cards.title: Shooting is not in any engine: offer the sword or the dodge instead
cards.text: Creators often ask for guns, bows or blasters. No genre can shoot: battle has a melee sword (in MR the right controller is the sword), tactics captures by moving, runner only walks. Say so kindly and offer the closest buildable thing: a battle option where enemies walk in and are struck up close, or a runner where red hazard rings are the 'shots' to dodge.
cards.use_when: the brief mentions shooting, guns, lasers, arrows, a sniper or a shooting gallery
do: Name the limit in one friendly line, then offer battle with the sword
Reframe 'shots' as red hazard rings or rain rings to step out of
Keep the sci-fi or space theme the creator wanted
avoid: Writing 'aim and fire' or 'collect ammo' in mechanics
Key art showing a gun or a muzzle flash

cards.title: No inventory or collecting items: use ordered checkpoints as the 'collection'
cards.text: Wishes like 'pick up keys', 'collect 10 gems' or 'open your bag' need an inventory that no engine has. In a runner, each checkpoint label can be the thing collected ('Find the jade key'), touched in a fixed order, and the score already rewards each one with +100. In tactics, the targets captured in order play the same role.
cards.use_when: the brief asks for items, keys, gems, loot, a backpack, power-ups or upgrades
do: Turn each wanted item into a checkpoint label in story order
Use the score (+100 per checkpoint) as the collection count
Use tactics targets as 'treasures to capture in order'
avoid: Promising free-order collecting or carrying items between levels
HUD rows for keys, ammo or bag slots

cards.title: No NPC conversations: put the story on the intro card and checkpoint labels
cards.text: Players cannot talk to characters and characters cannot answer. A 'talk to the village elder' idea becomes a still elder model beside the route plus a checkpoint label like 'Bring the lantern to the elder'. The story itself lives on the intro card (2-4 sentences) and in the order of the checkpoint labels.
cards.use_when: the brief wants talking characters, quests given by NPCs, dialogue choices or a guide who speaks
do: Write the story as 2-4 intro-card sentences
Make each NPC a scenery model next to a labelled checkpoint
Let the label carry the line the NPC would have said
avoid: Dialogue trees, choices or branching endings
Storyboard panels where the player 'asks' or 'answers' someone

cards.title: No voice chat or in-game talking: let real voices do it
cards.text: There is no voice chat in any mode. In MR this rarely matters: players in a shared floor session stand in the same real room and can simply talk, and spectators can call out hints. For remote friends, offer an online race with the live leaderboard instead of conversation.
cards.use_when: the brief asks for voice chat, team radio, walkie-talkie play or talking to remote friends
do: In MR co-located play, design moments where players naturally shout to each other
Offer a race with a live leaderboard for remote friends
Give spectators a cheering role from the side
avoid: Rules that depend on hearing a remote teammate
Puzzles that need one player to describe something to another over the game

cards.title: No crafting, building or base upgrades during play
cards.text: Crafting, building a base or combining items is not something any engine runs. Creative players can still get expression: in tactics they plan their own path to capture targets, and in a runner the route order and the race time show their skill. The creator, not the player, is the builder of the Land.
cards.use_when: the brief asks players to craft, build, farm, cook recipes or upgrade gear
do: Offer tactics as the 'planning and creating a solution' option
Present the creator's own Land editing as the building part
Use a farm or kitchen theme as scenery around a runner route
avoid: Mechanics like 'combine wood and stone' or 'build your tower'
Promising saved progress or upgrades between sessions

cards.title: No joystick, teleport or flying movement in MR
cards.text: In MR the player walks with their own legs on the real floor; there is no stick movement, teleport, jump or flight. Ideas like 'fly over the city' or 'run a 200 m track' must shrink to the real floor size. Use the void floor or tall scenery below to give the feeling of height while the player still walks a real route.
cards.use_when: an MR brief asks for flying, driving, jumping, a long track or a map bigger than the real floor
do: Fit the whole route inside width_m x depth_m minus 0.6 m edges
Fake height with the void floor and scenery below
Use PC if the creator really needs a big world to roam
avoid: Writing 'move with the thumbstick' in rules
A route longer than the floor allows
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Do not design for running in MR battle or runner
cards.text: Players in passthrough must walk, not sprint: real walls, furniture and people are near, and the battle engine is built so the player steps out of red rings rather than runs. Time limits that can only be beaten by running push players to unsafe speeds. Set time limits so a calm walk finishes with about 20-30 percent spare time.
cards.use_when: a design uses tight time limits, 'sprint', chase scenes or races in an MR space
do: Set timeLimit from walking pace (about 0.7-1 m per second plus stops) with spare time
Reward accuracy (no hazard hits) as much as speed
Write 'walk, do not run' in the rules
avoid: Chase themes where something runs after the player
A 60 s limit on a route that needs 70 s of walking
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Three options that are reskins of one idea
cards.text: A pirate course, a jungle course and a space course with the same loop are one game in three skins, and the checks reject them. The 3 options must use 3 different genres (battle, tactics, runner) and any two must differ on at least 2 of the axes aesthetic, loop, social and route. Change the core activity first, then the look.
cards.use_when: drafting the 3 options and they share a loop, route or social mode
do: Give each option its own genre and core loop
Vary social mode (solo, race, together) and route shape across options
Let the theme follow the brief but the play differ
avoid: Same core_loop text in two options
Only changing theme and lighting between options
cards.source: design practice; Luminate and design fixation studies, CHI 2024

cards.title: Under 3 m on a side, battle and tactics do not fit in MR
cards.text: When the MR space is under 3 m on its shortest side, only runner fits; battle needs room to step out of rings and tactics needs a board with walkable squares. All 3 options are then runners, so they must differ through loop, social mode, route shape and aesthetic instead of genre.
cards.use_when: an MR brief has width_m or depth_m under 3
do: Make all 3 options runners and vary loop (tour, dodge, story)
Vary route (loop, out-and-back, zigzag) and feelings
Offer PC as an alternative if the creator wants battle
avoid: Proposing a battle or tactics option for a 2.5 x 4 m room
Three runners that only differ in theme

cards.title: All options scored the same
cards.text: Giving every option 4/4/4/4 hides the real trade-offs and gives the creator nothing to choose on. Use the whole 1-5 scale and tie each score to a brief or venue fact in scores_why, for example mr_fit 2 because a tactics board squeezed into a 3 x 3 m room makes squares only about 0.3 m wide.
cards.use_when: writing scores for the 3 options
do: Let at least two options differ in at least one score
Name the fact behind each score in scores_why
Set confidence to low for untested combos
avoid: 5 everywhere
scores_why lines like 'good fit' with no fact

cards.title: Too many checkpoints in a small room
cards.text: A 3 x 3 m living room has only about 1.8 m of usable side after the 0.6 m edge margin, which allows 3-4 checkpoints spaced roughly 0.8-1.2 m apart. Eight checkpoints there would sit on top of each other and players would bump the walls. Count checkpoints from the usable floor: small rooms 3-6, halls 4-8, courts 4-10.
cards.use_when: a runner for a room under about 5 m on its short side
do: Use 3-4 checkpoints under about 3.7 m, 3-6 under about 6 m
Make the route a loop so it can be walked twice
Replay value from time, not from more stops
avoid: 8-10 checkpoints in a bedroom
Stops closer than the minimum spacing

cards.title: Hazards on or right next to the spawn or a checkpoint
cards.text: A red hazard circle at the start sends a player back before they have learned anything, and one touching a checkpoint makes it unfair to reach. Keep the spawn clear (about 0.8 m in small rooms, 1.2 m in halls, 1.5 m on courts) and keep a gap between each hazard edge and every stop (0.4, 0.7 or 1 m by size).
cards.use_when: placing hazards in a runner layout brief
do: Put the first hazard after checkpoint 1 or 2
Place hazards between stops, beside the straight line, so they are dodgeable
Keep hazard radius small in small rooms (about 0.35-0.45 m)
avoid: A hazard on the first step
A hazard covering the whole corridor so it cannot be passed

cards.title: Dark, spooky or neon themes in bright daylight
cards.text: Outdoor noon sun washes out glow, emissive colour and dark scenes in passthrough, so a haunted night theme in a sunny garden looks flat and grey. Outdoors by day choose bright, high-contrast themes with noon or morning lighting; keep spooky, neon and night for indoor spaces or after dark.
cards.use_when: an outdoor MR venue in daytime with a dark, spooky, glow or neon theme request
do: Pick noon or morning lighting with saturated scenery outdoors
Move the spooky version to the evening slot or indoors
Tell the creator why in one line
avoid: Spooky or neon lighting for an outdoor 2 pm event
Key art promising glowing effects under the sun

cards.title: Scary content for young children
cards.text: Children under about 8 in a headset cannot look away from a fright as easily as on a screen, and a scare can make them run into real walls. For young kids avoid ghosts that loom, sudden appearances and spooky lighting; use friendly creatures, toys, candy or farm themes with morning or default light. Keep any 'danger' cartoonish, such as puddles or sleeping dragons.
cards.use_when: players include young children or a family with small kids
do: Use friendly themes and soft lighting
Frame hazards as silly (mud, sticky jam)
Ask the creator about the youngest player age
avoid: Thai ghost models for a kindergarten
Jump scares or chase stories
cards.source: design practice; Yamada-Rice et al. 2017 on children and VR

cards.title: Text-heavy HUD
cards.text: A HUD with paragraphs, many counters or a quest log cannot be read while walking, and in MR text floating in view hides real obstacles. Keep 2-4 HUD items, short and numeric, such as timer, score and next checkpoint label; put the story on the intro card before play.
cards.use_when: writing the prototype hud and flow
do: Limit the HUD to timer, score, next goal and (battle) health
Use checkpoint labels of 2-5 words
Move story to the intro card
avoid: Mission text panels during play
More than 6 HUD items
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Boss fight at the start of a battle
cards.text: The battle engine runs chapters first and the boss at the end, and players need the early chapters to learn the sword and the step-out rings. A boss in chapter 1 skips the learning and ends the arc too early. Chapter 1 is a few grunts only, the middle chapters add shields and rain, and the boss closes the game.
cards.use_when: planning battle chapters or a storyboard that opens with the boss
do: Chapter 1: 2-4 grunts, no rain
Add shield then beast in later chapters
Put the boss in the climax storyboard panel
avoid: Boss intro in the first minute
All enemy kinds in the first chapter

cards.title: Beast enemy in the first chapter
cards.text: The beast is big and charges, and the check rejects it in chapter 1. Early chapters should teach one thing at a time: grunts to learn striking, then shields to learn hitting from the side, then a beast once players can step aside. In MR keep each chapter at 6 enemies or fewer; on PC up to 9.
cards.use_when: writing the battle config chapters
do: Grunts only in chapter 1
Introduce beast in chapter 3 or later
MR chapters: at most 6 enemies
avoid: A beast in chapters[0]
8 enemies in one MR chapter

cards.title: Tactics guards moving too fast in MR
cards.text: In MR the player has to walk onto a real square, which takes much longer than a mouse click, so guards must move every 3 s or slower. A 1.5 s beat is fine on PC but impossible to read while walking. The first board should also have at most 2 guards.
cards.use_when: setting tactics board beats and guard counts
do: MR: beat 3-3.5 s
PC: beat can start at 2.5 s and drop to 1.5 s on later boards
First board 0-2 guards, then build up
avoid: Beat under 3 s in MR
3 or 4 guards on board 1

cards.title: Do not design an exact or impossible tactics board
cards.text: The tactics engine builds each board from counts (piece, targets, guards, cracks, tables, beat) and proves it can be solved. The AI cannot place squares by hand, and intents like 'a trick board no one can solve' or 'trap the player' are not possible. Express difficulty with counts and piece choice instead.
cards.use_when: the creator wants a specific puzzle layout, a trap board or an 'impossible' level
do: Raise difficulty with more guards, cracks and targets, or a harder piece
Use the board story line to set the mood
Rook or queen boards feel easier; knight boards feel trickier
avoid: Describing exact square coordinates
Promising a board that cannot be won

cards.title: Storyboard without a climax
cards.text: A storyboard of 'start, walk, walk, end' shows no peak and is rejected. Panels go in play order, the first is the start, each beat is used once, and one panel is the climax: the boss, the last board with the most guards, or the final hazard run before the portal. Put the climax where spectators can see it.
cards.use_when: writing the prototype storyboard
do: Use start, middle, climax, end (or start, climax, end)
Make the climax the hardest or most visual moment
Say what the player physically does in the climax
avoid: Two middle panels and no climax
Climax hidden in a corner away from the audience
cards.source: design practice; Fullerton, Game Design Workshop

cards.title: Key art prompt with text, logos or UI
cards.text: The picture maker draws the key art from an English prompt, and asking for a title, score, health bar or logo produces garbled letters and a fake-looking image. Describe one moment of real play: camera, player view, what is on screen, setting, light. For MR say it is seen through a headset with the real room visible and only the floor changed. End with 'no text, logos or interface'.
cards.use_when: writing key_art.prompt or art.prompt_style
do: Write prompts in English only
Describe one frame within the engine's abilities
Add 'no text, logos or UI' at the end
avoid: Game title or Thai text in the picture
Showing mechanics the engine lacks, like guns or chat bubbles

cards.title: Route crowded into one corner
cards.text: Routes the model writes often bunch the checkpoints in one corner and leave most of the floor empty, which wastes the space and makes players collide. Spread stops across the whole area using the full width and depth, keep each pair inside the spacing range for the room size, and keep 0.6 m from every edge.
cards.use_when: writing a layout brief or route for a runner
do: Name the route shape (loop, zigzag, spiral) across the whole floor
Visit all four quarters of the area
Keep stops 1.2-4 m apart in small rooms, 1.8-6 m in halls, 2.5-9 m on courts
avoid: All checkpoints within 2 m of each other
A route hugging one wall

cards.title: Giving spectators tasks inside the play area
cards.text: Spectators cannot see the virtual floor and anyone stepping onto the play area is a collision risk for players in headsets. Never ask spectators to hold props, stand as gates or walk the route. Give them roles from outside the boundary: cheer, call out hints, watch the leaderboard on a screen, or take the next turn.
cards.use_when: writing spectator_view or spectator_plan
do: Keep spectators on one marked side outside the area
Place a key moment (hazard dodge, finish portal) facing them
Offer a leaderboard screen for races
avoid: 'Parents stand on the checkpoints'
Games where a spectator must touch the player
cards.source: Reeves et al. 2005, Designing the spectator experience (CHI)

cards.title: Sacred places and religious objects as game props
cards.text: Thai temples, Buddha images, monks and stupas carry deep respect; using a Buddha image as a hazard, a target to capture, a boss or something to step on or strike is offensive. Temple scenery can appear as respectful background far from the action, but never as something hit, captured or trampled. Prefer folklore spirits, nature, markets or fantasy kingdoms for game action.
cards.use_when: a Thai theme involving temples, Buddha images, monks or religious ceremonies
do: Keep temple models as distant decor, upright and undamaged
Use folklore or invented creatures for enemies and hazards
Ask about cultural rules in the constraints question
avoid: A Buddha image as a checkpoint to touch or a boss
Hazards placed on temple steps or stupas
Monks as enemies

cards.title: Royal symbols and real national figures in a game
cards.text: Royal emblems, portraits of the royal family, the royal crown and similar symbols are protected by law and custom in Thailand, so they must not appear as props, prizes, enemies or jokes. A 'kingdom' theme should use an invented fantasy court with its own made-up crest and characters.
cards.use_when: a Thai brief about kings, palaces, royal history or national pride
do: Invent a fictional kingdom name and crest
Use generic fantasy palace scenery
Keep historical themes respectful and non-violent
avoid: Real royal emblems or portraits
A real king as a boss or a chess piece to capture

cards.title: Recreating a named existing game, its characters or its look
cards.text: Briefs often say 'make it like' a famous game, cartoon or film. Never recreate a named existing game, its characters, logos, levels or signature look. Take the abstract feeling the creator loves (fast dodging, cosy exploring, block-like style) and build an original world with invented names on our engine.
cards.use_when: a brief names an existing game, franchise, character or film as the model
do: Ask what they love about it (pace, mood, challenge)
Invent original names, creatures and setting
Use our low-poly catalogue themes
avoid: Reusing a franchise's character names or costumes
Key art prompts that name a real game or studio

cards.title: Long sessions at events with queues
cards.text: At a booth or mall activation a 15-minute game means a queue of 40 minutes for the fifth family and headsets sitting idle during setup. Aim for 3-5 minutes of play per turn, a one-screen intro and a clear finish. Races of 2-6 players at once raise throughput if the floor is large enough.
cards.use_when: the venue is an event, booth, fair or mall with people waiting
do: Set session_minutes 3-5 and timeLimit around 120-240 s
Use a race for many players at once on large floors
Keep rules to 2-3 lines
avoid: 10+ minute experiences at a booth
Multi-chapter battles with long boss fights in a queue setting

cards.title: Ignoring real obstacles in the space
cards.text: A pillar, sofa, tree or table inside the floor is real and invisible to the route unless named. Ask about obstacles in the interview, write them in the brief, and route around them with at least 1.2 m clear walking width and nothing placed on them. Better still, use them: a pillar becomes the 'tree' the route circles.
cards.use_when: the venue has furniture, pillars, trees or any fixed object inside the floor
do: Record obstacles in the brief explicitly or as 'none'
Route around obstacles with margin
Theme the obstacle as part of the world
avoid: Checkpoints placed on a real table
A straight route line through a pillar
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Tasks that need looking up while walking
cards.text: Players in passthrough need to see the floor and the people near them. Putting the next goal high in the sky, or asking them to read signs above head height while walking fast, causes trips and collisions. Keep labels and goals at chest height or on the floor, and put sky-high scenery only where players stand still.
cards.use_when: placing checkpoints, labels or key scenery in an MR layout
do: Keep goals and labels between knee and eye height
Put tall hero pieces at the edge, viewed from a stop
avoid: Dragons to 'chase' across the ceiling
Labels only readable by looking straight up
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Sudden scares that make players run
cards.text: A jump scare in passthrough can send a player backwards into a wall or another person. Even in a horror event, build dread with lighting, slow-moving scenery and story, and keep the route clear so a startled step is safe. Never place a scare near the area edge.
cards.use_when: a horror or haunted brief in MR
do: Use the spooky or night preset and slow reveals
Keep 1.2 m clear and 0.6 m from edges at frightening spots
Warn in the rules that it is a scary walk
avoid: Things that leap at the player
A scare right at a wall or corner
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Void floor for beginners, kids or seniors
cards.text: The void floor turns the real floor into a bottomless drop with scenery below. It is dramatic but can cause vertigo, freezing or anxiety, especially for first-time VR players, young kids and seniors. Use it only for adults or teens who ask for thrill, in short sessions, and offer a normal floor version.
cards.use_when: considering the void floor option
do: Reserve void floor for thrill-seeking teens and adults
Keep sessions short and the route simple
Mention vertigo in risks
avoid: Void floor at a seniors' centre or kindergarten
Void floor with tight time pressure
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Races and many players in small rooms
cards.text: Under about 4 x 4 m there is room for 1-2 players only; four people walking the same small floor at once will collide. A 'race' there should be turn-based: each player walks alone and the online race leaderboard compares times. Save simultaneous races of up to 6 for floors over 10 x 10 m.
cards.use_when: a small room brief asks for a party race or a group game
do: Turn-based time trial with leaderboard
Others watch and cheer from outside
Shared floor only for 2 players who can see each other
avoid: 4 simultaneous players in a living room
Two lanes in a 3 m wide room

cards.title: Asking about room size for a PC game
cards.text: On PC there is no real room. Asking for floor size, obstacles or indoor light wastes interview turns and can leak into wrong fields. Once the creator says computer, skip the environment question and do not set venue, width_m, depth_m or indoor; spend the turns on players, feelings and session instead.
cards.use_when: the platform is pc
do: Skip the venue question
Treat spectators as friends watching the screen
Use PC themes: dark, ice, lava, forest, neon, desert
avoid: Setting width_m for a PC game
MR safety rules in PC rules text

cards.title: Asking questions whose answer changes nothing
cards.text: Every extra question delays the creator; the interview should take 4-7 questions and never more than 9. Skip anything with a sensible default (session 5 minutes, solo play for one player, default lighting) and write the default into the brief. Ask only what would change the 3 options, like floor size or the youngest player's age. Never ask for personal data such as names, schools, phone numbers or photos; age range and group size are enough.
cards.use_when: deciding the next interview question
do: Default session_minutes and play_mode when unanswered
Combine environment facts into at most 2 questions
Stop when platform, concept, players, feelings and environment are known
avoid: Asking about colours before knowing the floor size
A tenth question
Asking for a school name or children's photos
cards.source: design practice; Kuhn et al. 2023 CLAM on clarifying questions

cards.title: Time limits outside 30-3600 seconds or written in minutes
cards.text: game.timeLimit is seconds between 30 and 3600, or null. Writing 5 (meaning minutes) gives a 5-second game and is rejected. For a calm walk set it from route length; for submission or relaxing games use null so no one is rushed.
cards.use_when: filling game.timeLimit in the build step
do: Convert minutes to seconds (3 min = 180)
Use null for relaxing or kids' games
avoid: timeLimit 5 meaning 5 minutes
A limit so tight only running beats it

cards.title: Family living room 3 x 3 m: a gentle loop runner
cards.text: Brief: 'Something for my kids (6 and 9) in our living room, about 3 x 3 m, sofa on one side.' Decisions: MR; at exactly 3 m a side all three genres are allowed, but battle and tactics are cramped (tactics squares only about 0.3 m), so runner leads and the other two score low on mr_fit with honest reasons; 1 player at a time, turn-based with the online leaderboard for sibling rivalry; feelings discovery and submission; friendly toy or candy theme with default lighting; 3-4 checkpoints on a small loop, 1-2 tiny hazards after checkpoint 2; sofa listed as obstacle and kept outside the route. If the room were under 3 m, all 3 options would be runners. Key spectator moment: the portal faces the sofa where parents sit.
cards.use_when: a family plays in a small home living room
do: Runner as the lead, 3-4 checkpoints, loop route
Take turns and compare times
Session about 3 minutes, timeLimit null
avoid: Scoring a cramped tactics board as a 5 for mr_fit
Spooky themes for a 6-year-old

cards.title: School class in an 8 x 8 m hall: three genres for 30 students
cards.text: Brief: 'Grade 5 class of 30, school hall about 8 x 8, one hour.' Decisions: MR, medium space, 2-4 players at once while others watch from one side; feelings challenge and fellowship. Options: a runner race of 2 lanes with 5-7 checkpoints themed as a science journey; a tactics board on the floor (squares about 0.85 m) where classmates call out hints; a battle with grunts only in early chapters. Turns of 3-4 minutes so every student plays. Key moment: the finish portal on the audience side.
cards.use_when: a teacher brings a whole class to a hall
do: 3-4 minute turns, 2-4 players at once
Audience line along one wall
Leaderboard on a projector
avoid: One 15-minute solo session
Students waiting inside the play area

cards.title: Songkran outdoor booth at noon: bright water festival runner
cards.text: Brief: 'งานสงกรานต์ บูธกลางแจ้ง อยากได้เกมสนุก ๆ คนต่อคิวเยอะ' (Songkran outdoor booth, lots of people queueing). Decisions: MR outdoors at noon so noon lighting and bright water, flower and festival scenery, no dark or glow themes; 5 x 5 m floor, 1-2 players; 3-minute turns, timeLimit 150 s; 5 checkpoints like 'Pour water for luck', hazards themed as slippery puddles. Avoid temple or Buddha images as props; keep it a festive street. Key moment: the last hazard dodge right in front of the queue.
cards.use_when: a Thai festival event outdoors in daylight
do: Noon lighting, saturated colours
Short turns for throughput
Respectful festive theme
avoid: Spooky lighting under the sun
Real headsets near water splashes without cover

cards.title: Haunted night event for teens: slow-dread story walk
cards.text: Brief: 'Halloween night event for high schoolers, indoor hall 10 x 12 m, they want it scary.' Decisions: MR indoors at night, spooky lighting; original folklore spirits as scenery standing beside the route; runner with 6-8 checkpoints telling a ghost story, hazards as cursed ground; dread from lighting and slow reveals, no jump scares, nothing near the walls. Battle option: enemies walk in slowly from the edges, chapter 1 grunts only. Key moment: the final portal reveal facing the audience.
cards.use_when: teens want a horror experience at an evening event
do: Spooky or night preset indoors
Story in checkpoint labels
Clear 1.2 m route and calm pace
avoid: Jump scares that make players run
Sacred religious objects as horror props
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Kindergarten 5 x 5 m playroom: one tiny adventure
cards.text: Brief: 'Kids aged 4-5, a playroom, teachers help.' Decisions: MR, short 2-minute turns with headsets fitted by teachers; feelings discovery and submission; farm or friendly animal theme, morning or default lighting; runner with 4 big, clearly spaced checkpoints ('Say hi to the cow'), no hazards or only one soft one, timeLimit null. One child at a time, others sit on a mat outside the area. Key moment: each child reaches the portal near the mat and classmates clap.
cards.use_when: very young children play with adult supervision
do: No time limit, almost no hazards
Friendly animals, bright light
Teachers outside the area as spotters
avoid: Battle or chase themes
Long text on the intro card
cards.source: design practice; Yamada-Rice et al. 2017 on children and VR

cards.title: Seniors' centre: a calm garden walk with stops
cards.text: Brief: 'Elderly group, community room 6 x 8 m, many never used VR.' Decisions: MR indoors with studio or morning light; runner with 5 checkpoints spaced 2-3 m apart on a gentle loop, no hazards or very few, timeLimit null; theme a flower garden or old market; no void floor; seated rest chairs outside the area; labels at chest height. Tactics option with a rook (straight walks) and a 3.5 s beat for those who like puzzles. Key moment: arriving at the portal beside their friends.
cards.use_when: older adults or first-time VR users with mobility limits
do: No time pressure, wide spacing
Familiar calm themes
Rook board, 3.5 s beat for puzzle fans
avoid: Void floor or dark lighting
Battle with fast grunts
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Gamers at a PC: battle, tactics and a speedrun runner
cards.text: Brief: 'For gamer friends on a computer, they like hard stuff.' Decisions: PC, no venue fields; feelings challenge and expression. Options: battle with the lava theme, chapter 1 grunts, later shields, beast and rain, up to 9 enemies per chapter, then a boss; tactics with a knight first board at 2 guards and later boards at 1.5-2 s beats; a WASD runner speedrun with tight timeLimit and hazards. Scores differ: battle highest fun, tactics highest expression. Spectators are friends watching the screen and the leaderboard.
cards.use_when: experienced players on PC who want challenge
do: Use the PC theme list
Ramp difficulty across chapters and boards
Leaderboard for bragging
avoid: Asking for room size
Beast or 3+ guards at the start

cards.title: Museum education about dinosaurs: a timeline walk
cards.text: Brief: 'พิพิธภัณฑ์อยากให้เด็กเรียนรู้เรื่องไดโนเสาร์' (a museum wants kids to learn about dinosaurs). Decisions: MR in a 7 x 9 m gallery space, indoor default lighting; runner with 6 checkpoints in time order ('Meet the long-neck', 'Find the egg nest'), dinosaur models beside each stop as vignettes, hazards as tar pits; 4-minute turns; story told by labels. Tactics option: the player is a bishop crossing a fossil dig. Key moment: a giant dinosaur model at the end, visible to parents behind the rope line.
cards.use_when: an education or museum brief about a learning topic
do: Checkpoint order = learning order
Big models beside, not on, the route
Short labels with one fact each
avoid: Long reading panels during play
Dinosaur 'chase' scenes

cards.title: Brand activation in a mall: original mascot world, 3-minute race
cards.text: Brief: 'A snack brand wants a booth in the mall atrium, 8 x 10 m, lots of shoppers.' Decisions: MR indoors, neon or studio lighting; original candy-world scenery and invented characters, no copying of famous games or mascots not owned by the brand; runner race of 2-4 players, 5-6 checkpoints, timeLimit 180 s; leaderboard on a screen facing the walkway. Battle option: 3 short chapters with grunts as snack crumbs. Key moment: the finish portal facing the shoppers.
cards.use_when: a commercial booth in a busy mall with passers-by
do: Short turns and a public leaderboard
Original designs or brand-owned assets only
Finish facing the crowd
avoid: Recreating another company's game
Spectators pulled into the area for photos mid-game

cards.title: Fortal court 14 x 22 m: 6-player two-lane race
cards.text: Brief: 'Race for 6 friends at the Fortal court.' Decisions: venue fortal-court, indoor steady light so neon or spooky works; runner race with 8-10 checkpoints spaced 2.5-9 m, two lanes or a long zigzag using the full 22 m, hazards between stops; live leaderboard on the wall screen; spectators along the long side. Battle option for 2-3 players in their own space; tactics board squares at 1 m. Key moment: last hazard and portal near the spectator side.
cards.use_when: a group race at the Fortal court
do: Use the whole court length
Leaderboard on the wall screen
Up to 6 players at once
avoid: Ignoring the 4 doors along one wall
Placing stops within 0.6 m of walls

cards.title: Rooftop at sunset: city skyline as backdrop
cards.text: Brief: 'A rooftop bar event at sunset, open floor 6 x 6 m, adults.' Decisions: MR outdoors at evening, evening lighting; the real skyline becomes the 'edge of the world', so low scenery in front keeps the view; runner loop with 5 checkpoints and a slow pace; battle option with enemies coming in from the parapet side but stopping well inside; no void floor near real edges. Key moment: the final checkpoint faces the sunset where guests sit.
cards.use_when: an outdoor elevated venue with a great view
do: Evening lighting, keep scenery low
Keep 0.6 m plus extra margin from parapets
Use the view in environment_fit
avoid: Void floor on a real rooftop
Tall props hiding the skyline
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Tiny 2 x 2 m room: three different runners
cards.text: Brief: 'I only have a 2 x 2 m space in my bedroom.' Decisions: MR, under 3 m so all 3 options are runners; usable side is tiny, so 3-4 checkpoints spaced about 0.5-1 m, hazards radius about 0.35 m or none; options differ on loop and route: a story out-and-back, a tour loop played twice, a dodge zigzag with one hazard. Solo, 2 minutes. Suggest PC for battle or tactics if the creator wants them.
cards.use_when: a very small MR space
do: Runner only, 3-4 checkpoints
Vary loop, route and feeling between options
Offer PC as an alternative
avoid: Battle or tactics options
More than one player

cards.title: Chess club: walk-on boards with rising pieces
cards.text: Brief: 'Our chess club wants to be the pieces.' Decisions: MR in a 6 x 8 m room so the 6 x 8 board fits with squares about 0.8 m; tactics as the lead option: boards from rook to bishop to knight to queen, targets 2 then up to 5, first board 1-2 guards, beat 3-3.5 s; time race with leaderboard. Contrast options: a runner of 'opening moves' as checkpoints and a battle where pieces walk in. Key moment: capturing the last target while members shout move hints from the side.
cards.use_when: players who already love chess
do: Tactics first, guards on a slow beat
Increase difficulty by counts and piece
Spectators call hints from outside
avoid: Beat under 3 s in MR
Exact board layouts by hand

cards.title: Birthday party in a garden: treasure walk race by turns
cards.text: Brief: 'วันเกิดลูก 8 ขวบ จัดที่สนามหญ้าบ้าน ช่วงบ่าย เพื่อน 10 คน' (8-year-old's birthday, home lawn, afternoon, 10 friends). Decisions: MR outdoors daytime, noon lighting, bright candy or pirate theme; lawn 6 x 6 m with a tree listed as an obstacle and circled by the route; runner with 5 checkpoints as 'treasure' labels, 2 hazards as sticky jam; 2 kids at a time, 3-minute turns, leaderboard. Key moment: blowing-out-candles style finish portal near the cake table.
cards.use_when: a children's birthday party
do: Turns of 2 players, 3 minutes
Bright daytime theme
Tree as part of the route
avoid: Spooky light outdoors
10 kids on the floor at once

cards.title: Office team-building: shared floor together mode
cards.text: Brief: 'Team-building for 12 office staff, meeting room cleared to 9 x 9 m.' Decisions: MR indoors, studio lighting; 'together' runner on a shared floor where 3-4 colleagues see each other's avatars and must all reach checkpoints, 6-7 stops; tactics option as a team relay where each person plays one board and the team's total time counts; battle option with players back to back. Real talking replaces voice chat. Key moment: the team finish with everyone watching.
cards.use_when: a corporate group wants teamwork
do: Shared floor or relay of boards
Talking happens in the real room
Score the team, not the individual
avoid: Voice chat or role-play dialogue
Long single-player sessions

cards.title: Tourist night market in Chiang Mai: lantern walk
cards.text: Brief: 'Booth at a Chiang Mai night market for tourists, 5 x 6 m, evening.' Decisions: MR outdoors after dark so night lighting and glowing lanterns work; original Lanna-inspired market and lantern scenery, no temple objects as props; runner of 5 checkpoints ('Light the lantern'), hazards as puddles; 3-minute turns, multilingual-friendly short labels; intro card short. Key moment: the final lantern release checkpoint facing the walkway.
cards.use_when: an evening tourist market booth
do: Night lighting after dark
Respectful local theme
Short turns, short labels
avoid: Buddha images or monks as props
Long story text tourists cannot read

cards.title: Rainy season move indoors: a classroom swap
cards.text: Brief: 'It was going to be outside but it rains every afternoon, now a classroom 6 x 7 m with desks pushed aside.' Decisions: MR indoors, stacked desks listed as obstacles and kept outside the area; indoor light means spooky or neon themes now become possible; runner 5-6 checkpoints with a storm or jungle theme, battle with rain rings fitting the season, tactics squares about 0.75 m. Key moment: battle rain chapter in front of the doorway where classmates watch.
cards.use_when: the venue changed from outdoors to indoors
do: Re-ask floor size and obstacles
Revisit lighting for indoors
Use rain as a theme in battle chapters
avoid: Keeping the outdoor noon plan
Ignoring the stacked desks

cards.title: Solo relaxation after work: slow zen walk
cards.text: Brief: 'I just want to relax alone at home, 4 x 5 m spare room.' Decisions: MR, solo, submission and sensation; runner loop with 4-5 checkpoints like 'Breathe by the pond', no hazards, timeLimit null; ice, garden or morning lighting; tactics option with a rook and slow 3.5 s beat as a quiet puzzle; battle option clearly marked as the energetic one. 5-10 minutes. Spectators none.
cards.use_when: a single adult wants a calm experience
do: No time limit, few or no hazards
Soft lighting
Slow tactics as a quiet alternative
avoid: Leaderboards and countdowns
Void floor

cards.title: 'Make a fun game' with no details: what to resolve first
cards.text: Brief: 'ทำเกมสนุก ๆ ให้หน่อย' (make a fun game). Resolve in order: platform (headset or computer), who plays and how many, the top 1-3 feelings, then for MR the floor size, indoor or outdoor and spectators. With those five facts the engine choices follow: floor size sets genres and checkpoint counts, light sets lighting presets, age sets theme and hazards. Use defaults for session (5 minutes) and play mode (solo).
cards.use_when: a brief is a single vague sentence
do: Ask platform first
Ask size before theme
Write defaults into the brief
avoid: Proposing options before knowing the floor
Asking about colours first
cards.source: design practice; Kuhn et al. 2023 CLAM on clarifying questions

cards.title: 'A space adventure' in a 10 x 10 m hall
cards.text: Brief: 'Space adventure for teens, hall 10 x 10.' Decisions: MR indoor, neon or night lighting; options: runner story through 7 planet checkpoints with meteor hazards; battle on the neon theme where alien grunts walk in and the right controller is the energy sword (no blasters); tactics where the player is a queen crossing a space station board. Axes differ on loop, social and route. Key moment: the battle boss or the portal near the audience side.
cards.use_when: a sci-fi theme where creators may expect shooting
do: Sword instead of guns
Neon indoors
Three genres, three loops
avoid: Laser guns or ships to fly
Three planet-themed runners

cards.title: Computer lab lesson: PC tactics as a logic lesson
cards.text: Brief: 'Grade 8 computer lab, 40 minutes, teach logical thinking.' Decisions: PC, no venue; tactics leads: 4 boards rising from rook to knight, first board 1 guard, later beats 2-2.5 s, board stories about a logic quest; runner WASD option as a warm-up; battle option for the last 10 minutes as a reward. Class leaderboard on the projector. Students in pairs: one plays, one advises.
cards.use_when: a school using desktop computers
do: Tactics boards as lesson steps
Pair play for discussion
Leaderboard on projector
avoid: MR safety talk for a PC game
Hard first board

cards.title: PC story fan: a short fantasy saga across three genres
cards.text: Brief: 'I want a fantasy story game on my computer, not too hard.' Decisions: PC, narrative and fantasy; runner option as a story walk with 8 labelled checkpoints in a forest theme; battle option in forest theme with 3 short chapters (grunts, then shields, then boss) and a named original boss; tactics option with a knight crossing a castle board story by story. Easy settings: few enemies per chapter, slow beats. Storyboard climax = boss or last board.
cards.use_when: a PC player who wants story over difficulty
do: Narrative in intro card and labels
Gentle difficulty ramp
Original boss name and lore
avoid: Dialogue with NPCs
Hard boss in chapter 1

cards.title: Tech expo with first-time VR visitors: a 2-minute taster
cards.text: Brief: 'At a tech expo, most visitors have never worn a headset, booth 6 x 6 m.' Decisions: MR indoors, studio lighting; runner with 4-5 checkpoints and one hazard, timeLimit null or 150 s, intro of 2 lines; battle option with only 2-3 grunts per chapter and 3 chapters; staff spotter outside the edge. Session 2-3 minutes. Key moment: the first sword strike or the finish, seen from the aisle.
cards.use_when: most players are new to VR at a public event
do: Very short, very clear rules
One new idea at a time
Staff spotter outside
avoid: Void floor or spooky scares
Many enemy kinds
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Hall with two pillars: make the pillars part of the world
cards.text: Brief: 'Community hall 12 x 12 m but there are two big pillars in the middle.' Decisions: MR; obstacles recorded in the brief; runner route as a figure-eight looping around both pillars with 1.2 m clear width, pillars themed as ancient tree trunks with scenery kept off them; battle arena on the free half; tactics board fitted to the clear side only. Key moment: the hazard dodge between the pillars where the audience looks in.
cards.use_when: a venue with fixed obstacles inside the floor
do: Route around obstacles with margin
Theme the obstacle
Fit boards and arenas to the clear part
avoid: A straight line through a pillar
Board squares overlapping a pillar
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Two players at home: shared floor date night
cards.text: Brief: 'Me and my partner, living room cleared 4 x 4 m.' Decisions: MR, 2 players together on a shared floor (they see each other's avatars and the real room), 4-5 checkpoints on a loop, gentle hazards; evening lighting indoors; battle option where they take turns and compare chapters; tactics option as a team where one walks and one advises from the sofa. 5 minutes per round.
cards.use_when: a pair of adults at home
do: Shared floor for 2
Turn-taking for battle
One plays, one advises for tactics
avoid: Races of 2 at once in 4 x 4 m with crossing routes
Long sessions without rest

cards.title: Fitness-minded adults: an active battle with rain rings
cards.text: Brief: 'Gym members want something active, studio 7 x 7 m.' Decisions: MR indoors; battle as the lead with 5 chapters building from grunts to shields to beast, rain from chapter 3, max 6 enemies each, then a boss; stepping out of rings and swinging gives real exercise without running; runner option as an interval walk with timeLimit; tactics as a cool-down puzzle. Spectators watch movements through the glass wall.
cards.use_when: players want physical activity
do: Battle steps and swings for exercise
Rain rings later
Rest between chapters
avoid: Sprinting or jumping
More than 6 enemies per MR chapter

cards.title: Thai folklore for adults: original spirits, respectful setting
cards.text: Brief: 'ผีไทยแต่ไม่อยากให้ลบหลู่' (Thai ghosts but not disrespectful). Decisions: MR indoors at night, spooky lighting; use the catalogue's Thai ghost models as standing scenery beside a village route, with invented spirit names; temples only as distant background, never touched or stepped on; runner with 6 story checkpoints, battle where spirits walk in and are sent away with the sword. No Buddha images, monks or sacred rituals as game parts. Key moment: dawn finish at the portal.
cards.use_when: a Thai ghost or folklore theme
do: Invented spirits and village settings
Temples as distant decor only
Story told by labels
avoid: Monks as enemies
Sacred objects as targets

cards.title: Car park evening event 20 x 25 m: big race
cards.text: Brief: 'Evening event in an empty car park, 20 x 25 m, lots of teens.' Decisions: MR outdoors after dark, night or neon lighting; large space rules: runner race for up to 6 players with 8-10 checkpoints 2.5-9 m apart in two lanes; painted lines and lamp posts noted as obstacles; leaderboard on a portable screen. Battle and tactics run in a separate fenced section. Key moment: finish portal under the main lights where the crowd stands.
cards.use_when: a very large open outdoor floor at night
do: Large-space spacing
Lamp posts as obstacles
Finish near the crowd
avoid: Daytime glow themes
Players crossing each other's lanes

cards.title: Garden in the morning: dinosaur egg hunt walk
cards.text: Brief: 'Saturday morning in the garden, 7 x 8 m, kids 7-10, two trees.' Decisions: MR outdoors, morning lighting, bright dinosaur and jungle scenery; trees as obstacles circled by a loop route; runner with 6 checkpoints ('Find the blue egg'), 2 hazards as mud pits; tactics option with a rook on a 'nest board'; battle option with grunts as playful raptors in 3 short chapters. 2 kids at a time.
cards.use_when: kids playing outdoors in morning light
do: Morning light, bright colours
Trees as features
Gentle hazards
avoid: Night or spooky light
Beast in chapter 1

cards.title: Creator asks to combine two options
cards.text: Brief follow-up: 'I like the dinosaur look of option 1 and the race of option 2.' Decisions: keep the named parts (dinosaur theme and race social mode), keep it buildable, and still return 3 different options, for example a dinosaur runner race, a dinosaur battle with a leaderboard time, and a dinosaur tactics board race. Each still uses a different genre and differs on at least 2 axes.
cards.use_when: the creator requests a remix of earlier options
do: Keep the parts they named
Give 3 ways to combine them
Keep genres different
avoid: Returning one merged option
Dropping what they asked for

cards.title: Thai ghosts / ผีไทย: set the scare level by age before picking a spirit
cards.text: The same Thai spirit can be cute or terrifying, so pick the tone from the players first. Kids 6-9: round, big-eyed, glowing friends who are lost or hungry and need help home, morning or evening light, no gore, no faces close to the camera. Teens 13-17: eerie but not gory, spooky or night lighting, slow reveals at the side of the route, never a jump scare that makes a walking player run. Adults: folklore atmosphere and story, still no blood or organs, because the scenery is low-poly and gore reads as cheap rather than scary.
cards.use_when: any brief that mentions Thai ghosts, ผี, haunted or spooky with Thai culture
do: Ask or infer the youngest player before choosing a spirit
Kids: frame every ghost as someone to help
Teens: let ghosts stand beside the route and turn as you pass
Keep ghosts 1.5 m or more from the walking line in MR
avoid: Gore, entrails or blood at any age
Sudden scares that make a headset player run
Using the scariest spirit as the first thing kids see
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Mae Nak / แม่นาค: the loyal ghost wife, a love story first
cards.text: Mae Nak of Phra Khanong is a tale of a wife who waits for her husband even after death, so the strongest hook is love and loyalty, not horror. The catalog has her stilt house, canal banks, rowboats, a swinging cradle, a lullaby note marker and the famous long arm reaching for a dropped lime. For kids, the route can be "Help Mae Nak find the limes before dawn" with a lullaby at each checkpoint; for teens, the long arm reaching across the canal makes a great side spectacle beside a hazard. End at dawn with the portal so the story closes gently.
cards.use_when: a Thai ghost runner or story where a famous named folk spirit is wanted
do: Use canal, stilt house and cradle vignettes along a riverside route
Checkpoint labels that follow the story (cradle, lime tree, canal, dawn)
Lighting evening for kids, spooky for teens
avoid: Recreating the look or scenes of a specific Mae Nak film or series
Referencing her real shrine or turning worship into score
Making her a boss that is beaten up

cards.title: Krasue / กระสือ: the floating glowing head, toned without gore
cards.text: The krasue is a floating woman's head trailing glowing organs, which is too graphic as told. In low-poly, show only the head and a soft glowing ribbon trail (the catalog has green-glow, pink-coil and flying-trail versions plus a Krasue Queen boss). For kids it is a shy night-light spirit that drifts over the rice fields; for teens its trail can mark where a hazard is, and the Krasue Queen works as a battle boss name in a dark theme. Keep the trail abstract light, never organs.
cards.use_when: a brief wants a famous scary Thai ghost, a night-time glow or a battle boss with Thai flavour
do: Describe the trail as a glowing ribbon in prompts
Use night or spooky lighting so the glow reads
Pair with rice fields, banana groves and village huts
avoid: Drawing entrails, blood or a severed neck
Krasue in daylight outdoors where the glow vanishes
Putting the floating head at eye level right on the route

cards.title: Phi Pop / ผีปอบ: never design a "find the possessed villager" game
cards.text: In folklore the phi pop possesses a person and eats their insides, and real villagers, often older women, have been accused of being phi pop and driven out of their homes. So a game where players accuse or hunt a villager hidden in a crowd repeats a real harm. Use the catalog's old-woman and old-man phi pop as clearly supernatural, comic-grumpy spirits who steal snacks from the kitchen, and make the player return the snacks, not punish anyone.
cards.use_when: a brief mentions ผีปอบ, possession or a hidden-monster-among-villagers idea
do: Make phi pop obviously a ghost (glow, float), never an ordinary villager
Kids: snack-stealing grump, players carry snacks home along the route
Keep eating and organ details off screen
avoid: Accusation or witch-hunt mechanics
Elderly women as the default monster look
Gore about eaten organs

cards.title: Nang Tani / นางตานี: the banana-tree lady as a gentle guide
cards.text: Nang Tani lives in wild banana trees and is usually told as a beautiful, mostly harmless spirit in green, which makes her one of the best Thai ghosts for children and families. The catalog has the Tani banana-tree lady plus young, fruiting and tattered banana clumps, a firefly tree and glow mushrooms. Build a banana grove route where she points the way: each checkpoint is a banana clump with a soft glow, and the portal is a moonlit clearing. Evening lighting keeps faces friendly; night makes the green glow pop indoors.
cards.use_when: a family or kids brief that wants Thai folklore without fear
do: Banana grove vignettes 1.5 m beside the route
Labels like "Follow the green light"
Use her as the guide on the intro card
avoid: Turning her into a seductive figure for kids
Cutting down banana trees as a goal
Spooky lighting for under-8s

cards.title: Phi Am / ผีอำ: the sleep-pressure ghost needs care with bedrooms
cards.text: Phi Am is the spirit that sits on a sleeper's chest, the folk name for sleep paralysis, which is a real frightening experience for many people. For teens and adults, a haunted-house interior (the catalog has teak beds with mosquito nets, wardrobes ajar, rocking chairs, dust-sheet sofas and the Phi Am shadow sitter) makes a strong spooky runner indoors at night. For kids, skip the bedroom setting and show Phi Am as a sleepy heavy shadow who just wants a pillow, placed in a garden, not over a bed.
cards.use_when: a haunted house, bedroom or sleep-themed ghost idea
do: Teens: interior route room by room with spooky lighting
Keep the shadow sitter as scenery, not jumping out
Kids: move it outdoors and make it sleepy and comic
avoid: A bed scene where the player lies down or is pinned
Bedroom horror for under-10s
Text that describes real sleep paralysis symptoms

cards.title: Pret / เปรต: the tall hungry ghost works as a "feed them" goal
cards.text: Pret are very tall hungry ghosts with tiny mouths from Buddhist teaching about greed, and Thai children know them from temple murals. The playful, respectful angle is generosity: the catalog has tall and hunched pret, a Pret King boss, a pret-mouth target hoop and trays of throw food (rice balls, khanom krok, sticky rice). A runner where each checkpoint "feeds" a pret turns them from scary to sad-and-helped. In battle, Pret King can be a dark-theme boss name, but the line should be "send them to rest", not mockery of the teaching.
cards.use_when: a ghost theme for kids or a battle boss with a Thai folk name
do: Checkpoints as feeding stops with food props in vignettes
Keep the pret 2 m or more from the line, they are 3 m tall
Frame the end as the ghosts finally full and at peace
avoid: Recreating temple murals of the hell realms
Food thrown at elders or monks
Gags about the teaching itself

cards.title: Phi Ta Khon / ผีตาโขน: a joyful ghost parade, not a horror theme
cards.text: Phi Ta Khon is a festival in Dan Sai, Loei (usually around June or July), where people wear bright masks made from rice-steaming baskets and coconut-tree bases and dance through town. It is colourful, noisy and merry, so treat it as a parade theme: the catalog has a Phi Ta Khon festival mask figure and a mask jack-o-lantern. A runner that follows a parade street with banners and dancing mask figures beside the route suits families at noon or evening light, since the colours survive daylight.
cards.use_when: a festival, parade or Isan theme, or "Thai ghosts but fun"
do: Treat masks as festival art: bright, many colours, lined along the route
Label checkpoints as parade stops
Use noon or evening; the theme survives outdoor light
avoid: Spooky lighting and horror framing
Inventing fake ritual meanings for the masks
Calling it Halloween

cards.title: Phi Khamot / ผีโขมด: will-o-wisps as the kindest guide lights
cards.text: Khamot are floating lights in the dark fields that lead travellers astray in folklore. Flip it into a guide: the catalog has orb, flame and trio wisps plus firefly clusters and fog bands. A wisp hovering above each checkpoint gives first-time VR kids a target they can see from far away without reading text. The light reads only in night or spooky lighting indoors, or evening at a dim venue.
cards.use_when: a night route for young or first-time players who need visual wayfinding
do: Put a wisp above each checkpoint at 1.6-2 m height
Use fog bands only beside the route, not hiding hazards
Story line: "the lights lead you home"
avoid: Wisps that lead into hazards as a trick for kids
Glow themes outdoors at noon
More than one wisp colour meaning different things

cards.title: In battle, Thai spirits are sent to rest, not killed
cards.text: Thai ghost stories usually end with a spirit being calmed, given merit or let go, so slashing ghosts to death feels off to many Thai players and parents. Keep the battle engine as it is (grunts, shields, beasts, a boss) but write the chapter lines and boss intro as releasing restless spirits before dawn: "Calm the wandering spirits", "Free the Pret King". The verbs change the meaning with no change to mechanics.
cards.use_when: a battle game with Thai ghosts as enemies
do: Use dark or forest theme with lines about calming or freeing
Final chapter: dawn, the boss is set free
Boss names from folklore types, or invented
avoid: Chapter lines like "Kill the ghosts"
Monks, temple objects or sacred amulets as weapons in the story
Gloating victory text over a spirit

cards.title: Himmapan forest / ป่าหิมพานต์: a golden mythic sky world
cards.text: The Himmapan is the mythical forest of Thai art, full of hybrid creatures, which gives a fantasy world that is clearly Thai without touching anything sacred. The catalog has a full set: golden gates and sky portals, floating islands with golden salas and spires, lotus platforms, naga bridges, kinnaree, golden swans, white elephants and golden-leaf trees. It suits a runner as a "journey through the sky forest" or a void-floor dramatic finale, and the gold reads in daylight, so noon and morning work outdoors.
cards.use_when: a fantasy theme that should feel Thai, elegant, or for tourists
do: Name the realm and its creatures in the story
Use golden gate arches as checkpoint frames
Morning or evening light for warm gold
avoid: Putting Buddha images or temple chedis on the islands
Mixing in royal regalia as treasure
Too many gold props so hazards stop standing out

cards.title: Naga / พญานาค: a revered guardian, use as rails and allies, not a slain boss
cards.text: Naga serpents guard temple stairs and rivers and are honoured as protectors, especially in the Mekong region and Isan, where many people believe in them sincerely. Use naga as bridge railings, stair rails and gates (the catalog has naga-railed bridges, naga-head newels and a sweeping naga tail) and as a friendly guide in the story. If a battle needs a water serpent foe, invent a different creature (a "river wyrm" or "mud eel") with its own look rather than defeating a naga.
cards.use_when: a water, river or Himmapan theme, or a serpent enemy is wanted
do: Naga railing along a bridge section of the route
Story: the naga guards the river and lets you cross
Invent a non-naga serpent for any enemy role
avoid: A naga as the defeated boss
Stepping on naga heads as hazards
Joke or cute-dumb naga for adults in Isan

cards.title: Garuda / ครุฑ: a Himmapan bird is fine, the state emblem pose is not
cards.text: The garuda is a great half-bird hero of Himmapan art, but in Thailand a red and gold garuda with spread wings and raised arms is the royal and state emblem, seen on official buildings and documents. A game must not use that emblem look on badges, banners, prizes or as an enemy. If a creator wants a garuda, show it as a flying creature in the sky or perched far away, in a different pose and colour scheme, and never on a crest.
cards.use_when: a brief asks for garuda, a bird hero or a "Thai kingdom" crest
do: Garuda flying in the background sky or on a distant island
Invent the kingdom crest (a lotus, a star lantern)
Choose a different colour mix from red and gold
avoid: The spread-wing red-gold emblem pose anywhere
Garuda as an enemy or captured target
Garuda logo on the game title

cards.title: Kinnaree / กินรี: graceful bird-maidens for gates and dance moments
cards.text: Kinnaree are half-woman half-swan dancers of grace and beauty, known from Thai classical dance. The catalog has flying kinnaree, a circling pair, a kinnaree wing gate and a bird-maiden dancer. Use them as the gatekeepers of checkpoints (wings open as you approach) and as the sensation moment for spectators. Keep the costume graceful and covered, a cultural art form, and avoid sexualised poses.
cards.use_when: a Himmapan, dance, elegant or "beautiful Thai" theme
do: A kinnaree gate at the climax checkpoint facing spectators
Pair with lotus ponds and golden swans
Morning or evening light
avoid: Revealing or sexualised designs
Kinnaree as monsters or grunts
Using real dancers' photos as reference faces

cards.title: Singha / สิงห์: guardian lions that frame the start and finish
cards.text: Stone singha lions guard gateways in Thai and Lanna temples and palaces, which makes them natural markers for the start and the portal. The catalog has a stone singha guardian and a winged lion guardian statue. Place a pair either side of the spawn or the finish portal, facing outwards, 1.5 m clear of the walking line. On a tactics board story they can be the two "watchers" at the edge of a courtyard, but never pieces to capture.
cards.use_when: framing the entrance or finish of a Thai or Lanna themed game
do: Pairs, symmetric, at spawn or portal
Use as scenery outside the board in tactics
Combine with lanterns and tung banners
avoid: Singha as enemies or hazards
Placing them on the route where players brush past
Using a real brand's lion logo

cards.title: Songkran / สงกรานต์: Thai New Year water festival, 13-15 April
cards.text: Songkran is the Thai New Year, 13 to 15 April, the hottest time of year, known for water fights in the streets (Chiang Mai's moat is famous) and the gentle custom of pouring scented water over elders' hands for blessing. In a runner, checkpoints can be "Splash station" stops along a street with water jars, buckets, flower garlands and a moat bank, hazards as slippery puddles. Show the elder blessing as a calm vignette, not a joke. Noon and morning lighting fit the bright, sunny mood.
cards.use_when: a festival theme in March or April, a water theme, or a Thai New Year event
do: Street route with water jar and garland vignettes
Hazards as puddles or slippery tiles
A calm blessing vignette near the end
avoid: Splashing monks or elders as gags
Spooky or night lighting
Promising water-gun shooting (the engine cannot shoot)

cards.title: Songkran in MR: the water must stay virtual
cards.text: Creators planning a Songkran booth sometimes want real water play next to the game. Quest 3 headsets and controllers are not waterproof, and wet floors make walking players slip. Keep all water in the virtual scene, place the booth away from street water fights, and use a covered, dry floor; suggest spectators throw cheers, not water.
cards.use_when: an MR booth during Songkran or a water-play request
do: Ask where the booth is relative to water play
Dry, covered floor and a towel station
Virtual splash moments at checkpoints
avoid: Real water guns near players
Outdoor booth on a wet street
Water props on the real floor
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Loy Krathong / ลอยกระทง: float a light on the river
cards.text: Loy Krathong falls on the full moon of the 12th Thai lunar month, usually in November, when people float krathong (banana-trunk rafts with flowers, a candle and incense) on rivers to thank the water and let go of bad luck. It is calm and pretty, so the runner fits submission and narrative: walk a riverside route, each checkpoint lights a lantern, and the portal is the water's edge where you "float your wish". Night lighting indoors makes candles glow; the catalog has lotus lanterns, lily pads, piers and a krathong lantern.
cards.use_when: a festival theme in November, a calm couples or family experience, or a river theme
do: Riverside or canal route, portal at the water edge
Labels as wishes or thanks
Night lighting indoors, evening outdoors
avoid: Fast race or harsh hazards that break the calm
Foam krathong props (the culture now prefers natural ones)
Mixing in Halloween wording in November

cards.title: Yi Peng / ยี่เป็ง: Lanna lantern night in Chiang Mai
cards.text: Yi Peng is the Lanna festival held at the same full moon as Loy Krathong, famous in Chiang Mai for hanging lanterns (khom fai), star lanterns and sky lanterns (khom loi). A lantern trail runner is the natural fit: the route winds under Lanna hexagon and star lanterns, each checkpoint lights one, and the finale releases a sky lantern above the portal for spectators to see. Sky lanterns are now restricted for fire safety, so show them as a virtual-only moment and never suggest releasing real ones at the venue.
cards.use_when: a Chiang Mai, Lanna or lantern brief, especially October to November
do: Lanterns hung above or beside the route, never at head height on it
One rising virtual lantern as the climax
Night or evening lighting
avoid: Real sky lantern release or open flames
Temple ordination areas as the setting
Too many lights so hazards disappear

cards.title: Chiang Mai Flower Festival: floats and gardens, early February
cards.text: The Chiang Mai Flower Festival takes place on the first weekend of February with a parade of flower-covered floats and big flower displays in the park, during the cool, dry season. It makes a bright daytime theme: a garden route with giant flowers, a float parade of animal shapes, bougainvillea and marigold bushes. The catalog's garden set (giant daisy and flower-head platforms, petal pennants, bluebell lamps) works with Lanna lanterns on top. Noon or morning lighting is ideal and survives outdoors.
cards.use_when: a spring, garden or Chiang Mai daytime event, January to February
do: Float-shaped vignettes beside a parade route
Petal-pennant flags as checkpoints
Gentle, family pacing with few hazards
avoid: Night lighting that hides the colours
Copying a real company's sponsored float logo
Pollen and bee hazards for very young kids without care

cards.title: Vegetarian Festival / เทศกาลกินเจ: use the food and flags, not the piercing rites
cards.text: The Vegetarian (Jay) Festival runs nine days in the ninth Chinese lunar month (September to October), famous in Phuket and Bangkok's Chinatown, with yellow flags marked with the red character for jay, white clothing, vegetarian food stalls and firecrackers. Some processions include self-piercing by spirit mediums, which is sacred to devotees and too graphic for a game. Use the yellow-flag street food market as the theme: stalls, lanterns and a parade street, with no piercing, blood or trance figures.
cards.use_when: a brief mentions กินเจ, Jay, Phuket festival or a yellow-flag food market
do: Yellow flags and food stalls along a street route
Checkpoints as stalls to visit
Evening lighting for lanterns
avoid: Pierced faces, blades or fire-walking scenes
Making spirit mediums into monsters
Meat props in a vegetarian festival scene

cards.title: Bun Bang Fai / บุญบั้งไฟ: Isan rocket festival, May
cards.text: Bun Bang Fai is held in Isan (Yasothon is the best known) in May, before the rains, when villages build and launch home-made bamboo rockets to call the rain. It suits a high-energy theme: a runner through rice fields where each checkpoint "loads a rocket", and the finale launches one over the portal. The catalog has a bamboo rocket (bang fai) launcher, buffalo carts, rice granaries and sugar palms. Some parades include rude jokes and phallic props, so leave those out for family games.
cards.use_when: an Isan theme, a festival in April to May, or a launch-and-celebrate climax
do: Rice-field route with rocket launcher vignette at the end
Noon or evening lighting
Spectator moment: the virtual launch
avoid: Phallic or rude parade props
Players near real fireworks
Rockets as projectiles players fire (no shooting)

cards.title: Chinese New Year in Thailand / ตรุษจีน: red lanterns and lion dance streets
cards.text: Chinese New Year (January or February) is big in Bangkok's Yaowarat, in Phuket and in many Thai-Chinese homes: red lanterns, gold, red envelopes, oranges, lion and dragon dances and firecrackers. A runner down a lantern-lit market street (round Chinese paper lanterns, shophouses, fruit stalls) with the dragon or lion dancers beside the route makes a cheerful family theme. Keep ancestor altars and shrines as quiet background, not interactive props.
cards.use_when: a January to February event, a Thai-Chinese community, or a red-and-gold festive theme
do: Red lantern strings above the route edge
Checkpoints as "collect luck" stops (oranges, red envelopes)
Evening or night lighting
avoid: Ancestor altars or joss offerings as hazards
Accents or costumes that mock Chinese people
Real firecrackers near the play area

cards.title: After a festival date, rename the theme instead of dropping it
cards.text: A festival theme feels stale or wrong the day after the event, but the art is still useful. Rename it: Songkran becomes a "water splash festival", Loy Krathong and Yi Peng become a "lantern river night", Christmas becomes a "winter village" after 26 December, Halloween becomes a "ghost night" or "spirit festival" after 31 October. Keep the props, change the title, story and labels, and remove the dated wording from the intro card.
cards.use_when: a brief or event that runs past a festival's date, or a long-running booth
do: Check the event dates against the festival date
Swap dated words in title, story, labels
Keep the scenery and palette
avoid: Festival names in titles after the day
Countdown or "tonight" wording for a multi-week event
Rebuilding the whole scene just to rename it

cards.title: Thai night market / ตลาดกลางคืน: stalls, lights and a winding walk
cards.text: A Thai night market is rows of stalls under string lights, with food smoke, music and crowds, which maps neatly onto a runner: the route winds between stall vignettes and each checkpoint is a stall to visit ("Buy the meatball skewer", "Find the lantern seller"). The catalog has market stalls, sweets stalls, cloth stalls, fruit stalls with parasols, lantern posts and paper lantern strings. Night or evening lighting gives the right glow; hazards can be spilled ice or a puddle.
cards.use_when: a market, food, tourist or Chiang Mai evening theme
do: Stalls as vignettes 1 m or more beside the route
Labels as shopping errands
Night lighting indoors, evening outdoors
avoid: Stalls on the route that players walk into
Real shop or brand names on signs
Crowded corners where two lanes cross

cards.title: Floating market / ตลาดน้ำ: boats, canals and fruit
cards.text: Floating markets sell fruit, noodles and flowers from small wooden boats on canals, a classic central-Thailand image. The catalog's lotus city set has bobbing longtail fruit boats, flower boats, a sampan with a frog vendor, piers with pavilions, canal banks and mooring poles. Lay the route along the canal bank with boats drifting beside it; the canal itself can be a void-floor drop in VR, or simply water scenery in MR with a plank bridge to cross. Morning lighting fits, since markets open at dawn.
cards.use_when: a water, canal, food or central Thai theme
do: Route along the bank with one bridge crossing
Boats as moving scenery beside the path
Morning light, colourful fruit
avoid: Asking players to "step into a boat" in MR
Hazards placed on the bridge itself
Overdressing so the canal is not readable

cards.title: Rice fields / ทุ่งนา: open green paddies with village life
cards.text: Rice paddies are the heart of rural Thailand: flat green squares, raised earth paths between them, a wooden hut, buffalo, scarecrows and a rice granary. The raised paths form a natural grid, which fits a tactics board story ("cross the paddies without waking the scarecrows") as well as a calm runner. The catalog has rice granaries, buffalo carts, haystacks, scarecrows with ngob hats, sticky-rice baskets and banana trees. Morning or noon light suits daytime farm life; at night it becomes the stage for krasue and khamot stories.
cards.use_when: a countryside, farm, Isan or calm daylight theme
do: Tactics: describe the board as paddies and earth paths
Runner: zig-zag along paddy edges
Buffalo and huts as vignettes
avoid: Showing poverty as a joke
Buffalo as enemies
Too uniform, add huts and trees for landmarks

cards.title: Doi Suthep mountain feel: mist and forest, not the temple
cards.text: Creators in Chiang Mai often want "Doi Suthep", the mountain west of the city. Its sacred temple, golden chedi and naga staircase are a pilgrimage site, so do not recreate them as a game level. Capture the mountain feel instead: misty forest, mossy boulders, winding stone steps, viewpoint over a city of lights, cool morning air. Use fog wisps beside the route, old conifers and stepping stones, and a viewpoint portal at the top facing spectators.
cards.use_when: a brief asks for Doi Suthep, a mountain, a Chiang Mai landmark or a misty forest
do: Mountain path route that climbs in a spiral
Morning lighting with fog wisps
A viewpoint finale over a distant city
avoid: Recreating the real chedi or temple stairs
Climbing real stairs in MR
Monks on the route as scenery

cards.title: Old city moat and walls / คูเมือง: a square city with corner bastions
cards.text: Chiang Mai's old city is a square ringed by a moat and old brick walls with gates and corner bastions, and many Thai towns have similar old walls. This shape makes a loop route around a walled square, with each gate as a checkpoint and the corner bastions as landmarks. The catalog has brick city walls, bastions with banners, a city gate, laterite plaza tiles and lamp posts. Invent the city's name (as in "Phayakburi") rather than copying a real gate's sign.
cards.use_when: a Chiang Mai, old town or "kingdom" theme, or a loop route
do: Four gates as four checkpoints on a loop
Moat as water scenery outside the route
Evening lighting, lanterns on walls
avoid: Real gate names on signs
Walls placed where they hide spectators' view
Royal crests on banners

cards.title: Lanna style / ล้านนา: northern Thai teak, kalae and star lanterns
cards.text: Lanna is the old northern kingdom centred on Chiang Mai, with its own look: dark teak houses on stilts, crossed kalae boards on the gable tips, tung banners (long hanging flags), hexagon and star paper lanterns, woven bamboo, sticky-rice baskets and red, gold and deep green accents. In low-poly, lean on silhouettes: steep stacked roofs, long tung banners, a lantern line. It is warm and welcoming, and tourists recognise it, so it fits both a family runner and an elegant tactics courtyard.
cards.use_when: a northern Thai, Chiang Mai or "Thai but not Bangkok" visual direction
do: Name the style "Lanna-inspired" in prompts
Tung banners as checkpoint flags
Star lanterns hung at the route edge
avoid: Mixing in central Thai palace roofs and calling it Lanna
Temple ordination halls as the main building
Hill-community costumes as decoration

cards.title: Temples: distant backdrop only, never part of the action
cards.text: Temple scenery (chedis, halls, bell towers) can set the mood of a Thai world, but it must stay respectful. Keep any temple model at the far edge of the scene as backdrop, not on the route, not inside a battle arena, not as a tactics target or board feature, and never a hazard. Prefer ruined, generic or invented structures (a ruined bell chedi in an ancient forest) over anything that looks like a real active temple, and never build an interior with altars.
cards.use_when: any Thai theme where temple models are tempting
do: Place temple models 3 m or more outside the route
Prefer invented ruins and pavilions
Use them for skyline, not interaction
avoid: Battle enemies spawning from a temple
Checkpoints on temple steps
Temple interiors, altars or Buddha images

cards.title: Spirit houses and offerings: scenery to respect, never hazards
cards.text: Most Thai homes and shops have a spirit house (san phra phum) with daily offerings, and many players treat them seriously. The catalog has spirit houses, garlands, bai si towers, incense, fruit platters and even pig-head offerings. Place them as quiet vignettes beside the route, perhaps marking the start as "the guardian of this land", but never as hazards, things to kick, targets to capture, or score pickups.
cards.use_when: a Thai village, house or ghost theme that uses offering props
do: A spirit house vignette near the spawn as a welcome
Keep offerings upright, tidy and clear of the route
Story: the guardian spirit blesses the journey
avoid: Knocking over or stepping on offerings
Offering food as collectible points
Pig heads in kids' scenes

cards.title: Yantra, amulets and takrut: keep them invented and off the floor
cards.text: Yantra cloths, takrut scrolls and amulets are sacred to many Thai people, who wear and bless them. The catalog includes floating yantra and takrut pickups, which are acceptable when the patterns are clearly invented fantasy runes and they float at checkpoints. Do not place them on the floor to be stepped on, do not copy a real monastery's yantra design, and do not make amulets a gacha or loot reward.
cards.use_when: a design that uses yantra, amulet or talisman props
do: Floating at checkpoint height (1.2-1.6 m)
Invented patterns in prompts ("fantasy rune cloth")
A few as story items, not dozens
avoid: Floor hazards shaped as yantra
Copies of real sak yant designs
Amulets as random loot

cards.title: Thai street food stall: an errand route kids and tourists love
cards.text: Thai street food is a shared pride and an easy hook for any visitor: noodle carts, grilled meatball skewers, khanom krok in a dimpled pan, sticky rice in a woven basket, iced drinks in plastic bags. A runner where each checkpoint is "the next order" gives a clear goal and a fun finish ("Serve the hungry ghost" or "Bring dinner home"). The catalog has charcoal stoves, woks, skewers, khanom krok, sticky rice balls and coconut carts.
cards.use_when: a food theme, a tourist booth, or kids who need a simple goal
do: Checkpoint labels as orders ("Grab the khanom krok")
Stall vignettes with stove and parasol
Evening lighting for cooking smoke and lamps
avoid: Real restaurant or vendor names
Jokes about tourists being sick from food
Hazards shaped as food

cards.title: Mango sticky rice / ข้าวเหนียวมะม่วง: a gather-the-ingredients runner
cards.text: Mango sticky rice is sweet sticky rice with coconut milk and ripe mango, a favourite in the hot season (March to May). It gives a neat story loop for kids: four checkpoints gather the parts in order (mango tree, sticky-rice basket, coconut cart, the plate), the portal is the shared dessert table. The catalog has mango trees with fruit, sticky-rice baskets, young coconuts and toke dining trays. Noon or morning light keeps the yellow and white bright.
cards.use_when: a short kids or family runner with a food goal
do: Order the checkpoints like a recipe
Keep 4-5 checkpoints for under-8s
Finish at a table vignette spectators can see
avoid: Long text describing the recipe
Rotten or gross food gags
Dark lighting

cards.title: Muay Thai / มวยไทย: theme the world, the engine still swings a sword
