cards.text: Muay Thai is a national pride and a natural "battle" request, but the battle engine is a sword (PC: 3-hit combo and dash; MR: the right controller is the sword), with no punches, kicks or clinch. Offer a Muay Thai camp as the world and story (ring ropes, sandbags, tyres, training camp boards) with the sword battle, or a training-camp runner where checkpoints are drills. Treat the wai khru dance and the mongkhon headband as respected traditions shown in the intro, never as hazards or loot.
cards.use_when: a brief asks for Muay Thai, boxing, kicking or punching
do: Say kindly that the engine swings a sword, not fists
Offer krabi krabong (Thai sword art) as the honest fit
Runner alternative: a training-camp route
avoid: Promising punch or kick detection
Mocking the wai khru
Stepping over or kicking a mongkhon prop

cards.title: Krabi krabong / กระบี่กระบอง: the Thai sword art fits the battle engine
cards.text: Krabi krabong is a traditional Thai martial art with swords, staffs and shields, shown at cultural festivals and in historical dramas. It matches the battle engine honestly: the player holds a sword, shields block from the front, and a beast charges. Write the chapters as a warrior training to defend a walled old town, use forest or desert theme for a sun-baked field, and give the boss an invented name, not a real historical king or hero.
cards.use_when: a Thai warrior, historical or "Muay Thai but battle" brief
do: Story: train in a warrior camp, defend the town gate
Shield foes as the training partner chapter
Desert or forest theme
avoid: Real historical kings or national heroes as characters
Battles against neighbouring nations
Royal regalia as the boss reward

cards.title: Elephants / ช้าง: free and gentle, no riding, no chains, no tricks
cards.text: Elephants are the national animal of Thailand and beloved, and elephant tourism has moved away from riding, chains and circus tricks towards sanctuaries. Show elephants walking free in a forest, bathing in a river or as the gentle white elephant of Himmapan stories (the catalog has a white-elephant fountain, an island elephant and an elephant fruit merchant). Never put players on an elephant's back, never show hooks or chains, and never make an elephant a battle enemy or hazard.
cards.use_when: any theme with elephants, jungle, Thailand tourism or Himmapan
do: Elephants as calm scenery beside the route
Story: help a lost baby elephant back to the herd
Spectator moment: elephant spray at the finish
avoid: Riding seats, chains, hooks or performances
Elephants as beasts in battle
Painted elephants for selfies

cards.title: Isan (northeast Thailand) / อีสาน: rice, festivals and khaen music
cards.text: Isan is the large northeastern region with strong Lao-Thai culture: rice fields and sugar palms, sticky rice in woven baskets, wooden stilt houses, buffalo, khaen pipe music, mor lam songs, the Bun Bang Fai rocket festival and Phi Ta Khon in Loei. It is warm, lively and proud. Show it as cheerful and resourceful, with the music and festivals as the energy, not as "poor countryside".
cards.use_when: a brief mentions Isan, Lao-Thai culture, mor lam or the northeast
do: Rice-field and village vignettes, festival finale
Music stage props for a mor lam party
Noon or evening lighting
avoid: Poverty or accent jokes
Mixing Lanna lanterns in as "Isan"
Naga as an enemy (deeply believed in the Mekong region)

cards.title: Southern Thailand / ภาคใต้: islands, longtail boats and old towns
cards.text: The south is limestone islands, turquoise water, white beaches, longtail boats with ribbons on the bow, coconut palms, coral reefs and Phuket's Sino-Portuguese old town shophouses in pastel colours. It fits sunny noon runners (island hopping on plank bridges), an underwater reef world, or a pastel old-town street. The south is also home to Muslim communities, so mosques are backdrop with the same care as temples, and food scenes should not assume pork everywhere.
cards.use_when: a beach, island, Phuket, reef or southern Thailand theme
do: Island-hopping route with plank and rope bridges
Pastel shophouses for an old-town street
Noon lighting outdoors
avoid: Religious buildings in the action area
Pork props in a scene meant for a Muslim community
Tsunami disaster as a theme

cards.title: Central Thailand: river life, canals and ancient brick ruins
cards.text: Central Thailand is the Chao Phraya river plain: stilt houses over canals, floating markets, rice, and the brick ruins of old capitals with tree roots and leaning chedis. Ruined brick and laterite walls, broken pavilions and a giant bodhi tree give an "ancient lost city" feeling that is Thai without being an active temple. Keep any Buddha head in tree roots out: it is a famous real image that is sacred, not decoration.
cards.use_when: a canal, river, "ancient Thai city" or adventure-ruins brief
do: Ruined laterite walls and leaning chedis as distant scenery
Canal bank routes with plank bridges
Evening light on brick
avoid: The Buddha head in tree roots
Climbing ruins as checkpoints
Treasure-looting framing at real heritage sites

cards.title: Hill communities: no costumes as decoration, no "exotic" spectacle
cards.text: Northern Thailand is home to many highland peoples (Karen, Hmong, Akha, Lahu, Lisu and others) with their own languages, dress and beliefs. Do not use their clothing, faces or rituals as costumes, enemies, scenery "natives" or tourist spectacle, and never reference neck rings or other dress as a curiosity. If a creator wants a mountain-village feel, use terraced fields, mist, bamboo bridges and generic wooden houses; if a community wants its own story told, it should be designed with them.
cards.use_when: a northern mountain, trekking or "hill tribe" theme request
do: Use landscape (terraces, mist, bamboo) for the mountain feel
Suggest working with the community for their own stories
Invented characters with no specific ethnic dress
avoid: "Hill tribe" costumes or masks as props
Neck-ring or traditional dress as a gag
Highland villagers as enemies or background extras

cards.title: Buddha images: never props, targets, enemies or floor decor
cards.text: Buddha images are deeply sacred in Thailand; even tattoos or decor showing the Buddha cause offence, and placing one low or near feet is disrespectful. In FortalLand a Buddha image must never appear as scenery, a checkpoint, a hazard, a tactics target, a boss or a collectible, in any genre. If a creator asks for one, explain kindly and offer a lotus, a golden bodhi tree, a lantern or an invented guardian spirit instead.
cards.use_when: any brief that mentions Buddha, a temple game or a "holy statue"
do: Replace with lotus, bodhi tree or lantern symbols
Explain the reason in one friendly line
Check key art prompts do not include a seated Buddha
avoid: Buddha heads, statues or murals anywhere in the scene
"Collect the golden Buddhas"
Buddha images in key art backgrounds

cards.title: Monks and novices: never enemies, jokes or hazards
cards.text: Monks are highly respected in Thai society; women traditionally avoid touching them and people bow when meeting them. A monk or novice must not be an enemy, a comic character, a hazard, a chaser or a spectator gag. Most game stories need none; if a wise helper is wanted, use an invented hermit (ruesi-like but named and dressed as a fantasy sage), an old forest spirit or a talking animal instead.
cards.use_when: a story needs a wise helper, or a brief mentions monks or temple life
do: Use a fantasy sage, owl elder or kind spirit as the guide
Keep saffron robes out of character designs
If monks appear in a real-event backdrop, keep them distant and calm
avoid: Monk enemies, zombie monks or ghost monks
Monks in silly poses or chasing players
Saffron robes on a villain

cards.title: Royal symbols are off-limits: build an invented fantasy court
cards.text: Royal portraits, crowns, regalia, the royal garuda, royal flags, royal barges and the names of real kings or queens are protected by Thai law and custom and must not appear as props, prizes, characters, enemies or jokes. A "kingdom", "palace" or "prince" story should use an invented realm with its own name, crest (a lotus, a star lantern, a white elephant) and fictional characters with no resemblance to real royals, and the palace architecture should be fantasy, not a copy of a real palace.
cards.use_when: a brief mentions a king, palace, prince, princess or kingdom
do: Invent the realm name and a non-royal crest
Fantasy palace from Himmapan or sky-palace models
Characters as heroes, not monarchs
avoid: Crowns or regalia as a final treasure
Real palace look-alikes
Yellow royal-day colours with crests as a theme

cards.title: Head high, feet low: place respected things above foot level
cards.text: In Thai etiquette the head is the highest part of the body and the feet the lowest, so pointing feet at, or stepping over, respected things is rude. In MR the player's feet are the main interaction with the virtual floor: hazards and floor decals sit where people step. So never put faces of elders, spirit houses, lotus symbols, national flags or sacred patterns on floor tiles or hazards; place them as raised scenery beside the route and keep the floor to neutral ground, tiles and water.
cards.use_when: designing floor decals, hazards or tactics squares in a Thai theme
do: Floor = ground, tiles, water, leaves
Respected symbols raised at 1 m or higher, beside the route
Hazards as puddles, cracks, thorns or fire
avoid: Flags or faces as floor tiles
Lotus or yantra decals that players step on
Spirit houses at floor level on the route

cards.title: Castles and knights: a generic storybook kingdom
cards.text: A castle is the easiest theme for UK players and kids everywhere: towers, keeps, gatehouses, banners and a drawbridge. The catalog has round and octagonal towers, a castle keep, gatehouse, wall bastions, a banner hall and a throne dais. It fits all three genres: a battle defending the castle gate (forest theme), a tactics board as the castle courtyard (knight piece first, naturally), or a runner from the gatehouse to the throne. Keep crests invented and avoid any famous film castle or royal family.
cards.use_when: a medieval, knight, princess or UK heritage theme
do: Tactics: the knight piece in a courtyard story
Runner: gate, bridge, hall, tower, throne as checkpoints
Invented heraldry (a fox, a star)
avoid: A famous animated film castle silhouette
Real royal coats of arms
Crusades or religious war framing

cards.title: Halloween: pumpkins, witches and friendly frights, late October
cards.text: Halloween on 31 October is big in the UK and US and growing in Thailand: pumpkins, witches, black cats, bats, skeletons and trick-or-treat sweets. The catalog has a large party set (jack-o-lanterns, cauldrons, witch hats, bat bunting, candy bowls, sheet ghosts, cute skeletons) and a witch marsh world. For kids, keep it "spooky cute" in evening light; for teens and adults, spooky or night lighting indoors. Battle fits a dark theme with sheet-ghost chapters and a witch boss.
cards.use_when: an event in October or a spooky-cute party theme
do: Use spooky-cute for families, dark-eerie for teens
Trick-or-treat checkpoints ("Fill the candy bag")
Indoor or after-dark venues for glow
avoid: Running it past 31 October with the Halloween name
Gore, real weapons or horror-film killers
Mixing Thai sacred items into the party props

cards.title: Thai events: no Halloween wording from 1 November
cards.text: For Fortal events in Thailand the team stops using the word Halloween (ฮาโลวีน) in titles, intro cards, labels and promo from 1 November, even when the event runs on into November. The ghost content itself can stay: rename it as a "ghost night", "spirit festival", "Thai ghost party" or a Loy Krathong lantern night, and replace jack-o-lantern wording with lanterns. Check the event dates first whenever a brief has a spooky or pumpkin theme.
cards.use_when: a Thai event or booth that runs after 31 October with a spooky theme
do: Check the event dates in the interview
Rename to ghost night or spirit festival
Swap pumpkin wording for lanterns
avoid: "Halloween" in any title or label after 31 October
Countdown to Halloween text in November
Removing all ghosts when only the word must go

cards.title: Christmas: a winter village with gifts, 1-26 December
cards.text: Christmas fits December events in the UK and Thai malls alike: snowy pines, cabins, sleighs, gifts, lantern posts with wreaths and hot cocoa. The catalog's frost vale set has penguins, polar bears, a red sleigh, a frost elk, gift piles and glowing igloos. A runner "deliver the gifts before morning" with one gift stop per checkpoint is simple and cheerful. Keep it secular and generic: an invented gift-giver or animal helpers rather than a branded Santa design, and drop the name after 26 December.
cards.use_when: an event in December or a winter gift theme
do: Gift delivery checkpoints in a village loop
Evening or night lighting for lights and glow
Penguin or elk helpers as guides
avoid: A drinks brand's Santa look
Nativity scenes as game props
Christmas wording in January

cards.title: Bonfire Night (UK), 5 November: fireworks, not effigies
cards.text: Bonfire Night (Guy Fawkes Night) on 5 November is a UK tradition of bonfires and fireworks in parks on cold, dark evenings. A runner across a dark field with a virtual bonfire glow and a fireworks finale over the portal fits families. The tradition includes burning a "guy" effigy, which is uncomfortable for kids and a burning human figure is not something to put in a game; show fireworks and toffee-apple stalls instead.
cards.use_when: a UK event in early November or a fireworks theme
do: Night lighting, fireworks finale above the portal
Sparkler and toffee-apple stall vignettes
Keep the virtual bonfire 3 m or more from the route
avoid: Burning effigies
Fireworks as projectiles players fire
Real sparklers or fire at the venue

cards.title: British seaside pier: boardwalk, carnival rides and gulls
cards.text: The British seaside pier is a long boardwalk over the sea with arcades, carousels, candy floss and fish and chips. It is a perfect out-and-back or lanes runner: walk out along the pier with ride vignettes either side, and the portal at the end over the sea. The catalog's carnival set has bulb-lit boardwalks, carousels, popcorn stands, cotton-candy carts, ticket booths and ferris wheels. Noon lighting for a sunny day, evening for the bulb lights.
cards.use_when: a UK seaside, summer or funfair theme
do: Out-and-back route along a boardwalk
Rides as moving scenery beside the lane
Gulls and bunting for landmarks
avoid: A real pier's name or arcade brand
Void-floor sea drop for first-time players
Gambling machines as props for kids

cards.title: London-like city: generic big-city icons, invented names
cards.text: A UK city theme reads quickly with a few generic icons: a clock tower, red buses, black cabs, terraced houses, a river with bridges, rain and umbrellas. Use a clock tower and a river bridge from the catalog and keep it "a London-like city" with an invented name, so it stays original and does not need landmark permissions. A rainy evening palette with street lamps suits a runner chase through streets, and the river bridge makes a great midpoint checkpoint.
cards.use_when: a UK, London or city adventure brief
do: Invent the city name and the street names
Clock tower and bridge as landmarks
Evening lighting with street lamps
avoid: Exact replicas of named landmarks as the main set
Real shop or transport logos
Royal guards or palace as characters

cards.title: Ancient Egypt-inspired ruins: sand, sun and scarabs
cards.text: Desert ruins with sandstone blocks, obelisks, scarabs and sun discs make a bright adventure theme that survives daylight outdoors. The catalog's desert set has rotating sundials, scarabs rolling sand balls, sandworms, sliding stone blocks, mosaic plazas and sun banners, and the battle engine has a desert theme with the brightest base light. Use invented gods and pharaohs; avoid mummies of real people or tomb-looting framing, and do not label mixed ancient styles as Egyptian.
cards.use_when: a desert, pyramid, archaeology or adventure brief
do: Battle: desert theme, sand-beast as the beast
Runner: dig site to sun gate
Noon lighting outdoors
avoid: Real pharaoh names or real mummies
Mixing Maya and Egyptian art under one label
Treasure theft as the goal for a museum client

cards.title: Jungle sun-temple ruins: invent the culture, do not blend real ones
cards.text: The catalog's sun set (stepped pyramids, glyph steles, jaguar statues, macaw perches, cenote islands) is inspired by Mesoamerican ruins. Present it as an invented jungle civilisation with its own name, not as "Aztec" or "Maya", and do not mix it with Egyptian or Thai sacred art in one world. Avoid sacrifice imagery; the hook is lost jungle discovery, so discovery feelings and a winding runner fit best, with forest lighting and green glows.
cards.use_when: a jungle ruins or "ancient civilisation" adventure brief
do: Name the invented civilisation in the story
Discovery runner with glyph steles as checkpoints
Pair with jungle and waterfall scenery
avoid: Human sacrifice scenes
Labelling real cultures inaccurately
Blending three ancient cultures into one

cards.title: Norse-inspired: longhouses, frost and runes, invented
cards.text: A Norse-inspired world uses fjords, snowy pines, longhouses, forges, dragon-headed ships and runes. The catalog's frost vale, forge and dragon sets cover it, and the battle engine's ice and lava themes suit a "frost giant" or "forge dragon" story. Use invented runes and invented gods or heroes; some real runes and symbols have been used by hate groups, so do not copy runic symbols or rune lines from real sources.
cards.use_when: a viking, frost, dragon or forge adventure brief
do: Battle: ice theme with a frost-beast boss
Invented rune shapes in prompts
Longship and forge vignettes
avoid: Real runes or symbols copied as decoration
Named characters from a famous comic or film version
Gore and raiding of villages

cards.title: Japanese-inspired: torii, sakura and dojo, generic and respectful
cards.text: The catalog's ninja set has torii arches, pagoda islands, sakura trees, stone toro lanterns, koi ponds, red bridges, taiko pads and a moon-gate portal, which makes a calm or action theme. Torii and shrines are religious sites in Japan, so use torii as the gate of an invented world, not a real shrine, and never as a hazard. Avoid stereotyped accents, the rising-sun flag and recreating a famous ninja anime's headbands or villages.
cards.use_when: a Japanese, ninja, sakura or dojo theme
do: Torii as checkpoint frames, moon gate as the portal
Sakura and koi for a calm runner
Invent the village name
avoid: The rising-sun flag
A specific anime's symbols or characters
Shrine buildings as battle arenas

cards.title: Dinosaurs and museums: discovery with a roar
cards.text: Dinosaurs are loved by kids in every country and work for museums, schools and malls. The library has dinosaur island creatures and jungle scenery (tree ferns, ginkgo, monkey-puzzle trees, cliffs). A museum client usually wants learning: a runner where each checkpoint is a dinosaur with a one-line fact, finishing at a big skeleton or nest. In battle, a dinosaur can be the beast, but for young kids keep dinosaurs as giants to watch, not chasers.
cards.use_when: a museum, school, science or dinosaur brief
do: One short fact per checkpoint label
Big dinosaur as the spectator moment at the finish
Forest or noon lighting
avoid: Film-franchise park logos, gates or jeeps
Chase scenes that make kids run in MR
Long text panels

cards.title: Space: stations, planets and warp portals
cards.text: Space reads instantly at any age and suits neon or night lighting indoors. The catalog's space set has neon gantries, glass tube bridges, docking plazas, ringed planets, hologram arrows, UFO beams and a neon warp portal. Runner: a mission across a station with system checks as checkpoints; battle: neon theme with robot grunts; void floor: a walk across space for confident teens. Invent agencies, ships and aliens, and avoid real space agency logos.
cards.use_when: a sci-fi, space, astronaut or STEM brief
do: Mission-check labels ("Fix the oxygen")
Neon or night lighting indoors
Planets as far backdrop
avoid: Famous film starships or helmets
Real agency logos
Void floor for first-timers

cards.title: Pirates: treasure islands and harbour towns, kid-friendly
cards.text: Pirates suit kids and families: ships, docks, treasure chests, parrots, cannons and colonial harbour towns. The catalog has a deep pirate collection (ships, docks, fort walls, harbour towns by day and night, octopus tentacles, rocking decks). A treasure-map runner where each checkpoint is a map clue is a classic; tactics can be a ship deck board. Keep it comic adventure, invent the captain, and avoid famous film pirate looks.
cards.use_when: a pirate, treasure, harbour or sea adventure brief
do: Treasure-map clue labels
Harbour town vignettes beside the route
Noon or evening lighting
avoid: A famous film pirate captain look
Real-world piracy or violence on ships
Walking the plank as a punishment gag

cards.title: Toy room: giant toys at shrink-ray scale
cards.text: A toy world makes the player tiny among giant toys: spinning tops, jack-in-the-boxes, toy trains, dominoes, building-block bridges and a music-box carousel are all in the catalog. It is bright and safe for young kids and works in daylight. A tactics board as a giant chessboard on a bedroom floor is a natural fit. Keep toys generic: no famous brick, doll or figure brands.
cards.use_when: young kids, a living-room space or a playful tactics board
do: Shrunk-down story ("you got shrunk")
Building-block bridges for the route
Studio or noon lighting
avoid: Branded bricks, dolls or action figures
Creepy-doll horror for kids
Clutter that hides hazards

cards.title: Candy land: sweets, cakes and gummies
cards.text: Candy worlds are joyful and readable for under-10s: lollipops, gummy bears, donuts, cakes, cookie stepping stones and candy-cane lamps are in the catalog. They fit birthday parties and family malls. Hazards can be sticky jam puddles; battle can be the neon or forest theme with gummy grunts. Keep the colours saturated but use red only for hazards, and avoid branded sweets.
cards.use_when: a kids party, birthday or cheerful theme
do: Bake-a-cake checkpoint story
Hazards as jam or melted chocolate
Noon or studio lighting
avoid: Real candy brands
Red sweets near red hazard rings
Overeating jokes

cards.title: Ice and frost: crystal palaces and auroras
cards.text: Ice worlds are calm, clean and cool: ice palaces, crystal spires, frozen ponds, aurora ribbons and snowy pines. The battle engine has an ice theme for a frost-beast story, and the frost vale set brings friendly animals. Ice is a great escape theme in hot Thai months (March to May) and a natural Christmas-to-February theme in the UK. Pale blues wash out at noon outdoors, so prefer indoor or evening.
cards.use_when: a winter, frozen, "cool down" or crystal brief
do: Battle: ice theme, frost-beast boss
Aurora as the finale for spectators
Indoor lighting so pale blues read
avoid: A famous animated ice-queen look
Slippery-floor wording that makes MR players nervous
All-white scenes where hazards vanish

cards.title: Music world: piano bridges and drum stages
cards.text: A music world turns instruments into the set: piano-key bridges, guitar fretboard decks, giant snare-drum plazas, metronome arms and golden-note save stands. It suits concerts, schools and festivals, and can carry Thai flavour by adding a khaen or ranat-shaped stage prop in the story. Neon lighting gives a concert feel indoors. Avoid famous band names and song titles.
cards.use_when: a music, concert, school or party brief
do: Each checkpoint is a note of a tune
Stage vignettes facing spectators
Neon lighting indoors
avoid: Real band names or song lyrics
Loud sudden sounds as scares
Promising rhythm-game hit detection

cards.title: Farm: barns, tractors and friendly animals
cards.text: A farm is gentle and familiar in both the UK (barns, tractors, hay bales) and Thailand (rice, buffalo, chickens). The catalog's farm set has windmills, hay bales, scarecrows, tractors, sprinklers, pecking hens and patchwork-field platforms. A morning runner "wake up the farm" is great for kindergartens and seniors, with very soft hazards. Keep animals as friends, not enemies.
cards.use_when: very young players, seniors or a calm daylight theme
do: Morning lighting, 4-5 checkpoints
Animal vignettes as landmarks
Gentle hazards such as mud puddles
avoid: Slaughter or meat production scenes
Animals as battle enemies
Fast time limits for seniors

cards.title: Jungle: vines, waterfalls and hidden ruins
cards.text: The jungle works across cultures and covers both Thai forests and adventure stories: banyan trees, bamboo, ferns, vine curtains, river stones, rock arches and waterfalls. The battle engine has a forest theme (greens and warm torchlight) for a friendly adventure. Combine with gentle wildlife (birds, monkeys) and keep elephants as calm scenery. A discovery runner with hidden vignettes behind vines suits explorers.
cards.use_when: an adventure, nature or exploration brief
do: Battle: forest theme
Vine curtains as walk-through scenery beside the route
Waterfall as the finale
avoid: Tribal-people stereotypes as jungle "natives"
Dense props that hide hazards
Animals as cruel enemies

cards.title: Underwater reef: coral, jellyfish and sunken ships
cards.text: An underwater reef is magical and calming: coral arches, kelp, jellyfish lifts, giant clams, pufferfish, sunken-ship decks and a whirlpool portal are in the reef set. It fits southern Thailand stories and ocean-awareness themes for schools ("clean the reef" checkpoints). Night lighting makes glowing kelp and jellyfish shine indoors. Avoid drowning or shark-attack framing for young players.
cards.use_when: an ocean, reef, island or environment brief
do: Reef-cleaning or "find the turtle" story
Glowing kelp lamps along the route
Calm pacing, few hazards
avoid: Drowning, shark-attack or diving-danger stories
A famous animated fish
Void floor described as deep water for nervous players

cards.title: Robots and factories: neon battles and conveyor runs
cards.text: Robots are the best enemy theme for kids who should not fight "living" things: hitting a robot feels harmless. The battle engine's neon theme fits a robot factory; the robot set adds robot arms, stamping presses, conveyors, laser gates, drones and robot dogs. In a runner, a factory with sweeping lasers as hazards and "reboot the core" checkpoints gives a clear tech story. Invent the robots; avoid famous film robots.
cards.use_when: kids who want fighting without violence, a tech or STEM theme
do: Battle: neon theme, robot grunts, mech beast boss
Runner: factory with laser-gate visuals
Indoor neon lighting
avoid: Famous film robots or transforming cars
Robots that look like real people
Laser visuals in bright daylight where they vanish

cards.title: Superheroes: invent the hero, never a comic-book IP
cards.text: Kids often ask for a specific famous superhero. Explain kindly that FortalLand only makes original heroes, and offer an invented hero with a power that the engine shows well: a storm hammer, an arc shield or a nova gauntlet (all in the catalog's hero-tech set). Let the creator name the hero and pick its colours, so it feels theirs. Avoid any costume, symbol or name pattern that copies the big comic universes.
cards.use_when: a brief names a famous superhero or comic universe
do: Offer the creator naming and colour choice
Use hero-tech display pedestals as checkpoints
Battle in neon theme as a city defender
avoid: Famous costumes, logos or chest symbols
A hammer or shield that copies a famous design
Real celebrities as heroes

cards.title: Thai festival calendar: which themes fit which month
cards.text: January to February: Chinese New Year and the Chiang Mai Flower Festival (first weekend of February), in the cool season; March to May: hot season, Songkran (13-15 April), mango sticky rice and Bun Bang Fai rockets in May. June to July: Phi Ta Khon in Loei; September to October: Vegetarian Festival, rainy season (go indoors) and Halloween up to 31 October. November: Loy Krathong and Yi Peng at the full moon of the 12th lunar month, with no Halloween wording; December: Christmas in malls and the New Year countdown. Lunar festivals move every year, so check the exact dates.
cards.use_when: choosing a seasonal theme for a Thai event date
do: Match the theme to the event month
Check lunar festival dates for the year
Rename themes after their date
avoid: Songkran theme in December
Halloween wording in November
Assuming lunar festivals fall on the same day every year

cards.title: UK calendar and daylight: which themes fit which month
cards.text: UK seasons shape both theme and light. Winter (December to February) gets dark around 16:00, so night themes work even outdoors in late afternoon; Christmas fits 1-26 December. Spring (March to May) suits gardens and Easter-style egg hunts (keep it secular). Summer (June to August) stays light until about 21:00, so dark themes outdoors fail; seaside and festivals fit. Autumn: harvest, Halloween (31 October) and Bonfire Night (5 November).
cards.use_when: a UK event, or a creator who lists a month and an outdoor venue
do: Use the sunset time to pick outdoor lighting
Seaside in summer, ghosts in October
Bonfire Night just after Halloween
avoid: Night themes outdoors on a June evening
Religious Easter scenes as props
Halloween branding after 31 October for Thai teams

cards.title: Thai seasons decide indoor or outdoor play
cards.text: Thailand has a hot season (March to May, often above 35 C), a rainy season (June to October, sudden heavy storms) and a cool, dry season (November to February), the best time for outdoor events. In the north, February to April also brings smoke haze from field burning, so outdoor play in Chiang Mai can be unhealthy then. Headsets overheat in direct sun. Use outdoor themes from November to February and plan indoor venues for the rest.
cards.use_when: an outdoor Thai venue or a creator who mentions a month
do: Ask the month for outdoor briefs
Cool season for outdoor events
Shade, water and short sessions in hot months
avoid: Midday outdoor sessions in April
Outdoor plans in Chiang Mai haze season without a backup
Rainy-season events with no cover

cards.title: Themes that make good battle enemies
cards.text: The battle engine needs foes the player is happy to hit: robots (neon), lava or forge creatures (lava), frost beasts (ice), restless spirits sent to rest (dark), mummies or sand beasts (desert), goblin-like forest critters (forest). Map grunts to small foes, shields to armoured foes and the beast to the big one: robot drones, shield bots and a mech; imps, armoured golems and a lava beast. Avoid real animals people love, real peoples, monks or sacred beings as enemies.
cards.use_when: choosing the theme and boss of a battle option
do: Pick one of the six engine themes, then write story to match
Match grunt/shield/beast to small/armoured/big
Invent boss names
avoid: Elephants, naga or monks as foes
Real nationalities or ethnic groups as enemies
Human soldiers for young kids

cards.title: Themes that suit a tactics board
cards.text: A 6 x 8 tactics board needs a setting where a grid feels natural: a castle courtyard with stone tiles, a marble palace plaza, a rice-paddy field of earth paths, a market of stall rows, a floating market canal grid, a toy-room floor, a ship deck. Guards become castle sentries, scarecrows, market watchmen or toy soldiers; tables become stalls or haystacks. Keep sacred places off the board: a Lanna-style pavilion courtyard is fine, a temple courtyard is not.
cards.use_when: writing the story and board names of a tactics option
do: Name the grid in the story ("the courtyard tiles")
Guards as sentries or scarecrows
Tables as stalls, haystacks or crates
avoid: Temple courtyards or sacred objects as squares or targets
Themes with no natural grid (open sky, ocean waves)
Real royal palaces

cards.title: Themes that suit a runner route
cards.text: Runner themes need a path that makes sense to walk: a lantern trail, a market street, a parade, a canal bank, a pier, a mountain path, a castle tour, a treasure map. Choose a theme whose checkpoints can be named in a sequence (stall 1 to 5, gate to throne, recipe steps). Lantern trails and markets suit night; parades, piers and farms suit noon; ghost villages suit spooky.
cards.use_when: choosing the theme and route shape of a runner option
do: Pick a theme with a natural order of stops
Match lighting to the theme and venue
Name each checkpoint to tell the theme
avoid: A theme with no path (a single room scene)
Night themes outdoors in daylight
Labels that do not follow the theme

cards.title: Inspired-by is fine, recreating a named IP is not
cards.text: Creators often say "like" a famous game, film or cartoon. Being inspired by a feeling, a genre or a public-domain myth is fine; copying a named game, film, character, logo, level, costume or distinctive look is not. Thai folklore spirits, Greek myth and Himmapan creatures are traditional and free to use, but a specific film's version of them (its costume, scenes or title) is owned. Always ask what the creator loves about the reference and build that feeling in an original world.
cards.use_when: a brief names an existing game, film, cartoon, character or brand
do: Ask what they love about it (speed, cuteness, spookiness)
Use traditional folklore, not a film's version
Invent names for the world and characters
avoid: Character names or look-alikes from films and games
Brand logos on props
A level layout copied from a famous game

cards.title: Make an original twist in three moves
cards.text: To turn a reference into something original: (1) change the who: a different species, age or role (a gecko knight instead of a famous hero), (2) change the where: move it into a Thai or invented setting (a ninja story in a Lanna rice valley), (3) change the why: a new goal (bring the lanterns home, not save the princess). Combining two unrelated themes, such as Himmapan plus space or pirates plus floating market, often gives a fresh world the library still covers.
cards.use_when: the options phase needs a fresh theme or a creator wants "like X but ours"
do: Change at least two of who, where and why
Combine two catalog themes for a fresh mix
Give the twist a one-line pitch
avoid: A reskin with the same characters and names
Combining themes the catalog does not cover
Mixing sacred symbols into a mash-up

cards.title: No real people: celebrities, influencers, politicians or royals
cards.text: Creators sometimes want a famous singer, footballer, YouTuber or politician in their game. Using a real person's face, name or likeness needs their permission and can be defamatory or illegal (and royals are fully off-limits in Thailand). Offer an invented character with a similar vibe (a "rock star cat", a "football robot") and let the creator design it.
cards.use_when: a brief mentions a real celebrity, influencer, politician or the creator's friends by name
do: Offer an invented character with the same vibe
Let the creator pick its name and colours
Keep real names out of prompts and labels
avoid: Real faces or names in key art prompts
Politicians as enemies or jokes
Classmates or teachers as characters

cards.title: Each battle enemy kind asks the player a different question
cards.text: The battle engine has exactly three enemy kinds. A grunt (3 health, fast) asks "can you swing in time?", a shield (5 health, blocks hits from the front) asks "can you get to its side?", and a beast (14 health, charges with a red ring at your feet, hits for 2) asks "can you read the warning and move?". Design each chapter around which question it asks, not around a body count.
cards.use_when: choosing the foes list of any battle chapter
do: Name the question each chapter asks before picking numbers
Use shields to teach moving around a foe
Use a beast as the chapter centrepiece, not filler
avoid: Inventing other enemy kinds (archers, flyers, mages)
Treating all three kinds as interchangeable counts

cards.title: Chapter one is grunts only, and never a beast
cards.text: The checker rejects a beast in chapter 1, and for good reason: the first chapter is where the player learns that a swing hits and a red ring hurts. Use 2 to 3 grunts and no rain. On PC this is a short warm-up; in MR it gives a first-time headset player time to find the controller-sword before anything charges.
cards.use_when: writing the first chapter of any battle game
do: Chapter 1: 2-3 grunts, rain false
Make its line say what to do ("Cut them down")
avoid: A beast or rain in chapter 1
Opening with 5+ enemies to look exciting

cards.title: Add one new thing per battle chapter
cards.text: A clear ramp introduces one new element per chapter: first grunts, then shields, then the first beast, then rain, then a mix. When two new things arrive together the player cannot tell what hurt them. The last chapter before the boss is the only place where everything mixes.
cards.use_when: ordering 4-6 battle chapters
do: Write a one-word "new thing" next to each chapter while planning
Save the full mix for the chapter before the boss
avoid: Shield and beast debut in the same chapter
Rain arriving together with the first beast

cards.title: Pick the battle chapter count from the session length
cards.text: The engine takes 3 to 6 chapters and then adds the boss fight on its own. As a planning estimate, a chapter takes about 40 to 90 seconds and the boss 1.5 to 3 minutes, with a short pause between chapters. So 3 chapters fit a 3-5 minute event slot, 4-5 chapters fit 6-8 minutes, and 6 chapters suit 10 minutes or more for keen players. Confirm the real times in a playtest.
cards.use_when: the brief has session_minutes and the option is battle
do: 3 chapters for 3-5 min queues
4-5 chapters for 6-8 min
6 chapters only for 10+ min and keen players
avoid: 6 chapters in a 4-minute event slot
Counting the boss as one of the 3-6 chapters

cards.title: In MR a battle chapter holds at most 6 enemies
cards.text: In MR the player stands in a real room, so the checker allows at most 6 enemies in a chapter (PC allows 9). Enemies also walk at about 60 percent of their PC speed in MR. Treat 4 as a normal MR chapter and 6 as the climax; more bodies around a real person feels crowded and makes rings hard to escape in a small room.
cards.use_when: writing battle chapters for platform mr
do: Keep most MR chapters at 3-5 enemies
Use 6 only for the chapter before the boss
avoid: Copying a 9-enemy PC chapter into MR
Six enemies in a 3 x 3 m room

cards.title: On PC a battle chapter holds at most 9 enemies, and 9 is a peak
cards.text: A PC chapter may list up to 3 foe entries, each with 1 to 6 of one kind, with a total of at most 9. Nine is a showpiece for the last chapter before the boss, when the player has learned all three kinds. A typical PC ramp is 3, 5, 3 (with the first beast), 5 with rain, then 7-9.
cards.use_when: writing battle chapters for platform pc
do: Ramp totals like 3, 5, 3, 5, 8
Lower the count when a beast or rain joins
avoid: Every chapter at 9
More than 3 foe entries in one chapter

cards.title: Rain is a pressure chapter: fewer, weaker enemies under falling rings
cards.text: When a chapter has rain, warning rings keep dropping around the player (roughly one per second) for as long as enemies are alive. That already makes the chapter hard, so pair rain with 3 to 4 grunts and no beast. Use rain once in a short game and at most twice in a long one; it reads as a story moment (a storm, a curse, falling rocks, meteors).
cards.use_when: deciding which chapters get rain: true
do: Pair rain with grunts only
Name the rain in the chapter line ("Ash falls from the volcano")
Place rain in the middle third
avoid: Rain in chapter 1
Rain plus a beast plus shields in one chapter
Rain in every chapter

cards.title: Rain in MR makes real people step often: size the room for it
cards.text: In MR there is no dash: the player escapes a ring by stepping out of it with their own feet. Rain chapters therefore mean many quick steps. In a 3 x 3 m room or with first-time headset players, either skip rain or use it once with at most 3 grunts. In 5 x 5 m or larger it works well and looks great to spectators.
cards.use_when: an MR battle in a small room or for first-time VR players
do: Skip rain under 4 x 4 m
Use at most one rain chapter for first-time VR
Tell players to step, not run
avoid: Two rain chapters in a living room
Rain for seniors or young kids
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: The boss is one fixed fight: you choose only its name and intro line
cards.text: Every battle ends with the same boss behaviour: a large crowned warrior that slams red rings at the player, calls 2 grunts every few seconds, and gets faster with extra rings once below half health. The design only sets boss.name and boss.intro. Make the name and intro pay off the story the chapters told ("The Frost Warden wakes. Break the ice crown.").
cards.use_when: writing the boss of a battle game
do: Foreshadow the boss in an earlier chapter line
Write the intro as a call to action
Keep the chapter before the boss below the cap, since the boss adds grunts
avoid: Promising a dragon that flies or breathes fire
Describing boss attacks the engine does not have

cards.title: When the creator asks for a special boss, offer name, intro and theme
cards.text: Creators often ask for "a giant dragon boss" or "a robot boss with lasers". The battle engine has one boss model and one behaviour. Say so kindly and offer what does change: the boss name, its intro line, the theme colours around it, and the story the chapters build toward it. A lava theme plus "The Ember Tyrant" carries much of the dragon feeling.
cards.use_when: the creator describes a boss with unique attacks, flying or shooting
do: Offer name + intro + theme as the boss identity
Tell the creator plainly what the boss does
avoid: Promising a custom boss model or attack
Silently ignoring the wish

cards.title: Chapter titles and lines tell the story in order
cards.text: Each chapter has a title and one line shown when it starts. Read in order, the titles should form a story: arrive, meet resistance, face the beast, survive the storm, break in, face the boss. Keep each line one sentence, present tense, with the place and the threat ("The gate falls. Everything inside comes for you.").
cards.use_when: writing chapter titles and lines
do: Read all titles in a row: they should sound like a plot
One sentence per line, under about 12 words
avoid: Titles like "Wave 1", "Wave 2"
Lines that repeat the same sentence with different numbers

cards.title: Let each chapter line carry the hint for its new enemy
cards.text: The line is the only text a player reads at the start of a chapter, so it doubles as the tutorial. For shields say to hit from the side, for a beast say to watch its red ring and strike after it charges, for rain say to keep moving. Players then learn the counter inside the story instead of from a rules screen.
cards.use_when: a chapter introduces shields, a beast or rain
do: Shield line: "hit them from the side"
Beast line: "watch the ring, step out, strike its back"
Rain line: "keep moving"
avoid: Pure flavour lines with no hint on a new threat
Long rule text in the line
cards.source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

cards.title: Battle themes and the mood each one carries
cards.text: The battle engine has six themes. dark is purple night and torches for gothic dread; ice is cold blues, calm and clean, for frost or winter stories; lava is red and orange danger for a volcano or forge. forest is greens and warm torchlight for friendly adventure; neon is magenta and cyan for an arcade or cyber party; desert is warm sand with the brightest base light, for ancient ruins or sun.
cards.use_when: choosing config.theme for a battle game
do: Match the theme to the story world first
Use forest or desert for younger players
avoid: A theme name outside the six
dark for a cheerful kids story

cards.title: In MR pick the battle theme by the real light
cards.text: In MR only the floor and the enemies are drawn; the real room stays visible. In a bright hall or daylight, dark and neon look washed out, while desert and ice (the lightest themes) stay readable. In a dim hall or after dark, neon, lava and dark glow and feel dramatic. Red rings must stay readable on the floor in every case.
cards.use_when: an MR battle and the brief says indoor/outdoor and time of day
do: Bright venue: desert or ice
Dim venue: neon, lava or dark
Check ring readability in the prototype test questions
avoid: Neon in a sunny garden
Assuming the PC look carries into MR
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: A battle ramp for kids: short, grunt-heavy, one beast late
cards.text: For ages about 6 to 11 use 3 or 4 chapters: grunts, then shields with grunts, then one beast with 1-2 grunts, then an easy final mix. Use rain at most once and keep totals at 3-5. The player has 10 health and heals 2 after each chapter, so a gentle ramp lets most kids reach the boss, which is the moment they talk about afterwards.
cards.use_when: players are kids or families and the option is battle
do: 3-4 chapters
Totals 3-5 per chapter
One beast, late
Friendly theme like forest or desert
avoid: Two beasts in one chapter for kids
Gothic dread themes for under-8s
Rain twice

cards.title: A battle ramp for gamers: 5-6 chapters with combined threats
cards.text: Gamers want the combinations: shields that block while a beast charges, rain over a grunt pack. Use 5 or 6 chapters, two rain chapters, and a final chapter at the cap (9 on PC, 6 in MR). The end score adds a bonus for finishing fast and for health left, so tell them that speed and clean play raise the score.
cards.use_when: players are gamers or teens who want a hard fight
do: Combine shield + beast in the late chapters
Two rain chapters spread apart
Mention the time and health bonus in the rules
avoid: A flat ramp where chapter 5 equals chapter 2
Hiding how the score works

cards.title: MR battle needs at least 3 x 3 m of empty floor
cards.text: The arena is fitted to the room minus about 0.5 m on each side, so a 3 x 3 m floor gives a 2 m fighting area: enough for grunts and shields, tight for a beast charge (its warning ring is about 2.8 m across). From 4 x 4 m a beast is comfortable; 5 x 5 m is the template default. Under 3 m on a side the checker only allows runner options.
cards.use_when: an MR brief where the floor size is known
do: 3-4 m: grunts and shields, at most one beast
4 x 4 m or more: full mix
Under 3 m: offer runner instead
avoid: Proposing battle for a 2.5 x 3 m room
Two beasts in a 3 x 3 m room

cards.title: MR battle: the controller is the sword and the feet only step
cards.text: In MR the right controller holds the sword and a fast swing attacks; the player stands and steps, with no dash and no running. Enemies walk in slowly from the edges, and every threat is a red ring the player steps out of. Write rules and pitches around "swing and step": it is safe, and it is what spectators enjoy watching.
cards.use_when: pitching or writing rules for an MR battle
do: Rules: "Swing the right controller", "Step out of red rings"
Pitch the player as standing their ground
avoid: Promising a dash in MR
Telling players to run or dodge-roll
Two-handed or shield blocking moves

cards.title: PC battle: 3-hit combo and a dash are the whole move set
cards.text: On PC the player moves with WASD, aims with the mouse, swings a 3-hit sword combo (the third hit deals double damage and reaches further) and dashes with Space or right click, which briefly dodges attacks. That is the full kit. Good PC chapters are about using the dash to leave a red ring and the third hit to finish a shield or beast.
cards.use_when: writing pitch, rules or storyboard for a PC battle
do: Mention the dash in the beast chapter line
Show the third hit as the big moment in the storyboard
avoid: Promising magic, bows, blocking, jumping or pickups
Weapon upgrades between chapters

cards.title: Battle has no items, no co-op and no second weapon
cards.text: Creators often add upgrades, potions, a partner hero or a bow to a fight concept. The battle engine is one player, one sword, three enemy kinds, rain rings, one boss, health that refills by 2 after a chapter, and a score. Offer the closest real things: the heal between chapters as "rest at the campfire", score as bragging rights, spectators as the cheering party.
cards.use_when: the creator asks for power-ups, co-op, shooting or inventory in a battle game
do: Reframe the chapter heal as a story rest
Offer the score for competition between friends taking turns
avoid: Promising co-op or online battles
Promising loot or upgrades

cards.title: Battle score rules to write into the game card
cards.text: Score comes from kills (grunt 50, shield 80, beast 400), 200 for each cleared chapter, and on a win a bonus for speed and for health left. Write two rules from this: "Clear a chapter to heal 2 and gain 200" and "Finish fast with health left for a higher score". It gives friends taking turns something to compare.
cards.use_when: writing game.rules for a battle game
do: Mention the chapter heal and 200 bonus
Mention the speed and health bonus
avoid: Inventing combo multipliers or stars
Score rules that the engine does not count

cards.title: MR battle spectators watch a real sword fight with no visible enemies
cards.text: People beside an MR battle see a person swinging, turning and stepping out of invisible rings. That is funny and dramatic, so give them a place outside the floor edge with at least 1 m extra for the swinging arm, and let them cheer each "Chapter cleared". The boss is the loudest moment; spectators can cheer the boss health going down if a screen mirrors the game.
cards.use_when: writing spectator_view or spectator_plan for an MR battle
do: Spectators stand outside the edge plus 1 m
Invite cheering at chapter clears and the boss
avoid: Spectators inside the play area
Asking spectators to call out enemies they cannot see
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: The shield chapter is the battle game's little puzzle
cards.text: Shields block hits from the front, so the player must get to their side. In MR this means stepping around a slow enemy, which feels clever and is easy to read. Use 2 to 3 shields with 1 to 2 grunts as distraction; more than 4 shields becomes a wall that frustrates new players.
cards.use_when: the second chapter of a battle game, or teaching flanking
do: 2-3 shields + 1-2 grunts
Line: "Hit them from the side"
avoid: 5-6 shields in one chapter
A shield chapter with rain before players know the trick

cards.title: Budget the player's 10 health across the run
cards.text: The player has 10 health, regains 2 after each chapter, and beast and boss hits cost 2 while grunt hits and rain cost 1. Many beasts or long rain chapters drain health before the boss, which ends runs at the wrong moment. Aim for a run where an average player arrives at the boss with about half health.
cards.use_when: balancing a 5-6 chapter battle or a hard ramp
do: At most one beast per chapter before the final mix
Follow a rain chapter with a lighter one
avoid: Back-to-back beast chapters
Ending most runs before the boss

cards.title: Example battle plan: forest rescue for a family day (MR, 4 x 4 m)
cards.text: Theme forest; chapter 1 "Goblins at the gate": 3 grunts; chapter 2 "The bark shields": 2 shields, 1 grunt, line "Step around them, hit their side". Chapter 3 "The mud boar": 1 beast, 1 grunt, line "Watch the ring, step out, strike"; chapter 4 "Acorn storm": 3 grunts with rain. Boss "The Thorn King", intro "He has the fox cub. Win it back." Every MR chapter stays at 4 or fewer.
cards.use_when: need a worked example of a kid-friendly MR battle config
do: Copy the structure, change names to fit the brief
avoid: Copying the names verbatim for another brief

cards.title: Each tactics piece teaches a different way of seeing the board
cards.text: The knight jumps in an L over anything, so it teaches seeing hidden two-step paths. The bishop slides on diagonals and can only ever reach one colour, so it teaches routing around. The rook runs straight lines that tables stop, so it teaches lanes. The queen moves any way, so the board becomes a test of reading danger rather than finding a path.
cards.use_when: choosing the piece for each tactics board
do: Say in the board story what the piece is good at
Vary the piece between boards
avoid: The same piece on every board
Promising a king or pawn as the player piece

cards.title: A good tactics piece order: simple reading first, queen last
cards.text: The rook is the easiest piece to read (straight lines) and suits board 1 for kids and newcomers; the knight suits board 1 for puzzle lovers because its jump is a fun surprise. Put the bishop in the middle and the queen on the last board or two, where freedom meets the most guards. The build task asks for the pieces to vary.
cards.use_when: ordering 3-6 tactics boards
do: Kids: rook, knight, bishop, queen
Puzzle fans: knight, bishop, rook, queen, queen
avoid: Opening with the queen
Bishop first for young kids

cards.title: Give bishop boards fewer targets
cards.text: A bishop zig-zags to reach anything, so each target costs more moves and more beats under guard pressure. Code still makes the board solvable, but 5 or 6 targets with a bishop feels slow. Use 3 to 4 targets on bishop boards and spend the extra difficulty on guards instead.
cards.use_when: a tactics board where the piece is bishop
do: Bishop boards: 3-4 targets
Raise guards, not targets
avoid: 6 targets with a bishop
A bishop board as the first board for kids

cards.title: Pick the tactics board count from the session length
cards.text: The engine takes 3 to 6 boards. As a planning estimate a board takes about 45 seconds to 2 minutes on PC and longer in MR, where every move is a walk and guards wait at least 3 seconds. So 3 boards fit 3-5 minutes, 4-5 boards fit 6-10 minutes, and 6 boards suit a long session for puzzle fans. Confirm in a playtest.
cards.use_when: the brief has session_minutes and the option is tactics
do: MR events: 3-4 boards
PC puzzle fans: 5-6 boards
avoid: 6 MR boards for a 5-minute queue

cards.title: Guards ramp from at most 2 on board 1 to at most 4
cards.text: Each board has 0 to 4 guards, and the checker rejects more than 2 on the first board. Guards are the main difficulty knob because their attacked squares change every beat. A typical ramp is 1, 2, 2, 3, 4; for kids 0 or 1 guard on board 1 lets them learn how the piece moves before anything moves back.
cards.use_when: setting guards for a sequence of tactics boards
do: Board 1: 0-2 guards (0-1 for kids)
Add one guard every board or two
Final board: 3-4
avoid: 3 or more guards on board 1
Dropping from 4 guards back to 1 without a story reason

cards.title: You choose how many guards, not which pieces they are
cards.text: Code picks each guard's kind (rook, bishop or knight in rotation) and its patrol path when it builds the board. So a board story should not promise "two knights guard the vault" or "a rook patrols the hall". Describe guards by role in the story ("the night watch", "palace guards") and let the engine decide their moves.
cards.use_when: writing board stories or the prototype for a tactics game
do: Call guards by story role
Describe the guard count, not the guard pieces
avoid: Naming specific guard pieces in board stories
Promising hand-placed patrol routes

cards.title: Set the guard beat by who plays
cards.text: The beat is the seconds between guard moves (1.5 to 3.5). Slower is easier: there is time to look at the red and orange squares and plan. For kids or first-time players use 3 to 3.5 s throughout; casual adults on PC 2.5 to 3 s; puzzle fans on PC can end at 1.8 to 2 s. Shorten the beat by about 0.2 to 0.3 s per board at most.
cards.use_when: choosing beat values for tactics boards
do: Kids: 3-3.5 s on every board
Gamers PC: start 2.8, end 1.8-2.0
avoid: Beat under 2 s on board 1
Big jumps like 3.0 to 1.5 between boards

cards.title: In MR guards move every 3 s or slower, so ramp with other knobs
cards.text: Players walk the board in MR, so the engine never lets guards move faster than every 3 s, whatever the plan says. In MR use beats of 3 to 3.5 s and make later boards harder with more guards, more cracked squares and more targets instead of a faster beat. A plan that relies on a 2 s beat for its climax will feel flat in a headset.
cards.use_when: a tactics game on platform mr
do: MR beats: 3.0-3.5 s
Ramp with guards and cracks
avoid: Planning beat 2.0 as the MR climax
Telling MR players to hurry between beats

cards.title: MR board squares are fitted to the floor, up to 1 m
cards.text: The 6 x 8 board is scaled to the room: each square is the smaller of 1 m, width / 6 and depth / 8, and never below 0.5 m. A 6 x 8 m floor gives 1 m squares; 4.5 x 6 m gives 0.75 m; 3 x 4 m gives 0.5 m, where it is hard to stand clearly on one square. The player moves by standing on a legal square for about a third of a second.
cards.use_when: an MR tactics option and the floor size is known
do: Prefer 4.5 x 6 m or more (0.75 m squares)
Score mr_fit lower when squares come out near 0.5 m
Run the 8-square side along the longer wall
avoid: Promising big squares in a small room
Tactics in a room under 3 x 3 m

cards.title: MR tactics: walk, never jump, and keep the board edge clear
cards.text: A queen or rook move can cross the whole board, which in a 6 x 8 m room is several metres of walking in a headset. With a guard beat ticking, players may hurry. Tell them in the rules to walk, keep 0.6 m clear beyond the board edge, keep spectators off the board, and remember that after a hit the player walks back to the start ring.
cards.use_when: writing rules or the spectator plan for MR tactics
do: Rule: "Walk onto a green ring, never jump"
Keep a clear margin around the board
Mention walking back to the start ring after a hit
avoid: Encouraging a dash across the board
Real furniture left on the board area
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Tactics is a race on time with a leaderboard
cards.text: The run timer counts every board, each hit adds 5 seconds, and the player has 3 hearts. The leaderboard ranks by boards cleared, then by time, and asks for the next player's name, so it suits events where people take turns. Pitch it as "fastest clean run wins" and suggest showing the leaderboard on a screen for the queue.
cards.use_when: tactics for events, classes or friends taking turns
do: Pitch "fastest clean run" as the goal
Rule: each hit adds 5 s
Show the leaderboard to the queue
avoid: Promising online head-to-head chess
Promising stars or unlocks

cards.title: Wrap each tactics board in one story line
cards.text: Every board has a one-line story, and the run reads as a plot when the lines connect: sneak in, cross the hall, reach the vault, face the king. Common wraps that fit the mechanics: a heist (targets are treasures, guards are watchmen), a rescue (targets are keys taken in order), a ghost hunt (targets are spirits to catch). The rules stay chess; only the words change.
cards.use_when: writing board stories and the game story for tactics
do: Give the targets a story meaning
Make the last line the climax
avoid: Board lines that only describe the piece
Story beats that need new mechanics (doors that unlock, items to carry)

cards.title: Tables come with seated characters: use them for indoor stories
cards.text: Each table blocks a square (sometimes two side by side) and has cartoon characters sitting at it who cheer when you capture. That suits stories set in a cafe, library, classroom, banquet or night market. Tables also block a rook or bishop guard's line, so they make safe shadows on the board.
cards.use_when: a tactics story set indoors or among people, or the board needs shelter from line attacks
do: Use 2-4 tables in cafe or banquet stories
Mention tables as cover in the board story
avoid: Tables as hiding spots the player can enter
Describing tables as anything other than blocked squares

cards.title: Cracked squares are fixed traps that hurt when you land
cards.text: A cracked square costs a heart when the player lands on it; it never moves. Use 0 to 1 on early boards and 3 to 4 later, and give them a story name: thin ice, lava cracks, broken tiles, cursed stones. Because they are static, cracks reward planning rather than timing, which balances boards where guards already add timing pressure.
cards.use_when: setting cracks for tactics boards
do: Board 1: 0-1 cracks
Late boards: 3-4
Name the cracks in the story
avoid: 4 cracks on board 1
Describing cracks that open or move

cards.title: Targets set the length of a board more than its difficulty
cards.text: Each board has 2 to 6 targets captured in number order. More targets mean more moves and more beats, so a longer board, but not much harder if guards are few. Use 3 targets early, 4 to 5 in the middle and up to 6 late, and keep target counts lower in MR where every move is a walk.
cards.use_when: setting targets per board
do: Early: 3
Middle: 4-5
MR: rarely more than 5
avoid: 6 targets on board 1
Using targets as the only difficulty knob

cards.title: The king is the last target on the final board only
cards.text: Setting king: true makes the last target of that board a king. Use it on the final board as the story climax ("Take his guards, then take him"), with the other targets as his court. A king earlier in the run spends the climax too soon, and a run without a king needs another strong final line.
cards.use_when: writing the final tactics board
do: king: true on the last board
Final story line names the king
avoid: king: true on several boards
A king on board 1

cards.title: Escalate the target piece to show rising stakes
cards.text: target_piece sets how targets look: pawn, knight, bishop or rook. Targets do not move or fight back; the change is visual and narrative. Escalate across boards (pawns, then knights, then bishops, then rooks guarding the king) so players feel they are climbing toward the court.
cards.use_when: choosing target_piece across boards
do: Pawns on board 1, rooks near the end
avoid: Saying stronger targets fight back
Random target pieces with no pattern

cards.title: The AI chooses numbers; code places the board and proves it solvable
cards.text: For tactics the design gives each board a piece, a story line and counts (targets, guards, tables, cracks, beat, king). Code places everything and checks that every board can be solved. So never promise exact square positions, hand-made puzzle layouts or a specific trick in a prototype; promise the experience and the ramp.
cards.use_when: writing options, prototype sketch or build for tactics
do: Describe each board as a feeling plus numbers
Sketch the board with zones, not exact squares
avoid: "The target is on c5 behind the table"
Promising a particular puzzle solution

cards.title: Tactics teaches itself through floor colours
cards.text: Green rings show where you can move, orange numbered pieces are targets in order, red squares are attacked now, and light orange squares will be attacked after the next guard move. Board 1 should have few guards so players learn these colours. In rules, name the colours rather than chess terms, which helps kids and people who never played chess.
cards.use_when: writing rules for tactics, or players new to chess
do: Rules in colours: green = move, red = danger
Mention the "attacked next" warning
avoid: Chess notation in rules
Assuming players know how pieces move

cards.title: Turn one or two tactics knobs per board, not all five
cards.text: A tactics board has five knobs: beat, guards, cracks, tables and targets. Guards and beat change difficulty most, cracks add planning, tables can make it easier (shelter) or harder (blocked lines), and targets change length. Changing one or two per board makes the ramp readable; changing all at once makes a spike.
cards.use_when: planning a 4-6 board tactics ramp
do: Write which knob changes on each board
Pair a new piece with an easier board
avoid: New piece + more guards + faster beat on one board
No change at all between boards
cards.source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

cards.title: Tactics is not two-player chess: offer the time race instead
cards.text: Creators often imagine players playing chess against each other or against a computer opponent. In this engine one player is a piece, guards follow patrols on a beat, and targets wait to be taken. Offer turns on the same boards with the leaderboard (fastest clean run), or friends calling hints from the side.
cards.use_when: the creator asks for PvP chess, an AI chess opponent or co-op tactics
do: Offer the leaderboard race
Offer friends calling hints
avoid: Promising online matches
Promising guards that chase the player intelligently

cards.title: Tactics spectators become the hint crowd
cards.text: In MR people beside the floor see a player stepping square to square and stopping to think. They cannot see the board, but with a screen mirroring the game or after watching a few runs they love to shout hints. Put the spectators along the long side, show the leaderboard there, and present it as a calm, social puzzle rather than an action game.
cards.use_when: spectator_view for tactics at events, classes or families
do: Spectators on the long side of the board
Leaderboard on a screen nearby
avoid: Spectators walking onto the board to point
Promising spectators can see the board in MR without a screen

cards.title: Tactics serves challenge, discovery and expression, not sensation
cards.text: Tactics is slow and readable: the pleasure is finding a path (discovery), planning your own route (expression) and beating the clock (challenge). It is the best pick in a brief that mentions thinking, chess, puzzles, school or calm competition. It is the weakest pick for "wow", fast action or pure relaxation, so score fun honestly when the brief is sensation-led.
cards.use_when: mapping brief feelings to the tactics option
do: Lead with tactics for puzzle, school and strategy briefs
Score it lower on fun for thrill-seeking briefs
avoid: Pitching tactics as an action spectacle

cards.title: Example tactics plan: library heist for kids (MR, 5 x 7 m)
cards.text: Board 1: rook, "Sneak past the reading tables", 3 targets, 1 guard, 2 tables, 0 cracks, beat 3.5, target pawn. Board 2: knight, "Hop over the book piles", 3 targets, 1 guard, 2 tables, 1 crack, beat 3.5, target pawn. Board 3: bishop, "Slip along the diagonals", 3 targets, 2 guards, 1 crack, beat 3.2, target knight. Board 4: queen, "Take the Librarian King's keys", 4 targets, 3 guards, 2 cracks, beat 3.0, king true, target bishop.
cards.use_when: need a worked example of a gentle MR tactics ramp
do: Keep MR beats at 3 s or more
Copy the shape, not the words
avoid: Reusing this story for an unrelated brief

cards.title: Loop routes: the safe default for small and medium rooms
cards.text: A loop walks around the space and ends near the spawn, so the finish portal is where the queue and spectators already are. It uses the whole floor without crossing itself, which keeps the 1.2 m walking corridor simple. Use it for rooms under 4 x 4 m and as the default in 4 to 10 m spaces.
cards.use_when: choosing a runner route shape for a small or medium space
do: End the loop with the portal near the audience
Keep the loop at least 0.6 m from the edge
avoid: A loop crammed into one corner
Crossing paths inside a small loop

cards.title: Zig-zag routes fill long rectangular rooms
cards.text: A zig-zag goes back and forth across the short side while moving down the long one, so every leg is about the room width. It suits classrooms, halls and courts, and gives natural spots for hazards in the middle of each leg. Keep turns at the ends at least 0.6 m from the walls.
cards.use_when: a rectangular space where one side is about 1.5 times the other or longer
do: One checkpoint at each turn
Hazards mid-leg
avoid: Zig-zags with legs shorter than the stop spacing
Turning right at the wall

cards.title: Spiral routes build to a climax at the centre
cards.text: A spiral walks inward ring by ring, so the story naturally heads "to the heart" of something: the temple shrine, the dragon nest, the eye of the storm. Put the last checkpoint and the portal at the centre. It needs a fairly square space of about 5 x 5 m or more; in smaller rooms the inner turns get too tight.
cards.use_when: a square space and a story that goes deeper toward a goal
do: Portal at the centre
Labels that move inward ("outer wall" to "inner shrine")
avoid: Spirals under 5 x 5 m
A spiral on a void floor for first-time players

cards.title: Two-lane routes suit big spaces and side-by-side play
cards.text: Two parallel lanes let two players walk the length of a large space at the same time and stay apart, which is clear for spectators along the long side. It needs over 10 x 10 m (for example the 14 x 22 m Fortal court). Keep at least 1.2 m clear for each lane plus a gap between them.
cards.use_when: a large space with 2 or more players at once
do: Lanes along the long side, spectators parallel
Portal at the far end facing the crowd
avoid: Two lanes in a 6 m wide room
Lanes that cross

cards.title: Hub-and-spoke routes: a central camp with trips outward
cards.text: A hub route returns to a centre between trips to the edges, like a village square with paths to the well, the forest and the temple. Checkpoints still go in order, so alternate: spoke, hub, spoke. It fits discovery and story briefs in medium and large square spaces, and a big hero model beside the hub anchors the whole Land.
cards.use_when: a discovery or story brief in a square medium or large space
do: Alternate hub and spoke checkpoints
Hero scenery beside (not on) the hub
avoid: Hub routes in rooms under 5 x 5 m
Promising free choice of spoke order

cards.title: Out-and-back routes fit narrow spaces and corridors
cards.text: Out-and-back walks to the far end and returns, so it suits a long narrow garden path, a corridor or a strip of a car park. The turnaround is the story climax (the summit, the treasure), and the return leg can bring new hazards. Offset the return 1.2 m or more from the outward leg where the width allows, so walkers do not meet face to face.
cards.use_when: a long, narrow space (about 3 m wide or less)
do: Climax checkpoint at the far end
Offset outward and return legs
avoid: Outward and return on the same line
Out-and-back in a square room where a loop fits better

cards.title: Write checkpoint labels as short verb-first story beats
cards.text: Each checkpoint has a short label that tells the story. Write 2 to 4 words, verb first, saying what happens there: "Feed the dragon", "Light the lantern", "Wake the guardian". A label tells the player why they are walking, which turns a course into a story without any new mechanic.
cards.use_when: writing checkpoint labels for a runner layout brief
do: Verb first, 2-4 words
Each label names a thing the scenery shows
avoid: "Checkpoint 3"
Labels longer than a short line
Labels promising actions the player cannot do (talk, pick up)

cards.title: Arrange checkpoint labels as a five-step story arc
cards.text: With 5 to 7 checkpoints, a simple arc reads well: setup (arrive), two rising steps, a twist (something goes wrong), the climax, then the portal as the way home. Example: "Enter the temple", "Light the first candle", "Cross the spirit bridge", "The ghost awakes", "Return the bell", then the portal. Place the scenery for each step beside its checkpoint.
cards.use_when: planning 5-7 checkpoints with a story
do: Twist on the second-to-last or third-to-last stop
Climax just before the portal
avoid: All labels at the same emotional level
The climax on checkpoint 1
cards.source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

cards.title: Checkpoint count and spacing follow the room size
cards.text: Small spaces (under 4 x 4 m) use 4 to 5 checkpoints 1.2 to 4 m apart, and a very small room (about 2 x 3 m) only 3 to 4. Medium spaces (4 to 10 m) use 5 to 7, 1.8 to 6 m apart. Large spaces (over 10 m) use up to 10, 2.5 to 9 m apart. The layout checker enforces ranges like these, so plan within them.
cards.use_when: planning the checkpoint count for an MR runner
do: Small: 4-5
Medium: 5-7
Large: up to 10
avoid: 10 checkpoints in a living room
4 checkpoints spread across the Fortal court

cards.title: Put hazards mid-leg, visible from the previous stop
cards.text: Hazards are red circles on the route between stops (about 0.45 m radius in small rooms, 0.6 m medium, 0.8 m large) and must keep a gap from every checkpoint (0.4, 0.7 and 1 m). Place them in the middle of a leg so the player sees one coming after touching a checkpoint and steps around it. Give each a story name like "spirit puddle" or "lava crack".
cards.use_when: placing hazards in a runner layout brief
do: Mid-leg, in view of the last stop
Name each hazard in the story
avoid: Hazards right on top of a checkpoint
Hazards hidden behind a big model

cards.title: Use hazards sparingly for kids, more for gamers
cards.text: A hazard sends the player back to the last checkpoint and costs 25 points, so it doubles a leg. For kids, families and seniors use 0 to 2 hazards on short legs. For teens and gamers use about one per leg on later legs. Avoid hazards right before the portal on long legs: being sent back at the finish feels unfair.
cards.use_when: deciding how many hazards a runner has
do: Kids: 0-2 on short legs
Gamers: about one per later leg
avoid: A hazard on every leg for first-time VR
A hazard just before the portal on the longest leg

cards.title: Set a runner time limit from route length and walking speed
cards.text: The time limit is optional. Estimate the route length and divide by a walking speed: about 0.5 m/s for first-time headset users, kids or seniors, and about 1 m/s for confident players, then add 50 percent for reading labels and stepping around hazards. For young kids and relaxed tours skip the time limit; the finish time bonus already rewards speed.
cards.use_when: deciding game.timeLimit for a runner
do: Compute length / speed x 1.5
No limit for kids and tours
avoid: A tight limit that makes people rush in a headset
A limit without testing the walk

cards.title: Runner online modes: race for rivals, shared floor for togetherness
cards.text: In a race everyone walks their own copy of the Land with a live leaderboard, which suits friends and teens who want to compete. On a shared floor players see each other's avatars, which suits families and groups who want to walk the story together. Pick from the brief's play_mode and feelings: challenge points to race, fellowship to together.
cards.use_when: choosing the online mode for a runner
do: challenge or rivals: race
fellowship or families: shared floor
avoid: Race for young kids with parents
Promising voice chat or teams

cards.title: A race in one room puts real bodies on the same route
cards.text: Every racer walks the same route, so in one real room racers can walk into each other. Keep same-room races to large spaces (over 10 x 10 m) with a few players and staggered starts; or race across turns or different rooms, with the leaderboard comparing them. Under 4 x 4 m, do not race at all.
cards.use_when: a race in MR where several players share one floor
do: Stagger starts by a checkpoint or two
Race across turns in small spaces
avoid: Simultaneous racing in a small or medium room
Promising contact-free racing without a plan
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Void floor is dramatic but dizzying: use it with care
cards.text: The void floor turns the real floor into a bottomless drop with scenery below. It is a strong sensation moment for confident adults indoors, but it can make first-time headset users, kids and seniors freeze or feel unwell. Use it only with a slow walk, no time limit, no race, and say clearly at the start that the floor is solid.
cards.use_when: the brief asks for height, sky islands, space or "wow"
do: Confident adults, indoors, no time limit
Tell players the real floor is solid
avoid: Void for first-time VR, kids or seniors
Void with a race or tight time limit
Void with a spiral route
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Pick the runner lighting preset from the real light
cards.text: Presets are noon, morning, evening, night, spooky, neon, studio and default. Outdoors in daylight use noon or morning, because glow and dark themes wash out. Indoors with steady light, studio or evening keep colours readable. Spooky, neon and night work best in a dark hall or after dark.
cards.use_when: choosing lighting for an MR runner
do: Daylight: noon or morning
Dark hall or night: spooky, neon or night
avoid: Neon or spooky in a sunny garden
A preset name outside the list
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Pick a runner theme the scenery library really covers
cards.text: The runner dresses the route with 1,900+ low-poly models: Thai ghosts and temples, fantasy worlds, dinosaurs, pirates, toys, sci-fi, candy, ice, music, farm and animated rides. Choose a theme the library covers well and say it plainly in the layout brief ("Thai temple at night with lanterns"). Decor can be marked VR only so it is hidden in MR.
cards.use_when: choosing a theme for a runner option
do: Name a library theme in the layout brief
Group scenery into vignettes beside the route
avoid: Themes the library lacks (a real brand, a specific film)
Scenery on the walking line

cards.title: Dress the runner as vignettes beside a clear corridor
cards.text: Players walk the straight lines between stops, and nothing may stand within a 1.2 m corridor plus half the object's size. So scenery is grouped into small scenes beside the route (a dragon nest, a lantern stall), each tied to the checkpoint label next to it. Big pieces go to the edges and corners, small props line the route.
cards.use_when: writing the layout brief for a runner
do: One vignette per checkpoint story beat
Big models at the edges
Arches only with walkThrough
avoid: Models on the walking line
Scenery clustered in one corner

cards.title: Place the portal where spectators can see the finish
cards.text: The finish portal comes after the last checkpoint, and the finish is the moment spectators cheer. Put it on the side where people watch, with the last leg facing them. Keep the spawn clear (about 0.8 m in small rooms, 1.2 m medium, 1.5 m large) so players start without bumping into scenery.
cards.use_when: placing spawn and portal in an MR runner
do: Portal on the spectator side
Clear space around the spawn
avoid: Portal in a far corner nobody can see
Spawn surrounded by props

cards.title: Runner score rules to write into the game card
cards.text: Score is fixed: each checkpoint +100, each hazard step -25, and the finish +300 plus a time bonus. Write the rules from this ("Touch the stones in order", "Red circles send you back", "Reach the portal fast for a bonus") and keep game.rules to 3 to 5 short lines. Do not add stars, coins or combos the engine does not count.
