cards.use_when: writing game.rules for a runner
do: 3-5 short rules matching the real score
Name the story items in the rules
avoid: Invented collectibles or stars
Rules about combat or items

cards.title: Runner has no enemies: turn a chase wish into hazards and a clock
cards.text: When a creator wants monsters chasing players in a walking course, the runner cannot move enemies. Offer the closest real things: hazards named as the monster's traps, a time limit framed as "before the ghost wakes", spooky lighting and still scenery beside the route. If real enemies matter, propose the battle genre as another option.
cards.use_when: the creator asks for chasing enemies, combat or shooting in a runner
do: Hazards as the threat
Time limit as the pursuer
Offer battle as a separate option
avoid: Promising moving monsters on the course
Sudden scares that make people run

cards.title: Runner has no pickups: collecting is checkpoints in order
cards.text: Creators often say "collect 5 gems". The runner has no inventory or free pickups, but checkpoints touched in order can be the collection: label them "Take the red gem", "Take the blue gem", and show the gems as scenery at each stop. Say plainly that they are collected in a set order.
cards.use_when: the brief asks to collect, find or gather items
do: Label checkpoints as the items
Tell the creator the order is fixed
avoid: Promising free-order collection or an inventory
Hidden items with no checkpoint

cards.title: Route the runner around real obstacles in the room
cards.text: In MR the real floor is the play area, so pillars, tables or trees inside it must stay outside the walking route. Plan the route shape around them (a loop around a pillar, a zig-zag between two trees), keep 0.6 m clear of them and of the edge, and never place checkpoints or hazards against them. Mention each obstacle and its position in the layout brief.
cards.use_when: the brief lists obstacles inside an MR space
do: Shape the route around obstacles
Name obstacles in the layout brief
avoid: Checkpoints next to a real pillar
Hiding a real obstacle behind virtual scenery
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Under 3 x 3 m in MR, all three options are runners
cards.text: Battle and tactics need at least 3 x 3 m, so a smaller MR room gets three runner options. Each still has to differ on at least 2 of the 4 axes: vary the route (loop vs out-and-back), the loop type (story vs dodge vs tour) and the social mode. Use 3 to 5 checkpoints, small props, and no race.
cards.use_when: an MR space under 3 m on a side
do: Three runners that differ in route, loop and feeling
Small props only
avoid: A battle or tactics option in a 2 x 3 m room
Three runners that are skins of one idea

cards.title: PC runner: WASD walking, no room limits, same rules
cards.text: On PC the runner is played with WASD, with no real room. Skip venue and size questions and use the large-space ranges freely (up to 10 checkpoints). The void floor carries far less risk on a screen, so it can be the sensation hook here, and race or shared floor work the same online.
cards.use_when: a runner on platform pc
do: Up to 10 checkpoints on longer routes
Void floor as a visual hook
avoid: Asking about room size for PC
Assuming PC adds jumping or combat

cards.title: A calm runner tour for seniors, young kids or relaxing briefs
cards.text: For submission and relaxed feelings, make the runner a guided walk: no hazards or one gentle one, no time limit, morning or studio lighting, wide spacing, and labels that point at beautiful scenery ("Greet the elephants", "Ring the temple bell"). It is often the most comfortable first headset experience.
cards.use_when: the brief mentions relaxing, seniors, toddlers, or first time in a headset
do: 0-1 hazards, no time limit
Labels that point at scenery
avoid: Void floor or spooky lighting
Race mode

cards.title: Give each genre the part of the brief it serves best
cards.text: The 3 options must use 3 different genres, so let each show its strength: battle for sensation, fantasy and action challenge; tactics for thinking, planning and calm competition; runner for story, discovery and relaxed walking. Keep the same world from the brief in all three and change the verb: fight it, outwit it, explore it.
cards.use_when: writing the 3 options for any brief with a space of 3 x 3 m or more (or PC)
do: Same world, three verbs
Lead each pitch with the feeling it serves
avoid: Three options with the same mood
Forcing a genre to do what another does better

cards.title: One brief, three genres: "Thai temple spirits" for a school group
cards.text: Battle: "Guardian of the Temple", forest theme, 4 chapters of spirit grunts and shield-bearers, boss named "The Rain Naga". Tactics: "Temple Steps", 4 boards where the player is a rook, then knight, bishop and queen, taking candles in order past the night watch. Runner: "Lantern Night", a 6-checkpoint loop through Thai temple scenery with labels from "Light the gate lantern" to "Ring the great bell".
cards.use_when: need a worked example of three different-genre options from one brief
do: Same story world in all three
Different route or social axis for each
avoid: Copying this example to an unrelated brief

cards.title: Stretch a genre with story and theme, never with new mechanics
cards.text: What can change freely: titles, chapter and board lines, checkpoint labels, boss name and intro, theme, lighting and scenery. What cannot: the verbs. A battle cannot add shooting, a tactics board cannot add doors or keys that unlock, a runner cannot add enemies. Map each wish to the nearest real feature, say so in the option, and name the gap in risks.
cards.use_when: a brief wishes for something none of the genres does directly
do: Map the wish to a real feature (rain as a meteor storm)
List the gap honestly in risks
avoid: Describing a mechanic the engine lacks
Hiding the gap from the creator

cards.title: Common wishes and the real feature that answers each
cards.text: Shooting or magic: battle sword swings with a fiery theme; monsters to avoid: runner hazards or battle red rings; a treasure hunt or collecting: runner checkpoints or tactics targets, always in a set order. Sneaking: tactics guards and their red squares; things falling from the sky: battle rain. A giant final enemy: the battle boss with a custom name. Racing friends: runner race or the tactics leaderboard.
cards.use_when: translating a creator wish into one of the three genres
do: Answer each wish with a named engine feature
Offer the genre that fits it best
avoid: Saying "not possible" without an alternative

cards.title: Score mr_fit by how each genre uses this floor
cards.text: The same room fits the genres differently. A 3 x 3 m room is fine for a runner loop, tight for battle (about a 2 m fighting area) and poor for tactics (0.5 m squares). A 6 x 8 m hall fits tactics best (1 m squares) and battle well. Over 10 m the runner shines with long routes and races. Let these facts move the scores so the 3 options do not all score the same.
cards.use_when: scoring mr_fit for three options of different genres
do: Write the square size or arena size in scores_why
Use the whole 1-5 scale
avoid: All three options at mr_fit 4
Ignoring that tactics squares shrink in small rooms

cards.title: One game is one genre: do not merge battle, tactics and runner
cards.text: Creators sometimes ask for "a walking course with sword fights, then a chess puzzle". Each genre is its own engine, so one game cannot switch between them. Offer a combination inside one genre (a battle whose chapter lines tell the journey, a runner whose labels pose riddles), or suggest a series of separate games that share one story world.
cards.use_when: the creator asks to combine options of different genres into one game
do: Offer three ways to combine within a genre
Offer a shared-world series
avoid: Promising a hybrid game
Mixing genre fields in one build plan

cards.title: On PC every genre fits, so pick by feeling and player skill
cards.text: With no room limits on PC, all three genres always fit. Battle shines for gamers and action (combo and dash), tactics for puzzle fans and classrooms (click to move, beats down to 1.5 s), runner for story and casual explorers (WASD). Choose the recommended option by the brief feelings and how used to games the players are.
cards.use_when: a PC brief deciding between the three options
do: Recommend battle for action gamers
Recommend tactics for puzzle or school
Recommend runner for story and casual play
avoid: Asking about floor size for PC
Assuming MR limits on PC

cards.title: Knight boards: the jump over tables is the joy
cards.text: A knight moves in an L (two squares one way, one square across) and jumps over tables, guards and targets in between. Board 1 or 2 with a knight and 2 to 4 tables lets players discover that tables do not stop them, which feels like a secret. In MR one knight move is a walk of about 2.2 squares, roughly 1.1 to 2.2 m, so it stays short and safe.
cards.use_when: a board where the player is the knight
do: Give knight boards 2-4 tables so the jump matters
Story line: "Hop over the ..."
avoid: A knight board with no tables or cracks
Telling players the knight can be blocked by tables

cards.title: Bishop boards: diagonal walking and one colour only
cards.text: A bishop slides diagonally and stays on one square colour for the whole board, so half the board is unreachable. Code still places targets it can reach. In MR every diagonal square is about 1.4 times the walk of a straight square, so long bishop slides cross the room on a slant; tell players to look where they will stop before walking.
cards.use_when: a board where the player is the bishop, especially in MR
do: Put the bishop in the middle of the run
Rule: "You can only stand on one colour"
avoid: Bishop as the very first board for newcomers
Long diagonal slides in rooms under 4 x 5 m

cards.title: Rook boards: straight lines that tables cut short
cards.text: A rook slides any distance in a straight line and stops before a table or piece. That is the easiest movement to read, so a rook with 0 to 1 guards and 1 to 2 tables makes a good first board. In MR a full rook slide can be up to 7 squares, so remind players they may stop on any green ring along the line.
cards.use_when: a first or teaching board, or the player is the rook
do: Rook on board 1 for newcomers
1-2 tables so lines are cut short
avoid: A rook board with 4 guards early
Implying the rook must slide all the way

cards.title: Queen boards: many green rings, so the danger is reading
cards.text: The queen combines rook and bishop moves, so the board shows many green rings at once. The challenge moves from "can I get there?" to "which of these squares is safe after the next beat?". Use the queen on the last one or two boards with 3 to 4 guards and 2 to 4 cracks; on PC the beat can drop to about 2 s here.
cards.use_when: the final boards of a tactics run
do: Queen with 3-4 guards
Story line that names the risk ("So do your mistakes")
avoid: Queen on board 1
Queen with 0 guards (no challenge at all)

cards.title: Teach players to check the next-move warning before stepping
cards.text: A player loses a heart by landing on a red (attacked) square, by standing on an attacked square when guards move, or when a guard lands on them. The light orange squares show what will be attacked after the next guard move. So the winning habit is: pick a green ring that is neither red nor light orange, then move. Put this habit into the board 1 story line or a rule.
cards.use_when: writing rules and early board lines for tactics
do: Rule: "Before you step, check the orange squares"
Board 1 with 1 guard so the warning is easy to see
avoid: Rules that only mention red squares
Fast beats before players learn the warning

cards.title: Tactics solo: frame the run as beating your own best time
cards.text: The leaderboard is kept on the device that runs the game and shows the best finished time. At an event this becomes a shared ranking as people take turns on one device; at home it is a personal best to beat. Pitch solo play as a time attack ("beat your best clean run") and do not promise an online or worldwide ranking.
cards.use_when: tactics played alone at home or in a classroom
do: Goal line: "Clear every board as fast as you can"
Mention that each hit adds 5 s
avoid: Promising a global online leaderboard
Promising prizes or unlocks for times

cards.title: Tactics ramp templates for 3, 4 and 6 boards
cards.text: Three boards (MR events): rook 3 targets 1 guard 1 table 0 cracks beat 3.5; knight 3 targets 2 guards 2 tables 1 crack beat 3.5; queen 4 targets 3 guards 1 table 2 cracks beat 3.0, king true. Four boards (PC casual): rook 3/1/2/0 beat 3.0; knight 3/2/2/1 beat 2.8; bishop 4/2/1/2 beat 2.6; queen 4/3/2/3 beat 2.4, king true. Six boards (PC puzzle fans): knight 3/1, bishop 4/2, rook 4/2, knight 5/3, queen 5/3, queen 5/4 with king, beats from 2.8 down to 1.8 and cracks rising 0 to 4. Numbers are targets/guards/tables/cracks.
cards.use_when: need concrete board numbers for a tactics build
do: Adapt the template to the brief, keep board 1 at 2 guards or fewer
Keep MR beats at 3 s or more
avoid: Copying the PC beats into MR

cards.title: Set a board's mood with the ratio of tables to cracks
cards.text: You choose how many tables and cracks a board has, not where they go. Many tables and few cracks make a sheltered, busy room (a cafe, a library) where tables block guard lines. Few tables and many cracks make an open, dangerous field (a frozen lake, a lava floor). Match the ratio to the story line of that board.
cards.use_when: choosing tables and cracks for a board with a strong setting
do: Cafe or library: 3-4 tables, 0-1 cracks
Ice or lava field: 0-1 tables, 3-4 cracks
avoid: Describing exact table or crack positions
A lava story with no cracks

cards.title: Battle chapter templates for 3 and 4 chapters (PC)
cards.text: Three chapters: grunt 3; shield 2 + grunt 2; beast 1 + grunt 3; then the boss. Four chapters: grunt 3; shield 3 + grunt 2; beast 1 + grunt 2; grunt 4 with rain; then the boss. Both stay well under the PC cap of 9 and introduce one new thing per chapter.
cards.use_when: need concrete foes for a short PC battle
do: Rename chapters to fit the story
Keep the order of new things
avoid: Adding a beast to chapter 1
Using these counts in MR without checking the cap of 6

cards.title: Battle chapter templates for 5 and 6 chapters (PC)
cards.text: Five chapters: grunt 3; shield 3 + grunt 2; beast 1 + grunt 2; grunt 4 with rain; shield 2 + grunt 4 + beast 1. Six chapters: grunt 3; shield 3 + grunt 2; beast 1 + grunt 3; grunt 5 with rain; beast 2 + shield 2; shield 3 + grunt 4 + beast 2 (the full 9). Use six only for keen players and 10+ minute sessions.
cards.use_when: need concrete foes for a long PC battle
do: Give the last chapter the biggest mix
Follow the rain chapter with a different threat
avoid: Two rain chapters in a row
More than 9 enemies in a chapter

cards.title: Battle chapter templates for MR (cap of 6)
cards.text: Three chapters: grunt 2; shield 2 + grunt 1; beast 1 + grunt 2. Four chapters: grunt 3; shield 2 + grunt 2; beast 1 + grunt 2; grunt 3 with rain. Five chapters: add shield 2 + grunt 3 + beast 1 as the final mix (exactly 6). For six chapters insert beast 1 + shield 2 + grunt 1 before the final mix, and only in rooms of 5 x 5 m or more.
cards.use_when: need concrete foes for an MR battle
do: Stay at 6 or fewer per chapter
Drop rain for first-time VR or rooms under 4 x 4 m
avoid: PC templates copied into MR
Two beasts in one MR chapter in a small room

cards.title: Name the enemy kinds to fit the theme (the models stay the same)
cards.text: The theme changes the arena colours and light, but enemies keep the same look in every theme: bony warriors with glowing eyes, a shield-bearer, and a big beast. So rename them in chapter titles and lines with names that suit bones. dark: skeleton scouts, the shield wall, the war beast, cursed rain; ice: frost dead, ice-shield knights, the snow beast, hail; lava: ash soldiers, obsidian shields, the magma beast, falling embers. forest: bramble bones, bark shields, the mud boar, acorn storm; desert: tomb guards, sun shields, the sand beast, sandstorm; neon: glitch skeletons, firewall shields, the data beast, code rain.
cards.use_when: writing chapter titles and lines for a chosen battle theme
do: Pick names from the theme row
Keep names that fit a bony warrior look
avoid: Promising enemy models that match the theme (robots, animals, ice golems)
Names that suggest flying or shooting enemies

cards.title: Hazard gate: two circles with a clear gap between them
cards.text: Place two hazards side by side across a leg with a clear gap of at least 1 m between their edges, so the player walks through the middle like a gate. Frame it with a walkThrough arch or two posts beside the route and name it in the story ("the spirit gate"). It suits medium and large spaces; in small rooms one hazard is enough.
cards.use_when: a runner leg that needs a readable, fair challenge
do: Gap of 1 m or more between the hazard edges
Keep the gap from every checkpoint (0.7 m medium, 1 m large)
avoid: A gate narrower than 1 m
Gates in rooms under 4 x 4 m

cards.title: Hazard slalom: alternate circles along one long leg
cards.text: On a leg of about 5 m or more, place 2 or 3 hazards alternately a little left and right of the straight line so the player weaves between them. It reads as a river of stepping stones or a field of lava cracks. Use it once per route, on the longest leg, and only for teens, adults and gamers; it is too fiddly for small kids in a headset.
cards.use_when: a long leg in a medium or large space for skilled players
do: 2-3 hazards, alternating sides
One slalom per route
avoid: Slaloms on short legs or in small rooms
A slalom right before the portal

cards.title: Zig-zag pinch: a hazard on the inside of a turn
cards.text: On a zig-zag route, place one hazard on the inside of a turn, mid-way between two checkpoints, so players who cut the corner step in it and players who walk wide pass. It rewards looking ahead without adding a new rule. Keep the wide path at least 0.6 m from the edge of the area, and use it in medium or large rooms only.
cards.use_when: a zig-zag runner that needs a gentle skill test
do: Hazard on the inside of the turn, not on the checkpoint
Leave the wide line clear of scenery
avoid: A pinch that forces players toward a wall
Pinches at every turn

cards.title: Escalate a ten minute challenge in clear phases
cards.text: For a roughly 10 minute challenge, escalate in three readable phases: baseline from 0:00 to 3:30, about 30% stronger from 3:31 to 7:00, and about 50% stronger from 7:01 to 10:00. Existing units keep the stats they had when summoned, so later upgrades do not retroactively change them, and their level stays visible. The transferable lesson is to make escalation predictable and legible, whether through battle chapters or a runner route that becomes denser with hazards.
cards.use_when: Pacing a long session that needs a rising arc without surprising players with hidden stat changes.
do: Escalate in readable phases rather than continuously
Give each phase a clear milestone and stronger finale
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Make the climax require coordinated preparation
cards.text: Make a spectacular finale something players earn through coordinated movement, not a single button press. In the source, an 80 mana Meteor Shower creates impact zones that a Vanguard must run over to lock the target before a wide area strike and visual transformation. Adapt the reasoning within the engine as a final sequence of ordered checkpoints before the portal, so preparation creates anticipation and the finish feels collectively earned.
cards.use_when: Designing a memorable team finale or final objective that should involve bodies and communication.
do: Require several players or steps to prepare a climax
Place the decisive action in the play space before the payoff
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Balance powerful effects with cost and counterplay
cards.text: Pair powerful tactical effects with meaningful cost, limits, and a chance for opponents to respond. The source prices area turrets at 40 mana, an invisible stunning mine at 20 mana with a 5 second cooldown, and temporary 15 second power boosts at 50 to 60 mana. Hidden area damage plus stun can feel unfair, so in this engine prefer the visible red hazard circles and reserve dramatic moments for clearly signposted checkpoints or the portal finish.
cards.use_when: A creator asks for traps, stuns, or other high impact abilities that could remove player agency.
do: Show dangerous zones before players commit
Reserve strong effects for costly, limited moments
avoid: Invisible unavoidable punishment
Long or frequent surprise stuns
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Use a limited comeback window, not a permanent catch-up buff
cards.text: Trigger a comeback state only when a team is in clear crisis, such as holding under 20% of the field, and end it after recovery above 25%. A strong but bounded example doubles resource regeneration from 5 to 10 per second and permits only 2 activations, giving the losing side one counterattack opportunity without erasing the leader's advantage. Make the state and its remaining uses legible so players know they must plan the counterattack rather than rely on rescue.
cards.use_when: A competitive design needs comeback potential without making an early lead meaningless.
do: Set separate entry and exit thresholds.
Cap the number of comeback activations.
Show when the comeback state ends.
avoid: Leaving the losing team's buff active indefinitely.
Making recovery automatic without player planning.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Build accessibility by removing systems, not only shortening rounds
cards.text: For a fast casual mode, use a fixed 5-minute round with the winner decided only when time expires. Remove carrying, decks, mana management and armor exceptions, then give each role one immediate verb and cooldown-only skills; a frequently usable support action can have a 10-second cooldown. Add automatic pressure at a steady interval, such as every 10 seconds, so play continues even when participants do not coordinate.
cards.use_when: A standard game has too many rules for first-time or mixed-skill players.
do: Use one clear objective per role.
Replace resource economies with visible cooldowns.
Keep the round ending predictable.
avoid: Keeping every subsystem and merely increasing game speed.
Making success depend on a specialist role being present.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Redirect territory-shooter requests to supported contests
cards.text: Do not promise painting territory, guns, instant kills, unit summons or team territory control, because none of these engines supports them. For competition, offer an online runner race on separate copies with a live leaderboard, ordered checkpoints worth 100 each and a finish worth 300 plus a time bonus. For direct action, offer battle chapters using sword combos, dodging and a boss, and treat territory or faction war as theme and story rather than a simulated mechanic.
cards.use_when: The creator asks for a paint war, shooting match, commander units or territorial conquest.
do: Name the unsupported mechanic kindly.
Offer racing for competition or sword battles for action.
Preserve the desired fiction through labels and scenery.
avoid: Promising team painting or shooting.
Describing cosmetic territory theming as actual control mechanics.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Let one moving frontline carry the contest
cards.text: For a tug-of-war contest, have opposing forces seek the nearest rival and stop where they meet, so the clash itself draws a clear border instead of making players read several meters. Reward victories by advancing that border, and maintain free baseline pressure: the source releases 3 soldiers every 15 seconds without Mana. When adapting this to another engine, preserve the single readable struggle and steady rhythm rather than copying unsupported minions.
cards.use_when: Designing a territorial or back-and-forth contest that spectators and players must read instantly.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Use a slow, contested boss to break stalemates
cards.text: Reserve a boss for the middle or late game, and gate it behind visible preparation: a full charge, delivery to a marked summon point, then a Commander resource and skill check. Make the resulting threat slow, highly visible and hard to interrupt so the opposing team has time to respond; in the source, reaching the back line repaints 90% of the field, but killing the boss awards substantial territory instead. The design lesson is a dramatic finale with counterplay and a meaningful reversal, not an automatic win button.
cards.use_when: A match can stall and needs a coordinated climax that both teams can contest.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Make teamwork a short cross-role power window
cards.text: Express synergy as an explicit sequence in which one role creates an opening and another exploits a temporary empowerment, rather than as a passive bonus. The source uses a 10-second window for an enlarged Vanguard to paint trails again and a 15-second window for a Striker's shots to paint the floor directly. Clearly signal activation and expiry, and give the pair an immediate shared target so the short window produces a memorable coordinated push.
cards.use_when: Designing cooperative roles and wanting teamwork to produce visible, timed highlights.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Redirect shooter and territory-control wishes by their desired experience
cards.text: A request for a VR team shooter or territory-control battle often includes rifles, revives, mana cards and floor painting, none of which this engine supports. Say that plainly, then preserve the underlying wish: battle provides sword action, dodging and staged enemies; tactics provides spatial control through ordered captures and guarded squares; an online runner race provides group competition with a live leaderboard. When presenting three options, use these as three genuinely different genres rather than three versions of the unavailable shooter.
cards.use_when: A creator asks for 3v3 combat, gun roles, territory painting, revives or card-triggered team powers.
do: Name the unsupported mechanics before proposing alternatives.
Offer battle for direct action, tactics for spatial control, and an online runner race for group competition.
avoid: Promising rifles, mana cards, minion revives, floor painting, or role-specific abilities.
Presenting three options that are merely variations of one unsupported team-combat brief.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Build combat beats around a visible opening and a quick payoff
cards.text: A setup-and-payoff beat makes action feel cooperative and intentional: one event creates a clearly marked opening, and a quick physical response converts it into a strong result. The source uses a flashing floor marker lasting 2 to 3 seconds, a useful starting window to playtest for notice-and-respond actions. In this engine, recreate the rhythm within supported battle play through warning rings, a short dodge or reposition, then a sword response, rather than adding stuns or role abilities.
cards.use_when: A battle encounter feels like undifferentiated attacking and needs clearer pacing, readability and satisfying decisions.
do: Make the opportunity visible with a floor marker or warning ring.
Playtest whether a new player can notice, move and respond within the window.
Leave a recovery beat before introducing the next threat.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Make cooperation a visible two-step handoff
cards.text: Build team combos so one role creates an opportunity and another completes it, rather than asking everyone to act at once. Here, damage adds a Stun Marker and a floor light tells the Vanguard where to step, while another combo grants 15 seconds of enhanced attacks. Use a conspicuous world-space cue, a clear completion action, and an immediate result so teammates can coordinate without a tutorial.
cards.use_when: Designing cooperative roles, team abilities, or moments that should make spectators understand who helped whom
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Let planning resources recover during deliberation
cards.text: A strategic player should not become helpless while thinking: this economy generates 5 Mana per second up to a 100 cap, reaching full from empty in 20 seconds. Discarding an unwanted card refunds 15 Mana, giving players an emergency conversion from bad options into tempo. Pair steady regeneration with a capped reserve and a costly refund so recovery is possible but still requires a decision.
cards.use_when: Tuning a resource-driven role and checking that players always have a path back into play
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Guarantee a basic action inside a varied hand
cards.text: Keep one inexpensive, dependable card permanently available, redraw it after use with only a 1-second cooldown, and add variety through nine rotation cards drawn four at a time. The example basic unit costs 5 Mana, only one second of passive income, so a bad random hand cannot remove the player's ability to participate. This structure separates reliability from variety and makes each draw easier to read.
cards.use_when: Designing randomized hands, decks, or rotating action choices that must never leave a player stuck
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Express unit jobs through a readable cost ladder
cards.text: Give each unit a distinct tactical job and make its cost communicate commitment: 5 Mana for disposable lane filler, 10 for a fast raider, 20 for a self-destruct attacker, and 30 for a large territory-capturing unit. At 5 Mana per second, those costs imply roughly 1, 2, 4, and 6 seconds of saving, creating an understandable tempo ladder. Also distinguish battlefield consequences, such as whether a destroyed unit paints the floor, so players can predict the strategic effect before spending.
cards.use_when: Balancing several unit or action types whose purpose and opportunity cost should be quickly understood
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Build a five minute battle toward a boss climax
cards.text: For a short action session, use a three-part arc: minutes 0:00 to 2:00 establish the core fight with simple enemies, minutes 2:00 to 4:00 raise pressure and introduce the boss confrontation, and minutes 4:00 to 5:00 become a decisive final rush. Give the ending a clear resolution rather than letting intensity simply stop. In this engine, express the arc through successive battle chapters, enemy mixes such as grunts, shields and beasts, then the boss, with rain reserved for added late pressure.
cards.use_when: Structuring pacing and difficulty for a short battle game or chapter sequence.
do: Teach the core enemy response before adding mixed pressure.
Place the boss after the opening learning phase.
Make the last minute feel decisive and end clearly.
avoid: Starting with the boss before players learn the fight.
Keeping intensity flat across the whole session.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Redirect hero-skill territory control wishes
cards.text: Requests for summoned minions, turret drops, meteor attacks, boss armies, shooting weak points, or painting territory cannot be built by these engines, even when they fit a MOBA fantasy. Offer battle for close action with a sword, dash, telegraphed danger rings, chapters and a boss, or tactics for territorial-feeling play through ordered captures, guard patterns and route planning on a 6 x 8 board. In MR, preserve real walking and safety rather than simulating a battlefield with running players.
cards.use_when: A creator asks for MOBA hero abilities, team territory control, shooting, or summoned armies.
do: Name the unsupported mechanics kindly before proposing an alternative.
Choose battle for direct action or tactics for spatial conquest.
Keep MR encounters walkable with clearly telegraphed hazards.
avoid: Promising turrets, meteors, shooting, armies, or floor-painting systems.
Treating a theme or story as permission to add new mechanics.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Open with a short, spectacular movement burst
cards.text: For a timed area-control game, make the first 3 seconds unusually generous: every crossed row changes colour, creating instant visible progress before normal play begins. A midpoint race can add a capped bonus of 1 to 3 extra rows, scaled by the arrival-time gap, but this rewards an early lead and can snowball. Keep the opening easy to understand and treat the bonus as a dramatic kickoff, not the deciding mechanic.
cards.use_when: Designing the opening and scoring rhythm of a competitive movement game
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Make specialist roles depend on one another
cards.text: A 3v3, 10-minute match can divide expertise across physical area control and blocking, precision ranged play, and planning or unit management. The important pattern is interdependence, not three separate minigames: the commander can only deploy the ultimate boss after the vanguard physically places a summon box. Give the team's biggest moment a visible handoff between roles so every specialist contributes to it.
cards.use_when: A creator wants distinct team roles and cooperative highlight moments
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Translate territory-control wishes into supported competition
cards.text: If a creator asks for 3v3 territory control, ranged shooting, deployable turrets, or summonable units, explain that these mechanics are not available rather than reskinning them as promises. Preserve the underlying wish with a choice: timed tactics boards for planning and ordered captures, battle chapters for direct physical action, or an online runner race with a live leaderboard for group competition. Ask whether strategy, combat fantasy, or head-to-head rivalry matters most before choosing.
cards.use_when: A creator brings a team shooter or territory-control brief to this engine
do: Offer tactics for strategy, battle for action, or an online runner race for rivalry.
Identify the desired experience before selecting the closest genre.
avoid: Do not promise teams capturing floor colour, shooting, turrets, or boss summoning.
Do not describe an online race as shared territorial combat.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Make the boss a costly gamble, not a free power spike
cards.text: Gate a climax behind a substantial resource cost, such as the source's 90 mana, and make a failed skill check consume the attempt rather than merely delay a button press. Give the boss very high durability and very slow movement so its threat is readable, then balance its huge upside with a severe, visible penalty if it dies and make a second summon unlikely. In this engine, keep only the pacing lesson: build a chapter-end boss as a slow, readable, high-stakes finale, without promising mana, summoning, territory painting or stun systems.
cards.use_when: Designing a boss finale or a comeback moment with major risk and reward
do: Telegraph the slow approach so players have time to react
Make both the potential reward and the defeat penalty clear before commitment
avoid: A free boss that only adds power
An instantly repeatable summon after failure
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Converge a climactic clash on one shared objective
cards.text: When two major threats meet, turning their collision into a distinct duel phase concentrates attention instead of splitting it across the whole field. Give everyone the same immediate objective, focus the opposing threat, and use a bounded winner reward such as the source's 20% health recovery while the loser suffers the established defeat penalty. For FortalLand, reuse only the focus and phase-change lesson in a solo boss chapter: briefly change existing boss behavior and give the player one obvious priority using sword hits, dashes, warning rings and available enemies.
cards.use_when: A boss encounter has several threats and the player may not know what matters now
do: Announce the phase change through a clear behavior shift
Keep one dominant objective during the climax
avoid: Competing objectives with equal visual urgency
Promoting a two-boss or unit-control system the engine lacks
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Turn defense into readable vulnerabilities, not invisible math
cards.text: Defense becomes actionable when play can change it: the source uses repeated weak-point critical hits to break armor, after which every friendly damage source benefits, and distinguishes ordinary units from structures. Keep defense classes few and visibly different, and clearly explain any zero-damage result when attack is equal to or below armor. In this engine, express the lesson through existing behaviors, such as a shield blocking frontal hits and a beast telegraphing its charge, rather than adding armor statistics, critical hits, plasma weapons or structures.
cards.use_when: Designing battle enemies whose defense should change how the player approaches them
do: Give each defensive behavior a visible cue and a counter
Show when a successful hit changes the enemy's vulnerability
avoid: Unexplained immunity or zero damage
A hidden stack of armor classes and weapon exceptions
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

cards.title: Translate MOBA territory skills into supported objectives
cards.text: A request for painting team territory, summoning a 5 x 5 cannon turret on a 20-second cooldown, or clearing a 10 x 10 area with a meteor on a 30-second cooldown cannot be built directly. Preserve the intended push-and-defend tension with battle chapters containing grunts, shields and beasts, ending in a boss, or with tactics boards that require ordered target captures while avoiding guards. For a contest over progress rather than combat, use a runner race with ordered checkpoints and a live leaderboard.
cards.use_when: A creator describes MOBA-style territory control, deployable turrets, or large cooldown-based attacks.
do: Ask whether the desired feeling is defending against waves, outcapturing rivals, or escaping danger.
Offer battle chapters and a boss for the wave-defense fantasy.
Offer ordered tactics captures or a checkpoint race for territorial progress.
avoid: Promising team-color painting, turret placement, meteor attacks, or cooldown skills.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground casual mode GDD, example 2 (course material)

cards.title: Telegraph floor hazards before resolving them
cards.text: For a grid-based survival challenge, flash threatened tiles orange for 3 seconds, then turn lava tiles red and safe tiles green so players can read the state at a glance. In the PC proof of concept, a 10 x 20 grid, a circle for the player, WASD movement and 5 HP were enough to test the loop. Awarding 10 points for avoiding lava and subtracting 10 for being hit makes every round immediately legible; tune the warning time before adding visual complexity.
cards.use_when: Designing or prototyping a timed hazard-dodging game where players must move to safety.
do: Use a consistent warning, danger and safe colour sequence.
Test scoring and movement on a simple grid before producing final artwork.
avoid: Changing safe tiles without advance warning.
Adding decoration that obscures the red and green state colours.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal phygital game GDD, example 1 (course material)

cards.title: Prove competitive body-controlled Snake with simple PC inputs
cards.text: A two-player Snake concept can be tested before building its LED-floor controls: mark P1 and P2 standing positions in the simulation, map P1 to WASD and P2 to the arrow keys, and show both snakes on a simulated projector screen. Eating food lengthens a snake, while hitting its own head-to-body path or another player's tail kills it, creating direct competition through shared space. This cheap setup tests whether steering, growth and collision rules are understandable and fun before investing in physical tracking.
cards.use_when: Prototyping a multiplayer game whose final version uses floor positions or body movement as controls.
do: Give each player a separate, familiar input set.
Display both players and their trails in one shared view.
Test collisions between players as well as self-collisions.
avoid: Building physical tracking before validating the core competitive rules.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal phygital game GDD, example 1 (course material)

cards.title: Use a fail-safe casual round for walk-in groups
cards.text: For children, families and mixed-skill friends, teach the rules within 30 seconds and target rounds of 2 to 5 minutes. Adjust difficulty to the group, make fun more important than ranking, and let mistakes cost points rather than end the run. Confirm every success or error with immediate, distinct colour, sound or animation feedback.
cards.use_when: Shaping a relaxed walk-in game for a family venue or mixed-ability group
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal phygital game GDD, example 1 (course material)

cards.title: Split private MR action from public information
cards.text: Keep the player's attention on physical movement, while placing shared goals, time, scores and results on a wall screen that is visible from every angle. Treat the headset view as a private layer that bystanders cannot see, so spectators need public information plus readable player reactions to follow the game. This supports the useful venue pattern of head up for information and feet down for control.
cards.use_when: Planning information and spectator visibility for an MR venue game
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal phygital game GDD, example 1 (course material)

cards.title: Replace territory control with a visible checkpoint race
cards.text: If a creator asks for Territory War, do not promise floor tiles that change team ownership or a percentage-controlled map. Offer the closest supported contest instead: players walk separate copies of a checkpoint course, with a live leaderboard and results on a shared screen. For a gentler group, use the same course as an individual score challenge without forced ranking.
cards.use_when: A creator requests team territory control or tile-painting competition
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal phygital game GDD, example 1 (course material)

cards.title: Escalate pressure by shrinking safe choices
cards.text: Build difficulty across rounds by reducing safe choices rather than only speeding everything up: start with about 4 safe squares, end with 1, and place later objectives farther away. On hard boards, let the safe opportunity shift so players must read and follow the pattern. In this engine, express this through guard coverage, cracked squares and ordered targets in tactics, or tighter hazard spacing between checkpoints in a runner. Never use objective distance to force running in MR.
cards.use_when: Designing a difficulty curve for a spatial course or board
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Design assignment: a phygital game for LED floor and projection

cards.title: Translate HP victory into supported scoring
cards.text: Do not promise HP totals, damage or team elimination: these engines have no general health or combat-result system. Translate 'the side with more HP wins' into supported outcomes: checkpoint +100, hazard -25, finish +300 plus a time bonus, with a leaderboard for races. For MR battle, frame victory as clearing the chapters and defeating the boss rather than comparing team HP.
cards.use_when: A creator asks for health-based team win, loss and tie rules
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Design assignment: a phygital game for LED floor and projection

cards.title: Put live race stakes where spectators can watch
cards.text: A responsive floor arena becomes a group event when a big screen shows scores and time live, letting teams and onlookers follow the contest. For an online runner race, use the live leaderboard and place dodges, the last checkpoint and the portal where spectators can see players' bodies. Spectators should cheer or call hints from outside the route, never enter the play area for a task.
cards.use_when: Designing for friends, parties, school groups or team building with people watching.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

cards.title: Make the party-game goal understandable in seconds
cards.text: The venue's broad-age party zone succeeds with games whose rules are understood within a few seconds, whether played alone or in teams. Give a new Land one immediate goal, a visible next action and instant feedback; ordered checkpoint labels can carry the story without a long briefing. Add depth through route, timing and hazard placement rather than stacking extra rules.
cards.use_when: The creator expects mixed ages, first-time players or quick party rotation.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

cards.title: Build one shared spectacle worth remembering
cards.text: The 360-degree arena surrounds several players with one scene and full-view giant creatures, creating both immersion and a photo-worthy memory. Recreate that design beat with a chapter boss, a large beast or a dramatic final portal that everyone can anticipate and witness together. In MR, frame it against the real room and keep it visible to spectators instead of hiding the climax in a private UI moment.
cards.use_when: A group experience needs a clear climax or a memorable highlight beyond scoring.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

cards.title: Walk-in casual play needs instant goals and soft failure
cards.text: For families and friend groups, target a goal players understand within 30 seconds and rounds lasting 2 to 5 minutes. Let mistakes reduce score rather than end the session, reinforce every action with clear colour, sound and animation, and offer adjustable difficulty across varied bright themes. Keep rankings optional and design the same core activity for solo play or parallel group play so competition never blocks relaxed participation.
cards.use_when: A creator wants a relaxed, accessible venue game for mixed ages or walk-in groups.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Design assignment: a phygital game for LED floor and projection

cards.title: Telegraph danger, then escalate movement demands
cards.text: A readable movement round can use three distinct states: blinking orange warns for 3 to 5 seconds, green marks safety, and red confirms the hazard. Increase difficulty by shrinking the safe area from 4 grid cells toward 1, placing it progressively farther from players, and reserving a moving safe area for the hardest level. This creates a learnable rhythm before demanding faster or more sustained movement, while immediate feedback keeps failure understandable.
cards.use_when: Designing repeated hazard rounds or a difficulty curve around timed movement.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Design assignment: a phygital game for LED floor and projection

cards.title: Size movement and readability to the floor grid
cards.text: The reference play lane is 3 by 6 metres, divided into 10 by 20 cells of 30 by 30 centimetres, with stepping detected and light feedback shown immediately. Use that cell size to judge reachable distances and safe-area capacity, and separate communication by surface: floor colour for actions, a projected wall for prompts and animation, and a monitor for score, time and results. Two identical lanes can support parallel teams without requiring everyone to share one floor.
cards.use_when: Planning a real-floor group game, its information displays, or a two-lane layout.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Design assignment: a phygital game for LED floor and projection

cards.title: Lava Escape contrasts forgiving co-op with team survival
cards.text: In a 90-second single-lane version for 2 to 4 players, each timely safe-zone arrival earns 10 points and standing in lava loses 10, so errors never end play. The dual-lane version instead fields 2 teams of 2 to 4, gives each team 10 HP, subtracts HP according to how many members are caught, and awards the win to the team with more HP after 90 seconds. The comparison shows how the same telegraphed activity can shift from forgiving cooperation to optional rivalry by changing scoring, not by changing its basic rules.
cards.use_when: A creator needs cooperative and competitive variants of one short group activity.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Design assignment: a phygital game for LED floor and projection

cards.title: Play first, then choose a creative track
cards.text: For a one-day school game-design event, let students sample the medium before asking them to create: allow 20 minutes for orientation, safety and grouping, two 40-minute rotations covering four play stations, then a 20-minute scored group finale. After lunch, give students a choice of game creation, AI video or art, with 105 minutes of hands-on work. This sequence builds shared references in the morning and ownership in the afternoon.
cards.use_when: Designing an educational visit, workshop or event that combines playing games with making student work.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

cards.title: End a student workshop with a visible artifact
cards.text: Keep hands-on school groups to about 12 to 15 students so everyone can contribute. Reserve the final 40 minutes for finishing work and preparing presentations, followed by 20 minutes to screen every track's creations, award certificates and take a group photo. Give students a usable file to take back for a school portfolio; the public finale and take-home artifact make the day feel consequential rather than like an isolated demo.
cards.use_when: Planning the group size, final phase and lasting outcome of a school or youth creation workshop.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

cards.title: Short matches benefit from three genuinely different jobs
cards.text: This casual territory-control example uses a 5 minute, 6 player 3v3 match on a 5.5 x 11.7 m LED floor, with victory going to the larger colored area when time expires. Its roles separate bodily area capture, ranged clearing, and resource planning, so players can contribute through exertion, accuracy, or judgment rather than everyone doing the same task. Use this as a role-clarity reference when discussing group play, then express the desired experience through supported battle, tactics, or runner mechanics.
cards.use_when: A creator wants a short physical team contest with complementary player roles.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground casual mode GDD, example 2 (course material)

cards.title: Autonomous pressure keeps play moving without a leader
cards.text: Spawning 5 soldier minions every 10 seconds gives this territory match a baseline contest even if nobody performs the Commander role. The reusable lesson is to keep the core activity moving without constant input from an organizer or strategist, so a hesitant or absent leader cannot stall everyone's fun. In this engine, preserve that principle with self-running battle enemy chapters or an individually playable runner race rather than units players must command.
cards.use_when: A group concept depends on one confident player directing everyone else.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground casual mode GDD, example 2 (course material)

cards.title: Teach party games in ten seconds
cards.text: For casual venue and party play, aim for a goal players can understand in about 10 seconds. Use one immediately readable objective and let the first attempt teach the interaction, rather than front-loading instructions. This keeps the game approachable for newcomers and workable for both solo sessions and group rotations.
cards.use_when: Designing onboarding for a casual MR game with short rounds or rotating players.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

cards.title: Offer privacy for celebrations and teams
cards.text: Birthdays, private parties and company events benefit from a private play room rather than a shared public floor. Plan a hosted session with staff support throughout, so the group can focus on playing together instead of equipment or etiquette problems. Privacy is itself part of the event value, not merely a venue detail.
cards.use_when: A creator is designing for a birthday, private party, company event or established friend group.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

cards.title: Make breaks part of the social session
cards.text: Schedule a comfortable regrouping point between rounds where players can have snacks and drinks while watching friends continue. Treat it as the group's meeting place, not dead time outside the experience. This supports mixed energy levels and keeps nonplaying friends and families involved.
cards.use_when: Planning a multi-round venue session for friends, families, schools or other groups.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

cards.title: Redirect shooting requests to sword combat
cards.text: A creator inspired by outdoor co-op shooter attractions may ask for controller guns, but the engine cannot provide shooting. Say so kindly and offer MR battle instead: the right controller is a sword, enemies approach slowly from the edges, and players step out of red warning rings before chapters culminate in a boss. This preserves action, fantasy and physical dodging without inventing firearms or team assault mechanics.
cards.use_when: The creator asks for an MR shooter, gun combat or a co-op assault inspired by venue shooter games.
do: Offer the battle genre's close-range sword combat and readable dodge warnings.
Keep cooperative team planning as a discussion goal only if the selected online mode supports the session format.
avoid: Do not promise gun controllers, shooting, or team assault mechanics.
Do not copy an outdoor shooting theme into daylight without considering MR visibility.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

cards.title: Keep versus rounds short, symmetric, and easy to rematch
cards.text: For a friendly head-to-head contest, start with a 60 second round so the result arrives quickly and a rematch feels effortless. Give opponents mirrored or otherwise symmetric starting positions and equivalent opportunities, then make the win condition simply who captured or scored more. If the board is mirrored, count each logical scoring cell only once rather than accidentally doubling one side's territory.
cards.use_when: Designing a fast competitive race, score duel, or other repeatable contest for friends
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

cards.title: Translate territory capture wishes into supported competition
cards.text: When a creator asks to move around and capture territory, do not promise persistent cell ownership, territory control, power-ups, or combat because those mechanics are not available. Offer the closest supported fantasy: a tactics board about capturing targets in order while avoiding guards, or a runner race where players take ordered checkpoints and compare scores on a live leaderboard. Preserve the requested fast, friendly rivalry with short rounds and clear scoring rather than copying the unsupported mechanic.
cards.use_when: A creator describes Territory War, Splatoon-like claiming, or another territory-control game
do: Offer ordered target capture in tactics
Offer an ordered-checkpoint runner race with a leaderboard
Keep the competitive round brief and readable
avoid: Promising cells that remain owned or change ownership
Adding power-ups, combat, or remote multiplayer
Treating mirrored cells as extra scoring cells
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

cards.title: Reuse one core challenge across three session formats
cards.text: Offer distinct ways to frame the same challenge rather than inventing separate mechanics: a 30-second time attack compares how much each player achieves, an endless round continues until stamina runs out, and a tournament uses a bracket for 4 to 8 players. Choose time attack for quick turns and spectators, endless for personal endurance, and a bracket when the group wants a clear overall winner.
cards.use_when: A creator wants replayability, a party format, or several game modes around one core activity.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

cards.title: Prove the core loop before adding content
cards.text: Build in dependency order: first prove control input, movement, and the basic scene, then add round structure such as best-of-3 logic and clear win and lose states. Polish sound, visuals, and assets only after the game is playable, and leave power-ups, obstacles, and extra modes for last. This prevents optional variety from hiding a weak or incomplete core loop.
cards.use_when: Planning a prototype or deciding which requested features belong in the first playable version.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

cards.title: Short duel rounds keep party crowds rotating
cards.text: For a booth or party activation, structure a head-to-head contest as best of 3, with two equal 100 m rounds and a deciding third only if needed. First to 2 round wins takes the match, keeping the full session to 2-3 minutes. Equal goals and frequent resets make the result easy to follow, give a losing player a quick comeback chance, and limit spectator waiting.
cards.use_when: Designing a social race for an event, booth, or party with people waiting to play.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

cards.title: Make physical effort visibly drive progress
cards.text: When exertion is the core input, make the relationship immediate: faster movement produces faster progress, while no movement produces none. Set base speed to 0, scale acceleration with a tunable sensitivity multiplier, and smooth the result with lerp so motion stays readable rather than jittery. Keep the fantasy and on-screen progress aligned so both players and spectators can understand why someone is winning.
cards.use_when: Turning a physical action into speed, score, or another continuous race advantage.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

cards.title: Teach the action before a synchronized race start
cards.text: For an instantly learned party game, wait until both players have joined and are ready, then show one animated instruction that demonstrates the core action. Follow it with a visible 3, 2, 1 countdown so neither player gains an accidental start advantage. During play, show both competitors' progress toward the same finish continuously, making the goal and changing lead readable without further explanation.
cards.use_when: Onboarding first-time players into a short competitive game with one main action.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

cards.title: Settle XR mode, venue, players, and locomotion first
cards.text: Before designing mechanics, establish whether the experience is MR passthrough, VR, or MR with a VR fallback; whether the venue is already calibrated, an ordinary room, or a new space requiring a scan; and whether play is solo, co-located, or remote online. In MR, design for physical walking only and never promise joystick locomotion; reserve joystick movement for VR. These decisions determine the layout, multiplayer model, and fallback experience.
cards.use_when: Starting an XR concept whose display mode, venue, or multiplayer arrangement is still unclear.
do: Record display mode, venue readiness, player configuration, and locomotion at intake
Use real walking as the MR movement assumption and joystick movement only for VR
avoid: Deferring venue or player configuration until after mechanics are designed
Adding joystick locomotion to an MR concept
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

cards.title: Pause and require deliberate resume after headset interruption
cards.text: Treat headset removal or opening the system menu as an immediate game pause, since the player may no longer be able to see hazards or other people. Resume only after the headset is visible again and the player gives a fresh, explicit confirmation; require the previous input to be released first so a held button cannot restart play accidentally. This prevents the game from advancing while the player is disoriented or unattended.
cards.use_when: Designing pause and resume behavior for a headset game, especially one with physical walking or timed hazards.
do: Pause immediately when headset visibility is lost
Require a fresh, deliberate confirmation before resuming
avoid: Letting hazards or timers continue while the player cannot see the game
Allowing a held button to resume play automatically
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

cards.title: Turn a territory-control wish into a supported race
cards.text: A request for competitive territory capture cannot be implemented literally because the engine has no tile ownership or direct player conflict. Offer the closest supported contest: an online runner race where everyone walks or controls their own copy, touches 4 to 10 checkpoints in order, avoids hazards, and competes on a live leaderboard. Preserve the brief, party-friendly rivalry with an optional time limit and the standard score of +100 per checkpoint, -25 per hazard, and +300 for finishing plus a time bonus.
cards.use_when: A creator asks for Territory War, area capture, or direct competitive grid control.
do: Use an online runner race with identical courses and a live leaderboard.
Set a time limit and build the contest around ordered checkpoints, hazards, and finishing.
avoid: Do not promise capturable cells, direct invasion, mirror capture, or grid ownership scoring.
Do not describe the shared-floor option as competitive territory control; it only lets players see avatars.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

cards.title: Use a hard-stop one-minute party round
cards.text: For a quick party competition, a fixed 60-second round creates urgency without demanding a long commitment, and is suitable for an audience aged 8+. Keep the timer visible, end exactly at zero instead of inventing overtime, and define the tie result explicitly so the winner announcement is never ambiguous. In a runner design, pair the time limit with a simple published scoring rule so players understand whether to prioritize checkpoints, hazard avoidance, or a fast finish.
cards.use_when: Designing a short local or online competition for casual players, families, or groups.
do: Keep the objective to one sentence and the countdown visible.
State whether equal scores produce a draw before play begins.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

cards.title: Use symmetry to keep short duels fair and legible
cards.text: Symmetric competition makes fairness and relative progress easy to read: mirrored sides provide equivalent routes and starting conditions, while a blocked center initially separates rivals and an open center creates a more aggressive risk-versus-reward variant. If an action duplicates progress elsewhere, count each logical objective only once; the source scores just half its 10 by 6 grid for this reason. For a supported race, use identical course copies and a live leaderboard rather than implementing capture mirroring.
cards.use_when: Structuring a two-player contest or explaining why identical race courses and nonduplicated scoring matter.
do: Give competitors the same layout, start conditions, and scoring opportunities.
Explain any mirroring or duplication rule visually before scoring begins.
avoid: Do not award points twice for mirrored or otherwise duplicated progress.
Do not rely on spectators or players inferring a hidden symmetry rule.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

cards.title: Compose MR around the visible real venue
cards.text: In passthrough MR, treat the real room as the backdrop: do not add a sky, cover the real floor with an opaque virtual floor, apply a full-screen tint, or float objects without a clear physical reason. Let real walls occlude virtual objects so the scene feels grounded, and keep all decorative content switchable as one group when a venue needs an unobstructed view.
cards.use_when: Planning the visual composition and decoration of a passthrough MR game
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

cards.title: Keep MR feedback clear without moving the headset view
cards.text: Never shake or move the XR camera for impact feedback; use controller haptics and brief HUD flashes instead. Keep large flashes and dust effects at opacity 0.6 or below, and fade particles within 0.6 m of the head so they cannot obscure the player's view of real surroundings.
cards.use_when: Choosing impact, hazard, and celebration feedback for a walking MR experience
do: Use haptics and HUD flashes for hits or impacts
Cap large effect opacity at 0.6
Fade particles closer than 0.6 m to the head
avoid: Camera shake in the headset
Effects that hide real walls, people, or obstacles
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

cards.title: Scale MR creatures against real human bodies
cards.text: Build MR scenes at 1:1 scale, with one world unit equal to one metre, and judge sizes against the player's actual body rather than a desktop screen. As a useful upper range, humanoid enemies should be no taller than about 2.1 m and bosses around 2.7 m, preserving drama without making nearby creatures overwhelmingly large.
cards.use_when: Setting character, enemy, and prop dimensions for a room-scale MR game
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

cards.title: Use short race sets with clear comeback stakes
cards.text: For a party race session, a best-of-3 set gives players a concrete comeback arc without requiring a long campaign: announce each round winner and score, then reserve the champion celebration for the final result. A 2-1 finish feels meaningfully different from a single isolated win. In this engine, run the set as three separate races rather than promising built-in rounds, and offer replay immediately after the champion screen.
cards.use_when: Designing a repeatable competitive party session for friends or families
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

cards.title: Separate personal progress from shared race status
cards.text: A head-to-head race is easiest to follow when each player has a distinct personal view, while comparative progress and the match score occupy one consistent shared location. Keep secondary measures such as depth at the side so they do not compete with the main question of who is ahead. On PC this can be left and right views with central progress; in MR, put the shared comparison on a spectator leaderboard because bystanders cannot see the virtual course.
cards.use_when: Prototyping the HUD or spectator presentation for a two-player race
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

cards.title: High-contrast neon versus palette
cards.text: For a cyberpunk competitive prototype, use a dark purple-blue background (#0a0a1a to #16213e), neon red-pink (#ff0055) for Player 1, neon cyan (#00d4ff) for Player 2, gray (#333333) for neutral elements, and neon green (#00ff9f) for UI accents. Pair uppercase, letter-spaced monospace type with restrained motion: 0.5-second screen fades, 1-second timer and player pulses, a 2-second start-button pulse, and a 3-4-second title gradient cycle. In MR, favor this dark neon treatment indoors or after dark so daylight does not wash it out.
cards.use_when: Creating key art, a HUD mockup, or visual identity for a head-to-head neon arena concept.
do: Keep player colors consistent across markers, scores, and previews.
Reserve green for interface accents rather than a third player.
Test neon readability under the actual venue lighting.
avoid: Using glow as the only way to distinguish players.
Assuming dark neon scenes remain readable in bright daylight.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

cards.title: Fast competitive HUD and retry loop
cards.text: Storyboard a short competitive game as start screen, game screen, game over, then play again. The start screen should combine mode selection, player and control previews, a rules summary, and one large start action; during a 60-second round, keep the timer and both live scores above the playfield and control hints below it. End by naming the winner, showing both scores, and offering restart, so a loss leads directly to another attempt.
cards.use_when: Prototyping a timed score contest where players must understand controls and standings at a glance.
do: Show controls before play and keep them available during play.
Place timer and scores outside the main action area.
Make restart the primary game-over action.
avoid: Hiding rules or controls on a separate screen.
Letting animated titles compete with the timer and scores for attention.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

cards.title: Redirect territory-control wishes
cards.text: A creator asking for territory war may mean tile capture on entry, mirrored ownership, and two players sharing one keyboard; do not promise those mechanics. Offer battle chapters with distinct enemies and a boss for direct conflict, or a timed tactics board with ordered target captures and guard avoidance for spatial planning. If the real wish is score rivalry, use a race with a live leaderboard, while retaining red-versus-cyan arena styling as theme rather than unsupported territory mechanics.
cards.use_when: A creator asks for territory capture, local versus control, or a game modeled on this grid arena.
do: Identify whether the wish is combat, spatial planning, or score rivalry.
Map the wish to battle, tactics, or an online race respectively.
Preserve the versus fantasy through color and presentation.
avoid: Promising tile ownership, shared-keyboard multiplayer, or grid-capture rules.
Calling ordered tactics targets territorial control.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

cards.title: Give MR players a real escape window
cards.text: Telegraph area attacks for at least 1.3 seconds because a walking player needs roughly 1 second to move after seeing a signal. Make the warning ring match the damage area exactly, leave empty floor around it for escape, hold new attacks when the player is near a real wall or boundary, and never use knockback or forced movement. Warn about threats from behind with a screen-edge arrow and spatial audio rather than a full-screen tint.
cards.use_when: Designing MR attacks, hazards, or boss patterns that require physical dodging.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

cards.title: Budget XR visuals for the worst combat frame
cards.text: Do not base XR art direction on bloom or other post-processing, and disable shadows unless they are essential. Measure representative content before setting budgets, then test the densest case, such as a boss with all enemies and debris, and ensure no instanced batch overflows. Proven starting references are at most 40 meshes and 6k triangles for a boss, 12 draw calls for effects, and 40 monsters distributed across 8 instanced batches.
cards.use_when: Choosing enemy counts, boss complexity, and effects for a Quest XR battle.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

cards.title: Build a desktop preview for fast design checks
cards.text: Give every XR project a desktop preview with walking, aiming or interaction, a third-person camera, and explicit start and restart controls. Include autoplay for demos and captures, visible fps, draw-call and particle counts, opt-in invulnerability for testing only, and controls that isolate one enemy type or model. These tools make pacing, readability, and worst-case behavior inspectable without putting on a headset for every check.
cards.use_when: Prototyping or debugging an XR game and preparing demonstrations.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

cards.title: A passing build is not a playable game
cards.text: Verify the real play flow from entry through start, actions, damage, HUD updates, turns, and restart while checking performance and errors. Inspect every real-time capture visually, because automated tests can pass while the scene is unattractive, unreadable, or effectively unplayable. Before calling work finished, state plainly which features have not yet been tested in an actual headset.
cards.use_when: Validating a prototype before presenting it as complete to a creator.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

cards.title: Ask one decision-changing question at a time
cards.text: Interview the creator one question at a time, offer answer chips, and briefly explain why each answer matters. Ask when the goal is ambiguous or the answer would change the design; act when confident, stop when the brief is complete, and confirm the brief before designing. This elicits more useful preferences with less creator effort than an open prompt box.
cards.use_when: Starting a vague brief or deciding whether another clarification is worth asking
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Differentiate three options on explicit design axes
cards.text: Offer three genuinely different games, not cosmetic variants, and make their differences explicit on axes such as core play, pacing, social fit, venue demands, and intended feelings. Give each option reasons, risks, four scores, and an AI recommendation, but let the creator choose, modify, or remix. Explicit axes reduce design fixation, while a small structured set avoids choice overload.
cards.use_when: Turning a confirmed brief into design choices without steering the creator toward near-duplicates
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Approve a concrete prototype before building
cards.text: Before building, show key art, a storyboard, the player flow, a palette, and a code-drawn level sketch, then revise from creator comments until approval. Measure time to approval and compare the finished build with the approved prototype. These checks reveal whether the prototype communicates quickly and whether implementation quietly drifts from the agreed design.
cards.use_when: The creator needs to understand and approve the game before implementation
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Turn intended feelings into the evaluation target
cards.text: Record target players, context, session length, and intended feelings using the eight MDA aesthetics, then reuse those feelings as the evaluation target rather than treating them as mood words. Have persona bots walk the level and a judge check it against the brief, followed by a study with people. This tests whether the built game delivers the agreed experience, not merely whether it is valid.
cards.use_when: Checking whether a completed design still fulfills its experiential brief
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Put triangle detail where players see it
cards.text: For real-time XR art, budget about 15,000 to 25,000 triangles for a hero character, 3,000 to 6,000 for ordinary monsters, and under 250,000 for the whole scene. Spend triangles on curved silhouettes and shaded contours rather than flat surfaces, then review front, side, top and back captures before approval. This reserves detail for readable forms instead of invisible surface density.
cards.use_when: Planning or reviewing the visual asset scope for a real-time game
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

cards.title: Prototype beautiful heroes before promising them
cards.text: A reusable low-poly toon kit is a good fit for enemy groups, bosses and scene props, but it is not a safe basis for promising a cute or beautiful game-render-quality lead. When hero beauty matters to the creator, commission or generate a visual prototype first and approve that target before producing the cast. This exposes the fidelity gap early rather than after the production style is locked.
cards.use_when: A creator asks for exceptionally attractive or cute lead characters
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance
