cards.title: Make every strike produce local hit feedback
cards.text: Every object that can be struck should support a visible emissive flash, with independently controllable materials whenever characters must react separately. Shared materials can otherwise make several characters flash as one and blur which target was hit. A brief flash on the struck character gives immediate, local confirmation without adding extra UI.
cards.use_when: Designing readable feedback for melee hits or other strikes
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

cards.title: Hand over headset evidence, not assumed readiness
cards.text: With each headset prototype, provide a link that works on the target device, step-by-step controls, captures from the running build, and fps, draw-call and triangle figures when available. State plainly what has and has not been tested in the headset. A localhost link only works on the host computer, so headset review needs a deployed link.
cards.use_when: Preparing a playable XR prototype for creator review or playtesting
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

cards.title: Echo player mistakes on the spectator display
cards.text: Give spectators a dedicated visual reaction when a player triggers an important event, such as a glass ornament shattering when that player breaks a floor cell. Keep the effect decorative so it cannot alter gameplay, and make it brief and readable: shards can fall for 0.7 seconds and travel 0.6 metres before a fresh ornament appears after 1.5 seconds. Varying the motion and which ornament reacts keeps repeated events lively while preserving the cause-and-effect link.
cards.use_when: Designing a screen or viewing area for people watching a floor or room-scale game
do: Trigger the spectator effect directly from the real gameplay event
Use a short, exaggerated animation that reads from a distance
Reset decorations quickly so later events remain visible
avoid: Letting decorative effects change the game state
Using identical, mechanical motion for every repeated effect
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Use short rounds with explicit breathers
cards.text: For an active group score chase, start from 3 rounds of 60 seconds, an 8 second break between rounds, and a 3 second countdown before play. The breaks create a clear rhythm for checking scores and recovering without ending the session, while the countdown prevents a confusing start. Treat these as playtest defaults rather than fixed rules.
cards.use_when: Structuring session length and pacing for a physically active score-chasing game.
do: Show a countdown before each round.
Use inter-round pauses for recovery and score feedback.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Align reward tiers with rarity and celebrate real pickups
cards.text: Make value readable through a consistent visual ladder: in this design, six common bounties score 1 point, while the rarer most-wanted target scores 5. Bronze marks common rewards, silver the temporarily enlarged reward, and gold the rarest and most valuable. Play the coin-flip celebration only when a player actually collects a reward, not when it expires or is cleared, so the effect confirms player success rather than visual noise.
cards.use_when: Designing collectible value, score readability, and collection feedback.
do: Tie the strongest visual tier to the rarest high-value reward.
Reserve pickup animation for the player-triggered collection path.
avoid: Do not use success animation for expiry or teardown.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Space pickups beyond double their collection reach
cards.text: For position-based collection, keep item centres farther apart than twice the combined grab reach, or one standing position may collect two items. With a combined reach of 0.62 m, the danger threshold is 1.24 m: a 1.2 m minimum gap caused accidental double pickups, while 1.6 m provided reliable separation. Use the same reach-plus-margin calculation whenever spawn spacing is tuned.
cards.use_when: Placing floor collectibles or other proximity-triggered rewards that should be collected individually.
do: Calculate spacing from the combined player and item collection radii.
Add margin above twice that reach.
avoid: Do not set minimum spacing just below the double-collection threshold.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Give every input path the same brief button punch
cards.text: Use one button-feedback pattern whether activation comes from a mouse, LED floor, or another input route. A useful tuning is a 0.15 scale punch over 0.25 seconds with vibrato 6, returning automatically to the original scale so Start, Restart, and Exit remain pressable. If a button also has an idle breathing pulse, suspend and restart that pulse around the punch instead of letting both animations fight over scale.
cards.use_when: Prototyping responsive menus or floor-operated controls that must remain reusable.
do: Route all input methods through equivalent press feedback.
Keep reusable controls visible and pressable after activation.
avoid: Do not let idle and press animations compete for the same scale.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Make tracked movement stable before tying gameplay to it
cards.text: For a floor-positioned MR game, treat live positions as noisy: smooth the signal, ignore movements below about 0.03 m, and start with roughly 0.15 s of smoothing to reduce visible jitter. Reject implausible jumps and poses outside calibrated bounds, hold the last good position during brief signal gaps, then recover gradually rather than teleporting; useful starting limits are a 1 s pose age, 1 m bounds margin, and 2 m snap threshold. Playtest walking, stopping, and tracking loss, since sliding or sudden corrections can make checkpoint and hazard outcomes feel unfair.
cards.use_when: Designing or testing MR gameplay whose checkpoints, hazards, or movement depend on tracked player positions.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Handle tracked player loss without breaking the group
cards.text: Give each of the 2 to 4 players a stable slot and an explicit measured, predicted, or lost state with an input age. When tracking is lost, stop that player's ready state, cursor, answers, and attacks without pausing or reassigning everyone else; on recovery, require fresh input rather than replaying stale actions. Never let bots silently replace real tracking, and reset readiness and session state between rounds.
cards.use_when: Building a multiplayer floor tracked game where players can drop out, reconnect, or remain still between rounds
do: Display tracking loss and recovery clearly to players and operators
Require a fresh ready action after reconnecting or starting a new round
avoid: Refreshing a player's acceptance or readiness from an old frame
Reassigning identities when somebody reconnects
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Make every supported player count a complete game
cards.text: For selectable 2, 3, or 4 player sessions, build menus, playfields, and results from the chosen roster instead of discovering whoever happens to be in the scene. Check that every active player has an independent cursor, score, hit or answer grading, and a way to win or tie, while unused slots stay excluded. Use count dependent layouts and explicit physical progress units, for example two lanes per player in a path game, so adding players does not merely squeeze a two player screen.
cards.use_when: Designing a game with variable group size, shared cursors, competitive scoring, or count dependent layouts
do: Playtest 2, 3, and 4 player sessions independently
Include ties and missing players in results-screen playtests
avoid: Squeezing additional players into a fixed two player layout
Allowing inactive slots to score, answer, or appear in results
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Prove physical tracking separately from gameplay
cards.text: Prototype a tracked floor game with known metre points at the centre and corners, then test dropouts, long stalls, implausible jumps, and one tag disappearing while the others keep moving. Replay the same recorded cases before changing smoothing or jump thresholds, and keep prediction bounded. Mouse or bot play can validate menus and UI, and synthetic geometry can validate mapping, but neither proves real radio tracking accuracy.
cards.use_when: Turning a screen based prototype into a location tracked physical game
do: Keep labelled recorded tracking cases for repeatable playtests
Check both coordinate mapping and real hardware behavior before promising reliable movement
avoid: Treating successful mouse or bot play as validation of physical tracking
Retuning several tracking thresholds without a repeatable comparison
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Use an automatic Ready-to-countdown onboarding beat
cards.text: When players cannot pause with a keyboard, let the start press open a short Ready hold, then begin the 3-2-1 countdown automatically rather than chaining straight into play. Keep every in-round instruction, including Ready and prompts such as Walk, in one consistent headline position, and reveal hidden solution information only when the Memorize phase actually starts. This gives players a predictable moment to orient themselves without letting them study the answer early.
cards.use_when: Designing the start and memorize phases of a movement or memory game with limited input
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Finish outcome effects before the judging beat ends
cards.text: Budget the complete failure or success animation inside the state that displays it: in this project, all crack and shard runtime had to stay comfortably below the 1.3 second judging window. Do not merely start an effect at judgment and advance the state machine on a fixed timer, or the transition will cut it off. Treat the judging duration as an audiovisual budget and shorten or simplify effects when necessary.
cards.use_when: Timing breakage, scoring, or other outcome effects between rounds
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Separate player identity, game state, and surface decoration
cards.text: Give each player a hollow ring with a solid inner circle, and reuse that player's inner-circle color in their progress display so identity remains consistent across the HUD. On grid cells, place beveled borders and gloss beneath a live gameplay tint for hidden, safe, breaking, broken, or wrong states. Decoration can make surfaces feel like glass, but the state color must remain the top readability layer.
cards.use_when: Building readable player cursors and state-heavy floor or board cells
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Keep MR sword combat grounded and visually clear
cards.text: For an MR battle, make the right controller the sword: a fast swing attacks, real steps dodge red danger rings, and the trigger restarts after a run. Place the arena beneath the player's feet and align it with their initial view so the goal is immediately understandable. Hide tall decorative objects such as pillars and thrones in MR, leaving the floor and enemies readable against passthrough surroundings.
cards.use_when: Designing the interaction and arena presentation for a Quest 3 passthrough battle game.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC battle engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Escalate a battle boss without losing dodge readability
cards.text: Give the boss a clear targeted ground slam, then intensify the same pattern below half health by adding 3 extra warning rings and summoning weak grunts. This creates a readable second phase: the player already understands the main threat, while added rings test positioning and grunts divide attention. Keep the new pressure telegraphed rather than introducing an unrelated surprise attack.
cards.use_when: Designing or tuning a PC battle boss and its chapter climax
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC battle engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Make battle defense readable on the ground
cards.text: Build PC sword combat around a 3-hit combo whose third strike deals double damage, plus a dash on Space or right click that evades attacks. Telegraph danger with red circles on the floor, and treat the circle's flash as the deadline: players must leave before it flashes. Introduce these two verbs in a low-pressure opening so later difficulty tests timing and positioning rather than control discovery.
cards.use_when: Designing controls, telegraphs, or onboarding for a PC battle game.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC battle engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Escalate chapters before the boss
cards.text: Give each battle chapter a title, one story line, and a bounded enemy wave, with at most 6 enemies of each kind per chapter. Escalate by changing the mix of fast grunts, front-blocking shields, and charging beasts rather than only adding bodies. Use rain as an optional pressure layer of continuously falling red warning rings, then end with the boss chapter, which the engine adds automatically as "Face <boss name>".
cards.use_when: Planning the pacing and encounter sequence of a chapter-based battle.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC battle engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Anchor MR sword combat to the body and real floor
cards.text: Treat MR battle as a room-scale, embodied encounter: the player's head position is the hero, and the right controller is the sword. Size the arena in metres for the available MR floor instead of reusing a PC arena, then arrange enemies and dodge room around that physical space. Quest 3 passthrough with a local-floor reference keeps combat anchored to the real surroundings.
cards.use_when: Designing an MR battle layout or translating a PC sword-fighting concept to a headset.
do: Map the hero to head position and the sword to the right controller.
Configure the arena from the real floor dimensions in metres.
Leave physical room for movement and dodging.
avoid: Assuming the larger PC battle arena will fit an MR room.
Adding joystick locomotion or a disembodied weapon scheme.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC battle engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Make enemy roles readable through behavior and telegraphs
cards.text: Build each enemy around a clear loop of entering, chasing, winding up, striking, and causing knockback, with a hit flash confirming successful attacks. Give large foes a visible wind-up ring before they swing, and reserve abrupt bursts for special roles such as a beast charging at 3.4 times its normal speed. Separate hp, speed, body radius, attack reach, wind-up time, damage, score, and size so roles can be tuned without changing their basic behavior.
cards.use_when: Designing or tuning a PC sword-combat encounter with several enemy types
do: Telegraph heavy attacks with a ground ring and a wind-up interval.
Tune movement, reach, durability, and damage independently for each role.
Use hit flashes and knockback to make attack outcomes immediate.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC battle engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Pair combat stats with distinct silhouettes and independent flash materials
cards.text: Give enemy kinds immediately different silhouettes, such as a humanoid skeleton, a front-facing shield-bearer, a broad four-legged beast, and a crowned boss. Size and posture should communicate threat before the player reads the HUD, while each model needs its own materials so a hit flash affects that enemy without changing the others. Treat visual identity and combat stats as one role-definition pass rather than decorating enemies after tuning.
cards.use_when: Turning abstract enemy statistics into a readable battle roster
do: Differentiate body shape, facing defense, posture, and headgear by role.
Test recognition at normal play distance before refining detail.
Keep materials independent per enemy for localized damage feedback.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC battle engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Start desktop melee movement at 5.2 metres per second
cards.text: For a third-person desktop sword game, 5.2 m/s is a concrete starting run speed for WASD movement with mouse aim. Keep swing, combo window, dash, dash cooldown, invulnerability, and general cooldown as separate timers so responsiveness and punishment can be adjusted independently. Playtest whether players can reposition during enemy wind-ups before increasing enemy speed or damage.
cards.use_when: Establishing initial movement and defensive timing for a PC melee prototype
do: Begin run-speed tuning at 5.2 m/s, then test against attack telegraphs.
Separate dash, invulnerability, combo, and swing timers.
Check that dodging and attacking remain legible under mouse aim.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC battle engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Give battle states distinct HUD homes
cards.text: Separate persistent status from event feedback: health pips, score and clock stay visible, while chapter title and progress steps explain the current objective. Reserve the boss bar for the boss, a centre message for major prompts, and a hurt flash for damage; use start and end cards to frame play rather than crowding the arena.
cards.use_when: Designing the HUD and feedback for a chapter-based PC battle game.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC battle engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Fill warning rings before area strikes
cards.text: Telegraph every area attack with a red floor circle that visibly fills before striking everything inside, so the fill is the player's dodge timer. Reuse the same readable language for cursed rain chapters, where multiple warning rings fall from the sky, and clear the rings when the encounter resets.
cards.use_when: Designing dodgeable battle attacks or a rain chapter on PC.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC battle engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Use chapter rewards to sustain battle tempo
cards.text: Start battle scoring at 10 points per hit, with enemy kill values defined per enemy kind, then award 200 points and heal 2 health on each chapter clear. At victory, add bonuses for time left and remaining health at 100 points per health point; this makes clean play and efficient clears matter without requiring an inventory or upgrade system.
cards.use_when: Tuning scoring, recovery and replay motivation for a PC battle run.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC battle engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Spawn enemies away from the player with a grow-in
cards.text: Place ordinary enemies on an elliptical ring about 7 metres across in X and 5 metres in Z, away from the player, and place the king at the throne end for a deliberate boss entrance. A grow-in burst makes a new arrival legible before contact; small coloured tetrahedra with gravity, floor bounces and fading can also punctuate hits without persistent visual clutter.
cards.use_when: Staging enemy entrances and lightweight impact effects in the PC battle arena.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC battle engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Tune tactics boards with small, legible budgets
cards.text: Choose the player's movement identity first: knight, bishop, rook, or queen. A useful board budget is 2 to 6 ordered targets, 0 to 4 patrolling guards, 0 to 4 blocking tables, and 0 to 4 damaging cracked squares, with enemy movement every 1.5 to 3.5 seconds. Raise difficulty through route planning and patrol timing rather than filling every budget at once.
cards.use_when: Defining or balancing a sequence of chess-movement tactics boards.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Prove ordered routes and a safe opening
cards.text: Validate each board using the actual movement rules of its piece, checking that the player can reach target 1, then 2, and so on without crossing tables, cracks, or later targets. Also verify that no guard attacks the starting square at time zero, and reject or regenerate layouts that fail either check. Hand-authored layouts need the same solvability test as generated ones.
cards.use_when: Building fixed or generated tactics puzzles with ordered objectives and moving threats.
do: Test the complete ordered route, not just individual target reachability.
Reject layouts whose start is already attacked.
avoid: Assuming a plausible-looking layout is solvable.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Show present danger and the next beat separately
cards.text: Use two distinct danger states: red for squares a guard can capture now, and light orange for squares that will become capturable after its next move. This lets players plan around a moving threat instead of treating every warning as identical. In this ruleset, capture costs a heart, adds 5 seconds, and returns the player to the start, while losing all hearts ends the round.
cards.use_when: Designing readable turn-timing feedback and consequences for patrolling enemies.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Fit MR chess movement to real walking speed
cards.text: Lay the board on the real floor with squares between 0.5 and 1 m wide; a 6 by 8 m area gives 1 m squares for the default 6 by 8 board. Confirm a move only after the player stands on a legal square for about 0.35 seconds, preventing accidental moves while passing through. In MR, keep enemy moves at least 3 seconds apart so players have time to read threats and physically relocate.
cards.use_when: Adapting a screen-based tactics board to full-body movement in MR.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Prove every tactics board is solvable and fairly started
cards.text: Generate a tactics layout from its piece, targets, guards, tables, cracks and guard beat, then validate it with real chess movement: tables block entry, while live targets, enemies and the player stop sliding moves. Use a search to prove the player can travel from the start through every target in the required order without entering tables, cracks or later targets. Retry generation until that proof succeeds, and separately reject any board where a guard on the first square of its patrol attacks the start square.
cards.use_when: Designing or generating an ordered-capture tactics puzzle with moving guards.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Fit the chessboard to the real floor
cards.text: Size an MR tactics board in real metres, with each square between 0.5 and 1 m. The baseline is 6 columns by 8 rows; a 6 x 8 m play area therefore gives 1 m squares. Derive square size from the measured floor so every destination remains physically reachable.
cards.use_when: Laying out a walkable MR tactics board for a known play area.
do: Measure the real play depth before choosing square size.
Fit the 6-column by 8-row board using squares between 0.5 and 1 m.
avoid: Do not assume the default 6 x 8 m area is available.
Do not treat board scale as independent of the real floor.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Preview moves with clickable destination rings
cards.text: On PC, separate board inspection from movement: left-click a green ring to move, right-drag to orbit, and use the mouse wheel to zoom. Visible destination rings make legal moves readable before commitment, while distinct inputs prevent camera adjustments from causing accidental moves.
cards.use_when: Designing mouse controls and movement feedback for a PC grid tactics game.
do: Show legal destinations as green rings.
Keep movement, orbit and zoom on distinct mouse inputs.
avoid: Do not make camera orbiting or zooming trigger a move.
Do not leave players guessing which destinations are legal.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Build tactics around ordered captures and safe squares
cards.text: In a tactics board, the player embodies one chess piece and must follow its real movement rules, capture numbered targets in order, and never finish on a square attacked by a guard. Design up to 6 boards as a progression by changing the piece, target and guard counts, tables, cracked squares, and enemy beat; an example rook board uses 4 targets, 2 guards, 2 tables, 3 cracks, and a 2.4 second beat. Give each board a short story line that reinforces its movement lesson.
cards.use_when: Specifying or pacing chess-based tactics boards
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Prove generated puzzle boards are solvable
cards.text: Separate puzzle authorship from layout generation: the designer supplies the story and a compact board spec, while seeded generation places the actual pieces and obstacles. Validate every generated board with breadth-first search over legal movement, ordered captures, and attacked squares, and regenerate or reject any layout without a solution. This preserves variety without shipping an impossible challenge or relying on manual inspection.
cards.use_when: Creating procedural or AI-specified puzzle layouts
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Match each intro rule to its board colour
cards.text: Put one concise rule per line on the start card, and give its bullet the same colour used by the corresponding board explanation or marker. Keep the established order: green, orange, red, light orange, then brown. This lets players connect instructions to the board before moving, instead of decoding several unrelated symbols at once.
cards.use_when: Writing the tactics start card and visual rule legend
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Keep a PC tactics camera inspectable and the moves explicit
cards.text: For a PC board-game view, orbit the camera around the player piece, with a slow menu spin to reveal the 3D layout; let players right-drag to orbit and use the wheel to zoom. Left-clicking visible move rings keeps legal movement unambiguous, while a brief hit shake can add impact. Disable orbit and shake in MR, where the player's head controls the view.
cards.use_when: Designing camera, inspection controls, and move feedback for a PC tactics board game.
do: Anchor the orbit on the current player piece.
Show legal destinations as clickable rings.
Reserve drag and wheel input for orbit and zoom.
Use head-tracked viewing without camera shake in MR.
avoid: Making players guess which squares are legal moves.
Applying screen shake or automatic orbit to an MR headset view.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Stagger waves and leave recovery beats
cards.text: Structure a battle run as chapters followed by a final boss chapter, spawning each wave instead of releasing every enemy at once. Start with about 0.7 seconds before the first foe, stagger arrivals by 0.45 seconds, allow roughly 2.2 seconds between beats, and cap each enemy kind at 6 per chapter. This gives players time to read threats and recover while preserving escalation.
cards.use_when: Tuning the pacing and intensity of a chapter-based sword battle.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC battle engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Make frontal defense create movement decisions
cards.text: Build the PC sword attack as a readable 3-hit combo in a front cone, extending 70 degrees from center on each side for 140 degrees total. Shield enemies block frontal hits, so their defense creates a clear flank-or-reposition problem, while dash invulnerability frames provide a defensive timing tool. Give hits, blocks and dashes immediate visual feedback so players can learn the combat rhythm.
cards.use_when: Designing readable sword combat and enemy-specific counterplay on PC.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC battle engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Frame a battle floor with strong landmarks
cards.text: For a ruined-keep battle arena, combine a tiled combat floor with pillars, torches and banners around it, a throne as a distant focal landmark, and light ember effects for ambient motion. In MR, rebuild the floor tiles when the play area changes size. Keep decoration from obscuring enemies, attack openings or warning rings so atmosphere does not reduce combat readability.
cards.use_when: Composing a fantasy battle arena that must remain readable during play.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC battle engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Theme the whole lighting stack together
cards.text: Define each battle theme as a coordinated palette across background and fog, floor tile hue, torch light and sky light, rather than recoloring only decorative props. Changing these layers together keeps the arena visually coherent and preserves silhouettes. In MR, test dark, spooky or neon looks indoors or after dark because bright daylight washes out dark scenes and glow.
cards.use_when: Choosing visual themes and lighting for a battle arena.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC battle engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Use ambient onlookers to reward captures
cards.text: Add simple seated onlookers around a puzzle or tactics board who watch the player, gasp when approached, and cheer when a target is captured. These proximity and success reactions make a quiet planning game feel socially alive and confirm important moments without NPC conversations or extra mechanics. Keep them brief and ambient so they never obscure guard movement or board readability.
cards.use_when: A tactics game needs lively feedback and a sense of audience without adding dialogue or combat systems.
do: Have seated onlookers watch the player
Gasp when the player comes close and cheer on captures
Keep reactions secondary to board-state feedback
avoid: Adding conversations or tasks for the onlookers
Making ambient reactions compete with guard and target readability
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Make capture order and recovery readable
cards.text: For a tactics game with ordered captures, let every target sway gently but pulse only the next required target, so the sequence is visible without extra instructions. After a hit, blink the player piece throughout invulnerability to communicate both damage and temporary safety. Mark each successful capture with a brief confetti burst, about 1.2 seconds, so the reward registers without delaying the next decision.
cards.use_when: Designing moment-to-moment feedback for an ordered capture or avoidance board.
do: Pulse only the next target
Blink the piece during invulnerability
Keep capture celebration brief
avoid: Animating every target with equal emphasis
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Adapt board spectacle to the display
cards.text: On PC, frame a floor board with a hall, windows and a cheering crowd to give the match a sense of occasion, and add file letters along the board edge for orientation. In MR, hide room-scale scenery and retain the floor-level board, pieces and gameplay props so virtual walls do not conflict with the real room. Treat the crowd as presentation rather than another source of essential gameplay information.
cards.use_when: Adapting one tactics board between a computer screen and a passthrough headset.
do: Keep board coordinates visible at the rim
Remove virtual room-scale scenery in MR
Use crowd animation as nonessential atmosphere
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Telegraph danger and legal moves directly on the board
cards.text: Tint squares attacked now red and squares attacked next orange, and draw a ring on every legal destination. This separates immediate danger from the next guard beat and lets players plan without memorising invisible attack rules. Keep the board title, ordered targets and beat indicator visible so the overlay supports the current objective.
cards.use_when: Designing guard timing, movement choices or board readability for a tactics game.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Rank progress before speed and make hits cost time
cards.text: Sort the local leaderboard by boards cleared first, then completion time, so a slower player who finishes outranks a fast player who quits early. On a win, add a 5 second penalty per hit and report both the hit count and final time; on a loss, report the board reached. Keep separate lists for each rift, preview or demo so scores remain comparable.
cards.use_when: Tuning scoring, failure feedback or replay motivation for a multi-board tactics run.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Give each chess piece a distinct movement silhouette
cards.text: Animate movement as an eased hop from square to square rather than an instant teleport, using an arc around 1.6 for knights and 0.5 for other pieces. The higher knight jump makes its special movement legible while the landing clearly commits the move and resolves targets, cracks, attacks and heart loss. Preserve this readable landing moment even when the board theme changes.
cards.use_when: Choosing movement feedback that helps players understand piece rules and consequences.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Split tactics HUD into planning, urgency and run status
cards.text: Use the start card for the story and rules, then keep board title, target order and hearts persistently visible during play. Reserve large centre messages for important events, and give the guard beat and clock their own indicators so timing pressure does not obscure planning information. This hierarchy lets a new player learn the objective before the run while still reading state at a glance.
cards.use_when: Laying out onboarding and the in-game HUD for a timed, multi-board tactics game.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Give walking tactics a readable beat
cards.text: When movement means physically walking onto a square, keep the interval between enemy moves at least 3 seconds so players can read threats, move and reorient. Show the time until the next enemy step in seconds, and use that shared beat to pace planning rather than demanding rapid input.
cards.use_when: Tuning guard patrols and turn timing for an MR tactics board.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Make tactical danger queryable at a glance
cards.text: Base the player-facing board display on three live queries: which squares enemies attack now, where each enemy steps next, and which player moves are legal. Keep blocking rules consistent, including tables, guards and out-of-order targets, and make a live target stop a slide so the visible outcome matches the rules.
cards.use_when: Designing previews, highlights and move feedback for a grid tactics game.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Do not rely on a screen HUD in MR
cards.text: A DOM or screen-overlay HUD is invisible inside the headset, so put essential tactics information on an in-world canvas panel floating low in front of the player. Prioritise the current objective and enemy-move countdown, and avoid making players look far away from the floor board they are walking on.
cards.use_when: Prototyping objective and timer feedback for an MR board game.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC tactics engine (Vite + three.js template)

cards.title: Ask what surrounds the MR floor and who is watching
cards.text: After learning the clear floor size, ask a tap-to-select question about furniture along the walls, obstacles in the middle, windows or glass doors, and spectators. Treat visible edge furniture as possible story scenery, such as a nest border or mountain, while keeping the walking route clear of real obstacles. Knowing who watches also helps place discoveries and finish moments where they can share them; small homes may offer only 2 x 3 m rather than the 4.5 x 5 m initially expected.
cards.use_when: Scoping a room-scale MR game after the creator gives its dimensions
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: A young first-time VR player sets the whole pace
cards.text: Ask the child's age and VR experience early, then ask for up to three desired feelings to decide whether to emphasize discovery, fantasy, story, teamwork, wonder, or relaxation. For a first-time 6-year-old, use simple checkpoint labels, a shorter route, gentle hazards or none, no scares or startling moments, and no fast walking, running, or stressful time pressure. A calm five-minute shared adventure can fit bedtime better than a longer challenge.
cards.use_when: Designing for a young child, VR newcomer, or calming play session
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Confirm a concrete play brief before offering genres
cards.text: Before proposing options, restate the players, child's experience, room dimensions, shared mood, desired feelings, safety constraints, session length, and spectator arrangement in one short paragraph. Mark unprovided choices as defaults, such as a roughly 10-minute evening session with no extra spectators, so the creator can correct them. Do not let an early default erase later facts like a five-minute limit or Grandma watching from the sofa.
cards.use_when: Turning interview answers into a brief and preparing three options
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Ask who plays before shaping a party game
cards.text: For a vague multiplayer party request, establish the audience and simultaneous group size before choosing the layout. Families with young children need different difficulty and chaos from teen or adult groups, and 3–5 bodies sharing a real floor also changes collision risk. Use the answer to temper competitive pressure, visual busyness, and how much simultaneous movement the design asks for.
cards.use_when: A creator asks for a chaotic or multiplayer party game without specifying players
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Use desired feelings to choose the design direction
cards.text: Once the audience is known, ask for the top 1–3 target feelings rather than treating all party or adventure games alike. Fellowship points toward shared activity and laughter, challenge toward light competition, discovery toward exploration and surprises, and submission toward relaxed low-thinking play. For a first-time young player, discovery can become a calm treasure hunt while narrative can turn the same route into a story-driven quest.
cards.use_when: A brief has a theme or activity but no clear experience goal
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Measure the real floor and locate obstacles
cards.text: In MR, ask early for clear-floor dimensions and whether furniture sits in the middle or only around the edges; accept metres or paces, using 1 pace ≈ 0.75 m. Floor size and obstacles determine route shape, checkpoint or hiding-spot count, and safe walking lines. For a gentle home game, preserve a 1.2 m clear route, keep content off real furniture, and maintain a 0.6 m margin from area edges.
cards.use_when: Scoping an MR game for a living room or another creator-supplied space
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Make each checkpoint a bedtime story page
cards.text: A parent and VR-new six-year-old wanted discovery and a cozy narrative in a 4.5 × 5 m living room, with a 10-minute session. The design made each checkpoint a page in a baby-dragon bedtime tale, progressing from an empty shell to tucking the dragons in, so story labels supplied the narrative without adding unsupported mechanics. Gentle constraints were explicit: no scares, void floor, running prompts, or objects on furniture, plus a 1.2 m route and 0.6 m edge margin.
cards.use_when: Designing a short, gentle story adventure for a young first-time VR player and caregiver
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Turn a vague setting wish into concrete theme choices
cards.text: When a creator gives only a setting, such as wanting to play by the sea, respond with a small set of contrasting fantasies such as pirate treasure, an underwater world, animal rescue or a relaxed beach walk. The chosen theme becomes the anchor for the story, scenery and route, so settle it before detailed layout questions.
cards.use_when: The creator names a place or mood but has not chosen what players do or imagine themselves to be.
do: Offer 4 or 5 contrasting themes
Use the chosen theme to guide story, scenery and route
avoid: Asking for route or scoring details before the fantasy is clear
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Let audience and desired feelings set family-game pacing
cards.text: Ask who will play, including age, simultaneous group size and VR experience, then ask for up to three desired feelings before tuning the route. For children under 8 or ages 3 to 7 playing with parents and new to VR, sensation and fantasy usually call for a calm, beautiful shared walk with gentle hazards and no sudden scares; about 8 minutes is a useful default round. Group size affects required floor space, while first-time headset use calls for simpler controls and a shorter walk.
cards.use_when: Designing an MR experience for young children, parents or first-time headset users.
do: Ask age, group size and VR experience
Let young first-time players set a calm pace
Cap feeling choices at three
avoid: Treating all family games as challenge races
Adding scares to a sensation-led first VR experience
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Confirm the venue before promising glow-heavy MR visuals
cards.text: If the creator and editor disagree about the venue, confirm the actual location before developing the visual concept. Strong outdoor noon sun washes out glow, sparkle and dark scenes, while an enclosed indoor venue with stable light supports night, neon and ghostly effects; outdoors, morning or golden evening light is a better fit for beautiful scenery. Treat this as a design decision, not merely a lighting preset.
cards.use_when: The venue is contradictory or the concept depends on night scenes, glow, sparkle or a dark atmosphere.
do: Resolve venue conflicts explicitly
Match glow-heavy art to controlled lighting
Use morning or evening light outdoors
avoid: Promising strong glow for a sunny rooftop
Leaving contradictory venue selections unresolved
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Make a child's first MR adventure gentle and shared
cards.text: For a 6-year-old's first MR session, frame the floor as a cosy make-believe space and plan a gentle 10-minute adventure with no scares, simple discovery goals, and an adult playing alongside. In a clear 4.5 x 5 m living room, keep furniture such as the sofa and TV along the walls, leave the middle free of trip hazards, and use an easy walking pace. Safety and shared wonder matter more than challenge or score pressure.
cards.use_when: Designing a first-time MR experience for a young child and parent in a small home space
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Turn a checkpoint race into a story battle
cards.text: A walking engine can deliver combat fantasy without combat mechanics: label each checkpoint as a sword strike or defeated beast, make each hazard an enemy blow that knocks the player back, and end with the final blow. For 2-6 experienced adult friends in a 5-minute race, give everyone their own copy of a compact 5 x 7 m course and let the fastest finisher win. Keep decisive moments visible to friends watching from the doorway, and vary the fiction across fortress, siege, or monster themes without changing the rules.
cards.use_when: A creator wants an action or boss-fight fantasy but the available game only supports ordered checkpoints, hazards, and racing
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Use clear times to make solo chess tactics social
cards.text: For a PC chess-piece adventure, use the 6 x 8 board, ordered captures, and guards sweeping attacked squares on a beat as a short solo time trial. A 5-minute clear works for 2-6 teens and adults taking turns, including players with mixed experience, while the fastest time gives friends a concrete score to chase. Make the current target and threatened squares readable on the shared screen so spectators can follow and cheer without needing to play.
cards.use_when: Designing a short turn-taking tactics challenge for friends around one PC screen
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Ask age, group size and VR experience first
cards.text: Before proposing game options, establish the players' ages, how many play together and whether they have used VR. These answers determine route length, stage difficulty, suitable excitement and where an attendant may need to help: ages 4–7 need short, friendly routes, while ages 8–12 can accept more challenge. Give concrete choices such as solo, 2–3 friends or siblings, 4–6 with mixed experience, and first-time versus experienced VR users.
cards.use_when: Starting an MR design with only a theme or adventure concept
do: Offer concrete age, group-size and experience choices
Use the answers to tune route length, difficulty, excitement and supervision
avoid: Proposing options before establishing the audience
Assuming older children and VR newcomers want the same difficulty
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Turn target feelings into the option filter
cards.text: Once the audience is clear, ask which one to three feelings matter most, using concrete options such as wonder, role-play, story, challenge, cooperation, discovery or relaxation. Treat the chosen feelings as the filter for pacing, stages and atmosphere before generating game options. Children new to VR often benefit more from wonder and story than from difficulty, so do not automatically make challenge the core.
cards.use_when: Choosing among possible game directions after the player audience is known
do: Ask for one to three target feelings
Translate the chosen feelings into pacing, stages and atmosphere
Favor wonder, role-play and story over difficulty for VR newcomers
avoid: Defaulting to skill challenge for first-time VR players
Letting a long feature wish list replace an emotional target

cards.title: Make a spooky family walk cute and hand-holdable
cards.text: An 8-minute ghost-market walk for one family per round shows how to make a night theme gentle for children aged 3–7 with no VR experience. For 1–2 adults and 1–3 children, use cute ghosts, no frightening imagery or jump sounds, no running, no void floor and no upward-looking tasks while moving. Keep the route wide and clear enough for an adult to hold a child's hand, and aim for wonder and role-play rather than skill challenge.
cards.use_when: Designing a first-time MR walking experience for parents with young children
do: Keep ghosts cute and the walking pace slow
Provide a wide, clear hand-holding route
Use wonder and fantasy rather than challenge
Keep relatives and staff outside the route as watchers
avoid: Jump scares, frightening ghost imagery or sudden sounds
Running, void floors or looking upward while walking
Routes too narrow for an adult and child holding hands
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Age and VR novelty set the gentleness budget
cards.text: For a family request, ask the child's age band and whether each player has used VR before tuning hazards, duration, and text. For a first-time 6-year-old seeking cosy discovery, default to about 5 minutes of shared play, simple story labels, and no scary or rushed moments; choose a longer session such as 10 minutes only deliberately. Age and novelty affect comfort and comprehension, not just difficulty.
cards.use_when: A creator names a child audience but gives no difficulty or session-length requirements
do: Ask age and headset experience together
Use short labels and an unhurried shared default
avoid: Treating a first-time child player like an experienced gamer
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Ask for feelings as playable verbs
cards.text: When a creator supplies only a theme, ask them to choose up to three concrete desires such as exploring and finding secrets, pretending to be heroes, following a story, relaxing, or playing together. Use the leading feelings to decide whether the structure is a treasure hunt, story adventure, or challenge, then let them shape checkpoints, lighting, and pace. Exploring plus heroic pretending suggests discovery tasks with role-play, not added combat or time pressure.
cards.use_when: Turning a vague fantasy or family theme into a game structure
do: Offer concrete feeling choices
Carry the chosen feelings into pacing and checkpoint labels
avoid: Inferring difficulty from theme alone
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Seat family spectators outside the route
cards.text: In MR, family spectators see players' bodies and reactions, not the virtual floor or objects. Keep them safely outside the play area, such as on a sofa beyond the route, and place visible discoveries, dodges, and the finish where they can watch and cheer. They may call out encouragement or hints, but never give them a task inside the play area.
cards.use_when: Designing a home MR game with parents, grandparents, or friends watching
do: Include spectators in the social staging
Keep key moments visible from their seats
avoid: Placing spectators or their tasks inside the walking route
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Let the event purpose steer the genre
cards.text: For a brand or event game, establish the desired outcome before choosing theme or genre. Brand memory and crowd attraction favor a short, spectacular, easy win that leaves players smiling and gives passers-by a reason to stop, while a skill-focused event can sustain challenge and a leaderboard. When a creator selects several goals, repeat each one in plain language rather than silently simplifying it.
cards.use_when: A creator wants a public booth or event game but has not settled its theme or mechanics.
do: Ask what should be different for players or the crowd after playing
Restate multiple goals explicitly and invite correction
avoid: Starting with theme when the creator has not stated the event goal
Reducing several selected purposes to an easier but incorrect interpretation
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Design a booth play for player and queue
cards.text: A shopping-centre booth brief became one first-time VR player at a time, about 90 seconds per play, with the queue and passers-by watching the player's view on a TV. For this setup, design both experiences together: immediate visual spectacle readable from the aisle, plus light skill that onlookers can understand and cheer. A short runner course fits this wow-and-easy goal better than a long challenge, and family-safe assumptions were no horror, no void floor and no sudden scares.
cards.use_when: Designing a high-throughput MR attraction for mostly first-time players with spectators waiting nearby.
do: Budget roughly 90 seconds when a long queue must keep moving
Stage one readable wow moment and a small skill moment for both player and audience
Use a TV to show the player's view and keep only one person in the play area
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Offer assumptions, do not attribute them to the creator
cards.text: Never turn a helpful estimate into an apparent creator requirement. The AI introduced a 2-minute session without being asked, and the creator challenged it before revising it to 90 seconds for a large queue. Say something like 'For a busy queue, would 90 seconds work?' and use familiar labels such as 'relaxing, effortless fun' instead of expecting creators to know the term 'submission'.
cards.use_when: Filling in session length, audience or other missing brief details, or presenting specialist design vocabulary.
do: Mark durations and other unstated values as proposals
Ask about queue length and desired throughput before fixing session time
Pair specialist labels with everyday wording
avoid: Presenting an invented duration as something the creator already requested
Using internal jargon such as submission without a plain-language explanation
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Choose the genre that natively matches the described play
cards.text: When a creator already describes being a life-sized chess piece, capturing targets in order and avoiding attacked squares, recognize a direct tactics fit rather than reskinning another genre. Checkmate Run used a 6 by 8 board on a 6 by 8 metre indoor floor, routed around two real tables, and supported 2 to 6 teens and adults taking turns in a 5-minute race with friends cheering from one side. The lesson is to preserve the creator's core reasoning loop while letting the engine handle board generation and solvability.
cards.use_when: The creator's concept already names concrete movement, objectives and threats that clearly correspond to one available genre.
do: Match a fully expressed mechanic to its native genre
Preserve ordered objectives and threatened-square avoidance
Incorporate real obstacles as route-planning features after checking safety
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Compare platforms by whole-group participation
cards.text: When a creator wants a whole class involved but is unsure between MR and PC, explain the participation model before discussing theme: MR lets about 2 to 6 players walk at once while classmates watch and cheer, but needs Quest 3 headsets and clear floor, whereas PC is usually one player per screen and works best with several computers. Confirm actual device counts and the usable venue next, since two borrowed headsets and a desk-filled classroom may point to a two-player gym activity rather than a classroom PC game.
cards.use_when: The creator is undecided about platform and prioritises involving a whole class or group.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Keep queued MR rounds short and calm
cards.text: For a busy booth, prefer roughly 90-second turns over 2 minutes so the queue keeps moving. In a 3 x 3 m play area, do not rely on a countdown for excitement because players may rush and collide; create readable skill moments facing the aisle and end with a visible score that spectators want to beat.
cards.use_when: Designing a small public MR attraction with spectators and a waiting queue.
do: Budget about 90 seconds per turn when a large queue is expected.
Place one legible highlight where the aisle audience can see it.
Use score comparison to give spectators a reason to try next.
avoid: Using time pressure to manufacture excitement in a 3 x 3 m room.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Do not invent hand-catching to add skill
cards.text: A request such as catching bubbles with the hands expresses a wish for active skill, not permission to add unsupported input. Say that hand-catching is unavailable, then preserve the intent with mechanics the chosen genre actually supports, such as a more demanding ordered route and hazards in runner, or switching genres if combat or movement puzzles fit better; merely repeating a walk around two hazards is unlikely to satisfy a challenge brief.
cards.use_when: A prototype is called too easy and the creator requests an interaction the engine cannot perform.
do: Name the unsupported mechanic clearly and kindly.
Ask what kind of skill the creator wants, then use supported mechanics to provide it.
avoid: Promising hand tracking, catching, shooting, inventory or other unavailable interactions.
Calling a trivially repeated walking route a skill challenge.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Turn two headsets into a whole-class lesson
cards.text: A workable class pattern is two headset players racing for different teams while the other 30 of 32 students solve answers and cheer from outside the play area, using short rounds of about 3 minutes to rotate participation. In a prepared 10 x 10 m half-gym, keep the two lanes clearly separated with safe edge clearance, and label the leaderboard with team names rather than student names so classmates can collaborate without entering the lanes or being personally ranked.
cards.use_when: Designing an active learning game for a large class with very few headsets.
do: Give waiting classmates a thinking and cheering role outside the play area.
Use separate lanes and team names on the scoreboard.
Keep rounds near 3 minutes for rotation.
avoid: Letting spectators enter the active lanes.
Designing movement or scoring that encourages children to sprint.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Never invent the player's room dimensions
cards.text: Do not state a width, depth, or obstacle layout until the creator has supplied it; a invented measurement such as 5.25 m quickly destroys trust. For an MR design, ask for approximate width and depth, indoor or outdoor placement, and whether sofas, tables, or plants can be moved. If they are unsure, invite them to pace the room and report steps, then treat the result as an estimate.
cards.use_when: An MR creator has not yet described the real play space
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Make one-headset party queues part of the game
cards.text: For a children's party with one headset and roughly 6 to 10 guests, use solo turns of about 2 to 3 minutes so everyone rotates through without a long wait. Give waiting children spectator roles such as calling directions or counting objects, while keeping them outside the play area. Let the birthday child play first and last, and consider removing timers and scores when competition could cause arguments.
cards.use_when: Designing short MR rotations for a children's group
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Reserve the personal climax for the guest of honour
cards.text: A repeatable finale should fit a repeated turn: do not sing the birthday song and present candle cake after every child's run, since eight identical celebrations make the occasion feel strange. Give the birthday child the full personal climax on their turn, while friends receive a smaller completion moment such as earning a baby dinosaur to care for. This preserves both a satisfying ending for every player and the uniqueness of the celebration.
cards.use_when: A party game repeats but celebrates one specific person
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Create MR scares without provoking a sprint
cards.text: For a walk-only MR horror attraction, deliver medium-intensity suspense through theme, lighting, story labels, and deliberate hazards rather than jumpscares or chase moments likely to make players run. A 4 by 5 m indoor room can support roughly 4 minute solo queue turns, with the route kept clear of wall cabinets and corner sofas. Place spectators along a safe wall where they can cheer or call directions, and use indoor lighting so spooky colours and neon remain readable.
cards.use_when: Designing a thrilling MR queue attraction for newcomers
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Choose the learning mechanic from the desired outcome
cards.text: Ask what learners should remember or be able to do after playing before selecting a genre. For factual recall, put short prompts or facts on checkpoint labels; for an ordered process, make players visit steps 1, 2, 3 in sequence; for planning and decisions, use the tactics board. A request such as practising multiplication tables 6 to 9 is a recall goal, not enough by itself to justify a generic adventure.
cards.use_when: A teacher or creator requests an educational game but describes only the subject matter.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Design the whole class rotation, not only the headset round
cards.text: With 32 children, 2 headsets and a 50 minute lesson, calculate throughput using setup, instructions, play and realistic headset fitting time; a 30 second child-led handoff is likely too optimistic. Keep the roughly 30 waiting children active with team turns, projected questions and a live score, letting them answer by raised hands or paper cards without phones. Spectators stay outside the play area, and separate lanes support a race without players colliding.
cards.use_when: A class or group has far more players than headsets and limited session time.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Let young learners retry without losing their progress
cards.text: For children still practising a skill, avoid a punitive reset after a wrong answer, especially when the creator worries it will make them cry. Use a brief pause followed by another attempt so the race continues and the child gets immediate practice. Show the prompt to teammates as well so their help feels useful rather than turning failure into public embarrassment.
cards.use_when: Designing scored learning challenges for young or anxious players.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Do not present invented prototype choices as creator decisions
cards.text: A three minute round was displayed as though the creator had chosen it even though session length had never been discussed, causing confusion and distrust. Mark unrequested timings, themes and formats as AI proposals, and ask about constraints such as a 50 minute lesson and available projector before relying on them. Recheck the full schedule whenever round length or handoff time changes.
cards.use_when: A prototype needs defaults for session length, theme or display equipment that the creator never supplied.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Ask platform and feelings before detailed design
cards.text: Start with the creator's theme and platform, MR on Quest 3 with real walking or PC, because this answer removes whole branches of questioning. On PC, skip the real-room survey; on MR, usable floor size determines feasible genres and simultaneous players. Then ask for 1 to 3 desired feelings, such as playful spooky and challenging, to set the genre, atmosphere and intensity before discussing mechanics.
cards.use_when: Opening an interview with a vague theme and no settled game structure
do: Ask theme and platform first
Ask desired feelings before detailed mechanics
Reserve room questions for MR
avoid: Surveying furniture for a PC game
Treating a theme word as a complete genre brief
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Deliver a ghost chase without real running
cards.text: When a creator asks for running away from ghosts in MR, preserve the fantasy but state plainly that players will not really run. Create pursuit through brisk walking, dodging red danger rings and ghosts that follow. Build fear with lighting, atmosphere and an escalation from mild creepiness to intense suspense, not jump scares that could make a startled player run into real furniture.
cards.use_when: A creator wants a frightening chase or real running in a headset
do: Translate fleeing into brisk walking and dodges
Explain the safety constraint alongside the alternative
Escalate atmosphere from creepy to intense
avoid: Requiring real running
Using sudden scares that provoke flight
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Survey clear floor and remaining obstacles separately
cards.text: Ask for the empty floor actually available after tables and chairs are moved, not the room's nominal dimensions, and offer choices such as 3 x 3 m or 4 x 5 m. If the creator is unsure, accept an estimate and suggest pacing it off, then ask what remains: edge furniture, a central column or scattered obstacles. A wall cabinet or corner sofa changes the walking route, hazard placement and safe spectator positions even when the overall size is adequate.
cards.use_when: Planning an MR game in a club room, classroom or other furnished venue
do: Measure floor after movable furniture is cleared
Let an uncertain creator estimate by pacing
Map fixed obstacles before placing routes and viewers
avoid: Using total room dimensions as playable space
Assuming an empty rectangle from a size estimate
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Make one-headset queues socially competitive
cards.text: With one headset and visitors arriving in a queue, use solo turns rather than promising simultaneous team play. Let friends outside the play area cheer and call out directions, while a shared leaderboard supplies competition across turns without more hardware. This combines spectator laughter and fellowship with a reason to replay, and keeps spectators out of the walking space.
cards.use_when: Designing an MR showcase with one headset and a steady flow of visitors
do: Run one player at a time
Invite vocal help from outside the play area
Use a leaderboard for asynchronous competition
avoid: Promising simultaneous multiplayer without enough headsets
Giving spectators tasks inside the play area
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Make the learning outcome structure the route
cards.text: Ask what should remain with players after the game before choosing theme or competition format, because the learning outcome determines checkpoint sequence, labels, pacing, and round length. Turn ordered knowledge into the walking route itself: for planet order, begin at the Sun and visit planets outward, with short labels adding facts such as which are hot or cold. This teaches through movement without requiring quiz or conversation mechanics.
cards.use_when: A creator requests an educational game but initially describes only a subject or visual scene.
do: Ask what players should remember or be able to do after playing
Express that outcome through checkpoint order and short labels
avoid: Starting with visual theme before agreeing what players should learn
Adding unsupported quiz, dialogue, or inventory mechanics to make the game educational
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Turn limited headsets into team rotations and audience play
cards.text: When a whole class must participate but headsets are scarce, design team rotations and meaningful spectator participation rather than simultaneous headset play. With 32 students and 4 headsets, use 8 teams of 4; at 4 minutes per round, headset play alone takes about 32 minutes before changeovers. The other 28 students can watch from seating, call hints, cheer, and follow a leaderboard, while remaining outside the play area.
cards.use_when: Designing for a class or group whose player count greatly exceeds the available MR headsets.
do: Group players around the available headset count
Give waiting players safe roles such as hints, cheering, and leaderboard watching
Check total rotation time against the lesson period
avoid: Leaving waiting students with nothing to do
Giving spectators roles that require entering the play area
Promising that every student can wear a headset simultaneously
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Use half the gym for play and half for spectators
cards.text: In a shared school gym, let the court layout determine both the course and audience placement. For a 14 x 15 m half-court play area with basketball posts on both sides, seat waiting students on the other half and route around the posts, keeping walking paths 1.2 m clear, virtual content off real obstacles, and at least 0.6 m from area edges. Indoor gym lighting also keeps colours readable for a daytime space-themed game.
cards.use_when: An MR game shares a school gym with sports fixtures and a seated audience.
do: Separate play and waiting areas by court half
Route around fixed sports equipment with safe clearances
Use indoor lighting to keep virtual scenes readable
avoid: Building the course across basketball posts or other fixed equipment
Placing spectators inside the walking route
Assuming daytime automatically makes a dark space scene unreadable indoors
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Default young first-time MR players to comfortable wonder
cards.text: For mostly first-time MR players aged about 10 to 11, default to calm walking discovery rather than fright or vertigo. Avoid void-floor effects, sudden scares, and pressure to move quickly; create wonder through floating models, scale, lighting, and clearly ordered destinations instead. Ask about acceptable scariness and dizziness early because these constraints affect scenery, lighting, hazards, and pacing.
cards.use_when: Designing a school MR experience for children with little headset experience.
do: Ask about fear and dizziness constraints early
Create sensation through scenery, scale, and orderly discovery
Keep first-time interaction to comfortable real walking
avoid: Using a void floor for default child-friendly wonder
Adding sudden scares or fast, frantic movement to create excitement
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: A calm pair walk still needs a shared verb
cards.text: Walking through scenery can feel boring even when the creator asked for something relaxing. Give pairs a few effortless shared rituals at checkpoints, such as stopping together, mirroring a gesture, finding the same object, or responding to a short prompt, then let them continue at their own pace. For a roughly 3-minute public experience, use only a few of these beats and create engagement through fellowship rather than hazards, timing, or a leaderboard.
cards.use_when: A creator calls a walking experience calm but early feedback says players just walk or do nothing together.
do: Make the pair's interaction visible and easy to understand without instructions.
Keep participation optional and unhurried so the activity remains gentle.
avoid: Adding difficulty simply to make the walk less passive.
Promoting score or speed when the creator wants relaxation.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Read numbered choices back by name
cards.text: When a creator answers with only a list number, confirm both the number and its label before changing the design direction, and accept a later correction without argument. Words such as calm describe tone, not necessarily the desired feeling: a calm experience can centre on fellowship rather than submission. Carry the corrected choice into the next prototype so the pair interaction does not get replaced by a solitary relaxation walk.
cards.use_when: The creator selects from numbered choices tersely, or corrects the AI's interpretation of an earlier answer.
do: Say, for example, "5, Fellowship, doing it together" before proceeding.
Treat corrections as authoritative and revise downstream assumptions.
avoid: Inferring Submission solely because the requested mood is calm.
Continuing with an interpretation after the creator has clarified it.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Make the spectator show from visible body language
cards.text: MR spectators see players' bodies, not the virtual garden or checkpoints, so a shared experience needs a visible human performance. Place the pair's gestures, reactions, and finish on the side of the floor facing watchers, and keep the goal and rules simple enough that an onlooker can explain them after one round. Watchers may cheer or offer encouragement from outside, but never give them a role that requires entering the play area.
cards.use_when: Designing a public MR demo where visitors around the floor should understand and enjoy watching.
do: Schedule one or two clearly visible pair moments rather than constant subtle activity.
Use the surrounding audience as part of the social atmosphere.
avoid: Relying on virtual scenery alone to communicate the experience.
Giving spectators physical tasks inside the route.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Gentle defaults for first-time public MR
cards.text: For first-time headset visitors in a short public session, make the first action obvious and safe before introducing any story detail. On a small clear floor such as 4 x 4 m with two players, favour a simple open route, preserve a 1.2 m clear walking path and 0.6 m edge clearance, and confirm that spectators and furniture are outside it. Skip sudden scares, dizzying void-floor effects, punishing hazards, and score pressure; steady indoor light also keeps gentle colours readable.
cards.use_when: Planning a gentle drop-in MR experience for adults who are mostly new to VR.
do: Start with one reassuring step or checkpoint that teaches touching checkpoints in order.
Check real obstacles explicitly even when the creator calls the room clear.
avoid: Using surprise, dizziness, or penalties to create excitement.
Letting the route overlap the audience standing around the edges.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Estimate an unmeasured venue before planning the route
cards.text: When an MR creator cannot measure a gym, ask them to count paces and convert 1 pace to about 0.75 m, then mark a conservative play zone instead of assuming the whole venue is usable. A half basketball court can be estimated at roughly 14 x 15 m, leaving the other half for waiting players. Locate fixed obstacles such as basketball posts before deciding checkpoint spacing, simultaneous player count, and whether the route should loop or zigzag.
cards.use_when: A creator names a large venue but does not know its clear dimensions.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Give waiting teammates a real supporting role
cards.text: Choose simultaneous racing, rotating solo play, or cooperative teams before proposing options, because this determines scoring and what waiting players do. With eight teams of four, four headset wearers can walk while seated teammates help call out the next target and later teams chase a record. Since spectators cannot see the headset view, put the target sequence on an external screen or printed card and keep all helpers outside the play area.
cards.use_when: A class or large group has fewer play positions than participants and wants cooperation.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Use short solo turns for a first headset party
cards.text: For a first-time MR party with one headset and 6 to 10 five-year-olds, use solo turns of about 3 minutes in a clear 3 x 3 m indoor area. Keep the sofa and queue outside the walking route so family and friends can watch and cheer safely. Friendly scenery, no ghosts or jump scares, and a clearly visible finish suit young first-time players while keeping the rotation moving.
