cards.use_when: Designing a young children's party with one borrowed headset and no VR experience.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Fact-check learning content and its visual metaphors
cards.text: In an educational exploration game, have a teacher or domain expert review every label, sequence, and visual metaphor before final art. Creators caught a misspelled planet name and confusion between the asteroid belt and Kuiper belt, and distance from the Sun must not be treated as a simple temperature rule because Venus is hotter than Mercury. Red-orange and blue can support a broad hot-cold theme, but each stop also needs an accurate, distinct reveal so the learning route produces memorable wow moments.
cards.use_when: A game teaches real-world facts through themed checkpoints, colours, or scenery.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: A prop swap does not fix an unsupported interaction
cards.text: When a creator asks for a specific interaction, such as shining a flashlight so ghosts retreat, preserve the causal action rather than merely reskinning another mechanic. A flashlight that must be swung like a sword feels wrong because the requested verb was replaced, not supported. State the limitation kindly, then offer the closest real alternative, such as a timed escape route with hazards and checkpoints, and check that the fantasy still works in the prototype.
cards.use_when: A creator requests pursuit, light-based repulsion, combat, or another verb the available mechanics cannot perform.
do: Name the unavailable interaction and test the closest supported alternative with the creator.
avoid: Do not treat a requested interaction as satisfied by changing only the prop or animation.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Define the learning objective before the game wrapper
cards.text: For a vague request like "a maths game for my class," establish the exact skill and learner band before choosing genre, story, or scenery. Knowing that Year 4 students, about ages 8 to 9, need times-table practice determines the task content, reading load, and difficulty at every stop. Only then should preferences such as speed or teamwork decide whether that practice becomes a race, a cooperative challenge, or another wrapper.
cards.use_when: A teacher or parent proposes an educational game using only a broad subject such as maths.
do: Ask for the exact curriculum target and learner age before selecting a game structure.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Turn limited headsets into a short class rotation
cards.text: A class with only 4 headsets can play in groups of 4 while classmates watch, with roughly 4-minute sessions keeping rotation practical. For ages 8 to 9 and mostly first-time headset users, favour calm, safe walking and simple onboarding over intensity. In the example 7 x 8 m gym, benches and stacked chairs remained at the edges, so the clear route had to respect those obstacles. Keep spectators outside the play area, but let them cheer, call hints, and follow a leaderboard.
cards.use_when: Designing for a school class or other large group with fewer headsets than players and many spectators.
do: Rotate small groups through short sessions and give watchers safe, visible roles outside the floor.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Reconcile excitement and teamwork instead of choosing one
cards.text: When a creator selects both "fast and exciting" and "help each other as a team," treat these as goals to combine rather than forcing one to win. A short timed run can supply excitement while friends outside the route cheer or call hints, preserving fellowship without adding collisions inside the walking area. Confirm whether success means beating other players, beating the clock, or improving a team result before choosing the leaderboard and scoring emphasis.
cards.use_when: A creator chooses apparently competing feelings, such as racing against time and cooperating as a team.
do: Combine a clock-based challenge with cooperation that does not add physical traffic to the play area.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Age, party size and desired feelings set the brief
cards.text: Before choosing genre or difficulty for a children's event, ask the child's age, who will play together, and what equipment must be shared. Then ask for 1 to 3 desired feelings, such as story adventure, group laughter, discovery, gentle time racing, or relaxed walking. Young children call for non-frightening, short play, while cheering plus light racing points to a social, low-pressure challenge.
cards.use_when: Starting a game for a birthday, family gathering, or other mixed-player event.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: One headset can still serve a whole birthday party
cards.text: When 5 to 6 children share one headset, make the game explicitly turn based and keep individual attempts short. Add a visible timed leaderboard and moments that friends outside the play area can watch and cheer for, so waiting becomes shared play rather than a queue. Keep the competition light for an 8 year old's party.
cards.use_when: A group wants to play but hardware allows only one player at a time.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Measure the room, then locate every obstacle
cards.text: Ask for the usable floor size before proposing a route, accepting steps or comparisons with nearby objects when the creator does not know metres. Follow up on whether each obstacle lies inside or outside that area: a clear 3 x 4 m living room supports a different route from one with a TV table along an inner edge, which requires a detour and clearance. Also establish where spectators will stand.
cards.use_when: The creator gives an approximate room size or mentions furniture near the play area.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Offer fit constraints without inventing the theme
cards.text: Do not turn an early preference or room constraint into an unconfirmed game concept. In this session the AI announced a treasure hunt before the creator chose a theme and was corrected. Instead, explain only the constraint, such as a 3 x 4 m room best fitting a checkpoint walking course, then ask directly what the child loves and offer several varied theme examples. Mechanical fit and creative theme are separate decisions.
cards.use_when: Space or audience strongly suggests a genre, but the creator has not chosen a story or theme.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Sequence questions around design decisions
cards.text: Ask for the initial idea and platform first, because a PC game needs no real-room questions. Next establish player age, group size, headset count and prior VR experience, since these determine difficulty, session length and whether play must be turn-based. For MR, ask about the cleared floor and obstacles after those choices so the creator is not burdened with irrelevant venue detail.
cards.use_when: Opening a design interview with a vague game idea and an undecided or newly stated platform
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Turn one headset into a party race
cards.text: When 6 to 7 children share one headset, use short individual turns of about 3 minutes rather than promising simultaneous play, giving a full rotation in roughly 18 to 21 minutes. A race leaderboard lets waiting children follow and cheer, while they remain seated outside the walking route. For young players, keep the tone bright and avoid strong scares or surprises that could make them run.
cards.use_when: Designing an MR children's party with one headset and several waiting players
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Measure the cleared MR walking floor
cards.text: Ask for the empty floor left after furniture is moved, including its width, depth and fixed obstacles, rather than accepting the room's nominal size. If the creator has no tape measure, accept an estimate in steps using about 0.75 m per step. Treat anything smaller than 3 x 3 m as runner-only, and keep furniture such as a wall-side sofa outside the walking route.
cards.use_when: A creator describes a home MR venue but is unsure of its usable dimensions
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Lay out classroom play around obstacles and seated spectators
cards.text: For a class game where 4 students play while the rest watch, survey both fixed obstacles and spectator seating before laying out the route. In a 7 x 8 m gym with benches along the edges and children sitting on the sides, preserve a clear 1.2 m walking route and keep content at least 0.6 m from area boundaries. Spectators can cheer and watch bodies or a score screen, but should never have a task inside the play area.
cards.use_when: Designing an MR class activity with several active players and classmates watching.
do: Ask whether the floor contains pillars, stacked benches, or other fixed equipment, and where spectators will sit.
Keep a 1.2 m walking route clear, stay at least 0.6 m from area edges, and put watching children outside the route.
Let classmates cheer or follow a screen-based score display from the side.
avoid: Placing virtual prompts or tasks on benches, seated classmates, or other real objects.
Giving spectators a role that requires entering the play area.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Keep team maths failure individual and time pressure kind
cards.text: In cooperative learning games, separate individual failure from team progress: one child's wrong step should not send all 4 players back. For mental maths, do not tint wrong choices red in advance, because that gives away the answer; children should work it out and select the right number. When they ask to beat the clock but fear upset, make time pressure visible and exciting while keeping individual resets and timeout consequences gentle, and check that a small set such as 6 questions does not make the round feel thin.
cards.use_when: Tuning cooperative educational challenges for children who want excitement without harsh punishment.
do: Keep a wrong step's checkpoint reset individual rather than shared by all 4 players.
Present numerically neutral answer choices and focus practice on requested tables such as 7s and 8s.
Make the clock prominent and treat expiry as a gentle end or encouragement to retry.
avoid: Resetting the whole team because one child makes a mistake.
Marking incorrect answer choices red before players choose, since this reveals the answer.
Using a punishing timeout when the creator wants excitement without distress.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Turn a single headset into a short birthday party race
cards.text: For a birthday party with 5 to 6 friends and only one headset, use short sequential runs rather than simultaneous play: a roughly 3 minute course lets children take turns while friends and family cheer and follow scores from the room edges. A 3 x 4 m cleared living-room floor can support a compact race for an 8-year-old first-time player. Keep the theme friendly and avoid intense horror or jump scares, especially when the brief explicitly rules them out.
cards.use_when: Designing a children's MR party game with one headset and several guests.
do: Use one-player runs of about 3 minutes with a visible race score or leaderboard.
Keep friends and family outside the floor as cheering spectators.
Fit the route to the actual 3 x 4 m clear floor and use friendly dinosaur-themed discovery.
avoid: Designing simultaneous multiplayer when only one headset exists.
Using strong horror or jump scares for a young child's party.
Making turns so long that most friends spend the party waiting.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Establish platform and purpose before detailed mechanics
cards.text: Open the interview by establishing both platform and purpose, because these answers determine nearly every later design question. PC play skips real-floor size, surroundings, obstacles, venue, and indoor lighting, while MR play requires them. Knowing whether the creator wants party fun, learning, competition, or bonding then guides genre, cooperation, scoring, and session structure.
cards.use_when: Starting a new creator interview with only a loose theme or occasion.
do: Ask whether play is on a walking MR headset or a computer, and what the game should achieve.
For PC, omit venue, width, depth, and indoor questions.
For MR, use the answer to lead into room dimensions, obstacles, lighting, players, and spectators.
avoid: Asking PC creators for floor dimensions, obstacles, venue, or indoor lighting.
Choosing detailed mechanics before establishing whether the goal is party fun, group bonding, competition, or learning.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Redirect unsupported combat and conversation into performable alternatives
cards.text: When a creator asks for shooting or a mascot that talks and asks names, do not imply those systems exist. Offer the closest action fantasy instead: sword-based fruit slicing, with the brand mascot standing welcome, dancing, cheering during play, and appearing for the finale. This preserves the requested character and spectacle without promising dialogue or projectile mechanics.
cards.use_when: A creator describes Fruit Ninja-like action, shooting, or an interactive brand mascot.
do: Offer close-range sword slicing as the nearest action substitute for shooting
Give the mascot scripted appearances: greeting pose, dancing, cheering on hits, and a finish celebration
State the limitation kindly before presenting the alternative
avoid: Pretending a mascot can converse or ask the player’s name
Promising projectile fruit, shooting, or dialogue systems the engine lacks
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Design public booth play as a short, watchable score loop
cards.text: For a busy public booth serving mostly first-time players, design a one-player round around the queue budget, such as no more than 2 minutes per person. Pair immediate visual spectacle with score competition, but avoid difficulty so high that newcomers cannot finish or so low that score hunters lose interest. Keep the leaderboard visible to people waiting so the queue becomes part of the competition.
cards.use_when: The venue expects long queues, mixed experience levels, and rapid turn taking.
do: Cap the advertised session at the creator’s throughput limit, here 2 minutes per person
Combine easy-to-read action with score chasing and a leaderboard
Place rankings where waiting players can see them
avoid: Optimizing only for expert challenge
Leaving the score board invisible to the queue
Making newcomers endure a long session
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Subtract queues and furniture before sizing an MR game
cards.text: Measure the net empty MR play floor, not the whole booth: exclude queue space, giveaway tables, stages, and cables. A nominal 3 x 4 m booth can leave only about 3 x 3 m for play once those functions are removed, which supports standing play but sharply limits walking layouts. If the creator cannot give metres, accept step counts or familiar comparisons, or have them measure against a stated minimum.
cards.use_when: A creator gives booth dimensions for a public MR installation.
do: Ask for clear width and depth excluding tables, stages, cables, and queues
Subtract queue and service areas before selecting the game layout
Accept estimates in steps or comparisons, or recommend a minimum when the creator must measure
avoid: Treating total booth dimensions as playable space
Placing virtual action over queue furniture or cables
Choosing a genre before checking whether MR reaches 3 x 3 m
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Make requested spectacle and public scoring visible in the prototype
cards.text: In a spectacle-led action prototype, feedback such as colourful splash on a successful slice is part of the core fantasy, not optional decoration. Carry explicit requests such as a public leaderboard into every revision and show where waiting players will see rankings. A plain first pass can fail even if its mechanics are correct, so review both hit feedback and the competition display before approval.
cards.use_when: A creator approves a concept but asks for juicy hits, branding, or a missing score display.
do: Record named spectacle and leaderboard requirements as prototype acceptance checks
Show hit bursts or splashes prominently in the key scene
Include the queue-facing score view in the revised prototype
avoid: Treating decorative feedback as optional polish when it carries the fantasy
Dropping a requested leaderboard between prototype versions
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Redirect shooting requests to swordplay or dodging
cards.text: When a creator asks for shooting, acknowledge the action fantasy but state plainly that guns are unavailable. Offer the closest supported alternatives: in battle, the right controller becomes a sword for slashing nearby enemies; in runner, red floor circles can be framed as incoming shots or splashes to dodge. Let the creator choose between standing combat and walking avoidance, since that choice determines the whole game structure.
cards.use_when: A creator requests guns, projectile combat, or another unsupported action mechanic.
do: Name the missing mechanic, then offer two playable mappings and ask which action feel the creator wants.
avoid: Pretending that guns exist or silently substituting a mechanic without explaining it.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Never present an AI assumption as the creator's choice
cards.text: Do not describe an inferred duration or constraint as something the creator selected. One creator objected when a prototype claimed they had chosen 3 minutes; they actually needed roughly 1.5-minute rounds because many children would play. Present uncertain values as editable proposals, and ask about audience size and throughput before locking session length.
cards.use_when: A prototype fills in session length, audience, or other details the creator never confirmed.
do: Label unconfirmed numbers as proposals and explicitly invite correction during prototype review.
Ask about crowd size and desired turnover before fixing round duration.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Specify the fantasy centerpiece and hazard colors explicitly
cards.text: A generic dinosaur course became more exciting only after the prototype specified a large, visible, friendly T-rex and a cute greeting roar as the player entered the finish portal. Feedback also exposed an unreadable mud pit whose red or brown coloring was unclear. For character-led games, specify the fantasy centerpiece's scale, temperament, reveal location, and sound moment, while separately naming each hazard's material and color so decoration cannot be mistaken for danger.
cards.use_when: A child-friendly or character-themed prototype feels plain, or decorative terrain could be confused with hazards.
do: Describe the centerpiece model's size, emotional tone, placement, and sound cue.
Name hazard materials and colors explicitly in the visual specification.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Design a mall MR booth for throughput and bystanders
cards.text: For a busy branded mall booth, budget non-play space as deliberately as the MR floor: a 3 x 4 m booth can reserve a clear 3 x 3 m play area while the remainder handles the queue and a giveaway table. Use one player at a time and a 2-minute round when the queue is long, with side-on visibility for waiting visitors and passersby. A brand mascot can welcome, cheer, and celebrate the finish without NPC dialogue, while consistent indoor lighting keeps game colors readable for an all-ages drop-in audience.
cards.use_when: Planning a public promotional MR game with queues, spectators, and rapid player turnover.
do: Keep the MR floor completely clear and place queues, staff, and giveaways outside it.
Use a solo round short enough for turnover and a mascot loop that needs no conversation system.
Stage play where waiting visitors and passersby can watch from the side.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Design booth turns around queue flow
cards.text: For a busy public booth, treat throughput as a core design constraint: a creator facing a long queue may prefer a 90 second turn over an initial 3 minute round. Ask where spectators wait and face the biggest dodge and the finish toward the walkway, so watching builds interest without putting spectators in the play area. On a 3 x 6 m floor, also locate registration tables or counters before placing the route and visible highlights.
cards.use_when: Designing a short public demo with queues and passersby
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Stop interviewing when options are requested
cards.text: Use a small set of high-impact questions first: platform, desired feelings, approximate floor size, and obstacles or spectator position. Offer rough space choices such as 3 x 3 m or 3 x 6 m, and allow estimates in steps when exact measurements are unknown. If the creator says there are too many questions and asks to see concepts, end the interview and propose options using the constraints already captured.
cards.use_when: A busy creator becomes impatient during the design interview
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Build MR horror without startle reflexes
cards.text: For walking MR horror, create tension through story, slow approaching enemies, dim lighting and theme rather than sudden loud scares that could make players run into real furniture. Keep a 1.2 m clear route and stay at least 0.6 m from area edges; seated friends should watch from furniture outside the route. A night scene can use dim indoor light, but leave enough light for headset tracking, especially with first-time headset users taking solo turns.
cards.use_when: Designing a spooky room-scale game for adults new to headsets
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Replace talking NPC wishes with story beats
cards.text: If a creator asks for a character who talks to players, asks their name and cheers, do not promise NPC conversations or voice interaction. Offer the closest supported storytelling: an intro card, a clear goal line, and short checkpoint labels that address the player and advance the fantasy, with real spectators supplying the cheering. Preserve the requested emotional role rather than silently dropping it.
cards.use_when: A creator wants conversational characters or personalised spoken encouragement
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Map obstacles and audience sightlines together
cards.text: Before laying out an MR route, ask both what furniture or columns remain on the floor and exactly where waiting players will sit or stand. Keep the route off every real obstacle, and place the finish or biggest dodge where spectators can see it so friends can cheer. This check matters even in a seemingly adequate 4 x 4 m living room; a sofa along one wall can define the audience side.
cards.use_when: Planning a room-scale MR game for a home, party, or booth
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Size each round to the waiting queue
cards.text: For walk-up MR play, prioritize throughput with solo or 1 to 2 player rounds: about 3 minutes suits first-time, all-ages mall visitors, while 2 minutes works for a children's party where many players are waiting. Ask who will play and how many play simultaneously because those answers determine suitable difficulty, scariness, and round length. Make the visible action entertaining for the queue as well as the current player.
cards.use_when: Designing for parties, booths, or other rotating-player venues
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Choose platform before asking venue questions
cards.text: Ask early whether the game will use MR headsets or PC because that answer changes the entire design interview. PC needs no real-floor questions, while MR requires dimensions, obstacles, surroundings, and spectator positions. If the creator describes a physical booth and accepts headsets, proceed as MR and next establish the players and simultaneous group size.
cards.use_when: Starting a design conversation with an undecided or loosely specified platform
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Calibrate horror before choosing content
cards.text: When a creator only asks for a scary or haunted game, first establish player age and VR experience, then offer distinct intensity levels such as playful horror, tense and mysterious, or serious horror for adults. Use the answer to tune lighting, creature portrayal and mechanical simplicity, since first-time players need a gentler onboarding even when they are adults.
cards.use_when: A creator requests horror without specifying intensity or player experience.
do: Ask who will play and whether they have used VR before.
Offer named horror intensity levels rather than interpreting scary yourself.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Redirect unsupported combat and dialogue wishes
cards.text: If a creator requests guns, shooting or two-way character conversations, state the limitation plainly before continuing the design. Offer the closest supported fantasy: melee combat where the right controller becomes a sword and enemies approach, or story delivered through the intro and short stage labels such as a quest to send a spirit home. Confirm that the substitute preserves what they wanted, such as active ghost fighting or a strong narrative.
cards.use_when: A creator asks for shooting or interactive NPC conversations.
do: Name the unsupported mechanic directly.
Present the nearest supported mechanic and check acceptance.
avoid: Silently promising guns or conversational characters.
Treating a text label as equivalent to a full dialogue system.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Design for the cleared floor, not the room size
cards.text: For home MR, ask which furniture can be moved and derive the usable play rectangle rather than accepting the nominal room dimensions; battle and tactics need at least 3 x 3 m. Keep the walking route clear to 1.2 m, place nothing on real obstacles and keep activity at least 0.6 m from area edges. For friends taking turns, seat spectators along a wall or on furniture outside the route with views of dodges and the finish, and never let dim horror lighting hide real hazards.
cards.use_when: Planning an MR game in a furnished living room with several people sharing one headset.
do: Separate total room size from cleared playable size.
Ask where nonplayers will sit while others take turns.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: For a young child, settle who wears the headset
cards.text: Quest is manufacturer-recommended for ages 10 and up, so do not treat a 5-year-old wearing it alone as the default. Explain the concern kindly, then offer concrete arrangements: child plays slowly with an adult holding their hand throughout, an adult plays while the child watches or follows, or the group switches to PC. Who actually plays changes the whole design, so resolve this before choosing mechanics.
cards.use_when: A creator requests MR for a child under 10 or a first-time child player.
do: State the age guidance without presenting supported play as forbidden.
Ask whether the child or an adult will wear the headset.
Make adult assistance continuous if the young child plays.
avoid: Designing first and addressing the child's safety afterward.
Assuming a borrowed headset makes the plan suitable.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: A tiny living room forces the runner genre
cards.text: Measure the clear MR floor early, accepting a room comparison or a count of steps when the creator cannot give metres. MR normally needs at least 3 x 3 m for the genre range; below that, only runner fits, so all three options must be runners rather than promising battle or tactics. If an adult must walk beside or behind a child, include that accompanying movement when judging whether the route is clear.
cards.use_when: Sizing an MR game for a small home, especially with an adult guiding a child.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Ask for desired feelings, then preserve fear limits
cards.text: When a creator gives only a theme and occasion, ask them to pick 1 to 3 desired feelings, such as following a story, relaxing without fear or losing, exploration, wonder, or role-play; these choices distinguish games more usefully than decoration alone. Treat statements like "nothing scary" and "my child startles easily" as hard constraints on enemies, lighting, surprises, and failure pressure, not as a request to make a scary theme slightly milder. A cute narrative with relaxed play can satisfy both the requested theme and the child's limits.
cards.use_when: A creator names a theme but has not defined the experience, especially for a sensitive child.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Let young children finish gracefully
cards.text: For a children's attraction, even a planned 3-minute session may feel too long, so keep stages short and offer an early, celebratory ending when a child is struggling. Use a cute, non-threatening boss rather than relying on fear for excitement, and preserve the child's sense of success instead of forcing a loss.
cards.use_when: Designing difficulty, session length, and boss tone for young children or family venues.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Design the booth for people walking past
cards.text: A public attraction needs spectacle outside the headset or player screen, not just a fun game for the participant. Place visually readable highlights such as a giant mascot reveal where passersby can see the reaction, and offer a leaderboard on a booth TV to attract and involve spectators; confirm that the display connection is genuinely supported before promising it.
cards.use_when: A creator wants passersby to stop, watch, and join at a booth or event.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Keep the creator's named mascot exact
cards.text: Treat a named mascot, colour, and branded pattern as fixed creative requirements rather than loose inspiration. Substituting another animal can make a technically improved prototype feel wrong, so echo those details in the next version and ask before changing the character's species or identity.
cards.use_when: Turning a creator's character or brand description into prototype art.
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Adapt honestly to a tiny MR room
cards.text: Treat a creator's estimate of 3 steps by 3 steps as roughly 2.2 x 2.2 m, below the recommended 3 x 3 m for MR walking games; 4 steps is roughly 3 m. Check whether the area can be expanded, but respect a refusal caused by booking cost or lack of alternatives. In a fixed tiny room, offer only a short, gentle story route with no startling moments, and allow extra room when a child walks hand in hand with an adult.
cards.use_when: A creator describes a small living room in steps and wants a gentle game for a young child.
do: Ask once whether a larger free room or common area is available
If not, keep the course short, gentle and surprise-free
Reserve clearance for both bodies when an adult accompanies a child
avoid: Filling the full 3 x 3 m minimum with a route when an adult and child must share it
Adding scares or frantic movement to compensate for the tiny space
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Make waiting spectators part of the show
cards.text: When friends wait for one headset, design their experience as well as the player's: in passthrough they otherwise see a body walking and turning, not the virtual floor or cake. Put readable physical moments such as a dodge or finish where the group can watch, and use a TV view or leaderboard when available. Cheering and hints give the queue a role without assigning anyone a task inside the play area.
cards.use_when: A creator worries that friends watching or queuing will be bored during an MR game.
do: Place dodges and the finish where onlookers can see the player's body
Offer a leaderboard or mirrored screen when the venue setup supports it
Let friends cheer or call hints from outside the play area
avoid: Placing spectator activities or helpers inside the walking area
Assuming onlookers can see virtual scenery without a display
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Use reliable triggers for emotional climaxes
cards.text: Do not make a birthday climax depend on the headset somehow knowing that a child blew out a candle. A failed or ambiguous detection can turn the emotional peak into frustration, especially for a young child. Use a simple supported action such as touching the final checkpoint, or have an adult confirm the moment, so the celebration always resolves reliably.
cards.use_when: A story prototype includes a real-world gesture or celebration that the engine cannot reliably sense.
do: Replace implied sensing with a checkpoint touch or another supported action
If useful, let an accompanying adult trigger or confirm the celebration
Test the moment for clarity and emotional payoff, not technical cleverness
avoid: Claiming the headset can detect breath, candle flames or another unlisted real-world action
Making a young child repeat a fragile interaction before the story can finish
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Turn one headset into a short group race
cards.text: One headset does not prevent a social competition: let friends take turns on the same short course and compare times or scores while the others cheer. A four-minute zombie-escape round suits club play because several people can rotate without a long wait. Ask players' ages and whether they play simultaneously or sequentially, since those answers determine space, difficulty and whether a race structure fits.
cards.use_when: A group of friends has one Quest 3 and wants an exciting game with turns and cheering.
do: Use sequential attempts with comparable times or scores
Keep rounds near the requested four minutes
Frame hazards and checkpoints as escaping danger rather than unsupported combat
avoid: Treating one headset as a reason to ignore the waiting group
Promising simultaneous shared-floor play without enough devices
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Let real lighting decide whether glow can carry the theme
cards.text: Ask early whether the venue can be fully darkened, merely dimmed, or must stay bright before promising a lantern, neon, spooky, or night theme. Bright real light washes out dark scenes and glow; even a dimmable gym with window light needs high-contrast colours and readable scenery rather than reliance on darkness. If the room cannot get dark, keep the night-market story through props and labels but adjust the palette, or move spooky play indoors after dark.
cards.use_when: A creator requests a glowing night market, neon world, or dim horror scene in MR.
do: Ask whether lights can be turned off or only dimmed
Use strong contrast and visible scenery when ambient light remains
Reserve darkness-dependent scares and glow for suitably dark venues
avoid: Promising darkness when windows or fixed lights remain
Making faint glow the only way to read objectives
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Simplify a first VR round before adding content
cards.text: For children trying VR for the first time, make the first 4-minute round teach through play: brief instructions, a simple ordered route, few hazards, and checkpoint labels that make the next goal obvious. Start near the low end of the engine's 4 to 10 checkpoints rather than filling the short session with navigation complexity. Avoid intense horror and startling events that could provoke running, especially in a race with teachers and classmates watching.
cards.use_when: Planning a short MR session for VR newcomers, especially primary-school groups.
do: Keep instructions short and demonstrate the goal
Start near four checkpoints with a simple route and few hazards
Use wonder and cooperative cheering rather than intense fear
avoid: Long tutorials inside an already short round
Dense hazards or complex routing for first-time players
Sudden scares that could make children run
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Deliver an NPC voice request as staged story beats
cards.text: Do not promise spoken NPC dialogue or conversation when a creator asks for a character such as Mae Nak to talk: the engine supports neither NPC conversations nor voice chat. Offer the closest supported storytelling by putting her short lines into ordered checkpoint labels, establishing relationships on the intro card, and using scenery and lighting changes for escalating dread. This preserves character presence without inventing an unavailable mechanic.
cards.use_when: A creator approves the story but asks for a character to speak or converse with the player.
do: Write the character's short lines into ordered checkpoint labels
Use the intro card to establish relationships and motivation
Build dread with scenery, lighting, and reveals between beats
avoid: Promising recorded speech or interactive conversation
Adding a mechanic merely because it fits the horror theme
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Size a busy booth for queue flow, not maximum play
cards.text: For a walk-in booth with long queues, choose round length and simultaneous players after measuring only the clear floor, excluding counters and other obstacles. A 4 x 4 m MR area with a corner obstruction supports about 1-2 players safely; solo rounds of roughly 3 minutes maximize throughput, while 5 minutes gives a fuller experience. Show a live leaderboard on a spectator screen so people in the queue can follow scores without entering the play area.
cards.use_when: Designing a public MR attraction where session turnover and waiting spectators matter
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Redirect impossible wishes to the feeling behind them
cards.text: When a creator requests shooting or a mascot that can answer children's questions, state the limitation clearly and offer the closest achievable experience: swordplay against slowly approaching enemies for action, or a visible mascot that welcomes players, cheers successful hits and waves at the finish for character presence. Confirm that the substitute is acceptable, then continue the interview rather than dwelling on the refusal or implying the feature exists.
cards.use_when: A creator asks for combat or character interaction the available engine cannot support
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Make branded action welcoming for young first-time players
cards.text: For elementary-age children new to headsets, express the brand through visible, nonverbal details such as a brand-coloured sword and a mascot that greets and cheers. Keep the climax cute rather than frightening, and combine simple action with a visible score goal when the creator wants both excitement and competition. Capture requests made after option selection, such as sword colours and boss tone, as explicit prototype art direction.
cards.use_when: Turning a family brand brief into a child-friendly action-game prototype
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Turn one headset into a social score race
cards.text: When friends want to compete but share one headset, design short solo turns with a visible score or survival-time leaderboard rather than simultaneous multiplayer. Waiting friends can watch and cheer from outside the play area, but should never receive a task inside it. A wish for both scares and "who survives longest" calls for horror staging plus a score race, not necessarily cooperative play.
cards.use_when: A group requests competition, survival, or shared play with limited hardware.
do: Ask how many headsets are available before proposing multiplayer
Use sequential scored turns and a spectator-visible leaderboard
avoid: Promising simultaneous multiplayer when the group shares one headset
Giving waiting friends roles inside the play area
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Convert rough room descriptions into a safe floor plan
cards.text: When an MR creator cannot give metres, ask for an estimate in walking steps or a comparison with a familiar room, then verify it before building. Measure the floor after movable tables are cleared and record fixed obstacles such as a corner sofa. Keep routes 1.2 m wide, put nothing on real obstacles, and keep action at least 0.6 m from the area edge.
cards.use_when: The creator describes an MR venue only approximately or mentions furniture.
do: Ask for steps or a familiar-room comparison when dimensions are unknown
Verify the cleared floor and preserve 1.2 m routes and 0.6 m edge clearance
avoid: Treating a step estimate as an exact build dimension
Placing virtual scenery over a sofa or other fixed obstacle
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Stage MR horror with dim light and safe pressure
cards.text: For MR horror, ask when play happens and whether the lights can be dimmed: bright daylight washes out dark scenes and glow, while controllable indoor light keeps them readable. If one startle feels too ordinary, increase dread through pacing and slow enemies approaching from behind or the edges, not by adding sudden scares that make players run. Keep startling moments away from hazards and avoid tasks that require looking up while moving quickly.
cards.use_when: A creator wants zombies, jump scares, pursuit, or friends to scream.
do: Ask about time of day and control over room lights
Build pressure with slow approaching enemies and visible warnings
avoid: Relying on dark visuals in bright daylight
Using repeated untelegraphed jump scares that could trigger running
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Fit a branded battle into a three-minute mall queue
cards.text: A 4 x 4 m mall booth with a corner counter and a long queue can support a 3-minute solo MR sword battle for elementary-age visitors. Assume most children are new to VR, use immediate one-action onboarding, keep the counter out of the cleared route, and show the live leaderboard to parents and people waiting. A mascot that cannot converse can still welcome players and cheer at the start and finish. Plan VR for ages 10 and up, with close adult supervision for younger children.
cards.use_when: Designing a high-throughput MR booth for children, families, and passing spectators.
do: Target a 3-minute solo round with immediate onboarding
Show the leaderboard to parents and the queue
Use the mascot as a nonverbal greeter and cheerleader
avoid: Using a long tutorial for first-time young players
Making the mascot converse when the engine cannot support dialogue
Hiding the score from the queue
cards.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

cards.title: Explain follow-ups and confirm the brief before designing
cards.text: Keep a fixed set of required design fields, but make follow-up questions adaptive and briefly explain why each non-obvious question matters. End the interview with a one-screen brief covering concept, players, group size, VR experience, intended feelings, venue or environment, session length and play mode, then require an explicit confirmation or edit. Never request personal data while trying to fill design gaps.
cards.use_when: Starting a creator interview or deciding whether enough information exists to propose games
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Set intended feelings before choosing mechanics
cards.text: Choose the intended player experience early, using the 8 MDA aesthetics: sensation, fantasy, narrative, challenge, fellowship, discovery, expression and submission. Designers reason from mechanics toward aesthetics, but players encounter the resulting feelings first, so record the aesthetic goals before selecting a genre or mechanic. Reuse those goals later as criteria for judging generated content and alternatives, with fellowship especially relevant to group play.
cards.use_when: Turning a creator's broad wish into design goals or evaluating whether options preserve the desired experience
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Offer three genuinely different options with visible trade-offs
cards.text: Present three options, each with a pitch, core loop, player and venue fit, risks, scores for fun, player fit, platform fit and buildability, plus one recommendation. Declare different design axes such as dominant aesthetic, core mechanic and social structure, and verify that the options differ on at least two axes so they do not collapse into one game with three skins. A small set suits non-experts comparing complex whole-game concepts, while alternatives also elicit more critical feedback and reduce fixation better than a single proposal.
cards.use_when: Generating concept choices for a non-expert creator
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Keep the creator in charge of the AI recommendation
cards.text: The AI may recommend one option, but the creator makes the final choice and can request changes before anything is built. Explain how every score was derived rather than showing bare numbers, because scores and recommendations can induce acceptance even when the advice is wrong. Where over-reliance is a concern, ask the creator to state an initial preference before revealing the AI recommendation, while accepting that this extra step may feel less smooth.
cards.use_when: Presenting scores and a recommended concept without letting the AI quietly take over the decision
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Require fresh input after an MR interruption
cards.text: When a player removes the headset or the session pauses, do not resume movement or attacks from a button that was already held. Wait until every control is released, then require a new press so the game cannot continue acting on its own while the player is disoriented.
cards.use_when: Designing pause, resume, or headset removal behavior for a physically played MR game
do: Clear held input on pause and require release followed by a fresh press on resume
Playtest interruptions while movement or attack controls are held
avoid: Resuming immediately from the input state captured before the interruption
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

cards.title: Separate enemy roles by silhouette, not recoloring
cards.text: Give each enemy type a distinct silhouette so players can read its role at a glance, and reserve palette swaps for elemental variants, teams, or skins of the same type. A small role named palette can keep colors consistent across a cast, with emissive accents limited to focal details such as eyes or a core.
cards.use_when: Creating key art or a model palette for a game with several enemy roles and themed variants
do: Test enemy recognition as solid black silhouettes
Reuse one shape with themed colors only when its gameplay role stays the same
avoid: Making different enemy roles differ only by color
Adding glow everywhere instead of using it to mark focal details
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

cards.title: Compare parallel concepts before refining one
cards.text: Develop several concepts in parallel before investing in one detailed design. Research on parallel prototyping links it to better design results, greater divergence, and increased self-efficacy, so use the creator's comparison and critique to reveal preferences. Keep each alternative quick to assess, then refine the chosen direction.
cards.use_when: A creator has a broad brief and needs to choose a game direction without becoming anchored to the first proposal.
do: Make the alternatives differ in a consequential design dimension, not just theme or naming
Ask the creator to compare the options before converging on one
avoid: Presenting three superficial variations of one idea as meaningful alternatives
Refining the first generated concept before the creator has compared directions
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Clarify only ambiguity that changes the design
cards.text: When a brief is vague, ask the clarification whose answer would most change the design, rather than running through a full questionnaire. Work on eliciting preferences and selectively clarifying ambiguous questions supports using dialogue to expose consequential unknowns. For low-impact gaps, state a provisional assumption and keep the conversation moving.
cards.use_when: A creator gives an ambiguous or incomplete request and the next useful question is unclear.
do: Identify ambiguity that would materially change the experience or its feasibility
State provisional assumptions for minor details and invite correction
avoid: Using a long questionnaire to resolve every uncertainty
Asking detailed questions whose answers would not change the proposed game
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Use deliberate variation to counter design fixation
cards.text: Treat polished AI-generated concepts as prompts, not as evidence that the right direction has been found. Research on generative AI and design fixation makes deliberate divergence important: vary a fundamental design dimension between proposals and ask the creator what possibility is missing. This prevents surface-level variations from masquerading as exploration.
cards.use_when: The first generated proposal looks convincing and subsequent ideas are beginning to resemble it.
do: Change a core mechanic, player role, or experience goal between alternatives
Ask what direction is absent before selecting a concept
avoid: Letting visual polish make the first proposal feel settled
Generating more ideas without changing their underlying design assumptions
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Build the mission and route before the scenery
cards.text: Generate a level in two stages: first turn the brief and intended feelings into a mission, ordered objectives and playable route, then dress that route with theme and scenery. This keeps decoration from determining play and makes failures easier to locate: repair the mission or route before adjusting visual layout.
cards.use_when: Turning a creative brief into a playable level layout
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Separate meaningful level design from geometric placement
cards.text: Let the design model specify relations such as before, beside, visible from and clear of, while a solver places objects and enforces geometry. Well-formed output does not prove a meaningful or playable level, so validate semantics separately and use a path-planning agent to test reachability and walkability on the actual MR floor plan. Track schema failures, rule violations and meaning failures separately rather than treating every rejection as the same problem.
cards.use_when: Generating and validating layouts for a real play space
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Playtest with contrasting personas and brief-based targets
cards.text: Create 4 to 6 personas from the intended audience and play styles, such as curious child, cautious parent with child, goal-rusher and wanderer, then run at least 30 seeded simulations per persona per level. Fit walking speed and dwell time to a few real headset traces, and measure completion, session time against the brief, area coverage, idle or lost time, crowding, near-misses, boundary clearance and checkpoint reachability. Judge success against the original players, target session and intended feelings, not merely whether the level can be completed.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a generated MR level before inviting players
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Measure whether generated options truly offer different games
cards.text: Do not assume three proposals are meaningfully different because their themes differ. Plot the three options, and outputs across many briefs, on two-dimensional comparisons such as pacing against spatial spread, then check whether options separate and different briefs produce different level shapes. Use the results to revise generation toward genuinely distinct play experiences.
cards.use_when: Presenting divergent design options to a creator
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Preserve creator agency when scoring options
cards.text: Let the creator rank or choose among design options before revealing the AI's preferred option, so the recommendation does not anchor their judgment. Show what each score is derived from and explicitly mark uncertain scores rather than presenting a bare number. Allow remixing, such as taking the mechanic from option B and the theme from option A, then regenerate the combined design.
cards.use_when: Presenting and comparing AI-generated game concepts with a creator.
do: Let the creator rank or select options before revealing the AI recommendation.
Explain each score's inputs, flag uncertainty, and record acceptance or override rates.
Support combinations such as the mechanic from one option and the theme from another, then regenerate.
avoid: Leading with the AI recommendation and anchoring the creator.
Showing unexplained scores as if they were certain.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Approve a complete paper prototype before building
cards.text: After the creator picks a concept and before building, make a paper prototype with a logline, 3 design pillars, a 4 to 6 colour palette, key art, a 3 to 4 panel session storyboard, screen contents, minute-by-minute flow, and a top-down level sketch. Add 2 to 4 questions that a later playtest must answer. Revise as often as needed from creator comments, keep every version, and require the build plan to follow the approved prototype.
cards.use_when: Turning a selected game option into an agreed, buildable design.
do: Prepare a logline, three pillars, visual direction, storyboard, flow, level sketch, and playtest questions.
Revise from creator comments and retain each version.
Make the approved prototype the contract for the build plan.
avoid: Building a playable level before the experience has been agreed.
Omitting the playtest questions or allowing the build to drift from approval.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Do not let the first image choose the game
cards.text: Keep the initial game options text-only so an attractive generated picture does not decide which concept the creator selects. Once prototyping begins, treat key art as a cheap visual hypothesis and drive revisions from the creator's comments rather than attachment to the first image. This preserves exploration of visual directions while letting the creator judge experience goals before production geometry.
cards.use_when: Using text-to-image generation during concept selection or visual prototyping.
do: Keep initial concept comparisons text-only.
Treat generated key art as a disposable visual hypothesis.
Generate alternatives when comments reveal a different desired experience.
avoid: Attaching generated images to the initial options.
Treating the first attractive image as a settled art direction.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Generate the MR route from the real venue
cards.text: For room-scale passthrough MR, treat the real venue as visible game context and change only the floor layer. Put the venue's size, indoor or outdoor status, lighting, walls, and spectators into the design brief, then fit the route to the detected walkable floor while keeping clear of walls and using the available area. Real walking is the only locomotion, so every path and interaction must remain reachable within that actual room.
cards.use_when: Designing a passthrough MR game for a specific physical room or venue.
do: Gather size, indoor or outdoor setting, light, walls, and spectator presence.
Generate content on detected walkable floor and fit the route to that room.
Use real surroundings as visible context while replacing only the floor.
avoid: Assuming the virtual world can hide the venue.
Adding joystick locomotion or placing content outside the walkable floor.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Capture the venue as structured play data
cards.text: Before laying out an MR game, record walls, exits, obstacles, spectator zones and lighting as structured data rather than a prose description. Snap content to real planes and adapt placement to the room's physical and social context, because site conditions shape play and plane snapping makes placement faster and better. Keep real people and objects visible: this improves usability with little loss of immersion.
cards.use_when: Turning an MR venue description into a playable layout
do: Ask for walls, exits, obstacles, spectator positions and light conditions.
Use real walls, views and audiences as part of the scene.
avoid: Inventing a replacement virtual room when the real room can support play.
Treating venue notes as unstructured flavor text.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Give spectators a deliberate viewing plan
cards.text: MR spectators see players' bodies but not the virtual floor, so add a spectator plan to both the brief and the build. Specify where they stand, provide a shared screen view such as a leaderboard or floor projection, and stage dodges and finishes where their reactions are easy to read. Friends and parents can cheer or call hints, but never assign them a task inside the play area.
cards.use_when: Designing an MR game that friends, parents or an audience will watch
do: Choose a safe spectator zone outside the route.
Make important player actions visible without seeing the headset view.
Use a shared display for game state or results.
avoid: Placing spectators inside the walking course.
Assuming bystanders can understand play from the virtual action alone.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Budget walking comfort and bystander safety
cards.text: Real walking gives more natural movement and presence than walking-in-place or flying, so keep it but budget session length, route length, rest points and stricter limits for children; screen comfort with the SSQ when testing. Keep routes 1.2 m clear, content off real obstacles and at least 0.6 m from area edges, with no sudden scares or fast walking while looking up. Warn about nearby bystanders with combined audio and visual distance cues, which work better than either cue alone.
cards.use_when: Setting MR route length, session duration and safety behavior
do: Include rest points and child-appropriate session limits.
Playtest fatigue, dizziness and route clearance.
Pair visual proximity warnings with audio.
avoid: Maximizing walking distance to make an experience feel substantial.
Using surprise effects that could trigger running.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Let code verify geometry while the model designs meaning
cards.text: Have the model generate layout candidates inside a schema and external validation loop rather than asking it to verify its own spatial reasoning. Build in two stages, route first and scenery second outside a computed keep-clear corridor, with code auto-fixing small geometry slips and at most 2 feedback-driven repair rounds. This division matters: LLM-only repairs reduced blocking objects only from 38 to 30 to 24, while code fixed them in one pass.
cards.use_when: Building or repairing an AI-generated MR floor layout
do: Validate structure and gameplay meaning externally.
Reserve a clear corridor before placing decoration.
Cap model repair rounds at 2 and let code handle deterministic fixes.
avoid: Relying on repeated self-critique to solve precise geometry.
Placing scenery before the route is verified.
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Use bots to rank levels, not replace players
cards.text: Treat automated playtesting as decision support: correlate bot and judge predictions with real players on the same levels before trusting them. An LLM judge can score intended aesthetics plus player and venue fit, using randomized option order, several samples or models with agreement reported, length caps, and independent checking rather than unchecked self-judging. Compute safety as a hard gate from telemetry, never as an LLM opinion.
cards.use_when: Using simulated players or LLM judges to evaluate and revise a generated level
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Playtest the intended feeling at the venue
cards.text: Compare the revised level against the unrevised version with players in the actual venue, and ask directly whether they felt each intended feeling. Use PXI as the main experience scale rather than GEQ, whose factor structure did not replicate; measure sickness with SSQ before and after. In MR passthrough, interpret presence items about realness carefully, and keep questionnaires short: in-headset items can change response variance without changing means.
cards.use_when: Planning an experience playtest, especially for an MR game in its real venue
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Make child playtests short, consented and observable
cards.text: Obtain parental consent and the child's own assent, secure ethics approval first, and allow either to stop the session at any time. Keep sessions short, screen for sickness, use pictorial short-form questions, and include parent observation. Do not rely on an adult's consent or questionnaire responses alone to infer that a child is comfortable.
cards.use_when: Playtesting a game with children or family groups
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Keep the creator in control of AI recommendations
cards.text: Make alternatives differ on explicitly declared axes and verify that difference, so the creator avoids fixation on minor variations of one idea. Explain the basis of scores and recommendations. Let the creator rank the options before revealing the AI's preferred pick, reducing over-reliance while preserving a useful recommendation.
cards.use_when: Presenting AI-generated game options or recommending one direction to a creator
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

cards.title: Define a session policy for lost player tracking
cards.text: For a tracked multiplayer MR session, decide in advance what happens when a required player is lost: pause the session initially, preserve their last visible position if useful, and remove them from actions, collisions, and scoring. Add a grace period only after measuring real tracking losses, rather than letting stale positions affect play. This keeps races and shared-floor sessions fair and avoids unsafe confusion around a stationary avatar.
cards.use_when: Designing multiplayer MR play where tracking loss could disrupt safety or scoring
do: Pause when a required player loses tracking
Exclude lost players from scoring and interactions
Tune grace periods from measured session data
avoid: Letting stale positions keep scoring or colliding
Inventing a grace period before real measurements
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Verify shared MR tracking with real players
cards.text: Before promising a shared-floor MR game, test the full intended player count with independent tracked people, not bots or keyboard substitutes. Simulated fallbacks can hide a failed real-player lookup, while a healthy global signal can hide one rejected player, so monitor connection, last valid update, and position validity per player. Repeat the test after reconnects and roster changes, with explicit recovery when tracking is lost.
cards.use_when: Prototyping or playtesting multiplayer MR with tracked players
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Design the active roster before multiplayer play
cards.text: Define the actual active roster separately from technical capacity: for a 2 to 4 player game, give every participant a stable slot and a unique physical tracker identity. Size ready screens, play lanes and result attribution for that roster, and explicitly test three players as well as two and four so an odd-sized group does not expose silent bot substitution or layout assumptions.
cards.use_when: Planning or playtesting a tracked multiplayer floor game
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Make tracking loss a fair game state
cards.text: For each player, specify what missing, predicted and invalid position input means during play instead of treating one latest position as proof that everyone is tracked. Decide what silence does, such as pausing that player rather than registering steps or failures, and test dropout and recovery with real bodies before accepting the design.
cards.use_when: Defining movement rules and failure handling for physical tracking
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Choose floor triggers and test bodily interference
cards.text: Choose explicitly whether an action requires a foot press, remaining in a tracked spot for a dwell, or a test-only input; clear action state at each round and define whether LED feedback should hold. On site, test simultaneous players, path crossings, occlusions, dropouts and recovery, and record measured update rate, latency and position error rather than trusting configuration values.
cards.use_when: Prototyping tracked floor interactions or multiplayer movement
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Test tracked groups with simulated players disabled
cards.text: For a tracked group game, verify every player slot with a real participant before judging movement, pacing, or lane balance. In Deepspace, slots P3 to P6 silently became bots moving at 1.7 m/s whenever a real pose was unavailable, so a full-looking six-player test could hide broken tracking. Use stable player-to-tracker assignments, check each participant individually, and keep simulated players as an explicit test mode rather than an invisible fallback.
cards.use_when: Preparing or playtesting an MR game with several tracked participants
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Make tracking loss visibly fail safe
cards.text: Treat missing, stale, or out-of-area tracking as unavailable input, not as a valid position at the nearest edge. Clamped coordinates and automatic fallback actors can make the game appear responsive while outcomes no longer match the player's body. Pause scoring and hazard consequences for that player, show a clear tracking-loss state, and resume only after their position is valid again; a connected receiver alone does not prove that every player is tracked.
cards.use_when: Designing recovery and feedback for body-tracked MR play
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Stage the boss entrance before play begins
cards.text: Give a boss fight a short, unambiguous opening beat: the portal grows from zero to full size, the boss emerges, the portal shrinks away, and only then does play begin. A one-time entrance separates anticipation from action, makes the boss arrival memorable, and prevents players from mistaking the introduction for a moment when they should already react.
cards.use_when: Designing the opening presentation and readiness cue for a battle game's boss encounter.
do: Play the portal opening and boss emergence once per fight
Delay active play until the entrance has finished
Close the portal by shrinking it to mark the transition into play
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Start boss rosters equal, then tune by feel
cards.text: For repeated boss fights, select from a boss roster with weighted randomness so encounters vary without requiring new mechanics. Start with equal weights, test each boss individually, then adjust frequencies only after learning which encounters deserve to appear more or less often; weights alter relative likelihood, not a guaranteed fraction over a few sessions.
cards.use_when: Choosing how often different bosses appear across repeated battle sessions.
avoid: Treating a weight as a guaranteed appearance percentage
Tuning roster frequency before every boss has been tested individually
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Treat tracking loss as a participation state
cards.text: When a player's position stops updating, freezing their avatar is not enough: scoring, hazards and other rules may still act on the stale position. Mark that player explicitly unavailable, pause or exclude their participation according to one consistent policy, and preserve their identity when tracking returns rather than silently assigning another input source. This matters most in shared-floor or competitive play, where a dropout must not create an unfair hit, score or ownership change.
cards.use_when: Designing multiplayer play where player positions can drop out or become stale
do: Expose unavailable as an explicit player state
Use one consistent pause or exclusion policy
Restore the same player identity on recovery
avoid: Letting stale coordinates keep scoring
Silently switching a player to another input source
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Validate readiness with a fresh player action
cards.text: A selection countdown can force a session to start, but it cannot prove that every player is present and tracked; the source's 50-second timer could force readiness without validating players. Require a fresh, attributable action such as a step, press or hold before marking each player ready, and keep that one-time readiness signal separate from continuous movement input. Revalidate a player after hardware loss instead of treating an old position or held input as consent to continue.
cards.use_when: Onboarding several tracked players before a timed or competitive session
do: Confirm each player with a new deliberate action
Separate readiness events from movement targets
Recheck readiness after tracking loss
avoid: Using a timeout alone as proof that players are ready
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Build boss chapters from four waves
cards.text: For a chaptered action game, start with four enemy waves before each boss; tuning converged on four after trying three, four, and five. You can remove pauses between waves for relentless pressure while retaining a separate stage-transition countdown and a pause after the boss dies, giving intensity a clear beginning and end.
cards.use_when: Pacing chapters and bosses in a battle game
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Give respawning players three seconds of grace
cards.text: Start with about 3 seconds of post-respawn protection, rather than 1.5 seconds, so players can reorient before taking damage again. Treat this as a playtest starting point, not a universal value: the doubled timing came from a different death model, so immediate danger, spawn position, and whether the player loses health or is destroyed all affect the right grace period.
cards.use_when: Tuning deaths, respawns, and early-game frustration
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Make shared-station turn order survive walkaways
cards.text: When several visitors share an interactive station, establish priority in join order at each round reset and whenever the active player changes. A visitor who steps away and later returns should rejoin the queue rather than reclaim an old turn; this keeps ownership legible and prevents stale claims from blocking newcomers.
cards.use_when: Designing turn-taking for a public or group installation
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Leave room for tracking lag in walking challenges
cards.text: For position-tracked walking games, tune interactions for delayed and smoothed movement rather than instant input: this setup caps normal UWB motion at 1.8 m/s, predicts at most 0.35 seconds ahead, and treats poses older than 1 second as stale. Use broad checkpoints and hazards, avoid rapid precision dodges, and never depend on movements finer than the 0.08 m position dead zone. Test recovery after tracking errors as well as normal play, since position jumps over 0.75 m may be rejected.
cards.use_when: Setting hazard sizes, movement speed, or dodge timing in a tracked walking game
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Make floor input recover from stuck sensors
cards.text: On pressure-sensitive floors, expect debris, water, a dropped bag, or an overly sensitive sensor to report a press that never ends. Temporarily ignore a cell held longer than any intentional player stance, then restore it automatically after it goes quiet; provide a test view that distinguishes active and muted cells. Set the hold timeout well above the longest deliberate stand, and the gap tolerance above the controller repeat interval of roughly 10–170 ms, so normal packet gaps do not reset the hold.
cards.use_when: Building or playtesting a game that uses a pressure-sensitive floor
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Design foot input for repeats and sensor faults
cards.text: A pressure floor repeats an occupied cell several times per second and provides no release event, so game actions must tolerate repeated messages rather than assume clean press and release pairs.
