Trigger once per footfall or deliberately accumulate dwell time, preserve each packet's arrival time, and discard stale packets because a delayed frame is indistinguishable from a new step. Temporarily mute cells that stay active longer than a real step, and show muted cells differently from fresh presses so faults are visible without becoming gameplay input.
cards.use_when: Building or playtesting interactions driven by stepping on sensor cells
do: Debounce repeated cell events or intentionally accumulate them into dwell actions
Timestamp arriving steps and reject stale input
Mute abnormally long activations and distinguish them in diagnostics
avoid: Scoring once for every repeated sensor packet
Depending on a hardware release event
Treating a stuck cell as continuous player intent
cards.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

cards.title: Thai temple night festival: gold, deep indigo, lantern orange
cards.text: Palette: #1f1b4d night indigo, #d4a017 temple gold, #f28c28 lantern orange, #2e8b57 banyan green, #e0262b hazard red. Reads best indoors or after dark: the gold and lantern orange glow against indigo. In MR daylight the indigo turns grey and the gold looks flat, so switch the lighting preset to evening and lean on gold rather than glow. The hazard colour #e0262b (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.
cards.use_when: A Thai temple fair, wat at night, merit-making festival, naga and temple scenery
do: Put the 5 hex values straight into art.palette and name them in lang
Scenery theme to pair: ow-himmaphan, Thai temples from Thai Halloween
Keep the hazard colour only on danger (rings, enemy tells, cracked squares)
avoid: Adding a second red or orange to the decor, it steals the warning signal

cards.title: Songkran water fight: splash cyan, white, sunny yellow
cards.text: Palette: #19b5e6 splash cyan, #f7f7f2 powder white, #ffd23f sunny yellow, #ff6fa8 flower pink, #d7263d hazard red. Made for MR daylight outdoors: high-value cyan and yellow survive bright sun, and white reads as wet stone. Indoors under warm light it still works but tone the white to cream so it does not glare in the headset. The hazard colour #d7263d (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.
cards.use_when: A Songkran, water, summer splash or beach festival brief, especially outdoor and noon
do: Put the 5 hex values straight into art.palette and name them in lang
Scenery theme to pair: ow-village, ow-reef props, bazaar stalls

cards.title: Art style is always stylized low-poly, flat shaded: vary mood, not technique
cards.text: Every FortalLand game uses the same 1,900+ low-poly flat-shaded models, so the prototype art must promise exactly that. Vary the mood with palette, lighting preset and silhouette size, never with realistic, painted, pixel or anime styles that the build cannot match.
cards.use_when: Writing art.style and art.prompt_style for any prototype
do: Start art.style with "low-poly" in lang
Describe mood words: cozy, eerie, epic, festive
Name the lighting preset you expect (noon, evening, spooky, neon)
avoid: "Realistic", "photoreal", "cel-shaded anime", "pixel art" in prompt_style
Promising textures or detail the catalog lacks

cards.title: MR key art: first-person through the headset, real room visible, only the floor changed
cards.text: For MR the honest key art is the player view: a real room (walls, windows, people) with the game floor replacing only the real floor and low-poly objects standing on it. The code already adds the MR view line, so the prompt should describe the real room concretely (a school hall with windows, a living room sofa at the edge).
cards.use_when: key_art.prompt for any MR game
do: Name 2 real room details from the brief environment
Put the game objects at 1-4 m distance on the floor
Include a hand or controller at the bottom edge only if needed, kept simple
avoid: Virtual sky, walls or ceilings replacing the real room
Showing the player flying or running

cards.title: MR alternative: over-the-shoulder of a player in the real room
cards.text: A third-person shot of a person wearing a headset in the real space, with the virtual floor and objects drawn around them, explains MR to people who have never tried it. Use it when the brief stresses spectators or families watching.
cards.use_when: MR games for events, first-time VR players, or where the creator must pitch to others
do: Show one player from behind at waist height, 2-3 m away
Show spectators at the edge of the frame, outside the play area
avoid: More than 2 players in frame, FLUX blends faces and limbs
Visible text on the headset

cards.title: PC battle key art: low third-person behind the hero mid-combo
cards.text: Camera 2-3 m behind and slightly above the sword hero, the boss or a beast charging in from the far side, a red warning ring on the ground between them. One clear action pose (sword swing or dash) sells the 3-hit combo and dash in one frame.
cards.use_when: key_art.prompt for a PC battle game
do: Describe one hero, one big enemy and at most 3 small grunts in the distance
Name the theme ground (ice, lava, forest)
avoid: Crowds of enemies, FLUX merges them into mush
Guns, bows or magic bolts the engine lacks

cards.title: MR battle key art: player view, controller as sword, enemies walking in from the room edge
cards.text: Show the player view in the real room: a low-poly sword where the right controller would be, 2-3 grunts or a shield enemy walking slowly in from the wall side, a red ring glowing at the player's feet. This is exactly what the MR battle engine does, so the picture does not overpromise.
cards.use_when: key_art.prompt for an MR battle game
do: Enemies 2-4 m away at the real floor edge
Red ring near the bottom of the frame
avoid: Enemies jumping from the ceiling or walls
Player running or leaping

cards.title: Tactics key art: high three-quarter view of the whole 6 x 8 board
cards.text: A board game sells through its board. Use a high 45-60 degree view showing the whole board, the player piece (knight, rook...) as a large figurine, 1-2 guard pieces and a glowing target square. In MR show the board lying on the real floor of the room.
cards.use_when: key_art.prompt for a tactics game on PC or MR
do: Say "6 by 8 checkered board seen from a high angle"
Name the player piece type
One target clearly highlighted
avoid: Close-ups where the grid is not visible
Asking FLUX for exact square counts; accept roughly a board

cards.title: Runner key art: looking down the route toward the portal
cards.text: Put the camera at walking height looking along the route: a checkpoint marker close, one red hazard circle on the path, and the glowing portal at the far end framed by theme scenery. The eye travels the route the way the player will.
cards.use_when: key_art.prompt for a runner on PC or MR
do: One leading line (path) from bottom to the portal
One hazard and one checkpoint, no more
avoid: A route shown from too high, it reads as a map not a game
Many hazards that make it look impossible

cards.title: Pick the climax moment, not the start screen
cards.text: Only one picture is drawn, so draw the storyboard climax: the boss turning, the last target captured, the portal opening. A start-of-game picture looks empty and sells nothing.
cards.use_when: Choosing what key_art.prompt shows
do: Copy the climax panel action into the prompt
Write the caption as a short exciting line in lang
avoid: Menus, title cards or lobby scenes
The quiet tutorial area

cards.title: FLUX schnell draws text, hands and crowds badly: design around them
cards.text: FLUX schnell is fast but garbles letters, fuses fingers and melts groups of more than 2-3 characters. Keep prompts to one hero subject, few secondary shapes, no readable signs, and hands either hidden or holding a simple object.
cards.use_when: Writing any key_art.prompt
do: Max 1 main character and 3 minor ones
Say "blank sign" or omit signs
Use big simple props instead of detailed hands
avoid: Scoreboards, banners with words, logos
Close-up hands, dancing groups, crowds

cards.title: Key art prompt order: camera, subject, action, setting, light
cards.text: The code appends the view, the low-poly style and the palette, so the prompt itself should be 1-3 sentences in this order: camera angle, main subject, what happens, setting, light. 40-90 English words is enough; longer prompts dilute the subject.
cards.use_when: Writing key_art.prompt text
do: Example: "Low angle behind a small knight, a giant ice beast charges across a frozen arena, a red warning ring glows between them, cold blue dusk light."
avoid: Repeating the style or palette (code adds it)
Thai words in the prompt, it is checked and rejected

cards.title: No HUD, score or words in the key art
cards.text: The picture is an in-game moment without interface, so health bars, timers and titles stay out of key_art.prompt. HUD is listed separately in hud. Words in the prompt make FLUX draw fake letters, which look broken and cannot be translated.
cards.use_when: Any key art that mentions score, timers or titles
do: Describe the HUD in hud only
Convey score with visual objects (a glowing target, a portal)
avoid: "with the title FortalLand at the top"
"score 300 shown"

cards.title: MR key art must not replace the real walls or sky
cards.text: Only the floor changes in MR, so a key art with a fantasy sky or castle walls around the player promises something the headset will never show. Big scenery should stand on the floor and be lower than the real room, or be marked VR only.
cards.use_when: MR prototypes with grand themes (castle, space, ocean)
do: Put towers or trees on the floor inside the room
Let the real ceiling or sky stay visible
avoid: Full fantasy skyboxes
Underwater fog filling the whole room

cards.title: Titles: 1-3 words, sayable in Thai and English, one concrete image
cards.text: A good title is short enough to shout across a venue and names one concrete thing: "Lantern Run", "Naga Gate", "Ice Knight". Thai players should be able to say the English or the Thai version without awkward sounds. Avoid generic words like "Adventure", "Quest", "World" on their own.
cards.use_when: Writing prototype.title
do: Noun + verb or adjective + noun
Check it is under 16 characters
Offer a Thai form that keeps the same image
avoid: "Super Fun Adventure Game"
Puns that only work in one language
Brand names you do not own

cards.title: Title examples that work bilingually
cards.text: Examples: "Krathong Glow", "Ghost Market Dash", "Knight of Ice", "Tuk-Tuk Rush", "Dino Steps", "Temple Chess". Each names the theme and hints at the verb in 2-3 words.
cards.use_when: Needing inspiration for a title in th or en
do: Mirror the core loop verb (dash, steps, guard, catch)
avoid: Copying existing game or film titles

cards.title: Logline: you are X, you do Y, because Z is fun
cards.text: One sentence: who the player is, what they physically do, and the hook. "You are the last lantern keeper, walking the night river to relight 6 krathongs before the ghosts drift in." It must describe the real verb of the genre (walk, step out of rings, swing, move like a knight).
cards.use_when: Writing prototype.logline
do: Include a number (6 lanterns, 3 chapters, 90 seconds)
Use the genre verb
avoid: Abstract taglines ("an unforgettable journey")
Verbs the engine lacks (shoot, build, talk)

cards.title: Pillars must be testable choices, not adjectives
cards.text: A pillar is a rule every part must serve, so it must be able to reject ideas. "Every danger is seen 2 seconds before it hits" rejects instant traps; "Fun and exciting" rejects nothing. Write 3 pillars: one for feeling, one for play, one for the real space or players.
cards.use_when: Writing the 3 prototype.pillars
do: Good: "Kids can finish without reading"
Good: "Spectators see every big moment"
Good: "Always one step from safety"
avoid: Vague: "Beautiful graphics", "Immersive", "Fun for everyone"
3 pillars that all say the same thing
cards.source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

cards.title: Derive one pillar from each top MDA feeling in the brief
cards.text: Map the brief feelings to concrete pillars: challenge becomes "Fail fast, retry in 3 seconds"; fellowship becomes "Friends race side by side and see each other"; discovery becomes "Every checkpoint reveals a new view"; submission becomes "No way to lose, only to be faster"; narrative becomes "Each checkpoint is one line of the story".
cards.use_when: Turning brief.feelings into pillars
do: Keep the MDA word out of the pillar, write the behaviour
avoid: Pillars unrelated to the brief feelings

cards.title: Battle storyboard: first wave, mixed wave, boss, victory
cards.text: Start: 2-3 slow grunts walk in, the player learns to swing. Middle: a shield enemy plus grunts, the player must hit from the side, rain rings fall. Climax: the boss or beast charges, the player steps out of a red ring and lands the combo. End: the arena calms, score and time shown.
cards.use_when: Writing storyboard panels for a battle game
do: player_does in MR: swing, turn, step out of a ring
player_does on PC: 3-hit combo, dash
avoid: A beast in the first chapter (checked)
MR players running or dodging by sprinting

cards.title: Tactics storyboard: read the board, first capture, beat the guards, last target
cards.text: Start: the player sees the board, their piece and 1-2 guards, and plans the first move. Middle: they capture targets in order while counting guard beats. Climax: the last target sits next to an attacked square and must be taken on the right beat. End: the board clears, time goes on the leaderboard.
cards.use_when: Writing storyboard panels for a tactics game
do: player_does in MR: walk onto a square
Mention the piece type in every panel
avoid: More than 2 guards on board 1 (checked)
Real-time chasing, guards move on a beat of 3 s or slower

cards.title: Runner storyboard: spawn view, first hazard, final stretch, portal
cards.text: Start: the player sees the first checkpoint and the story card. Middle: hazards appear between checkpoints, touching one sends them back. Climax: the last checkpoint and the most dramatic view (void drop, big creature). End: the portal, the score with time bonus.
cards.use_when: Writing storyboard panels for a runner
do: Tie each panel to a checkpoint label
player_does: walk to, step around, touch
avoid: Jumping, climbing or collecting items
Climax in a corner spectators cannot see

cards.title: player_does uses the body verb, not the story verb
cards.text: Captions tell the story ("The ghost queen wakes"); player_does says what the body does ("steps left out of the red ring and swings twice"). Creators judge buildability from player_does, so keep it physical and possible.
cards.use_when: Filling storyboard[].player_does
do: MR: walk, turn, step, swing, stop
PC: move with WASD, click to attack, dash
avoid: "Defeats the queen" without saying how
Verbs like shoot, pick up, talk

cards.title: Use 3 panels for 2-3 minute games, 4 for longer
cards.text: Short sessions have no real middle: start, climax, end is honest. Games of 4 minutes or more need a middle panel to show the twist or difficulty step. Each panel needs its own beat and one must be the climax.
cards.use_when: Deciding storyboard length
do: 3 panels: start, climax, end
4 panels: start, middle, climax, end
avoid: Two middle panels or no climax (checked)

cards.title: In MR put the climax where the audience can see it
cards.text: Spectators see bodies, not the game, so the climax should be a big body action (turning to face the boss, a wide step out of a ring, walking through the portal) placed on the side nearest the audience zone.
cards.use_when: MR storyboards with spectators in the brief
do: Say in the caption where the audience is
Match the climax position to the sketch zone
avoid: Climax in the far corner
Tiny hand-only actions at the climax

cards.title: Battle HUD: health, chapter, enemies left, score
cards.text: A battle player needs four facts: how much health is left, which chapter of how many, how many enemies remain, and the score. On PC add a dash cooldown. Keep it to 4-5 items.
cards.use_when: Writing hud for a battle game
do: Health hearts or bar
Chapter 2/4
Enemies left
Score
avoid: Mana, ammo or inventory slots the engine lacks

cards.title: Tactics HUD: board number, targets captured, guard beat, timer
cards.text: Tactics play is planning on a beat, so the HUD shows the board (1/5), captured targets in order (2/4), a guard beat indicator that ticks before guards move, and the race timer for the leaderboard.
cards.use_when: Writing hud for a tactics game
do: Board 1/5
Targets 2/4 in order
Guard beat ring
Timer
avoid: Move history lists or text-heavy hints

cards.title: Runner HUD: checkpoint count, score, timer, next label
cards.text: The runner engine tracks checkpoints in order, score (+100 checkpoint, -25 hazard, +300 finish) and optional time limit. Show checkpoint 3/6, the next checkpoint label as the story line, score and timer. In a race add live position.
cards.use_when: Writing hud for a runner
do: Checkpoint 3/6
Next: "Feed the dragon"
Score
Timer or time left
avoid: Lives counters, the engine resets to the last checkpoint instead

cards.title: Kids HUD: 2 items, icons not numbers
cards.text: For players under 9, show at most 2 HUD items as icons: progress (lit lanterns 3 of 6) and one danger cue. Numbers, timers and scores can live on the spectator screen for parents instead.
cards.use_when: hud when the brief players are young kids
do: Progress as icons
Move score to the end screen
avoid: Timers counting down for small kids
Text instructions in the HUD

cards.title: MR HUD stays low and few: nothing that needs looking up while walking
cards.text: In passthrough the HUD floats in view, so keep it to 2-4 items near the lower edge or on the wrist. Players walking must keep their eyes on the floor. Big messages appear only when the player is standing still (start, chapter break, end).
cards.use_when: MR hud lists
do: 2-4 items
Flash major info at stops
avoid: Long text, minimaps, top-of-view elements
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Runner flow, 2 minutes, 5 checkpoints
cards.text: 0:00 story card and first view. 0:10 checkpoint 1, an easy straight. 0:30 first hazard pair. 0:50 checkpoint 3 with the best view. 1:20 tight zig-zag hazard. 1:40 last checkpoint. 1:50 portal and score. Short loops suit spaces under 4 x 4 m.
cards.use_when: Runner sessions of 2 minutes or small MR spaces
do: About 20 s between checkpoints
avoid: More than 6 checkpoints in 2 minutes

cards.title: Runner flow, 5 minutes, 8 checkpoints with a twist
cards.text: 0:00 intro card. 0:15 checkpoints 1-2 teach hazards. 1:30 checkpoint 3, story turn. 2:30 checkpoints 4-5, denser hazards. 3:30 the dramatic view (void floor section or big creature). 4:20 checkpoint 8. 4:40 portal, score and time bonus. 4:50 leaderboard.
cards.use_when: Runner sessions of 4-6 minutes in medium or large spaces
do: Put a calm stretch after the hardest part
avoid: Same hazard density the whole time

cards.title: Battle flow, 3 minutes, 3 chapters and a boss
cards.text: 0:00 title and stance tip. 0:10 chapter 1: 3 grunts. 0:50 chapter 2: grunts plus a shield. 1:40 chapter 3: rain rings start. 2:20 boss or beast. 2:50 victory and score.
cards.use_when: Battle games in MR or PC around 3 minutes
do: MR: at most 6 enemies per chapter (checked)
5-10 s breather between chapters
avoid: A beast in chapter 1 (checked)

cards.title: Battle flow, 8 minutes, 5 chapters for PC players
cards.text: 0:00 intro. 0:20 ch1 grunts. 1:30 ch2 shields. 2:45 ch3 first beast. 4:00 ch4 rain plus mixed. 5:30 ch5 hard mix up to 9 enemies. 6:45 boss. 7:40 results. Long battles fit PC better than MR, where arms tire after about 4-5 minutes of swinging.
cards.use_when: Long battle sessions, mostly PC gamers
do: Offer a shorter MR variant
avoid: 8-minute MR sword sessions for first-time VR players
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Tactics flow, 5 minutes, 4 boards
cards.text: 0:00 rules card with the piece moves. 0:20 board 1: 2 targets, 1 guard. 1:20 board 2: 3 targets, 2 guards. 2:40 board 3: new piece, cracked squares. 3:50 board 4: guards on a faster beat. 4:45 time to leaderboard.
cards.use_when: Tactics sessions around 5 minutes
do: Change the piece or one rule per board
avoid: More than 2 guards on board 1 (checked)

cards.title: Tactics flow, 2 minutes, 2 boards for events
cards.text: 0:00 show the knight move on the floor. 0:15 board 1: 2 targets, 1 guard. 1:00 board 2: 3 targets, 2 guards. 1:50 time on the leaderboard. Short and repeatable for queues at events.
cards.use_when: Event booths with queues, first-time players
do: Keep the same piece for both boards
avoid: New rules in the last board of a short session

cards.title: Flow steps every 20-60 seconds, ending with results
cards.text: Write 4-8 flow steps from 0:00 to the end, roughly every 20-60 s, including the intro card at 0:00 and the results or leaderboard as the last step. The last timestamp should match brief.session_minutes within 15 s.
cards.use_when: Writing prototype.flow for any genre
do: Format t as "m:ss"
One sentence per step
avoid: A flow that ends at the climax with no results
Steps longer than 2 minutes

cards.title: First-time VR players: add 15-20 s of standing still at the start
cards.text: People new to headsets need a moment to look around and trust the floor. Start the flow with 15-20 s where nothing threatens them, then introduce the first verb.
cards.use_when: MR flows when brief.vr_experience is low
do: 0:00 look around, 0:15 first task
avoid: Enemies or hazards in the first 10 s
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Battle sketch: arena with player start in the middle, spawn edges as danger
cards.text: Draw a battle as shape "arena": start at the centre (0.5, 0.5), danger zones at the edges where enemies walk in (r 0.1-0.15), the boss zone on the far side, and the audience zone outside the edge where people stand.
cards.use_when: sketch for any battle game
do: danger at 2-3 edges
audience at y 0.95
avoid: Zones in the centre ring where the player stands

cards.title: Tactics sketch: board shape with start corner and goal on the far side
cards.text: Draw tactics as shape "board": start at a near corner (about 0.2, 0.85), targets as story zones, guards as danger zones, the last target as the goal near the far side. In MR add the audience beside the long edge.
cards.use_when: sketch for any tactics game
do: Use small r (0.05-0.08) so zones look like squares
avoid: A route path; boards do not need one

cards.title: Runner sketch: route with 3-12 path points in walking order
cards.text: Draw a runner as shape "route" with a path of at least 3 points (checked) in walking order, start at the first point, goal (portal) at the last, danger zones on the path between, story zones at key checkpoints. Keep points 0.08 inside the square edge for the 0.6 m safety margin.
cards.use_when: sketch for any runner
do: Loop: return near start
Zig-zag: alternate x 0.2 and 0.8
avoid: Fewer than 3 path points
Path along the very edge of the square

cards.title: MR audience zone sits outside the play area on the side the brief names
cards.text: Put the audience zone where real spectators will be (a long wall, a doorway, chairs), just outside the play area, and bend the route or arena so the climax happens on that side. Never place audience inside the walking area.
cards.use_when: MR sketches when the brief has spectators
do: audience x or y at 0.95-1.0
Climax zone within 0.3 of it
avoid: Audience in the middle of the floor
Hazards right next to the audience edge

cards.title: PC sketches skip the audience zone
cards.text: On PC spectators watch the screen, so there is no audience place in the level. Use the zones for start, goal or boss, danger and story only.
cards.use_when: sketch for a PC game
do: Spend the zone budget on story spots
avoid: Audience zones on PC levels

cards.title: Sketch with 4-8 zones: one start, one goal or boss, the rest earn their place
cards.text: Up to 10 zones are allowed but 4-8 read best. Every zone kind tells the creator something: start, goal or boss (both required by the check), 1-3 danger, 1-2 story, 1 audience in MR.
cards.use_when: Any prototype sketch
do: Name zones in lang with the story word ("Ghost Gate")
avoid: 10 tiny zones that clutter the plan
Missing start or goal (checked)

cards.title: Small MR room under 4 x 4 m: one loop, big zones
cards.text: In a living room or small classroom the sketch is a tight loop of 4-5 points with large zones (r 0.15-0.25), because a 3 m room only fits about 4 steps per side. Only runner fits below 3 m.
cards.use_when: MR sketches for small spaces
do: Loop path of 4-5 points
avoid: Long zig-zags in tiny rooms
Battle or tactics under 3 x 3 m (checked)

cards.title: Good playtest questions are observable and specific
cards.text: Ask what you can see happen, with a threshold: "Do 4 of 5 first-time players step out of the first red ring within 2 seconds?" Bad questions ask for opinions ("Is it fun?") that players answer politely and that do not tell you what to change.
cards.use_when: Writing prototype.test_questions
do: Name the player group, the moment and a number
One question per pillar
avoid: "Did you like it?"
"Is the art good?"

cards.title: Battle playtest questions
cards.text: Examples: "Do players turn to face enemies coming from behind within 3 seconds?", "How many players get hit by the first rain ring?", "Do MR players stop swinging from arm tiredness before the boss?", "Does the shield enemy make players walk around it?"
cards.use_when: test_questions for battle
do: Watch arm fatigue in MR
avoid: Asking players to rate difficulty 1-10 only

cards.title: Tactics playtest questions
cards.text: Examples: "Can a first-time player say how a knight moves after board 1?", "How many players step on an attacked square on board 2?", "Do players stop and count the guard beat or rush?", "Does anyone walk off the board edge in MR?"
cards.use_when: test_questions for tactics
do: Count mistakes per board
avoid: "Was the puzzle clever?"

cards.title: Runner playtest questions
cards.text: Examples: "Do players find checkpoint 2 without help?", "How many hazards hit per run, and where?", "Do players read the checkpoint labels aloud?", "Does anyone hesitate at the void floor edge longer than 3 seconds?"
cards.use_when: test_questions for runner
do: Mark where hazards hit on the sketch
avoid: "Was the story interesting?"

cards.title: Playtest questions for kids
cards.text: Examples: "Can a 7-year-old finish without an adult explaining?", "Does any child look scared or stop moving at the ghost?", "Do kids point and tell parents what they see?" Watch faces and bodies, kids rarely say they are confused.
cards.use_when: test_questions when players are kids
do: Watch with a parent present
avoid: Asking kids for written feedback

cards.title: Playtest questions for spectators and groups
cards.text: Examples: "Do spectators cheer or call out at the climax?", "Can parents tell who is winning from the leaderboard screen?", "Do waiting players watch or look at phones?" The audience is part of the MR game.
cards.use_when: test_questions when the brief has spectators or a race
do: Observe the audience zone too
avoid: Only questioning the player

cards.title: Playtest questions for seniors and first-time VR players
cards.text: Examples: "Does anyone ask to stop in the first minute?", "Do players walk at normal pace or shuffle?", "How many reach for a real wall for balance?" These reveal comfort problems before fun problems.
cards.use_when: test_questions for seniors or first-time VR
do: Note pace and balance
avoid: Long sessions before comfort is checked
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Bad playtest questions and their good rewrites
cards.text: "Is it too hard?" becomes "How many tries does board 2 take?". "Is the theme cool?" becomes "Do players name the theme without being told?". "Is MR fun?" becomes "Do players look around the room in the first 30 seconds?"
cards.use_when: Reviewing test_questions before sending
do: Rewrite every yes/no opinion into a count or a time
avoid: Leading questions ("Wasn't the boss amazing?")

cards.title: Revising from comments: change only what was asked, keep the rest word for word
cards.text: When the creator comments on a prototype, copy every field they did not mention unchanged and edit only the named parts. Rewriting everything makes them re-review and lose trust that their approved parts survive.
cards.use_when: A prototype request that includes creator comments
do: List mentally which fields the comment touches
Keep title, pillars and palette unless named
avoid: Regenerating the whole prototype
Silently changing the genre

cards.title: Follow the ripple: one change may need its linked fields updated
cards.text: Some comments ripple: "make it night" changes palette, prompt_style and key art light; "add a boss" changes the storyboard climax, the sketch boss zone and the flow; "make it 2 minutes" shortens the flow and may drop the middle panel. Update the linked fields and nothing else.
cards.use_when: Applying a creator comment
do: Map: mood to art and key_art, length to flow and storyboard, place to sketch
avoid: Updating the flow but leaving a 5-minute storyboard

cards.title: When a comment asks for a mechanic the engine lacks, offer the nearest one
cards.text: If the creator asks to "add shooting" or "let them pick up keys", keep the prototype and swap in the closest buildable thing: shooting becomes the sword or stepping out of rings; keys become checkpoints labelled "Key 1, Key 2" in order. Say so kindly in the caption.
cards.use_when: Comments requesting unsupported mechanics
do: Name the replacement in the changed panel
avoid: Promising the mechanic in the key art
Ignoring the comment

cards.title: Change key_art.prompt only when the look or climax changed
cards.text: Each new key art costs a FLUX picture and the creator's attention. Rewrite key_art.prompt when the comment changes the theme, mood, palette, climax or platform; otherwise keep it identical so the same picture can be reused.
cards.use_when: Revisions where the picture may or may not need redrawing
do: Keep the prompt string exactly the same when unchanged
avoid: Tiny wording edits that trigger a redraw

cards.title: Revision example: "too scary for my 6-year-old"
cards.text: Keep title, route and flow. Change art.mood to playful, prompt_style to spooky-cute, palette dark base up one step, key art to a smiling ghost, storyboard climax captions to surprise rather than threat, and add a test question about children stopping in fear.
cards.use_when: Comments that the prototype is too scary
do: Soften the mood fields only
avoid: Removing the theme entirely when they only asked for softer

cards.title: Revision example: "we will play outside at noon now"
cards.text: In MR an outdoor noon venue kills dark and neon looks. Keep the game and story; switch palette to a daylight-safe variant, lighting to noon, remove glow words from prompt_style, and redraw key art with sun and real sky visible. Mention the change in art.mood.
cards.use_when: MR revisions where the venue light changes
do: Raise the darkest palette colour above about #3d5a80
avoid: Keeping a neon palette for noon outdoors

cards.title: Every prototype field must tell the same game
cards.text: Check that the logline verb appears in the storyboard, the climax appears in the key art, the HUD tracks what the flow describes, and the sketch zones match the storyboard places. A creator spots mismatches instantly and stops trusting the plan.
cards.use_when: Final check before replying with a prototype
do: Read logline, climax panel and key art together
avoid: A boss in the storyboard but no boss zone in the sketch

cards.title: Do not let the theme stretch the genre in the prototype
cards.text: A pirate tactics game is still a piece walking a 6 x 8 board; a dragon runner still walks checkpoints and avoids red circles. Theme dresses the engine, it does not add ships to sail or dragons to ride.
cards.use_when: Prototypes with strong themes
do: Describe themed versions of real mechanics (guards as pirate crew)
avoid: Captions promising sailing, flying or riding

cards.title: Battle flow, 2 minutes, MR event version with 2 chapters and a beast
cards.text: 0:00 look around, sword appears in the right hand. 0:15 chapter 1: 3 slow grunts from one wall. 0:50 chapter 2: grunts from two sides plus rain rings. 1:25 a beast charges in as the finale. 1:50 victory and score. Short enough for queues and for arms that tire fast in MR.
cards.use_when: MR battle at events, first-time VR players, sessions of about 2 minutes
do: At most 6 enemies per chapter in MR (checked)
Use the beast only after chapter 1 (checked)
avoid: A full boss fight squeezed into 2 minutes with 4 chapters

cards.title: Battle flow, 3 minutes, PC version with dash taught early
cards.text: 0:00 hero intro and controls. 0:10 chapter 1: 4 grunts, learn the 3-hit combo. 0:45 chapter 2: 2 shields, learn to dash behind them. 1:30 chapter 3: up to 9 mixed enemies with rain. 2:20 boss. 2:50 score and time. PC players tolerate denser chapters than MR players.
cards.use_when: PC battle sessions around 3 minutes
do: Teach one verb per chapter: combo, then dash
avoid: Introducing shields and rain in the same chapter

cards.title: Runner flow, 8 minutes, 10 checkpoints in 3 acts
cards.text: 0:00 story card. 0:20 act 1, checkpoints 1-3, open easy path. 2:30 act 2, checkpoints 4-7, hazard pairs and a story turn at 5. 5:00 calm view stretch, no hazards. 5:45 act 3, checkpoints 8-10, densest hazards or void floor. 7:30 portal. 7:45 score, time bonus, leaderboard. Needs a space over 10 x 10 m or PC.
cards.use_when: Long runner sessions, large venues or PC tours
do: Use the maximum of 10 checkpoints
Plan one rest stretch at mid-session
avoid: 8 minutes in a small room, players loop the same few metres

cards.title: Tactics flow, 8 minutes, 6 boards with a new piece every 2 boards
cards.text: 0:00 rules card. 0:20 boards 1-2 with the rook: 2 then 3 targets, 1-2 guards. 2:30 boards 3-4 with the knight, cracked squares appear. 5:00 boards 5-6 with the queen, guards on a 3 s beat and tables blocking lines. 7:30 final time, leaderboard. Good for puzzle fans on PC or a calm MR hall.
cards.use_when: Long tactics sessions for players who enjoy planning
do: Introduce one new piece or rule every 2 boards
avoid: Guards faster than every 3 s
Six boards of the same piece

cards.title: Classroom learning: chalk green, paper white, pencil yellow, ink blue
cards.text: Palette: #2f5d50 chalk green, #fbfaf5 paper white, #ffcf33 pencil yellow, #2d5bd1 ink blue, #e5262f hazard red. Made for a real classroom under fluorescent light, where everything stays readable. In daylight by windows the paper white can glare, so keep it on small props and use chalk green for the ground. The hazard colour #e5262f (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.
cards.use_when: Educational games for schools, quiz-style runners where checkpoints are lesson steps
do: Put the 5 hex values straight into art.palette and name them in lang
Scenery theme to pair: ow-library, ow-village
Keep the hazard colour only on danger (rings, enemy tells, cracked squares)
avoid: Adding a second red or orange to the decor, it steals the warning signal

cards.title: Office team-building: slate, teal, warm coral, clean white
cards.text: Palette: #3c4a5c slate, #1fa59a team teal, #ff8a65 warm coral, #f5f7fa clean white, #d7191c hazard red. A calm grown-up palette for meeting rooms and lobbies under office light. Coral is warm but clearly lighter than the hazard red, so keep it on goals and team markers. In daylight it still reads well. The hazard colour #d7191c (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.
cards.use_when: Corporate team-building, adult groups, office events
do: Put the 5 hex values straight into art.palette and name them in lang
Scenery theme to pair: ow-herotech, ow-garden
Keep the hazard colour only on danger (rings, enemy tells, cracked squares)
avoid: Adding a second red or orange to the decor, it steals the warning signal

cards.title: Tropical beach: lagoon turquoise, white sand, palm green, sunset coral
cards.text: Palette: #23c6c8 lagoon, #f6e7c1 white sand, #3f9b4f palm green, #ff8c69 sunset coral, #7b2cbf urchin purple hazard. Outdoor daylight friendly, like a real beach. Coral and sand are close to warm hazard colours, so hazards turn urchin purple, which stands out on sand and water alike. Indoors raise saturation a step. The hazard colour #7b2cbf (urchin purple hazard) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.
cards.use_when: Beach, island holiday, surfing or summer trip themes above water
do: Put the 5 hex values straight into art.palette and name them in lang
Scenery theme to pair: ow-pirate, ow-reef, ow-sun
Keep the hazard colour only on danger (rings, enemy tells, cracked squares)
avoid: Adding a second red or orange to the decor, it steals the warning signal

cards.title: Autumn harvest: maple orange, wheat gold, plum, pine
cards.text: Palette: #d9622b maple orange, #e8c35a wheat gold, #5e2750 plum, #2e5e4e pine, #00b4d8 frost cyan hazard. Warm all over, so a red hazard would hide among leaves; hazards become frost cyan. Pine and plum give the dark anchors. Works indoors and in soft daylight; at noon lift plum toward a lighter berry. The hazard colour #00b4d8 (frost cyan hazard) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.
cards.use_when: Harvest festival, autumn forest, rice harvest, thanksgiving-style themes
do: Put the 5 hex values straight into art.palette and name them in lang
Scenery theme to pair: ow-farm, ow-garden, ow-mushroom
Keep the hazard colour only on danger (rings, enemy tells, cracked squares)
avoid: Adding a second red or orange to the decor, it steals the warning signal

cards.title: Rainy season: storm grey, wet leaf green, umbrella yellow, puddle blue
cards.text: Palette: #5b6770 storm grey, #4caf50 wet leaf, #ffd400 umbrella yellow, #5fa8d3 puddle blue, #ff2d2d hazard red. Moody but not dark: grey sets the weather, yellow umbrellas guide the eye. Good indoors and on overcast days; on bright noon days the grey turns flat, so lean on yellow and green shapes. The hazard colour #ff2d2d (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.
cards.use_when: Thai rainy season, frogs and puddles, a cosy monsoon story
do: Put the 5 hex values straight into art.palette and name them in lang
Scenery theme to pair: ow-garden, ow-village, ow-witchmarsh
Keep the hazard colour only on danger (rings, enemy tells, cracked squares)
avoid: Adding a second red or orange to the decor, it steals the warning signal

cards.title: Chinese New Year in Thailand: lantern red, lucky gold, jade, ink black
cards.text: Palette: #c8102e lantern red, #f2c14e lucky gold, #00a86b jade, #1c1c1c ink black, #00e5ff electric cyan hazard. The festival is red by nature, so hazards must not be red: they become electric cyan, which appears nowhere in the decor. Rich indoors and at night like Yaowarat street lights; in daylight keep ink black small and let gold and jade carry contrast. The hazard colour #00e5ff (electric cyan hazard) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.
cards.use_when: Chinese New Year, Yaowarat street, dragon and lion dance themes
do: Put the 5 hex values straight into art.palette and name them in lang
Scenery theme to pair: ow-bazaar, ow-dragon, ow-lotuscity
Keep the hazard colour only on danger (rings, enemy tells, cracked squares)
avoid: Adding a second red or orange to the decor, it steals the warning signal

cards.title: School sports day: field green, team blue, team yellow, team purple
cards.text: Palette: #3fa34d field green, #1e63d6 team blue, #ffcc00 team yellow, #8e44ad team purple, #ff1a1a hazard red. Thai sports days use team colours; red is kept out of the teams so it can stay the hazard. Built for outdoor fields and gyms in daylight, where saturated primaries read from the stands. The hazard colour #ff1a1a (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.
cards.use_when: Sports day, team races, school competitions with colour teams
do: Put the 5 hex values straight into art.palette and name them in lang
Scenery theme to pair: ow-village, ow-olympus, ow-carnival
Keep the hazard colour only on danger (rings, enemy tells, cracked squares)
avoid: Adding a second red or orange to the decor, it steals the warning signal

cards.title: Race or shared-floor key art: two players, side by side, one clear leader
cards.text: For an online race or shared floor show exactly 2 player avatars or 2 headset players, one a step ahead, both heading to the same checkpoint or portal. Two figures is the most FLUX schnell draws cleanly, and a visible leader sells competition in one frame.
cards.use_when: key_art.prompt for race or together play modes
do: Give the two players different simple colours (blue and yellow)
Put the goal in the background between them
avoid: 3 or more players, faces and limbs merge
Players touching or passing items, the engine has no hand-offs

cards.title: Together storyboard: shared floor where players see each other, not a team mechanic
cards.text: On a shared floor players walk the same course and see each other's avatars, but there is no shared score or hand-off. Write beats around that: start, players gather at spawn; middle, one waits for or calls out to the other near a hazard; climax, they reach the last checkpoint together; end, both portals and both scores.
cards.use_when: Storyboards for play_mode together
do: Use calling out and waiting as the social verbs
Put both players in the climax panel
avoid: Promising carrying, combining items or team health
A climax only one player can reach

cards.title: Race HUD adds live position; shared-floor HUD adds nothing
cards.text: In a race each player walks their own copy, so add live position (2nd of 4) next to checkpoint count and timer, and mirror the leaderboard on a spectator screen. On a shared floor the other players are visible as avatars, so no extra HUD is needed.
cards.use_when: hud for race or together play modes
do: Race: position, checkpoint 3/6, timer
Shared: the normal runner HUD
avoid: Friend lists, chat or team bars the engine does not have

cards.title: Ask what the game is FOR before what it looks like (วัตถุประสงค์)
cards.text: Many creators are teachers, brands, HR teams or parents who need the game to do a job. Early in the interview, ask one question: what should be different for players after they play (they know a fact order, they remember a brand, they talked to colleagues, they relaxed)? The answer picks the genre, session length and whether there is a race far more than the theme does.
cards.use_when: the concept mentions a school, a client, an event, a team, a lesson, a booth or a goal beyond fun
do: Offer choices like: teach something, promote a brand, bring a team together, a party, relax, move more
Write the purpose into the concept line of the brief
Let the purpose decide play_mode and session_minutes when the creator did not
avoid: Asking about the purpose after the options are already drawn
Treating a learning or brand brief like a pure fun brief

cards.title: The purpose must ride on the core loop, not on top of it
cards.text: A purpose game works when the thing the player does again and again is itself the lesson, the message or the bonding. If the purpose lives only on the intro card while play is unrelated, players remember the play and forget the purpose. Check each option: if you deleted the theme, would the purpose still be present in what the player does?
cards.use_when: checking any option for a learning, brand, team or wellbeing brief
do: Map the purpose onto checkpoint order, tactics capture order or battle chapters
State in mechanics how the loop carries the purpose
avoid: A fun race with a fact screen at the end
A brand logo pasted onto an unrelated game
cards.source: Bruckman 1999, Can Educational Be Fun? (GDC); design practice

cards.title: Ordered checkpoints teach sequences (ลำดับเหตุการณ์)
cards.text: The runner forces checkpoints to be touched in order, so it is a natural teacher of anything that has a correct order: a life cycle, a process, a timeline, steps of an experiment. Give each checkpoint one short fact label in the true order, 4-8 stops, 1.5-3 m apart. Walking the order with the body helps it stick, and the order is the content, not decoration.
cards.use_when: the learning topic has stages, steps, eras or a fixed order
do: One fact per label, 2-6 words
Put a scenery model that shows the stage beside each stop
Use a loop route when the topic is a cycle, a line when it has a start and an end
avoid: Putting two facts on one label
Using checkpoints for a topic that has no order (e.g. a list of animals)

cards.title: Life cycle walk: butterfly, frog or rice plant
cards.text: A life cycle maps perfectly onto a loop runner. Butterfly: 'Tiny egg on a leaf', 'Caterpillar eats', 'Chrysalis rests', 'Butterfly flies', back to the leaf. Rice for Thai schools: 'Seed soaks', 'Seedling grows', 'Plant in paddy', 'Rice flowers', 'Golden harvest'. 4-6 stops in a loop, morning lighting, a big model of each stage beside its stop, hazards as hungry birds or dry cracked mud.
cards.use_when: a primary science lesson on growth, life cycles or farming
do: Use a loop route so the end meets the start
Make each stage model large and clearly different
Keep timeLimit null for under-8s
avoid: A straight line that hides the cycle
Scary predators chasing young children

cards.title: Thai history timeline by eras, not by kings
cards.text: For Thai history, make checkpoints eras in order: 'Ban Chiang pottery', 'Sukhothai script', 'Ayutthaya trade port', 'Thonburi', 'Rattanakosin city'. Show each era with buildings, boats, crafts and markets as scenery. Do not put real royal figures, portraits or royal symbols in the game; teach through places, objects and daily life, which is also easier to show in low-poly.
cards.use_when: a social studies or Thai history lesson, or a heritage museum brief
do: Use eras and everyday objects as the labels
Let the teacher name the people in the debrief
5-6 stops in a line from oldest to newest
avoid: Royal portraits, royal emblems or kings as characters
Battles between real historical armies as a battle option

cards.title: Solar system walk: planets in order from the Sun
cards.text: Spawn at the Sun and place 8 checkpoints, one per planet, Mercury to Neptune, so the order is learned with the feet. The real distances cannot fit any room, so space the stops evenly (1.5-3 m) and say on the intro card that the spacing is not to scale; a teacher can show real scale later. Night lighting indoors makes the planets pop; hazards as asteroid patches between Mars and Jupiter teach the belt's position.
cards.use_when: a science lesson about planets or space for ages 7-14
do: One planet name plus one fact per label ('Mars: red dust')
Hazards as the asteroid belt between stops 4 and 5
State that distances are not to scale
avoid: Implying the planets are evenly spaced in reality
More than 10 checkpoints (add the Moon in the story instead)

cards.title: Geography as a journey: river, regions or a trade route
cards.text: Geography works when the route is a real journey in miniature: the Chao Phraya from the northern rivers to the Gulf, or a trip through Thailand's regions north to south. Each checkpoint is a place in travel order with a landmark-type model (mountains, rice plains, a port, islands). The room's long side can stand for north to south so players feel direction.
cards.use_when: a geography lesson about a river, a country's regions or a route
do: Align the route with a real compass direction if the teacher wants
Use landscape models more than buildings
avoid: Real maps with text in the scenery
Placing sacred sites as checkpoints

cards.title: English vocabulary walk: one word per checkpoint with a picture model
cards.text: For Thai learners of English, each checkpoint label is one English word from a topic set (fruit, jobs, weather, prepositions) and a clear model of it stands beside the stop. Order can follow a story ('Wake up', 'Brush teeth', 'Eat breakfast', 'Walk to school') so the words are used in context. Players cannot type or answer in the game, so the teacher asks the class to say the words before and after.
cards.use_when: an English or foreign language lesson for kids or teens
do: Use a daily-routine or story order so words connect
Pick 5-8 words per game, picture-clear models
Set lang to en for the labels, keep the teacher's notes in Thai
avoid: Promising spelling tests or typed answers in game
Abstract words that no model can show

cards.title: Maths through movement: tactics pieces and number-sequence labels
cards.text: Tactics pieces are maths made visible: the rook moves in lines, the bishop in diagonals, the knight in an L of 2 and 1 squares. A board where the player must plan a capture order teaches counting squares, coordinates and planning. In a runner, checkpoint labels can be a number pattern ('2', '4', '8', '16') so the next stop is a prediction the class makes aloud before the player walks.
cards.use_when: a maths lesson on patterns, shapes, coordinates or logical steps
do: Use the knight board for older kids, the rook for younger
Ask spectators to predict the next number
avoid: Arithmetic drills with typed answers
Boards too hard for the age (more than 4 targets for under-10s)

cards.title: Tactics boards teach planning and algorithms
cards.text: A tactics board is a small algorithm: a fixed set of rules, a goal (capture targets in order) and obstacles (guards on a beat, cracked squares). Solving it means planning steps ahead, testing, and fixing a plan after a mistake, which is the core of computational thinking. Ask the player to say the plan out loud before stepping, then compare plan and result in the debrief.
cards.use_when: a computing, logic or problem-solving lesson
do: Start with 2 targets and one slow guard, then a second board with 3-4 targets
Have a partner outside the area write the planned moves
avoid: Fast guards that turn planning into reflexes
Only one board, so no chance to apply what was learned

cards.title: Teaching chess piece moves: one piece per board, simple to complex
cards.text: To teach how pieces move, give one piece per board in this order: rook (lines), bishop (diagonals), queen (both), knight (the L, hardest). The first board of each piece has no guards, only targets, so the player just learns the move; the second adds one guard to show attacked squares. In MR the body learns the shape of the move, which beginners often forget on a small board.
cards.use_when: a chess club, a school chess intro or parents teaching kids chess
do: Name the piece and its move in the goal line
Save the knight for last
avoid: Starting with the knight
Guards on the very first board of a new piece

cards.title: Battle as metaphor: germs vs the immune system
cards.text: The battle engine can teach a defence story: the player is a white blood cell, grunts are fast small germs, shield enemies are germs with a tough coat that must be hit from the side, the beast is a big infection, and the boss is the final wave. Chapter titles can teach stages ('The cut', 'The alarm', 'The big fight'). In the debrief, the teacher says where the metaphor is not true (cells do not use swords).
cards.use_when: a health or biology lesson about germs, the body's defence or hygiene
do: Name each enemy kind after a real germ type
Dark or neon theme indoors for an inside-the-body look
Spell out the limits of the metaphor in the debrief
avoid: Gory body imagery for young kids
Teaching that medicine is a sword (no medical claims)

cards.title: A battle metaphor that teaches a wrong idea
cards.text: Metaphors stick, including the wrong parts. If recycling is taught as 'slash the plastic monsters', kids may learn that waste disappears when you hit it. Before using battle for a lesson, list what each element stands for and check one wrong lesson it could teach; if the wrong lesson is the main takeaway, choose a runner where the correct order of actions is the content instead.
cards.use_when: battle is proposed for an education or awareness brief
do: Write the mapping: enemy = what, chapter = what, boss = what
Prefer a runner for process topics (sorting, recycling steps)
avoid: Violence as the answer to social topics
Enemies that represent people or groups

cards.title: Hazards as common wrong ideas
cards.text: Hazards can carry labels, so they can stand for misconceptions: on a solar system walk a red circle labelled 'Sun goes round Earth', on a food chain walk 'Plants eat soil'. Stepping in one costs 25 points and sends the player back, a gentle way to mark a wrong idea without quizzes. Keep it to 2-3 such hazards and discuss them in the debrief.
cards.use_when: a learning runner where the topic has known misconceptions
do: 2-3 labelled hazards, beside the route not on it
Short labels the class can read from the side
avoid: Hazards on the only path (forcing failure)
Mocking language in labels

cards.title: No quizzes, typed answers or multiple choice in any engine
cards.text: Teachers often ask for questions with answers. No engine can show a question and accept an answer, and routes are fixed, so there are no branching 'pick the right door' paths. Offer instead: the correct answer order as checkpoints, wrong ideas as labelled hazards, and the teacher asking questions out loud before and after play. The game is the experience; the quiz happens in the room.
cards.use_when: the brief mentions quiz, questions, test, answer, exam or choose the right answer
do: Say kindly that the game cannot ask questions
Turn the answers into the checkpoint order
Suggest a 2-minute verbal or paper quiz after play
avoid: Promising answer buttons, text input or branching routes
Rules like 'pick the correct gate'

cards.title: Write one observable learning objective
cards.text: A learning game needs one objective phrased as something you can see a student do afterwards: 'put the 5 rice stages in order', 'name 6 planets from the Sun', 'explain why the knight jumps'. Avoid 'understand' or 'learn about'. The objective decides the checkpoint labels, and it becomes the thing you check in the debrief.
cards.use_when: any education brief, before writing checkpoint labels
do: Use verbs like order, name, sort, explain, predict
Keep one objective per Land
avoid: Three objectives in one 4-minute game
Vague goals like 'have fun with science'

cards.title: Learning games by age band
cards.text: Ages 5-7: 4-5 checkpoints, labels of 1-3 words with picture-clear models, no time limit, no tactics guards. Ages 8-10: 5-7 checkpoints, short fact labels, tactics with rook or bishop and one slow guard. Ages 11-14: up to 8-10 checkpoints, cause-and-effect labels, tactics with knight or queen, battle as a metaphor. For MR, follow the headset maker's minimum age (Meta sets 10+ for Quest, with a parent-managed account); younger classes play on PC.
cards.use_when: an education brief where the players' age is known
do: Check the headset age rule before choosing MR for young classes
Scale label length with reading level
avoid: The same design for 6-year-olds and 13-year-olds
MR headsets for children under the maker's minimum age
cards.source: Meta Quest safety and age guidance; design practice

cards.title: Debrief after play: the learning happens in the talk
cards.text: Experience becomes learning when people reflect on it. Plan a 3-5 minute debrief with three questions: What happened, in order? Why was it in that order? Where is that true in real life? Players and watchers answer together. Put the debrief in the flow of the prototype so the teacher plans time for it.
cards.use_when: any education, team-building or museum brief
do: Add a debrief step to the prototype flow
Use the checkpoint labels as the discussion list
avoid: Ending the lesson when the last player takes the headset off
Debrief longer than the play

cards.title: Give each fact at the moment it is used
cards.text: Good games teach by putting information exactly where and when the player needs it, not in a manual first. In a learning Land, that means the fact sits on the checkpoint label the player is walking to, and the scenery beside it shows it. Keep the intro card for the story and goal only, and never put a reading wall before play.
cards.use_when: deciding where facts go in a learning game
do: Facts on labels and in scenery
Intro card: 2-4 sentences of story and the goal
avoid: A long text intro full of facts
Facts no player sees because they are only in the rules list
cards.source: Gee 2003, What Video Games Have to Teach Us About Learning and Literacy

cards.title: Which school topics fit the engines and which do not
cards.text: Fits well: sequences (life cycles, history eras, steps of a recipe or experiment), ordered lists (planets, food chains, journeys), movement rules and planning (tactics), defence or struggle stories (battle as metaphor). Fits poorly: open debate, reading comprehension, essays, arithmetic drills, anything that needs an answer typed or chosen. For poor fits, propose a game as the hook and keep the core task in class.
cards.use_when: a teacher names a subject and the AI must judge if a game helps
do: Name the fit honestly in options
Offer the closest fitting angle of the topic
avoid: Forcing a reading or debate topic into a runner
Promising the game covers a whole unit

cards.title: Class rotation: 30 students, few headsets, everyone busy
cards.text: With 2-4 headsets and 30 students, run stations: players in the area, a watching group with a simple sheet (write the checkpoint order you see, spot the hazards), and a group doing a related paper task. Turns of 3-4 minutes and a race of 2-4 players keep the queue moving; a full class rotation takes about 30-40 minutes. Watchers see bodies, so the sheet asks about what bodies do (where did she turn back?).
cards.use_when: a school class larger than the number of headsets
do: Session 3-4 minutes, race mode, leaderboard on a screen
Give watchers an observation task outside the area
avoid: 10-minute turns with 26 students waiting
Watcher tasks inside the play area

cards.title: Science fair or school project: students design the Land
cards.text: At a science fair, the learning can be in making the game: a student team picks a process, writes the checkpoint order and hazards, and explains each design decision on a poster. Visitors play a 2-minute runner and the team explains why each stop is where it is. The AI should help the students reason (why this order, why this hazard) rather than design it all for them.
cards.use_when: students are the creators, for a fair, a club or a project grade
do: Ask the students for the order and explain why each choice matters
Keep sessions at 2 minutes for fair visitors
avoid: Deciding everything so the students learn nothing
Long runs that block the booth

cards.title: A museum game sends visitors back to the real objects
cards.text: In a museum, the game should not replace the exhibits; it should make visitors look harder at them. Base each checkpoint on a real object in the nearby gallery ('Find the bronze drum'), and end the story with an invitation to go and see the real one. In MR passthrough, an exhibit visible beyond the edge of the play area can be the backdrop of the finish.
cards.use_when: a museum, gallery or heritage centre brief
do: Use exhibit names as labels
Close the story with 'see the real one in hall 2'
Face the finish toward a real exhibit if it is outside the area
avoid: Copying the whole exhibition into the game
Play area that includes cases or fragile objects

cards.title: Heritage craft as a process walk: Lanna umbrella or lacquerware
cards.text: Local crafts are perfect sequences. Bo Sang umbrella making: 'Cut the bamboo', 'Make the ribs', 'Stretch the saa paper', 'Paint the flowers', 'Dry in the sun'. Each stop shows the tool or the half-made object, so visitors learn the steps and the effort. Morning or noon lighting, warm wood and paper colours, one hazard as a wet paint puddle.
cards.use_when: a heritage, craft village or cultural centre brief in northern Thailand
do: Ask a craftsperson to check the order
Show tools and half-made items as scenery
avoid: Inventing steps that are not real
Turning a craft into a battle

cards.title: Local legends: tell them as legends, keep them respectful
cards.text: Local legends (a guardian spirit of a mountain, a city founding tale) make great narrative runners, but players should know it is a legend, not history. Say 'the old story says' on the intro card. Use original character designs, avoid making revered spirits into enemies or hazards, and ask a local guide or museum staff to check the telling.
cards.use_when: a heritage brief built on folklore or a founding story
do: Frame as 'the legend tells'
Revered figures as scenery or guides, never enemies
avoid: Battle against a revered spirit
Presenting a legend as fact in a school lesson

cards.title: Library reading programme: walk the story of a book
cards.text: A library can turn a book's plot into a runner: each checkpoint is a key moment in story order, and the finish invites the reader to the shelf where the book lives. Use public-domain tales or the library's own original stories, or get permission for a published book's names and look. Calm indoor lighting and 5-6 stops; kids who read the book first will recognise the order.
cards.use_when: a library, reading club or book week event
do: Plot points as labels in order
End with 'find the book on shelf B'
avoid: Copying a famous book's characters without permission
Long passages of book text in the game

cards.title: Brand activation: which success goal matters most?
cards.text: Brand clients mean different things by success: dwell time at the booth, a photo moment people share, high throughput (players per hour), a leaderboard with prizes, or one clear message remembered. Each pulls the design a different way (throughput means 2-minute turns, dwell means watchable races, message means story labels). Ask the creator to pick the top one.
cards.use_when: a brand, product, mall or sponsor booth brief
do: Offer choices: many players, long crowd watching, photos, prizes, a message
Write the chosen goal into constraints
avoid: Optimising for everything at once
Assuming the client wants a long immersive story

cards.title: Booth throughput: players per hour = headsets x 60 / (turn + changeover)
cards.text: Changeover (fit headset, 20-second brief, clean, reset) takes about 1-2 minutes. With 4 headsets, a 3-minute turn and 2-minute changeover give 4 x 60 / 5 = 48 players per hour; a 2-minute turn gives 60. If the client expects 500 players a day over 8 hours, that needs about 60 per hour, so 2-minute turns. Do this maths before choosing session length.
cards.use_when: an event or booth where the number of players matters
do: Ask the expected visitors per day
Choose session_minutes from the maths
Use timeLimit to enforce the turn
avoid: 5-minute games at a booth that needs 60 players per hour
Forgetting changeover time

cards.title: Brand look without ads inside gameplay
cards.text: Carry the brand through the world, not through billboards: use the brand palette for the floor and props, make the finish portal area in brand colours, and design an original world that fits the brand's values (fresh, playful, premium). Avoid pop-up ads, slogans on every prop and logo text in key art. Logos belong on the booth, the queue sign and the leaderboard screen, where people read them.
cards.use_when: a brand wants its identity in the game
do: Use the brand palette in the prototype palette
Put the logo on the physical booth and screen
One brand hero object as scenery at most
avoid: Logo text in the key art prompt
Products as obstacles or hazards

cards.title: Never make the product a hazard or an enemy
cards.text: If a drink can is a hazard players must avoid, or a snack is an enemy to slash, the game tells players to avoid the product. Make the product the goal or the reward: a giant model at the finish, checkpoint labels that follow the product's story ('Pick the fresh leaves'), or the theme of the world. Hazards should be the problem the product solves (thirst, dull days), shown as neutral things.
cards.use_when: a brand brief where products might appear in the game
do: Product as the finish or hero scenery
Hazards as the problem, not the product
avoid: Products as enemies, hazards or things to destroy
Competitor products in any role

cards.title: One brand message per game
cards.text: A 2-3 minute game can carry one message, not five. Pick one sentence the client wants remembered and build the story card (2-4 sentences) and the checkpoint labels around it, for example a coffee brand's 'from mountain farm to cup' becomes 5 stops in that order. Extra messages go on the booth, not in the game.
cards.use_when: the client lists many messages, features or products
do: Ask for the one sentence to remember
Make the checkpoint order tell that sentence
avoid: Every checkpoint naming a different product feature
Rules text used as advertising

cards.title: The photo moment happens outside the headset
cards.text: Spectators and cameras see bodies, not the game, so the shareable moment is real: the player's victory pose at the finish, a friend's reaction, the leaderboard screen with their nickname. Put the finish portal where a photo spot with the brand backdrop sits behind the player, and let staff take the photo (with consent) after the turn. A screen showing the player's view helps the photo tell the story.
cards.use_when: a brand or event brief that wants social media photos
do: Finish facing the photo backdrop
Screen with the leaderboard or player's view next to the photo spot
avoid: Expecting players to take photos inside the headset
Photos of minors without parent consent

cards.title: Leaderboard prizes that stay fair and keep people coming
cards.text: A prize leaderboard draws repeat visits but can make late visitors feel they cannot win. Reset the board every hour or every session block and give a prize per block; use nicknames or team colours, never real names or phone numbers. Everyone plays the same Land with the same timeLimit so scores compare. Announce the current top score so the queue has a target.
cards.use_when: a booth with prizes for top scores
do: Hourly or daily resets
Nicknames only on screen
Same Land and timeLimit for all
avoid: One all-day board where the morning winner can never be beaten
Collecting personal data in the game for prizes

cards.title: Design the queue: watching is the trailer
cards.text: The queue is where people decide to stay. Place it along the side where the players' turns and the finish are visible, show the leaderboard and a short looped video of the player's view, and give a 3-rule card people can read in 20 seconds. Pre-brief in the queue so the in-headset time is all play.
cards.use_when: an event booth with queues
do: Queue faces the play area and the screen
Rules in 3 short lines with pictures
avoid: Queue behind a wall where nothing can be seen
Explaining rules only after the headset is on

cards.title: Staff operation plan for an event booth
cards.text: Plan staff before the event: about 1 staff per 2 headsets to fit, brief and spot players, plus 1 person on the queue. A spotter stands at the edge to stop players drifting out of the area. Write a 3-line script for staff (welcome, the goal, the safety rule) and a reset step between turns (restart Land, wipe headset, check the floor is clear).
cards.use_when: any staffed booth, event or activation
do: Put the staff script in the build notes
Name a spotter position on the sketch
avoid: One person running 4 headsets and the queue
No reset step so the next player starts mid-game

cards.title: No personal data in the game, even for brand leads
cards.text: The game should never ask for names, phone numbers, emails, schools or photos. Leaderboards use nicknames or team colours. If a brand wants leads, that happens outside the game, on the client's own form with clear consent, and is not a condition for playing. This also keeps children safe at public events.
cards.use_when: a brand or event wants data, sign-ups or contact details
do: Nicknames or colours on boards
Say lead collection is the client's separate, consent-based step
avoid: Asking players for contact details to play
Showing children's names on a public screen

cards.title: Team-building: compete or cooperate? (ทีมบิลดิ้ง)
cards.text: Ask what the HR team wants people to feel: competing teams (energy, rivalry, good for sales teams) or one team together (trust, communication, good for new or mixed teams). Race mode with a leaderboard serves rivalry; shared-floor together mode or a relay where the team's total time counts serves cooperation. A mix (teams race each other, members cooperate inside a team) suits most groups.
cards.use_when: a corporate, HR or staff event brief
do: Offer: teams against teams, everyone together, or a mix
Score teams, not individuals
avoid: Individual rankings that embarrass the slowest colleague
Assuming every office loves competition

cards.title: Relay of short boards: every member plays, the team total counts
cards.text: Split the team so each person plays one 1-2 minute turn: a tactics board or a short runner section, and the team's summed time or score goes on the board. Everyone contributes once, nobody carries the team alone, and teammates outside the area can call out plans. Use 3-4 boards of rising difficulty so the team chooses who plays which.
cards.use_when: team-building with groups of 4-8 per team
do: Let the team assign players to boards (planning is the point)
Show team totals on a screen
avoid: One star player doing all the turns
Boards so hard that a member fails publicly

cards.title: Teammates outside the area become the navigators
cards.text: There is no voice chat, so make real talking the teamwork: the player in the headset sees the world, and teammates outside see the body and the screen with the player's view, calling out 'next stop is left' or 'guard moves next beat'. Communication becomes the game. Keep callers outside the play area behind a line on the floor.
cards.use_when: team-building, families or classes where watchers should help
do: Screen with the player's view facing the callers
A floor line callers stay behind
avoid: Callers walking into the area to point
Voice chat features in the rules

cards.title: Mixed-ability teams: walking pace, no running, optional effort
cards.text: Office groups mix ages, fitness levels and comfort with VR. Design for walking pace (no running in MR), checkpoints 2-3 m apart, few or slow hazards, and battle chapters without rain for the first round. Let each person choose their role: player, caller or scorekeeper. The goal is that the least sporty person enjoys it.
cards.use_when: corporate groups with mixed ages and fitness
do: Gentle first round, harder optional second
Offer non-headset roles
avoid: Physical challenges that reward the fittest
Fast guard beats or beast enemies in round one

cards.title: Team debrief: link the play to how the team works
cards.text: End team-building with a 10-minute talk: What helped us? What did the callers do that worked? Where did we lose time? What would we do differently in round 3? Link one answer to real work (how we hand over tasks). Without this, it was a fun break; with it, the team names a behaviour to keep.
cards.use_when: corporate or club team-building
do: 3-4 open questions in the build notes
Use the leaderboard as a discussion prompt, not a judgement
avoid: Ranking individuals in the debrief
Skipping the debrief because time ran out

cards.title: Forcing everyone into a headset
cards.text: Some people cannot or do not want to wear a headset (motion sickness, glasses, pregnancy, anxiety, make-up). If the only way to join is to play, they sit out and the event fails its purpose. Design roles that need no headset: caller, plan writer, scorekeeper, judge of the best victory pose. Mention these roles in the options.
cards.use_when: team, school or family events where everyone should take part
do: List 2-3 non-headset roles
Make opting out normal, not a confession
avoid: Pressuring hesitant people to play
Team scores that punish teams with fewer players

cards.title: Birthday party: the birthday child is the star of the story
cards.text: Let the birthday child choose the theme from 3 (dinosaurs, space, candy) and write the story around them ('Help the dino find the giant cake'). With 8-12 kids and 2 headsets, use 2-minute turns in pairs so everyone plays twice in an hour, and give the birthday child the first and the final run. The finish is the cake model, and the real cake comes right after.
cards.use_when: a birthday party at home, a venue or a garden
do: Theme chosen by the birthday child
2-minute turns, everyone gets the same number
Celebrate every finish, not only the winner
avoid: Using the child's real name or photo in the game
Ranking guests so someone cries at their own friend's party

cards.title: Family day: grandparents and grandchildren play together
cards.text: On a shared floor in together mode, a grandparent and a grandchild walk the same Land and see each other's avatars. Use a gentle runner: checkpoints 2.5-3 m apart, no time limit, 1-2 hazards, studio or morning light, no void floor. Labels can invite talk ('Grandma's old market', 'Feed the buffalo'), so the older player tells stories while the child leads.
cards.use_when: a family event, company family day or community day with mixed ages
do: Together mode, no time limit
Labels that invite memories and talk
Wide clear route for slower walkers
avoid: Races that pit grandparents against kids
Void floor or fast hazards

cards.title: Family game night at home on PC: take turns on a tactics board
cards.text: On PC, a family can share one computer: tactics boards become a puzzle the family solves together, one person on the keyboard while the others plan out loud. Use 3-4 boards of rising difficulty and let a different family member drive each one. Runner Lands with WASD suit a quick turn for each person, with the time board making a friendly family challenge.
cards.use_when: a family that will play on a home computer
do: Rotate who drives each board
Choose bright cheerful themes
avoid: Battle themes too dark for young siblings
Very hard boards that only the oldest child can solve

cards.title: A calm game removes pressure: no timer, no race, few hazards
cards.text: For relaxation (submission), take away the things that create pressure: timeLimit null, solo or together mode instead of race, 0-2 hazards placed well off the route, and no leaderboard on display. The score still exists in the engine, so say on the intro card that there is no rush. The player's own pace is the design.
cards.use_when: a brief about relaxing, unwinding, a break, calm or mindfulness
do: timeLimit null
Solo or together mode
Hazards off the main walking line or none
avoid: Race mode or a public leaderboard
Hazards every 2 m

cards.title: Calm tour route: wide loop, long sightlines, gentle labels
cards.text: A relaxation runner is a tour: a wide loop with stops 2.5-3 m apart, open sightlines so the next checkpoint is always visible, and nature or garden scenery with slow animated rides (a turning windmill, floating lanterns). Labels are gentle invitations, not orders: 'Rest by the pond', 'Watch the clouds', 'Listen to the bamboo'. Morning or evening lighting gives soft colour.
cards.use_when: designing the route and labels for a calm game
do: Loop route with 5-6 spacious stops
Invitation-style labels
Morning or evening lighting
avoid: Tight zig-zags and dense props
Neon flashing or night horror lighting

cards.title: Gentle mood without a soundtrack setting
cards.text: The engine's game settings have no music track, so do not promise a soundtrack. Create the calm feel visually: soft lighting presets, slow-moving scenery, open space, soft palette (sage, sand, sky blue). If the venue wants music, it can play quiet music on its own speakers in the real room, which players in passthrough hear naturally.
cards.use_when: a relaxation brief that asks for calming music or sound
do: Say the venue can play its own quiet music
Carry mood with light, slow motion and colour
avoid: Promising in-game music, breathing audio guides or narration

cards.title: No health or therapy claims for calm games
cards.text: A calm walk can feel restful, but the game must not claim to treat stress, anxiety, depression, pain or any condition. Describe it as 'a quiet walk in a garden world', not therapy. If a clinic or therapist uses it, they decide how it fits their practice. Avoid words like heal, cure, therapy or reduces anxiety in titles, stories and pitches.
cards.use_when: wellbeing, clinic, spa, elderly care or mental health briefs
do: Describe the experience, not an outcome
Leave clinical framing to professionals
avoid: 'Reduces stress by 40%'
'Therapy game' in the title

cards.title: Sensory-friendly sessions: predictable and easy to stop
cards.text: For players who are sensitive to busy input (some autistic players, anxious first-timers, older adults), design for predictability: show the route from the spawn, no void floor, no sudden appearing models, soft lighting, few props, no time limit. Tell them before play that lifting the headset or saying stop ends it any time. A quiet hour at an event helps.
cards.use_when: sensory-friendly sessions, special needs groups or very nervous first-time players
do: Full route visible from spawn
Explain how to stop before play
Studio or morning lighting
avoid: Void floor, scares, flashing neon
Crowded noisy booth placement

cards.title: Estimate walking distance honestly from the route
cards.text: Distance walked is about the sum of the gaps between stops: 7 checkpoints 2.5 m apart plus spawn and portal is roughly 20 m, so a single runner lap is short. A 10 x 10 m route with 10 stops 3 m apart is about 30-35 m. One step is about 0.75 m, so 1,000 steps needs about 750 m, which is many rounds. Frame runner fitness as gentle movement, not a workout.
cards.use_when: a fitness or step-goal brief for a runner
do: Calculate metres from the sketch
Offer several rounds if the goal is more distance
avoid: Promising step counts or calories
Claiming a 3-minute walk is exercise

cards.title: Movement goals in MR still mean walking, never running
cards.text: In passthrough MR, running risks collisions and falls even in a cleared space, and headsets slip. Effort comes from more walking, turning, stepping out of rings, squatting to see low details, and arm swings in battle, not speed. Set time limits generous enough that a brisk walk wins.
cards.use_when: fitness, sport or high-energy briefs in MR
do: Time limits that a brisk walk can beat
Effort from steps, turns and swings
avoid: Sprint challenges
Time limits only runners can meet
cards.source: Meta VR comfort and MR design guidelines; design practice

cards.title: MR battle as interval movement: chapters are sets, gaps are rest
