cards.text: Battle in MR is the most physical genre: the controller is the sword and red rings make players step. Treat each chapter as a set of 45-90 seconds and the gap between chapters as rest. Add rain rings in middle chapters for extra stepping, and keep the boss short. A 3-4 chapter game makes about 5 minutes of real movement.
cards.use_when: a fitness, active play or energetic adults brief
do: 3-4 chapters with rising effort
Rain in middle chapters, not the first
avoid: Back-to-back chapters with no breather
Beasts in chapter 1

cards.title: Active play safety: heat, sweat, breaks and spotters
cards.text: Active headset play warms people fast. Keep active turns to 5-10 minutes, offer water, add breaks between rounds, and use wipeable face covers. Outdoors at noon in Thailand, heat and glare add up, so prefer evenings or shade. A spotter watches the area edge, and swinging arms need 1 m of clear space around each player.
cards.use_when: fitness or high-energy sessions, especially outdoors or with many rounds
do: Short turns and breaks
Clear 1 m around swinging players
Shade or evening for outdoor sessions
avoid: 30-minute non-stop sessions
Two battle players within arm reach
cards.source: Meta VR comfort and safety guidelines; design practice

cards.title: No step counting, heart rate or calorie tracking
cards.text: The engines track checkpoints, hazards, time and score, not steps, heart rate or calories. Do not promise fitness stats in the HUD. If the purpose is a step goal, use the score and finish time as the progress measure, and suggest players use their own phone or watch if they want steps.
cards.use_when: the brief asks for calories, steps, heart rate or fitness tracking
do: Use time and score as progress
Suggest personal devices for steps
avoid: Fitness stats in the HUD
Health claims about calories burned

cards.title: Chiang Mai city promotion: a journey through the old city
cards.text: A tourism runner can walk the old city as a journey: 'Enter at Tha Phae Gate', 'Cross the moat', 'Lanna wooden house', 'Sunday walking street', 'Khao soi stall', 'Lanterns over the river'. Use Lanna-style buildings, the moat and lanterns as scenery, and the mountain on the skyline as a silhouette. Keep temples as respectful backdrop scenery, never checkpoints to stomp or hazards.
cards.use_when: a tourism office, hotel lobby or city promotion booth for Chiang Mai
do: Real place names as labels
Evening lighting for lanterns
End by pointing visitors to the real places
avoid: Temples or Buddha images as props to step on
Sacred sites as hazards

cards.title: A tourism game is a teaser for the real place
cards.text: The purpose of a tourism game is that players want to go. Show a short taste of 5-6 places, not the whole city, and end the story with a real-world invitation ('The lanterns are real: see them at the river tonight'). Staff can hand a paper map after the turn. A game that feels complete leaves no reason to visit.
cards.use_when: tourism, hotel, airport or city promotion briefs
do: Pick 5-6 highlights
Close the story with a real place to visit
avoid: Rebuilding a whole city in one Land
Fantasy elements that confuse what is real

cards.title: International visitors: picture-first, very short labels
cards.text: Tourist booths get visitors who read neither Thai nor much English. The game text is in one lang (th or en), so make labels 1-3 words, choose English for mixed tourist crowds, and let the scenery carry the meaning (a lantern, a noodle bowl, a gate). Staff demonstrate with gestures, and the 3 rules have pictures on the booth sign.
cards.use_when: festival, airport, hotel or tourist attraction booths
do: lang en for international crowds
Labels 1-3 words
Picture rules sign at the queue
avoid: Long story text
Puns or idioms that do not translate

cards.title: Festival booth: Yi Peng and Loy Krathong evening walk
cards.text: During Yi Peng and Loy Krathong in Chiang Mai, an evening booth can run a lantern and krathong walk: 5 checkpoints in festival order ('Fold the banana leaf', 'Add flowers and candle', 'Light the lantern', 'Make a wish', 'Float on the river'), evening or night lighting, water and lantern scenery. Outdoor at night, glow reads well. 2-minute turns for big crowds.
cards.use_when: a festival booth in November in northern Thailand
do: Evening lighting outdoors after dark
Festival steps as labels in order
2-minute turns
avoid: Mocking or trivialising the rituals
Fire hazards themed as lanterns burning people

cards.title: Fair competition: everyone plays the identical Land
cards.text: Competition is only fair if every player faces the same thing. Use one fixed Land, the same timeLimit and the same lighting for all heats, and do not change the layout during the event. Tactics boards are already built and proven solvable by code, so every board has a fair answer. Change only between event days, and announce it.
cards.use_when: leaderboards, tournaments, school competitions or prize events
do: Freeze the Land before the event
Same rules card for all
avoid: Editing hazards mid-tournament
Different layouts for different heats

cards.title: Repeatable skill: practice run, then scored runs
cards.text: Competitive games need a skill that grows with tries: a route with a faster line around hazards, or a tactics board with a shorter capture path. Give first-timers one practice run that is not scored, then 2-3 scored runs with the best counting. This keeps the board about skill, not about who already played before.
cards.use_when: tournaments and return-visitor leaderboards
do: One unscored practice for newcomers
Best of 2-3 scored runs
avoid: Single runs where first-time players are always last
Courses with no better line to learn

cards.title: Event tournament: heats of 2-6 racers, then a final
cards.text: In race mode each player walks their own copy of the Land with a live leaderboard, so heats of 2-6 run side by side if the space allows. Run 3-minute heats through the day, keep a top-scores board, and hold a final at a fixed time when the crowd is biggest. The final is the spectator moment: put the finish portals on the crowd side.
cards.use_when: a competition at an event, mall or school fair
do: Heat size fitted to the floor size
A scheduled final on the big screen
avoid: Knockout brackets so long that players wait an hour
Finals in a space the crowd cannot see

cards.title: Wheelchair users in MR: wide route, gentle turns, larger stops
cards.text: A seated player in a wheelchair can play an MR runner because the headset tracks their position as they roll. Make the route at least 1.5 m wide with no tight turns, stops 2.5-3 m apart, few hazards placed away from the turning circle, and a smooth floor without cables. Tactics squares of 1 m are tight for wheelchairs; prefer the runner or a PC game.
cards.use_when: a player or group includes wheelchair users or people who need to sit
do: Route 1.5 m wide, smooth floor
Few hazards, no tight zig-zags
PC as an equal alternative
avoid: Tactics boards with small squares
Battle with rain rings for seated players

cards.title: Seated play default: offer PC as a full version, not a lesser one
cards.text: When players must stay seated (bed-bound, limited stamina, a hospital ward, an office desk), PC is the natural platform: all three genres work with mouse and keyboard. Present it as the full game, with the same story and Land, so seated players are not given a smaller experience.
cards.use_when: the brief mentions seated players, limited mobility or no space to walk
do: Same story and theme on PC
Tactics for players who prefer slow thinking
avoid: Calling the PC version a 'lite' version

cards.title: Low vision and colour blindness: contrast and shapes
cards.text: Hazards are red circles, so pick a ground colour that is not red, brown or green (sand, pale grey, blue) so they stand out for red-green colour blind players. Use studio or noon lighting indoors, large and simple scenery shapes, and checkpoints with clear tall markers nearby. Avoid fog, night or neon when players have low vision.
cards.use_when: players include older adults, low-vision or colour-blind players, or the brief asks for accessibility
do: High-contrast palette with a neutral floor
Bright lighting presets
Big simple landmark models
avoid: Green or brown floors under red hazards
Night, spooky or neon for low vision

cards.title: Simple language for labels, rules and story
cards.text: Write for the weakest reader in the group (young kids, second-language players, people with learning disabilities): labels of 2-4 words, verb first ('Find the boat'), rules of 3 short lines, story of 2-3 short sentences with everyday words. Picture-clear scenery repeats what the label says, so reading is a help, not a gate.
cards.use_when: kids, mixed-language groups, special education or any accessibility brief
do: Verb-first labels of 2-4 words
3 rules maximum
avoid: Idioms, jokes that need culture knowledge, long sentences
Meaning that lives only in text

cards.title: Special education class: one small success, repeated
cards.text: For a special education class, aim for a guaranteed success: a short runner of 4 checkpoints in a 4 x 4 m space, no hazards or one well off the route, no time limit, bright lighting and a big friendly finish. A teacher or aide stays at the edge and can talk the student through. Playing the same Land twice builds confidence; the second run is often the joyful one.
cards.use_when: special needs schools, inclusion programmes or therapy-adjacent groups
do: 4 checkpoints, no time limit
Same Land replayed
Aide at the edge talking
avoid: Scores shown as rankings
New layouts every turn

cards.title: Playtest a learning game: can they do the objective after?
cards.text: Check learning, not just enjoyment. After play, give players the checkpoint facts on paper cards shuffled and ask them to put them in order (2 minutes); compare with a group who did not play, or with a quick check before play. Also watch: do players read labels aloud, do watchers argue about the order? If they enjoy it but cannot order the cards, the facts are decoration.
cards.use_when: planning test_questions for an education prototype
do: A 2-minute card sort after play
Note who reads labels aloud
avoid: Measuring only 'did they like it'
Testing with adults when the players are 8

cards.title: Playtest a brand activation: count, time and watch
cards.text: Measure what the client cares about: players per hour, average queue length, how long passers-by stop to watch (dwell), photos taken at the photo spot, repeat players, and whether players can say the brand message in one sentence afterwards. Count over a fixed 30 minutes and compare with the throughput maths.
cards.use_when: test_questions or a pilot for a brand or event booth
do: Tally players and watchers per 30 minutes
Ask 5 players to say the message back
avoid: Collecting personal data to measure
Judging success only by the client's feeling

cards.title: Playtest team-building: watch the talking, not the score
cards.text: For a team game the evidence is communication: how often teammates call to the player, whether quiet members speak, whether the team changes its plan between rounds, and whether everyone had a role. Note laughter and high-fives. A great score with silent teammates means the game did not do its job.
cards.use_when: test_questions for a corporate or club team game
do: Count callouts per round
Note who has no role
avoid: Using only the leaderboard as success
Ignoring people who sat out

cards.title: Playtest a calm game: do players slow down and look around?
cards.text: Signs of a working relaxation game: players walk slower on the second half than the first, stop to look at scenery, turn their heads, and take the headset off smiling rather than rushing out. Ask one question after: on 1-5, how calm do you feel now compared to before? If players hurry to the portal, something (a timer, a hazard, the score) is still pushing them.
cards.use_when: test_questions for a submission or wellbeing prototype
do: Time each half of the route
Ask a 1-5 calm rating, no medical scales
avoid: Measuring speed or score as success
Clinical questionnaires without a professional

cards.title: Playtest active play: effort, safety and willingness to repeat
cards.text: For movement games, observe minutes of active play, how many chapters or rounds players finish, near-misses at the area edge, and whether players want another go. A simple effort question after play (on 1-10, how hard did that feel?) shows if it is too easy or too much. Any near-miss with a wall or another player means the layout needs more clearance.
cards.use_when: test_questions for a fitness or active battle prototype
do: Ask a 1-10 effort rating
Log every near-miss at the edge
avoid: Pushing players to keep going when tired
Measuring calories

cards.title: Playtest tourism and museum games: do they go to the real thing?
cards.text: The best evidence that a museum or tourism game worked is behaviour after the headset: visitors walk to the related exhibit, ask staff where the real place is, take a map, or name a place they want to visit. Count these over a session. If visitors leave the booth and go elsewhere, the game was a ride, not a doorway.
cards.use_when: test_questions for museum, heritage or tourism prototypes
do: Count visitors who ask or go to the real place
Note which checkpoint they mention
avoid: Counting only number of players
Surveys that ask for contact details

cards.title: Playtest a competition: is it fair and worth repeating?
cards.text: Check that scores spread out (not everyone the same, not one runaway winner), that newcomers improve on their second run, and that nobody complains a heat was unfair. Watch return rate: do players rejoin the queue to beat their score? Many ties mean the course needs a skill line; one dominant player with huge gaps means a beginner board is needed.
cards.use_when: test_questions for a leaderboard or tournament design
do: Compare first and second runs
Track rejoin rate
avoid: Judging by the top score only
Changing the course mid-test

cards.title: Playtest family and inclusive games: did everyone play and enjoy?
cards.text: For families, parties and accessibility briefs, success is inclusion: every person who wanted to play finished at least once, the youngest and oldest both smiled, helpers (parents, aides) needed to step in rarely, and nobody was left watching all session. Note who needed help and where on the route; that spot needs a wider path, a simpler label or a removed hazard.
cards.use_when: test_questions for family, party, senior or accessibility prototypes
do: Note finish rate by age group
Mark on the sketch where help was needed
avoid: Testing only with fit adults
Counting only the winner

cards.title: In MR the player sees the real place, only the floor is replaced
cards.text: Quest 3 passthrough shows the real walls, people, sky and light; the engine only swaps the floor for the Land's ground and stands models on it at 1:1 scale. Design every option as a layer on top of a real place, not as a sealed virtual world. Ask what is around the floor, because that is half of what the player will see.
cards.use_when: Any MR brief, before proposing themes or scenery.
do: Ask what surrounds the floor (walls, windows, sky, trees, people)
Describe in environment_fit what the player sees beyond the floor
avoid: Promising a fully enclosed fantasy world in MR
Ignoring the real ceiling or sky in the key art prompt
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Everything stands at real 1:1 scale on the real floor
cards.text: A 1 m model in the Land is 1 m tall in the room, next to real furniture and people. A 4 m dragon in a 3 m high living room clips through the ceiling visually, while the same dragon on a car park looks huge and right. Size hero pieces against the real ceiling height and the floor size, not against an imagined world.
cards.use_when: Choosing hero pieces and prop sizes for an indoor or small venue.
do: Keep indoor hero pieces under about 2.5 m tall unless the ceiling is high
Use tall pieces outdoors or in halls
avoid: Huge models in low rooms
Tiny props in a 20 m car park where they disappear
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Use the real walls as the edge of the world
cards.text: Players can see the real walls, so make them part of the fiction: the fortress wall, the edge of the island, the end of the map. Place the route so it turns before the walls with at least 0.6 m to spare, and put low edge scenery near the walls so the change from virtual floor to real wall feels intended.
cards.use_when: Indoor venues with visible walls on most sides.
do: Name the walls in the story (the castle wall, the ice cliff)
Line the edges with low scenery that frames the real wall
avoid: Routes that point players straight at a wall at speed
Fighting the walls with scenery that pretends they are not there

cards.title: A real skyline or garden becomes the backdrop for free
cards.text: On a rooftop, car park or garden the real sky, trees and buildings fill the view above the floor. Pick themes that agree with them: a city skyline suits sci-fi or heroes, trees suit forest, dinosaurs or farm, open sky suits pirates or islands. Put the finish portal so players face the best view when they arrive.
cards.use_when: Outdoor venues with a visible horizon.
do: Match the theme to what is on the horizon
Face the finish towards the best real view
avoid: Space or underwater themes in bright midday outdoors
Facing the finish at a blank wall or a parked car

cards.title: Turn the real crowd into the in-game audience
cards.text: In a hall or at an event, the people standing around are visible in passthrough. Frame them as the arena audience, the villagers or the race fans. The story can say the crowd is watching your trial, which makes cheers feel part of the game and makes players perform for them.
cards.use_when: Events, halls and booths where spectators stand around the play area.
do: Mention the watching crowd in the intro story
Put the finish facing the spectators
avoid: Stories where the player is alone in an empty world while 30 people are visible
Asking the crowd to do in-game tasks

cards.title: The void floor is dramatic but makes people dizzy
cards.text: The void floor turns the real floor into a bottomless drop with scenery below. It is a strong wow moment but triggers fear of heights, slower walking and discomfort, especially for first-time VR players and seniors. Use it for short, slow sections with confident adults, never for kids or races.
cards.use_when: When a creator asks for heights, sky islands or falling scenery.
do: Offer it only for adults or experienced players
Keep the route short and slow when the void is on
Warn on the intro card
avoid: Void floor in races or timed runs
Void floor for kids 6-9, seniors or first-time VR
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Mark backdrop pieces VR only so they vanish in MR
cards.text: Decor can be flagged VR only so it is hidden in MR and shown only in full VR. Use it for walls, ceilings, skies and tall backdrops that would otherwise float through the real room or block the view of real walls and people. Floor-level scenery stays visible on both.
cards.use_when: A Land that will be played both in MR and in full VR.
do: Flag backdrop walls and ceiling pieces VR only
Keep floor-level scenery visible in MR
avoid: Tall backdrops that overlap real walls in MR

cards.title: There is no joystick movement in MR, the route must fit the real floor
cards.text: In MR players move only by walking, so the whole route, every checkpoint and the portal must lie inside the real empty floor. A creator who wants a long journey gets it through loops, zig-zags and story labels, not distance. Offer a spiral or out-and-back route instead of teleporting or scrolling worlds.
cards.use_when: When the creator imagines a big world or a long trip in a small space.
do: Use loops, spirals or zig-zags to lengthen the walk
Make each checkpoint label a new place in the story
avoid: Promising teleport, flying or joystick movement in MR
Routes longer than the floor allows

cards.title: Living room: small, furniture, 1-2 players
cards.text: A typical cleared living room gives 3 x 3 to 4 x 5 m of floor, with sofas, tables and a TV at the edges and warm indoor light. It fits 1-2 players, a short loop of 4-5 checkpoints and small props. Family members watch from the sofa. Cosy themes (toys, candy, farm, small dragons) fit better than epic battles.
cards.use_when: The creator plays at home.
do: Ask them to measure the empty floor after pushing furniture back
Use small props and a short loop
Make the sofa side the audience side
avoid: Races or 4 players at once
Routes that pass within 0.6 m of a glass table

cards.title: Classroom: desks to move, a class watching
cards.text: A classroom is about 7 x 8 m but desks fill it; after pushing them aside the clear floor is often 4 x 6 m. Light is steady fluorescent, good for colour. 1-3 students play while 25-35 watch, so turn taking and spectator moments matter more than length. Learning themes (Thai history, planets, animals) with checkpoint labels as facts work well.
cards.use_when: A teacher or school group plans to play in a classroom.
do: Ask for the clear floor after desks move, not the room size
Keep plays to 2-3 minutes so the whole class gets a turn
Use checkpoint labels as short facts
avoid: Long solo plays while 30 students wait
Assuming the whole room is empty

cards.title: Hall or function room: big, indoor, good for groups
cards.text: A school or hotel hall often gives 12 x 20 m or more of clear floor with steady light and sometimes a stage. It supports races of up to 6 players, long routes and two lanes. Lights can often be dimmed, which makes spooky and neon themes possible. Spectators stand along the sides or sit on the stage.
cards.use_when: Events in a school hall, hotel ballroom or community hall.
do: Ask whether lights can be dimmed
Plan two lanes or a race
Put the finish in front of the stage or seating
avoid: Using only a small corner of a big hall
Routes that cross the doors people walk through

cards.title: Sports hall or gym: court lines, echo, wide floor
cards.text: A gym or futsal court gives 15 x 25 m or more of flat floor with painted lines. Light is bright and even. Basketball hoops and wall bars stand at the edges, and benches give spectators a clear view. It suits races, sports or hero themes and long routes.
cards.use_when: Playing in a school gym, sports hall or covered court.
do: Use the court lines to align lanes
Seat spectators on the benches along one long side
avoid: Routes under hoops or near wall bars
Ignoring the echo when planning loud spectator moments

cards.title: Garden or lawn: daylight, trees, uneven ground
cards.text: A garden offers 5 x 8 m up to large lawns, but grass is uneven, there are trees, paths and garden furniture, and daylight washes out glow. Players walk slower on grass. Bright themes (farm, dinosaurs, pirates, candy) fit; dark or neon themes do not. Trees inside the floor must be listed as obstacles and the route kept away from them.
cards.use_when: Outdoor play in a garden, park or school field.
do: Ask about trees, slopes, holes and sprinklers
Use noon or morning lighting
Choose bright, saturated themes
avoid: Spooky or neon themes at midday
Hazards that need quick steps on wet grass

cards.title: Car park: huge and flat, but traffic and sun
cards.text: An empty car park gives 20 x 30 m or more of flat hard floor, ideal for long routes, two lanes and 6-player races. The risks are cars, kerbs, drains, strong sun and heat. Only use it when it is closed to traffic. Big hero pieces read well against open sky.
cards.use_when: Large outdoor events or tests in a car park.
do: Confirm it is closed to cars and fenced or staffed
Keep routes off kerbs and drains
Play in the evening or in shade for comfort
avoid: Assuming the whole car park is safe
Dark themes in midday sun

cards.title: Rooftop: skyline view, wind and edges
cards.text: A rooftop gives a dramatic city skyline but has parapets, vents, wind and sun. Keep the route at least 2 m from any roof edge or low railing, much more than the usual 0.6 m, because a player stepping back cannot see what is behind. Sci-fi, heroes or night city themes work best in the evening.
cards.use_when: The creator wants to play on a building rooftop.
do: Keep 2 m or more from roof edges and railings
Use evening or night lighting for city themes
Face the finish at the skyline
avoid: Void floor on a rooftop
Hazards that push players backwards towards an edge

cards.title: Mall atrium: crowds, bright light, passers-by
cards.text: A mall atrium offers about 8 x 12 m with bright mixed light, shiny floors, escalators and a constant crowd of passers-by. It is good for brand events and showing off, but people may walk into the area. Put a barrier or staff around it, keep plays short (2-3 minutes) and design big visible moments for the crowd.
cards.use_when: Promotional events in shopping malls.
do: Ask for a barrier or rope around the floor
Keep plays to 2-3 minutes
Put the leaderboard screen facing the walkway
avoid: Dark themes under skylights
Long plays with a queue of shoppers

cards.title: Event booth: 3 x 3 to 6 x 6 m and a fast queue
cards.text: Exhibition booths usually give 3 x 3, 3 x 6 or 6 x 6 m of floor with strong show lighting and noise. Most players are first-time VR and want a quick taste, so 90 seconds to 3 minutes per play with a clear goal works best. The booth lives on throughput and on how fun it looks from the aisle.
cards.use_when: Trade shows, game shows and expos.
do: Design for 2-3 minute plays
Face the key moments to the aisle
Plan queue entertainment on a screen
avoid: 5 minute plays that stall the queue
Routes that cross the booth entrance

cards.title: Fortal court: 14 x 22 m, steady light, 2-6 players
cards.text: The Fortal court (XR Arena, Chiang Mai) is an indoor 14 x 22 m floor with walls on all sides, painted court lines, 4 doors along one long wall and steady indoor light. Staff and families watch along one long side and a wall screen can show the leaderboard. It fits long routes, races, two lanes and spooky or neon themes.
cards.use_when: The creator plays at the Fortal court (venue fortal-court).
do: Use the preset instead of asking for size
Put key moments along the spectator long side
Show the race leaderboard on the wall screen
avoid: Routes through the doors on the long wall
Asking the creator to measure the court

cards.title: Under 3 x 3 m only the runner genre fits
cards.text: If either side of the MR space is under 3 m, battle and tactics do not fit: enemies need room to walk in from the edges and the 6 x 8 board needs squares a person can step on. All 3 options must then be runners that differ in theme, route and feeling instead. The builder checks this.
cards.use_when: MR brief with width or depth below 3 m.
do: Make all 3 options runners with different loops and moods
Use 3-4 checkpoints
avoid: Proposing battle or tactics in a 2 x 3 m room

cards.title: Under 4 x 4 m: 1-2 players, a short loop, no race
cards.text: A floor under 4 x 4 m is a small play area: plan 1-2 players, a short loop of 4-5 checkpoints and small props. A live race needs parallel space and does not fit, so offer a solo time attack with a leaderboard instead. From about 3.7 m on the shortest side the builder's small rules apply (3-6 checkpoints, 1.2-4 m between stops, 8-30 objects); below that the tiny-room rules take over.
cards.use_when: Small MR floors such as a living room or booth.
do: Plan a loop or figure-eight of 4-5 checkpoints
Offer a solo time attack instead of a race
avoid: Live races with 3 or more players
Big hero pieces that eat the floor

cards.title: 4 x 4 to 10 x 10 m: 1-4 players, loops and zig-zags
cards.text: Medium floors such as a cleared classroom or a small hall fit 1-4 players, loops or zig-zags and 5-7 checkpoints. When the usable side is 5-10 m the builder expects 1.8-6 m between stops, a 1.2 m clear circle around the spawn and 15-50 objects. Shared floor play works well with 2-3 players.
cards.use_when: Medium MR floors.
do: Use 5-7 checkpoints 1.8-6 m apart
Pick loop or zig-zag routes
avoid: Two-lane races under 8 m wide
Checkpoints closer than 1.8 m

cards.title: Over 10 x 10 m: up to 6 players, long routes, races
cards.text: When the usable side is 10 m or more (for example the 14 x 22 m Fortal court) the builder uses large rules: 4-10 checkpoints 2.5-9 m apart, a 1.5 m clear circle around the spawn and 20-80 objects. This is where races, two lanes and hub-and-spoke routes shine. Fill the space with 3-12 vignettes so long walks do not feel empty.
cards.use_when: Halls, courts, gyms and car parks.
do: Use 7-10 checkpoints 2.5-9 m apart
Offer races or two lanes
Place vignettes along the longer legs
avoid: Huddling a short loop in one corner
Stops more than 9 m apart with nothing between

cards.title: Judge size by the shortest side minus 1.2 m
cards.text: The builder measures the usable floor as the shortest side minus 0.6 m on each edge. A 4 x 8 m space is really 2.8 m usable, which counts as small, not medium. Always reason from the shortest side, because the route must turn inside it.
cards.use_when: Any time a size rule is applied.
do: Subtract 1.2 m from the shortest side before choosing rules
Mention the usable size in environment_fit
avoid: Using the long side or the area to pick a size class

cards.title: A shortest side under 3.7 m triggers the tiny-room rules
cards.text: The builder subtracts the 0.6 m edge margin on both sides, so any floor whose shortest side is under about 3.7 m has less than 2.5 m usable and gets tiny rules: 3-4 checkpoints, stops spaced about 45 percent of the usable side (at least 0.5 m), hazard radius 0.35 m, a 0.6 m spawn circle, 2-4 vignettes and 8-20 objects. A 3.5 x 5 m bedroom is tiny, not small. Plan a tight circuit where the story labels and one hero piece carry the experience.
cards.use_when: The shortest side of the MR floor is between 2 and 3.7 m.
do: Check the shortest side against 3.7 m before choosing a checkpoint count
Plan 3-4 checkpoints in a tight circle around one hero piece
avoid: Planning 5 or more checkpoints for a 3 x 4 m room
Hazards that force side steps toward furniture

cards.title: Keep everything at least 0.6 m from the edge of the floor
cards.text: Players overshoot targets, swing arms and step backwards. Keep checkpoints, hazards, the portal and the route at least 0.6 m inside the edge of the measured floor, and more next to glass, stairs or roof edges. The builder applies 0.6 m by default.
cards.use_when: Placing any marker in MR.
do: Treat the outer 0.6 m as a no-go strip
Add extra margin near glass, stairs and drops
avoid: Checkpoints on the edge of the floor
Hazards that make players step outward
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Keep a 1.2 m corridor clear along the walking route
cards.text: Players walk the straight lines from spawn through the checkpoints in order to the portal. No object may stand within 0.6 m plus half its footprint of those lines, which gives a 1.2 m corridor. Arches and gates can sit on the line only if marked walkThrough. This keeps players from flinching at virtual props they think are solid.
cards.use_when: Dressing the route with scenery.
do: Line props along the sides of the corridor
Use walkThrough arches to frame the path
avoid: Rocks or trees on the walking line
Narrow gaps between props players must squeeze through

cards.title: Real obstacles inside the floor must stay off the route
cards.text: A pillar, tree or table inside the floor is a real thing players can hit. List it in obstacles, keep the route and markers well away from it (at least 0.6 m plus a margin) and consider dressing it with a virtual piece of the same footprint, such as a rock around a pillar, so it reads as part of the world.
cards.use_when: The creator mentions a pillar, tree, table or other fixed object.
do: Ask for each obstacle and roughly where it is
Route around it and dress it as a landmark
avoid: Placing a checkpoint beside a pillar
Pretending the obstacle is not there
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Convert paces to metres: 1 pace is about 0.75 m
cards.text: Many creators do not know the size in metres. Ask them to walk the empty floor and count normal steps: 1 adult pace is about 0.75 m (a child's pace is shorter, about 0.5 m). 6 paces by 8 paces is about 4.5 x 6 m. Round down, never up.
cards.use_when: The creator does not know the floor size in metres.
do: Offer count your steps as a quick-reply choice
Round the result down to the nearest half metre
avoid: Rounding up
Using a child's step count with the adult conversion

cards.title: If the size is unknown, assume a small floor and say so
cards.text: If the creator cannot give the size even in paces, assume the safe case: a 3 x 3 m floor indoors, 1-2 players, a short loop. Write the assumption into the brief and tell the creator the game can scale up if they later measure a bigger space. Guessing big risks routes that run into walls.
cards.use_when: The creator does not know or skips the size question.
do: Assume 3 x 3 m indoors
Write the assumption into the brief
Ask once more with paces as an option
avoid: Guessing a large floor
Finishing the interview without any size for a space venue

cards.title: Ask for the empty floor, not the room
cards.text: Rooms include furniture; the play area is only the floor that is clear. Ask how big the empty floor you can walk on is, and offer quick choices such as about 3 x 3 m, 5 x 5 m, 10 x 10 m or bigger, and I will count my steps. The answer changes genre, player count and route, so it is required for a space venue.
cards.use_when: Interview step about the environment.
do: Offer 4-5 size choices plus a paces option
Explain in why that size decides how many can play
avoid: Asking for room size only
Skipping the size question

cards.title: Space checkpoints so players walk, not shuffle
cards.text: Stops too close together make players shuffle in place; too far apart and the walk feels empty. The builder checks 1.2-4 m between stops on small floors, 1.8-6 m on medium and 2.5-9 m on large. Aim for the middle of the range and vary it so the route has rhythm.
cards.use_when: Placing checkpoints in the layout brief.
do: Aim for the middle of the spacing range
Alternate a short and a long leg
avoid: Equal spacing everywhere
Several stops at the minimum distance in a row

cards.title: Hazards sit on the route but leave room to step around
cards.text: Hazards are red circles that send the player back to the last checkpoint. In MR the player must see them early and step around them without leaving the corridor. Keep hazards at least the builder's gap from each other (0.4 m small, 0.7 m medium, 1 m large floors) and away from the edge, so the dodge is never toward a wall.
cards.use_when: Adding hazards to an MR route.
do: Place hazards where the dodge is toward open floor
Give 2-3 m of sight line before each hazard
avoid: Hazards just after a sharp turn
Hazards that force a step into the edge margin

cards.title: Keep the spawn clear so players start calmly
cards.text: Players put the headset on at the spawn and take a moment to adjust. The builder keeps a clear circle around it: 0.8 m on small floors, 1.2 m medium, 1.5 m large. Put the spawn near the entrance and the staff side so helpers can reach players quickly.
cards.use_when: Choosing where the spawn goes.
do: Put the spawn near the staff and entrance
Face the spawn toward the first checkpoint
avoid: Spawning players facing a wall
Props inside the spawn circle

cards.title: Bright daylight washes out glow and dark themes
cards.text: In sun, passthrough is bright and virtual glow, neon and dark colours look faded. Outdoors in daylight choose bright, saturated themes with strong silhouettes and the noon or morning preset. Save spooky and neon for indoors or after dark.
cards.use_when: Outdoor or window-lit venues in daytime.
do: Pick noon or morning lighting
Use bold colours and big shapes
avoid: Neon or spooky themes at midday
Small glowing markers as the only cue
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Steady indoor light keeps colours readable
cards.text: Halls, classrooms and the Fortal court have even artificial light, so most themes read well. The studio or default presets match it; spooky and neon work if the room lights can be dimmed. Ask whether the lights can be changed, because it opens darker themes.
cards.use_when: Indoor venues.
do: Ask whether lights can be dimmed
Use studio or default when the lights stay on
avoid: Assuming a dark room the venue cannot provide

cards.title: After dark, spooky, neon and night presets shine
cards.text: Outdoors after sunset or in a dimmed hall, glow and dark palettes pop and spooky or neon themes feel strong. But passthrough gets grainy in low light and players see real obstacles less well, so keep some room light on, widen clearances and slow the pace.
cards.use_when: Night events, evening outdoor play or dimmed halls.
do: Use night, spooky or neon presets
Keep some real light so tracking and safety work
Widen corridors and slow the route
avoid: Pitch dark rooms where tracking fails
Fast timed routes at night
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Default lighting preset by venue
cards.text: Garden or car park at midday: noon. Morning outdoor events: morning. Sunset rooftop or garden: evening. Living room or classroom with lights on: default or studio. Hall or court with dimmable lights: spooky or neon for dark themes, studio otherwise. Outdoors after dark: night. Pick the preset that agrees with the real light the player will see.
cards.use_when: Choosing the lighting field in options or build.
do: Match the preset to the real light and time
Explain the pick in environment_fit
avoid: Night preset in a sunlit garden
Noon preset in a dim hall

cards.title: Ask when it will be played, not only where
cards.text: The same garden is a bright dino park at 11:00 and a ghost trail at 19:00. Ask the time of day for any venue with windows or open sky; it decides the lighting preset and which themes are possible. Offer quick choices: morning, midday, evening, night, indoors without windows.
cards.use_when: Interview, outdoor or window-lit venues.
do: Ask time of day together with indoor or outdoor
Record it in time_of_day
avoid: Choosing a dark theme before knowing the time

cards.title: Sun patches from windows fade colours on part of the route
cards.text: A room can have even light except where sunlight falls through a window, and that patch moves over the day. Inside it, virtual colours and hazard circles fade while the rest of the route looks fine, so a player can walk into a hazard they did not see. Ask where the sun falls at play time and keep hazards and checkpoints out of that patch, or close the curtains.
cards.use_when: Indoor venues with large windows, especially east or west facing.
do: Ask where direct sun falls at the planned time
Keep hazards out of sunlit patches
avoid: A hazard right in a sunbeam
Assuming the light at the test visit matches the event time
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Design for walking, never running
cards.text: Players in headsets misjudge real distances and may miss small real objects. Time limits and races must be beatable at a brisk walk. In battle the player steps out of rings, never sprints. Write walk, do not run into the rules of every race.
cards.use_when: Any timed, race or battle design in MR.
do: Set time limits a walking player can beat
Add walk, do not run to the rules
avoid: Time limits that need sprinting
Hazards that need a jump or lunge
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: No sudden scares that make people run
cards.text: A jump scare makes people step back or bolt, and in MR that can mean a wall or a person. Build horror with slow dread: dim light, Thai ghost scenery seen from far away, story labels. Keep scary pieces beside the route and visible early, never popping up in front of a player.
cards.use_when: Spooky or horror themes.
do: Use slow reveals and atmosphere
Place scary models beside the path, visible early
avoid: Monsters appearing right in front of the player
Scares near walls or edges
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: No tasks that need looking up while walking fast
cards.text: Looking up while walking hides the floor and real obstacles and causes trips. Put checkpoint labels and targets at chest to eye height. Tall scenery is fine to admire while standing still at a checkpoint.
cards.use_when: Placing labels, targets and hero pieces.
do: Keep interactive things between knee and eye height
Put tall wow pieces near stops, not mid-leg
avoid: Targets high above the route
Labels that must be read while looking up
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Offer a seated or standing-still way to play
cards.text: Some players cannot or should not walk around: limited mobility, some seniors, a tiny room. The PC platform serves seated players, and in MR battle the player mostly stands in place and steps out of rings. Mention the alternative so the creator can include everyone.
cards.use_when: Players with limited mobility or very small spaces.
do: Suggest the PC version for seated players
Keep MR battle steps small
avoid: Designs that assume everyone can walk 50 m
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Avoid motion sickness: the floor must stay still
cards.text: In MR the player walks for real, so the main sickness risks are a bottomless floor and anything that moves the world instead of the player. Keep the floor stable, avoid the void floor for sensitive players, and use animated rides as scenery, never as something players stand on. Fast spins to find the next checkpoint also cause discomfort, so keep the next stop roughly ahead.
cards.use_when: Constraints mention motion sickness, or players are new to VR.
do: Keep the next checkpoint within a 90 degree turn
Use animated rides as scenery only
avoid: Void floor for sensitive players
Routes with many 180 degree turns
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Default session length: about 4 minutes in MR
cards.text: Most MR walking plays feel complete in 3-5 minutes and stay comfortable. First-time players and events want 2-3 minutes; a home game with keen adults can run 8-10 minutes across chapters. If the creator does not say, use 4 minutes and write it into the brief.
cards.use_when: Session length is unknown.
do: Default to 4 minutes
Use 2-3 minutes for events and young kids
avoid: 15 minute single plays in a headset
No time cap at a queue event
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Plan rest breaks between chapters for long sessions
cards.text: Heat, headset weight and eye strain build up over time, faster in warm venues. If the whole experience runs over 10 minutes, split it into chapters of 3-4 minutes with a short break in which the player can lift the headset or sit down. In battle, the chapter by chapter structure gives natural break points before the boss; in runner, the intro card of a second Land can act as one.
cards.use_when: The creator wants a long session or repeated plays by the same person.
do: Add a break after every 3-4 minute chapter
Put the hardest part right after a break, not at the end of a long stretch
avoid: One continuous 20 minute play
A boss fight after 12 minutes without a break
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Quest 3 is heavy for small children: keep their plays short
cards.text: The headset weighs around half a kilo, which is a lot for a young child's neck, and the fit is loose on small faces. For kids 6-9 keep plays to 2-3 minutes, avoid long periods of looking down, and have a helper adjust the strap. Check the manufacturer's age guidance for the venue.
cards.use_when: Players include young children.
do: Cap plays at 2-3 minutes for under-10s
Plan an adult helper per child
avoid: 10 minute plays for 6 year olds
Designs that need long head tilts
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: At events plan hygiene and turnover between players
cards.text: Each change of player needs wiping the face pad, fitting the strap and a short briefing, about 60-90 seconds. Plan the play length and throughput around it. Disposable face covers and a second headset that alternates keep the queue moving.
cards.use_when: Public events with many players.
do: Budget 60-90 s between players
Suggest two headsets that alternate
avoid: Forgetting changeover time in throughput estimates

cards.title: Hot outdoor venues overheat players and headsets
cards.text: In midday Thai sun, headsets overheat and players sweat into the face pad, and sunlight falling into the lenses can damage the screens. Prefer shade, morning or evening times, and outdoor plays of 2-3 minutes. Store headsets lens-down in the shade between players.
cards.use_when: Outdoor daytime venues in hot weather.
do: Suggest shade or morning or evening play
Shorten outdoor plays to 2-3 minutes
avoid: Long midday sessions in direct sun
Leaving headsets lens-up in the sun
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Draw the headset boundary on the floor that was measured
cards.text: The game only knows the size the creator gave; on site, the safety net is the boundary drawn in the headset. Tell the creator to clear the floor first, then draw the boundary on that same floor, so the Land, its 0.6 m margin and the boundary all match. If the drawn boundary is smaller than the brief, rebuild with the smaller size rather than playing past it.
cards.use_when: Before the first play at a new venue.
do: Clear the floor, then draw the boundary
Rebuild if the boundary is smaller than the brief
avoid: Playing a Land bigger than the drawn boundary
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: One spotter watches the floor during group plays
cards.text: On a shared floor players see each other's avatars but still misjudge distance, and real people may wander in. One staff member or parent stands at the edge with a clear view of the whole floor, ready to call stop. Design routes that flow in one direction so players never walk toward each other head-on.
cards.use_when: Shared floor play or events with several players at once.
do: Plan one spotter per floor at the edge
Make routes flow in one direction
avoid: Routes where two players cross head-on
Spotters standing inside the play area

cards.title: Kids 6-9: short, bright, forgiving, few words
cards.text: Young children read slowly, scare easily and tire fast. Use 2-3 minute plays, 4-6 checkpoints with labels of 2-4 words, few hazards, no time limit or a generous one, bright high-contrast colours and friendly themes (animals, candy, toys). In tactics use slow guards (4 s or more) or a board with one guard.
cards.use_when: Players are young children.
do: Labels of 2-4 words
Generous or no time limit
Bright, friendly themes
avoid: Spooky themes
Long intro text
Void floor

cards.title: Kids 10-12: give real challenge and a score to beat
cards.text: Older children want to win and to beat their friends. They read short sentences, handle hazards and a time limit, and love leaderboards. Mild spooky themes such as cute Thai ghosts work. Keep plays 3-4 minutes and let the challenge rise across checkpoints.
cards.use_when: Players are 10-12 years old, for example a school class.
do: Add a time limit and a leaderboard
Raise hazard density toward the end
avoid: Babyish themes
Real horror

cards.title: Teens: competition, style and showing off
cards.text: Teens care about looking cool to the friends watching and beating each other. Races, leaderboards, neon and hero themes, tactics guards at 3 s and battle bosses fit. Keep text short and let them restart quickly.
cards.use_when: Players are teenagers.
do: Offer a race or leaderboard
Use bold neon or hero themes
avoid: Childish story text
Slow tutorials

cards.title: Adults at home or with friends: longer, harder, a bit of nostalgia
cards.text: Adults who choose to play (a game night, a team outing, a birthday) are past the novelty and want a real game: 6-10 minutes across chapters, a time limit that bites, a leaderboard among friends. Themes that call back to childhood (pirates, dinosaurs, toys) or local legends land well. They are self-conscious in front of colleagues, so avoid poses or moves that look silly and let the competition be the show.
cards.use_when: Adult players who have tried VR before or play for a social occasion.
do: Offer chapters and a tight time limit
Use nostalgic or local-legend themes
avoid: Childish story text
Moves that make adults look silly in front of colleagues

cards.title: Seniors: steady floor, slow pace, large clear text
cards.text: Older players may have balance or vision limits. Keep the floor stable (no void), no time limit or a generous one, wide corridors, large high-contrast labels and calm themes (temples, gardens, history). Offer the PC version for anyone unsteady on their feet.
cards.use_when: Players include seniors or grandparents.
do: No void floor, no time pressure
Large high-contrast labels
Offer a seated alternative
avoid: Fast hazards
Low-contrast dark themes
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Mixed-age families: one route, two levels of challenge
cards.text: A family group can have a 6 year old and a grandparent at once. Design for the youngest: short, bright, safe. Older players chase the time bonus and avoid hazard penalties while kids simply finish. Shared floor play lets a parent walk beside a child.
cards.use_when: Family groups with mixed ages.
do: Shared floor so a parent can walk beside the child
Speed bonus as an optional challenge
avoid: Difficulty tuned for teens
Scary themes

cards.title: First-time VR players need a calm first minute
cards.text: First-timers spend the first 30-60 seconds looking around and checking that the floor is really there. Put the first checkpoint close and in plain view, no hazards before it, and save the wow for the second half. Keep the intro card to 2 sentences.
cards.use_when: Events or briefs where most players have never used VR.
do: First checkpoint 2-3 m ahead in plain view
No hazard before checkpoint 2
avoid: Tight time limits from the start
Void floor
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Experienced gamers want depth and mastery
cards.text: Players used to VR or games read the rules fast and look for mastery. Give tighter time limits, denser hazards, tactics boards with 3 s guards and a strict capture order, or battle chapters mixing shield and beast enemies with rain. The leaderboard keeps them replaying.
cards.use_when: Players are gamers or VR regulars.
do: Tighter limits and more hazards
A leaderboard for replay
avoid: Long tutorials
Only easy content

cards.title: School classes: many turns, everyone watches
cards.text: With 30 students and 1-2 headsets, the game is mostly watched. Plays of about 2 minutes, a class leaderboard on a projector and checkpoint labels that teach a fact give the watchers a role: they learn and cheer. Use team names so turns feel fair and no personal data is shown.
cards.use_when: Classroom or school event briefs.
do: 2 minute plays
Leaderboard on the projector
Facts as checkpoint labels
avoid: 5 minute plays
Student names on the leaderboard (use team names)

cards.title: Tourists: local culture, little text, quick to understand
cards.text: Tourists may not read Thai and often play only once. Use visual storytelling and very short labels, Thai temples, ghosts or local legends as scenery, and a 2-3 minute play. The experience should be photo worthy for the friends watching.
cards.use_when: Tourist venues or visitors from abroad.
do: Minimal text, strong visuals
Local culture themes
avoid: Long story cards
Jokes that depend on the language

cards.title: Limited mobility: smaller loops, no stepping tasks, or PC
cards.text: For wheelchair users or people who cannot walk far, long MR routes and battle ring dodges exclude them. Offer the PC platform, or a small runner loop with wide flat corridors of 1.5 m and no hazards that need side steps. Ask what they need without asking for medical details.
cards.use_when: The brief mentions wheelchairs, injuries or limited mobility.
do: Offer the PC version
Wide corridors and no hazard steps
avoid: Asking for medical details
Ring dodges as the only mechanic
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Keep in-headset text short: labels under 5 words
cards.text: Text in a headset is harder to read than on a phone, and walking players only glance at it. Keep checkpoint labels to 2-5 words, the goal to one line and the story card to 2-4 short sentences. Young players and tourists need even less.
cards.use_when: Writing labels, goals and story text.
do: Labels of 2-5 words
Story of 2-4 sentences
avoid: Paragraph labels
Rules lists over 4 items

cards.title: High contrast colours for markers, more for kids and seniors
cards.text: Markers must read against both the virtual floor and the real light. Hazards are red, so keep the floor palette away from red and orange. Pair light floors with dark props or the reverse, and avoid low-contrast palettes for kids, seniors and daylight venues.
cards.use_when: Choosing the palette and floor theme.
do: Keep the floor away from red tones
Check the palette for daylight readability
avoid: Red or orange floors that hide hazards
Grey on grey palettes

cards.title: Tactics guard beat by player: 4-5 s for kids, 3 s for gamers
cards.text: In tactics guards move every 3 s or slower. Walking onto a square in MR takes time, so for kids, seniors and first-timers use 4-5 s per beat and few guards; gamers and teens can handle 3 s. A beat that is too fast turns planning into panic and tempts people to rush.
cards.use_when: Designing tactics boards in MR.
do: Slow the beat for young or new players
Use fewer guards on the first board
avoid: Beats under 3 s
Many guards on the first board

cards.title: Set time limits from walking speed and player type
cards.text: Estimate the walk: a brisk adult covers about 1 m per second plus a few seconds at each checkpoint. Give kids and first-timers about double that walking time, adults 1.5 times, gamers 1.2 times. Or leave the limit off and let the time bonus reward speed.
cards.use_when: Setting timeLimit.
do: Estimate route length, then apply the multiplier
Leave it null for relaxed or family games
avoid: Limits based on running speed

cards.title: Spectators see bodies, not the game
cards.text: People watching from the side see players walk, turn, step and react, but not the virtual floor. Design moments with visible body language: a sidestep around a hazard, a pause at a checkpoint, arms raised at the portal. A screen with the leaderboard gives them the rest.
cards.use_when: Any MR design with an audience.
do: Plan 1-2 visible body moments
Describe spectator_view honestly
avoid: Assuming spectators understand what the player sees

cards.title: Put key moments on the spectator side
cards.text: Find where people stand and place a hazard dodge and the finish portal on that side, 1.5-3 m from them and inside the edge margin. They then see faces and reactions instead of backs. The layout brief must say which side the spectators are on.
cards.use_when: Placing the finish and highlight hazards.
do: Finish portal facing the audience
One hazard on the spectator side
avoid: Finish in the far corner
Key moments with the player's back to the crowd

cards.title: Show the race leaderboard on a screen
cards.text: A TV or projector with the live leaderboard turns watchers into fans and gives the queue a reason to stay. Place it where spectators and the queue can both see it, not where players in headsets walk toward it.
cards.use_when: Races, events, classes, the Fortal court wall screen.
do: Put the screen beside the queue
Use nicknames or team names
avoid: Real names or personal data on screen

cards.title: Let parents and friends cheer and call out hints
cards.text: Spectators can shout left or one more. Design moments where a hint helps: a checkpoint behind a prop, a hazard the player has not noticed yet. This creates fellowship without any spectator task inside the area.
cards.use_when: Family or friend groups watching.
do: Place one checkpoint so it is fun to call out
Mention cheering in spectator_plan
avoid: Spectators walking into the area to help

cards.title: Never give spectators a task inside the play area
cards.text: Anyone standing on the floor is a real obstacle that players cannot see as part of the game. Spectator roles stay outside the edge: cheering, watching the screen, choosing the next player.
cards.use_when: Any design that involves spectators.
do: Keep spectator roles outside the boundary
avoid: A friend standing at a checkpoint
Spectators holding props on the floor
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Entertain the queue at events
cards.text: At booths the queue is the next set of players and the crowd that draws others in. Show the leaderboard or a looping trailer on a screen and let the queue watch players react. A short 2-3 minute play keeps the wait short.
cards.use_when: Events, booths and malls with a queue.
do: Leaderboard or trailer on a screen facing the queue
Keep plays short
avoid: A queue that faces a blank wall

cards.title: Race or shared floor: pick by space and goal
cards.text: In a race each player walks their own copy and sees a live leaderboard; in a shared floor players see each other's avatars. Races feel competitive, but players on the same real floor can still collide, so they need a large floor or players taking turns. Shared floor suits families and teamwork.
cards.use_when: Choosing play_mode with more than one player.
do: Race on large floors or as turns
Shared floor for families and teamwork
avoid: Simultaneous races on a small floor

cards.title: Cap players at once by area: about 8 square metres each
cards.text: When several people share one real floor (a shared-floor game or a simultaneous race), each walking player needs about 6-10 square metres to move without bumping into others. Divide the floor area by 8 and round down, then cap at 6: a 4 x 5 m floor fits 2, a 7 x 7 m floor fits 6 on paper but 4 is safer with hazards to dodge. More people than that means turns, not a bigger group.
cards.use_when: Setting group_size for a shared-floor or simultaneous MR game.
do: Divide the floor area by 8 square metres and round down
Lower the count if the route has many hazards
avoid: Filling the floor to the cap with kids who move unpredictably
Counting floor area that is inside the 0.6 m edge margin

cards.title: Two mirrored lanes for a fair side-by-side race
cards.text: On floors over about 8 m wide, split the floor into two mirrored lanes with at least a 1 m gap so two players race at once without crossing. Spectators love seeing them side by side, and mirrored lanes keep the race fair.
cards.use_when: Two-player races in halls, courts or car parks.
do: Mirror the checkpoints exactly
Keep a 1 m buffer between lanes
avoid: Lanes that cross
Lanes on floors under 8 m wide

cards.title: Turns plus an all-day leaderboard replace live races at busy events
cards.text: When more people want to play than the floor can hold, let them play one or two at a time and compete on a leaderboard that runs all day. A player who finished can come back to see if they still lead, and the next player knows the score to beat before putting the headset on. Reset the board at a fixed time and announce the leader.
cards.use_when: Events and classes with more players than space.
do: Run one leaderboard across the whole day
Tell each player the score to beat before they start
avoid: Holding people back to race everyone at once
Leaderboards with real names

cards.title: Estimate throughput: players per hour
cards.text: Players per hour = 60 / (play minutes + changeover minutes) x headsets. A 3 minute play with a 1.5 minute changeover on 2 headsets gives about 26 players per hour. Use this to set the play length the event can afford.
cards.use_when: Event planning with a target number of players.
do: Ask how many people are expected
Shorten plays if throughput is too low
avoid: Ignoring changeover time

cards.title: On PC skip every question about the real room
cards.text: A PC game has no real floor, so do not ask about size, surroundings, obstacles or venue, and do not set venue, width_m, depth_m or indoor. Spend those questions on players, feelings and session instead.
cards.use_when: The creator chooses platform pc.
do: Skip the environment questions
Ask more about players and feelings
avoid: Asking for floor size on PC

cards.title: On PC, friends watch the screen, not the body
cards.text: PC spectators see the same screen as the player, so they understand everything that happens. Loud visual feedback on hits, checkpoints and the finish makes watching fun, and hot-seat turns with a leaderboard work well for friends.
cards.use_when: PC games played with friends nearby.
do: Make hits and checkpoints visually loud
Offer hot-seat turns
avoid: Designing body-language moments that only matter in MR

cards.title: PC players expect WASD, mouse look and quick restarts
cards.text: On PC the runner is played with WASD and battle uses a third person sword with a 3-hit combo and a dash. Players expect standard controls, instant restarts and tighter challenge than in MR, because nobody walks a real floor. Routes can be longer and hazards denser than in MR.
cards.use_when: PC options and build.
do: Keep standard WASD and mouse
Tighten timing compared to MR
avoid: Copying MR walking time limits to PC
Custom control schemes

cards.title: Ideas too intense for MR belong on PC
cards.text: On PC nobody walks a real floor, so a fast pace, darker and scarier themes, dense hazards and dramatic heights are safe. When the creator wants something that breaks an MR safety rule (sprinting, jump scares, a long void walk), say why it is unsafe in a headset and offer PC as the home for that idea, or a gentle MR version alongside it.
cards.use_when: The creator asks for speed, scares or heights that MR cannot do safely.
do: Explain the MR safety reason in one line
Offer the PC platform for the intense version
avoid: Porting intense PC ideas straight into MR
Refusing the idea without an alternative

cards.title: Loud venues drown out game sound: make every cue visual
cards.text: Events, malls, gyms and halls are loud, and music or a crowd covers headset audio. Any cue that matters (a hazard, the next checkpoint, the time running out) must also be visible: the red hazard circle, the checkpoint label, the timer. Treat sound as a bonus layer, and remember the crowd can be the soundtrack: cheering at the finish is part of the show.
cards.use_when: Events, malls, gyms or anywhere with music or a crowd.
do: Make every important cue visible
Put the finish where the crowd can cheer
avoid: Story told only through audio
Warnings that are only a sound

cards.title: Rain and wind outdoors need a covered fallback
cards.text: Quest headsets are not waterproof, and wet grass or tiles become slippery. Wind blows hair into faces, moves loose decorations and can push light barriers onto the floor. For any outdoor plan ask about a covered fallback (a tent, a porch, an indoor room) and design a version of the Land that fits it.
cards.use_when: Outdoor venues, especially in the rainy season.
do: Ask for a covered fallback space and its size
Keep loose barriers and banners well outside the floor
avoid: Playing in drizzle
Outdoor-only plans in the rainy season

cards.title: The real floor surface changes how fast players can walk
cards.text: Players feel the real floor under the virtual one. Smooth tiles and court floors allow a brisk walk; carpet is safe but rugs with edges catch feet; grass is uneven and slower; polished stone can be slippery in socks. Ask what the floor is, remove rugs and cables, and lengthen time limits on grass or carpet.
cards.use_when: Any MR venue, before setting time limits and hazard density.
do: Ask what the floor surface is
Remove rugs and cables from the floor
Add time on grass or thick carpet
avoid: Tight time limits on grass
Playing in socks on polished floors

cards.title: Low light, mirrors and glass walls can break headset tracking
cards.text: The headset tracks itself with its cameras. Very dark rooms, large mirrors, glass walls, and plain featureless floors or walls can make it lose its place, so the virtual floor drifts or freezes. Keep the room moderately lit, cover big mirrors, and keep the route away from glass walls, which players also may not see in passthrough.
cards.use_when: Dim venues, dance studios with mirrors, glass shopfronts or atriums.
do: Keep some room light on
Cover large mirrors
Keep 1 m or more from glass walls
avoid: Pitch dark spooky rooms
Routes along a mirror wall or glass shopfront
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Young kids play with a parent at the edge or as a second player
cards.text: A child of 6-9 often wants a parent close. Either the parent stands at the edge as the spotter and calls out hints, or the parent wears a second headset and plays on a shared floor beside the child. A parent walking on the floor without a headset is a real obstacle the child may not expect, so avoid that.
cards.use_when: Families with young children.
do: Offer a shared floor so a parent can play beside the child
Or put the parent at the edge as the spotter
avoid: A parent walking on the floor without a headset
Races between a parent and a small child on one floor

cards.title: Wheelchair users in MR need wide turns and labels at seated eye height
cards.text: A wheelchair needs about 1.5 m to turn around, so make the corridor at least 1.5 m wide and leave a 1.5 m circle at each checkpoint and at sharp turns. A seated player's eyes are about 1.2 m above the floor, so keep labels and targets low. Choose a smooth hard floor, no hazards that need side steps, and no void floor.
cards.use_when: A wheelchair user will play in MR.
do: Make corridors and turns 1.5 m wide
Keep labels at seated eye height
Use a smooth hard floor
avoid: Hazards that need side steps
Thick carpet or grass
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Temples, schools and museums need respectful themes
cards.text: In a temple ground, a school or a museum, the theme must fit the place: no ghosts or horror on temple grounds, no violence-themed battle in a primary school, quiet play near prayer halls or classrooms in session. Ask the host about rules on photos, shoes, sound and opening times, and lean on discovery and narrative themes that tell the place's own story.
cards.use_when: Venues with cultural, religious or educational rules.
do: Ask the host about rules and quiet hours
Use the place's own story as the theme
avoid: Thai ghost themes on temple grounds
Loud play near prayer halls or classes

cards.title: Stairs, stage edges and ponds near the floor need extra margin
cards.text: The 0.6 m edge margin assumes a flat wall or open floor beyond the edge. If the floor ends at stairs, a stage edge, a pond, a pool or a balcony, keep everything at least 2 m away from that side and point the route away from it, because a player stepping backwards cannot see it.
cards.use_when: The floor borders stairs, a stage edge, water or a drop.
do: Ask what is just beyond each edge
Keep 2 m from drops and water
avoid: Hazards that make players step back toward a drop
Finishing on a stage edge
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Give every player a 30 second safety briefing
cards.text: Before the headset goes on, tell each player three things: walk, do not run; the boundary will appear if you get close to the edge; take the headset off or raise a hand to stop. At events the intro card can repeat walk, do not run in the rules list. It costs 30 seconds and prevents most accidents.
cards.use_when: Events, classes and first-time players.
do: Brief walk-do-not-run, the boundary and how to stop
Repeat walk, do not run in the rules
avoid: Putting headsets on players with no briefing
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: At home, close the doors and keep pets and small children off the floor
cards.text: In a living room the risks are not the walls but things that move: a dog, a toddler, a sibling walking through, a door that opens into the floor. Ask the creator to close doors, keep pets out and agree that nobody crosses the floor during play. Put the spawn on the side away from the door.
cards.use_when: Home play in a living room or bedroom.
do: Close doors and keep pets out
Spawn away from the door
avoid: Routes that pass a door that opens inward

cards.title: Start from a one-sentence premise: you are X, you must Y, before Z
cards.text: Before writing any label, chapter or board line, write the premise as one sentence with a role, an action and a stake: "You are the last lantern carrier and must relight 6 shrines before the ghosts wake." Every other line in the game should trace back to it. If the premise needs two sentences, the story is too big for a 1-8 minute play.
cards.use_when: the concept is chosen and you are about to write the story, labels or chapters
do: Write role + action + stake in one sentence
Use the premise as sentence 1 or 2 of the intro card
Check each label against it: does this line serve the premise?
avoid: Premises that are only a setting ("A spooky temple")
Two goals at once ("save the village and win the race and find the treasure")
cards.source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

cards.title: Split checkpoints into three acts: arrive, trouble, triumph
cards.text: Map the checkpoint count onto a short three-act shape. With 4 checkpoints use 1-2-1, with 6 use 2-2-2, with 8 use 2-4-2, with 10 use 3-4-3. Act 1 labels set up the world and the task ("Enter the reef"), act 2 labels raise trouble ("Swim past the eels"), act 3 labels pay off ("Wake the pearl queen"). The portal is the curtain call, not a fourth act.
cards.use_when: writing 4-10 checkpoint labels for a runner with narrative as a feeling
do: Decide the act split before writing labels
Put the hardest hazard in act 2 and the payoff label in act 3
Make the act 3 labels name the thing promised on the intro card
avoid: Ten labels at one emotional level
Using act 1 to explain backstory instead of moving

cards.title: Quest chain: each checkpoint makes the next one possible
cards.text: A quest chain links stops by cause: "Wake the bell keeper", "Ring the old bell", "Open the river gate", "Free the boats". Nothing is carried or unlocked by the engine; the checkpoint order already forces the sequence, so the words only need to imply that each step leads to the next. This makes 5-7 checkpoints feel like one task instead of a list.
cards.use_when: the brief wants a story with purpose and the route has 5-7 checkpoints
do: Let each label imply the result of the previous one
Show the change in scenery (a gate model beside "Open the river gate")
avoid: Saying a door really unlocks or an item is needed (no inventory)
Chains longer than 7 links in a short play

cards.title: Rescue structure: find each captive, then go home through the portal
cards.text: Rescue is the easiest story to read: each checkpoint is someone or something freed ("Free the first kitten"), hazards are what holds them (thorns, a curse ring, fire), and the portal is home. Put a still model of each captive beside its checkpoint so the label points at something visible. For kids use animals or toys; for adults use villagers or spirits.
cards.use_when: a runner for kids or families, or any brief that says "help" or "save"
do: Count the captives in the goal line ("Free 5 kittens, then go home")
Show each captive as a scenery model at its checkpoint
avoid: Captives that follow you (the engine has no followers)
Rescue from violence in kids games; use cages, sleep spells, ice

cards.title: Escape structure: the place is closing, the portal is the only way out
cards.text: In an escape the danger is behind you and the portal is the exit. Labels count down places passed ("Out of the cell", "Past the kitchen", "Up the stairs", "The last door") and hazards are the closing threat (lava, alarm rings). A time limit fits naturally ("before the volcano blows"), so set timeLimit and mention it once in the story. Escape suits challenge, sensation and races.
cards.use_when: a runner that should feel urgent, or a race
do: Write labels as places passed, not tasks done
Name the time limit in story words ("before sunrise")
avoid: Calm wandering words in an escape
A threat that is described but never shown; place hazards or scenery for it

cards.title: Delivery structure: you carry something precious from start to finish
cards.text: A delivery story gives one object the whole journey: a lantern flame, a letter, a dragon egg. The object exists only in words (the engine has no carrying), so state it on the intro card ("You carry the last warm ember") and let labels be the stops on the way ("Shelter from the snow", "Cross the frozen lake", "Reach the cold village"). The portal is the handover.
cards.use_when: a runner with a journey feeling, a tour, or a gentle family story
do: Name the carried thing on the intro card
Make the last label or the goal the handover ("Bring the ember to the village")
avoid: Rules or labels that say "do not drop it" (nothing can be dropped)
Asking players to hold a real object while walking in MR

cards.title: Collection structure: a numbered set the player completes
cards.text: Collection works when the set has a clear count and a reason: "5 lost stars to put back in the sky". Touching a checkpoint is the collecting, so labels can repeat a pattern on purpose ("Star 1: the well", "Star 2: the windmill"). Give the set a payoff in the last label or goal ("Light up the sky"). Kids love counting up, and the HUD already shows checkpoint progress.
cards.use_when: a runner for kids, families or first-time VR players, or a submission feeling
do: Use the same noun with a number plus a place
Say the total on the intro card and in the goal
avoid: Collecting with no reason or payoff
Promising to use the collected things later (no inventory)

cards.title: Tour structure: each checkpoint is one sight with one fact or feeling
cards.text: A tour treats checkpoints as stops on a guided walk: "See the floating market", "Visit the spirit house", "Watch the elephants bathe". Each label names the sight and the vignette beside it shows it. Add no threat words; use hazards lightly as natural obstacles (puddles, sleeping dogs). Tours suit tourists, seniors, educators and brands showing a place.
cards.use_when: tourists, school visits, brand showcases or a submission or discovery brief
do: One sight per label, named plainly
Let the intro card say where the tour goes and how many stops
avoid: Packing several facts into one label
Danger words in a relaxing tour

cards.title: Mystery with a reveal at the end: a clue in each label, the answer in the last
cards.text: A short mystery plants a question on the intro card ("Who stole the moon?") and lets each label add a clue the scenery shows ("Follow the silver footprints", "Check the empty nest"). The last checkpoint label gives the answer ("The owl kept it for her chicks"). The reveal must sit in the last label (or the boss intro in battle), because the engine has no ending screen to write on.
cards.use_when: a runner or battle with narrative or discovery, played solo or together (not a race)
do: Ask the question on the intro card
Make the last label the answer, not one more clue
avoid: Clues that need paragraphs
Reveals that need every label read, in a race where players skim

cards.title: Battle arc across chapters: outskirts, defences, heart, boss
cards.text: Across 3-6 chapters let the place move inward: chapter 1 at the edge ("The Frozen Pass"), middle chapters at the defences ("The Shield Wall", "The Hunting Grounds"), the last chapter at the boss's door ("Below the Throne"), then the boss. Moving through named places makes the fight feel like a journey even though the arena itself does not change.
cards.use_when: writing chapter titles for a battle game
do: Read the titles in order: they should move closer to the boss
Use the theme (ice, lava, forest, neon, desert, dark) in the place names
avoid: Titles that are only numbers or difficulty words ("Hard Wave")
Jumping to the boss lair in chapter 1

cards.title: Give each enemy kind a story meaning and name it in its chapter line
cards.text: The engine has three foes, so the words decide who they are. Grunts are fast and weak: a swarm (imps, ice sprites, sand rats). Shields block from the front: a wall of guards (stone soldiers, palace guards). Beasts are big chargers: the boss's pet (a lava hound, a forest boar). Rain is a sky threat: hail, falling embers, a curse. Mention the main foe in its chapter line ("Stone guards lock shields at the gate") so players know what is coming. Re-check after choosing foes: falling danger only when rain is true, a big creature only when a beast is in that chapter.
cards.use_when: writing chapter lines once each chapter's foes are chosen
do: Match the line to the main foe kind in that chapter
Name rain as weather or a curse when rain is true
avoid: Describing archers or flying foes (not in the engine)
Calling a chapter of grunts "the giants"

cards.title: Tactics arc across boards: the piece changes because the story does
cards.text: Boards should vary the piece, and each change needs a story reason: start as a knight sneaking in ("Leap the garden walls"), become a rook in the long halls ("Charge the straight corridors"), a bishop in the chapel ("Slip along the diagonal pews"), and end as the queen ("Take back the throne"). The piece change reads as growth or disguise, not as a rule change.
cards.use_when: writing 3-6 board stories for a tactics game
do: Tie each piece to the place of that board
Save the queen or the king target for the last board
avoid: Board stories that ignore which piece the player is
Changing piece with no word about why

cards.title: The boss is the story payoff: name it twice before it appears
cards.text: A boss lands when players already know it. Name it on the intro card ("the Ash King sleeps under the mountain"), hint at it in a middle chapter line ("His hounds smell you"), then let boss.intro deliver ("The Ash King rises. End this."). A boss who appears without warning feels like a random big enemy, not an ending.
cards.use_when: writing the story card, chapter lines and boss for a battle game
do: Mention the boss name on the intro card
Hint at it in one chapter line before the last
Write the boss intro as the climax sentence
avoid: A boss name first seen in boss.intro
A boss unrelated to the chapters' theme

cards.title: Label length: English 2-5 words, Thai about 6-16 characters
