cards.text: English labels read best at 2-5 words and under about 24 characters ("Ring the old bell"). Thai has no spaces between words, so count characters: aim for about 6-16 Thai characters ("ตีระฆังเก่า", "จุดเทียนดวงแรก"). Thai labels over about 20 characters blur in a headset while walking. If a label needs a comma, it is two labels.
cards.use_when: writing checkpoint labels in either language, especially for MR
do: Read the label aloud in under 2 seconds
Cut adjectives first, keep the verb and the noun
avoid: Thai full sentences with particles and pronouns as labels
Commas, brackets or two clauses in one label

cards.title: Thai labels start with the verb too, and drop the pronoun
cards.text: Thai naturally puts the verb first in commands, so labels should read like a friend telling you what to do: "ปลุกยักษ์วัด", "ข้ามสะพานหมอก", "ช่วยลูกเป็ด". Drop "คุณ", "เรา" and "จง"; they make the label long and stiff. Good: "จุดตะเกียง". Bad: "คุณจะต้องจุดตะเกียงให้สว่าง".
cards.use_when: writing checkpoint labels with lang = th
do: Verb + object, sometimes + one place word
Everyday verbs: ไป, หา, ช่วย, ปลุก, จุด, ข้าม
avoid: "จง..." commands (sounds like a textbook)
Starting every label with "ด่านที่ 3:"

cards.title: Numbered progress in labels when the set repeats: "Bell 2", "Last bell"
cards.text: When checkpoints are a set (bells, stars, lanterns), a number in the label tells players how far they are: "Bell 1: the gate", "Bell 2: the pond", "Last bell: the tower". In Thai: "ระฆังที่ 1 ประตูวัด", "ระฆังสุดท้าย บนหอ". Use Arabic digits so every player reads them fast, and name the final one "Last" or "สุดท้าย" to signal the climax.
cards.use_when: a collection or chain runner with repeated checkpoint types
do: Number + place for each repeat
Switch to "Last" for the final one
avoid: Numbers with no place (players cannot tell the stops apart)
Thai numerals in labels

cards.title: Checkpoint labels: bad drafts and good rewrites
cards.text: Bad "Checkpoint 2" becomes "Cross the rope bridge". Bad "Now you must find the very old ancient lantern" becomes "Find the old lantern". Bad "Talk to the monk" becomes "Visit the monk" (no dialogue). Bad "Pick up the key" becomes "Reach the key stone" (no carrying). Bad Thai "ท่านจงเสด็จไปยังศาลา" becomes "ไปที่ศาลา". Bad "Zone C" becomes "Into the bamboo".
cards.use_when: reviewing a draft list of checkpoint labels
do: Rewrite any label that names a number, a zone or an impossible action
Keep the verb and the visible noun
avoid: Labels that only describe geography with no action
Labels copied from another game

cards.title: Safe label verbs: actions done just by arriving
cards.text: A checkpoint is touched by walking into it, so the best verbs happen on arrival: reach, enter, cross, visit, light, wake, ring, free, find, greet, bless, see, pass. In Thai: ไปถึง, เข้า, ข้าม, ไปหา, จุด, ปลุก, ตี (ระฆัง), ปล่อย, หา, ไหว้, ดู. Avoid verbs that need hands, buttons or speech: pick up, throw, open with a key, talk, ask, buy, build, shoot.
cards.use_when: choosing verbs for checkpoint labels
do: Pick an arrival verb that fits the scenery at that stop
Vary verbs across the route
avoid: Hand verbs (pick up, throw, craft)
Speech verbs (ask, tell, answer)

cards.title: Six labels starting with "Find" read like a shopping list
cards.text: When every label opens with the same verb ("Find the cat", "Find the hat", "Find the bat"), players stop reading after the second. Unless it is a deliberate numbered set, vary the verb so each stop has its own moment: "Spot the cat", "Wake the owl", "Cross the creek", "Free the fox". In Thai, rotate between หา, ปลุก, ข้าม, ช่วย, จุด.
cards.use_when: a draft label list where most labels share a first word
do: Use at least 3 different verbs in 5-7 labels
Keep repetition only for numbered sets
avoid: The same verb on every label by accident
Fancy synonyms that are harder to read ("Procure")

cards.title: There is no ending screen: land the ending on the last label
cards.text: The game card has no finish-message field, and the portal only ends the run with the score. So the story's ending must live in the last checkpoint label ("Return the moon to the sky") and in what the goal line promised. Make the last label the resolution, not another errand, and give the portal a meaning on the intro card ("then the gate takes you home").
cards.use_when: writing the final checkpoint label and the intro card of a runner
do: Write the last label as the payoff
Name the portal's meaning on the intro card (home, the exit, the next world)
avoid: Planning a victory speech or ending text the engine cannot show
A last label that is a minor errand

cards.title: Intro card in 4 short sentences: world, you, trouble, go
cards.text: The story field is 2-4 sentences read once before play. A reliable shape: 1) the world ("The river spirits lost their lights."), 2) who you are ("You are the lantern child."), 3) the trouble and the stake ("The ghosts wake at midnight."), 4) the call to action ("Light 5 lanterns and get home."). With only 2 sentences, merge 1+2 and 3+4. Keep each sentence under about 15 words.
cards.use_when: writing game.story in the build step or in a pc_battle or pc_tactics game card
do: Second person "you" from sentence 2
End on an action the player does right away
avoid: Opening with history and dates
A fifth sentence of lore

cards.title: Goal, story and labels must agree on the numbers and the final thing
cards.text: If the goal says "Light 5 lanterns" there must be 5 lantern labels, and the story must not say "6 shrines". If the boss is "the Frost Warden" on the card, boss.name must match exactly. Players trust the card; a mismatch reads as a bug. Check counts and names across goal, story, labels, chapter lines, board stories (against the targets and guards of each board) and boss before submitting.
cards.use_when: the last check before submitting a build, pc_battle or pc_tactics answer
do: Count labels against the goal number
Use the exact same spelling for names everywhere
avoid: Vague counts in the story ("a few lanterns") while the goal says 5
A boss with two different names

cards.title: Rules list: 3-4 items, one plain verb each, in play order
cards.text: The schema allows up to 8 rules for a runner and 6 for PC battle and tactics, but players read 3-4. Order them as played: what to do, what to avoid, how to finish. Runner example: "Walk to the glowing points in order", "Red circles send you back", "Step into the gate to finish". Use plain mechanic words, with at most a story word in brackets.
cards.use_when: writing game.rules in the build step
do: One rule per line, starting with a verb or the thing to avoid
Put the finish rule last
avoid: Rules that repeat the story
More than 5 rules for kids or first-time VR players

cards.title: Write rules in plain words with the story word beside them
cards.text: Rules must be understood by everyone, so lead with the mechanic and add the fiction once: "Do not step in red circles (the lava pools)", "Capture targets in order (the stolen jewels)", "Step out of the red rings (the dragon's fire)". Thai: "อย่าเหยียบวงแดง (บ่อลาวา)". The story word carries the theme; the plain words keep the rule clear.
cards.use_when: rules for a themed game where the fiction renames hazards or targets
do: Mechanic first, story word in brackets
Reuse the story word from the labels
avoid: Only the story word ("Avoid the Ember Wounds")
Rules that hide what actually happens

cards.title: In MR, one rule is always about walking safely
cards.text: Walking players in a real room need one safety rule on the card: "Walk, do not run", or for battle "Step, do not jump". Thai: "เดินนะ ห้ามวิ่ง". Put it second or third, not first, so it is read without opening the card like a warning sign. It matters most in races, which make people speed up.
cards.use_when: any MR game card, especially races and battle
do: Include a walk-not-run rule in MR
Word it kindly and short
avoid: Leaving safety only to staff
Long legal-style warnings on the card
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Rule lists that work for each genre
cards.text: Runner: "Walk to the points in order", "Red circles send you back", "Finish at the gate". Battle on PC: "Click to swing, 3 hits make a combo", "Dash out of red rings", "Clear every chapter, then beat the boss". Battle in MR: "Swing your right controller like a sword", "Step out of red rings", "Beat the boss". Tactics: "Move like your chess piece", "Capture targets in order", "Never stop on a square a guard attacks".
cards.use_when: writing rules for battle, tactics or runner
do: Name the input in plain words on PC
Start from 3 lines and add only what the brief needs
avoid: Explaining how every chess piece moves in the list
Rules about mechanics the genre lacks

cards.title: Chapter title 1-3 words; chapter line one sentence under 12 words
cards.text: Titles are names of places or moments ("The Ash Road", "Ember Storm", "ถ้ำลาวา"); lines are one present-tense sentence about what happens now ("The road splits and the hounds come running."). Thai lines stay under about 30 characters: "ฝนไฟตกลงมา หลบให้ทัน". The line shows as a chapter starts, mid-action, so it must read in 2 seconds.
cards.use_when: writing the title and line of each battle chapter
do: Present tense, one sentence
Put the danger word near the start of the line
avoid: Lines that explain controls (use the rules list)
Titles over 3 words

cards.title: Boss names: a title plus one strong noun, easy to shout
cards.text: Good boss names are 2-4 words that say what the boss rules or is made of: "The Ash King", "Frost Warden", "Mother of Thorns", "ราชาเถ้าถ่าน", "เจ้าแม่น้ำแข็ง". Players and spectators should be able to shout it. Avoid apostrophes, invented syllables and names that only work in one language if the game may be made in the other.
cards.use_when: writing boss.name for a battle game
do: Title + element or domain
Match the theme (lava, ice, forest, neon, desert, dark)
avoid: Random syllable names ("Xyrrthak")
Names of real gods, kings or religious figures

cards.title: Boss intro: what wakes, then what you must do, in 1-2 short sentences
cards.text: boss.intro is the climax line. Write it as an event and a call: "The Ash King rises from the ember throne. Break his crown." Thai: "ราชาเถ้าถ่านตื่นแล้ว ล้มมันให้ได้". Use 5-15 words. The boss fight is fixed (ring slams, summoned grunts, faster below half health), so promise a fight, not a special attack.
cards.use_when: writing boss.intro for a battle game
do: Short event + imperative
Reuse the boss name exactly
avoid: Describing fire breath, flying or phases the engine does not have
Long villain speeches (no dialogue)

cards.title: Board story: one line under 12 words naming the targets and the guards
cards.text: A tactics board line says what the targets and guards are in story terms: "Steal the 3 crowns before the night watch turns." Thai: "ขโมยมงกุฎ 3 ชิ้น ก่อนยามหันมา". Mention a target count only if it matches the board's targets number. Use the piece's nature when it helps ("Leap the hedges, rider").
cards.use_when: writing the story line of each tactics board
do: Target meaning + guard meaning in one line
Match any number to the board's targets
avoid: Lines about moves the piece cannot make
Lines that describe the room only

cards.title: Give each chess piece a role that matches how it moves
cards.text: The piece the player is should feel like a character: knight = a rider or a frog that jumps over things, bishop = a monk or a shadow sliding on diagonals, rook = a battering cart or a castle golem charging in straight lines, queen = the hero, free in every direction. Write the role into the board story ("As the monk, slip along the diagonal halls").
cards.use_when: tactics boards where the brief wants fantasy or kids need a hook
do: Mention the role once per board
Pick roles that fit the theme (Thai temple: elephant, naga, temple cat)
avoid: Roles whose movement contradicts the piece (a "flying" rook)
Calling the player only "the knight piece" with no fiction

cards.title: Save the king for the last board and call it the climax
cards.text: Setting king: true on the final board makes the last target a king, a natural climax: "Corner the Rat King in his hall." Earlier boards build toward it ("His guards are getting nervous"). Thai: "ต้อนราชาหนูให้จนมุม". The intro card can name the king from the start so the last board pays it off.
cards.use_when: the final board of a 3-6 board tactics game
do: king: true only on the last board
Name the king on the intro card
avoid: A king on board 1
A king never mentioned before the final board

cards.title: A time limit needs a story reason: before sunrise, before the tide
cards.text: If timeLimit is set, say why in the story ("Get out before the volcano wakes", "ก่อนพระอาทิตย์ขึ้น") and state the minutes once in the goal or rules ("You have 3 minutes"). A clock with a reason feels like tension; a clock without one feels like a test. For submission or young kids, prefer no time limit and no clock words.
cards.use_when: a design with a time limit, or deciding whether to add one
do: Tie the timer to a world event
State the minutes once as a plain number
avoid: Hurry words in a relaxing game
Different times in the story and in timeLimit

cards.title: Thai: write like a friendly person speaking, not a textbook
cards.text: Use everyday polite spoken Thai: "ไปช่วยลูกช้างกัน", "ระวังวงแดงนะ". Avoid formal written words that feel like an exam or a government notice: "ปฏิบัติภารกิจ", "ดำเนินการ", "กรุณาหลีกเลี่ยง". Avoid royal register (ราชาศัพท์) entirely unless the creator asks for a royal story, and even then keep it respectful and short.
cards.use_when: any text with lang = th
do: Read the line aloud: would a teacher or an older sibling say it?
Use ไป, มา, ช่วย, หา, ระวัง, เลย
avoid: ราชาศัพท์ and court language
Bureaucratic words (ดำเนินการ, ปฏิบัติ, ทำการ)

cards.title: Thai pronouns: drop them, or use "เรา" for warmth
cards.text: Thai sentences work without a subject, so most lines need no pronoun: "จุดตะเกียงให้ครบ 5 ดวง". When the intro card needs one, "คุณ" is neutral for adults and "เรา" makes kids and families feel included ("เราต้องช่วยลูกเต่ากลับบ้าน"). Avoid "ท่าน" (stiff) and "เจ้า" (old period drama, unless the theme is fantasy), and never use rude pronouns.
cards.use_when: writing intro cards and lines in Thai
do: No pronoun in labels
คุณ for adults, เรา for kids and families
avoid: ท่าน in game text
Mixing คุณ and เรา on one card

cards.title: Thai for kids 6-10: short common words, no heavy Pali or Sanskrit vocabulary
cards.text: Children read slowly in a headset. Use words they know: "ผี" not "วิญญาณ", "ยักษ์" not "อสุรกาย", "ช่วย" not "กอบกู้", "บ้าน" not "ที่พำนัก". Keep lines to about 10-20 characters and add playful sound words sparingly ("ว้าว", "ปุ๊ง!"). Friendly creature names beat scary ones: "ผีน้อยขี้เหงา" works, while a folklore ghost famous for gore may frighten young kids.
cards.use_when: lang = th and players are kids or families with young children
do: Swap long formal words for daily words
Cute or funny names for spirits and monsters
avoid: Long compound words
Folklore ghosts known for gore

cards.title: Thai loanwords: keep the common ones, avoid long transliterated names
cards.text: Some English words are normal Thai: บอส, ด่าน, เกม, ทีม. But transliterated names like "เดอะ ฟรอสต์ วอร์เดน" are hard to read and sound awkward; give a Thai name with meaning instead ("ผู้คุมน้ำแข็ง"). Prefer "จุด" over "เช็คพอยต์", "ภารกิจ" over "มิชชั่น", "คะแนน" over "พอยต์". Brand and product names stay in their official form.
cards.use_when: a Thai game whose ideas came from English, or translating names
do: Make a Thai name with meaning for each boss or place
Keep official brand spellings as given
avoid: Spelling English names in Thai letters
English words mixed into every line

cards.title: Thai particles: none in labels, light ones on the intro card
cards.text: ครับ and ค่ะ give the game's voice a gender and add length, so leave them out of labels, chapter lines and rules. On the intro card and goal, a light นะ, เลย or กัน adds warmth: "ไปช่วยกันเลย!", "ระวังวงแดงนะ". Do not stack them ("นะคะจ๊ะ"). Use even fewer for teens and adults.
cards.use_when: any Thai text, especially labels and rules
do: Zero particles in labels
At most one soft particle per sentence on the card
avoid: ครับ or ค่ะ at the end of rules
Baby-talk particles for teens

cards.title: Thai lines with a balanced rhythm or internal rhyme stick
cards.text: Thai ears love two balanced halves and a sound echo (สัมผัส): "ข้ามสะพาน ผ่านม่านหมอก", "จุดเทียน เวียนรอบเจดีย์", "หนีให้ไว ไฟไล่หลัง". Use it on the intro card, the goal or 1-2 key labels, not everywhere, and only while the line stays short. A rhyme that forces a strange word is worse than no rhyme.
cards.use_when: Thai intro cards, goals and key labels for any audience
do: Two halves of 3-5 syllables
Use the rhyme on the climax label
avoid: Forced rhymes with odd words
A rhyme on every label (sounds like a chant)

cards.title: Thai sacred places and objects get respectful verbs only
cards.text: Temples, Buddha images, spirit houses, monks and the royal family must never be enemies, hazards, tactics targets or things to break, steal or kick. Use respectful verbs: "ไหว้ศาลพระภูมิ", "จุดธูปที่วัด", "ไปกราบพระ". Folk spirits can be playful opponents; sacred objects are places of safety or blessing in the story.
cards.use_when: Thai temple, spirit or folklore themes
do: Make sacred places the safe goal or a blessing stop
Use ไหว้, กราบ, จุดธูป beside temple scenery
avoid: A Buddha image as a boss, hazard or tactics target
Monks as guards to sneak past

cards.title: English for UK audiences: British spelling and words, plain sentences
cards.text: When lang = en and the players are in the UK, use British spelling and words: colour, centre, metre, sweets (not candy), queue, torch (not flashlight), mum. Keep sentences short and literal; UK families respond well to gentle understatement and dry humour ("The dragon is mildly annoyed."). Avoid American sports metaphors and dollar signs.
cards.use_when: lang = en and the venue or players are in the UK
do: British spelling on the card and labels
Light dry humour for families and adults
avoid: US terms (candy, flashlight, mom)
Hype words on every line ("AWESOME!")

cards.title: Switching language: rewrite the line, do not translate word for word
cards.text: A label that works in English may be long or flat in Thai, and Thai rhymes vanish in English. When the same game is made in both languages, keep the meaning, the count and the names, then write each line fresh: "Ring the old bell" becomes "ตีระฆังเก่า", "Cross the misty bridge" becomes "ข้ามสะพานหมอก". Puns and rhymes are rewritten as new ones or dropped.
cards.use_when: a creator wants both th and en versions, or a comment asks to change lang
do: Keep the same number of labels and the same names
Re-check length limits in the new language
avoid: Literal translations that keep English word order in Thai
An English pun spelled in Thai letters

cards.title: Voice for kids 6-10: warm, playful, clear, one idea per line
cards.text: Kids follow concrete, kind tasks: helping animals, finding friends, waking sleepy giants. Use exclamations warmly but sparingly ("Help the baby turtles home!"), make villains silly rather than evil ("the Grumpy Snow Troll"), and keep every line one idea. Parents often read the card aloud, so it must sound good spoken.
cards.use_when: players are kids 6-10
do: Helping and finding verbs
Silly villains, cute captives
avoid: Death, blood or real-world fears (getting lost, strangers)
Sarcasm and irony

cards.title: Voice for teens: confident, a little dangerous, never talking down
cards.text: Teens switch off at baby words and over-explaining. Write short, cool lines with real stakes: "Nobody leaves the fog. Except you." Labels can be terse ("Past the hounds", "Don't look back"). Mild menace and dry jokes work; cute mascots and "Great job!" do not. Make the challenge explicit: time, rank, the leaderboard.
cards.use_when: players are teens 13-17, school groups or youth events
do: Terse labels and a bold boss name
Mention the leaderboard or time in a race
avoid: Childish words and exclamation marks everywhere
Lectures or morals on the card

cards.title: Voice for families: sayable aloud, so parents can cheer and hint
cards.text: In MR, parents watch from the side and call out. Labels with a clear, shoutable noun let them join in ("Go to the bell!", "The duck, the duck!"). Keep scares mild, make humour work on two levels (a pun for parents, a silly image for kids) and use "together" words when play is together. Avoid anything a parent would have to explain afterwards.
cards.use_when: players are families, or parents watch from the side
do: A visible, nameable noun in every label
Humour that works for both ages
avoid: Hidden-meaning labels spectators cannot follow
Scary content that needs a parental warning

cards.title: Voice for adults: atmosphere and wit, still short
cards.text: Adults enjoy tone: dread, irony, nostalgia, a mystery. Lines can carry mood words ("The tide brings back what it took.") and boss names can be grim ("The Drowned Abbot"). They still read in a headset, so length limits do not change. Adults at events are often first-time VR players too, so keep the rules plain even when the story is rich.
cards.use_when: players are adults: events, date nights, corporate groups
do: One mood word per line
Let the mystery or irony sit on the intro card
avoid: Long literary sentences
Assuming adults know game jargon

cards.title: Voice for brands: the product is the hero object, not ad copy
cards.text: A brand game reads like a story, not a banner. Make the product or mascot a visible hero object (the golden bottle at the summit, the mascot to free) and use the brand name at most in the title and on the intro card. Labels stay story beats ("Climb to the golden bottle"), never slogans. Follow the brand's words-to-avoid exactly and make no health or price claims.
cards.use_when: a brand, sponsor or product launch brief
do: Brand name in the title or card only
The product as the final checkpoint or the portal's meaning
avoid: Slogans or prices in labels
Product claims the creator did not give

cards.title: Voice for educators: one true idea per label, the story carries the lesson
cards.text: In a school game each checkpoint can teach one simple fact through its label and scenery: "Visit Mars, the red planet", "Find the coral that feeds the fish". Keep facts short, true and checkable; if unsure, use a story label instead. The intro card frames learning as a mission ("Your rocket must visit 5 planets"), not a test.
cards.use_when: educators, school trips or learning goals in the brief
do: One short, true fact per label
Frame learning as a mission
avoid: Quiz questions in labels (players cannot answer)
Facts you are not sure about

cards.title: Voice for first-time VR players: reassure, then invite
cards.text: Newcomers worry about the headset more than the game. The intro card can open calmly ("Look around. The floor has changed, the room has not.") and the rules should say plainly what touching and finishing look like. Keep the first label easy and close ("Step to the first light") so the first success comes within seconds.
cards.use_when: players are new to VR or MR
do: A calm first sentence on the card
A first label that is obvious and near
avoid: Opening with danger or a countdown
Jargon like "spawn", "hitbox", "HUD"
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Fantasy: name the role and give it a title
cards.text: Fantasy (being someone else) lives in the role words. Open the card with a titled role ("You are the Ember Knight", "เราคือผู้ถือตะเกียงคนสุดท้าย") and let labels be the role's duties ("Guard the shrine"). The boss should be the role's natural enemy. A role without a title is just "the player".
cards.use_when: fantasy is a top feeling in the brief
do: A role with a title in sentence 1 or 2
Labels that are the role's duties
avoid: Calling the player "user" or "player" in the story
Roles that need abilities the genre lacks (a wizard who casts spells in a runner)

cards.title: Submission (relaxing): soft verbs, no threats, no clocks
cards.text: A relaxing game uses calm verbs (wander, visit, light, rest) and gentle images (lanterns on water, a sleepy cat, falling petals). Leave out timeLimit, alarm words and villains. Hazards, if any, become gentle things to step around (puddles, sleeping frogs). The intro card can invite rather than command: "Take a slow walk through the lantern garden."
cards.use_when: submission is a top feeling, or players are seniors or anxious first-timers
do: Invitation wording on the card
Calm, sensory nouns in labels
avoid: Countdowns, "hurry", "danger"
A boss-style climax

cards.title: Discovery: hint, do not spoil
cards.text: Discovery labels promise without giving away: "Follow the glow", "Behind the waterfall", "Peek into the old well". The scenery beside that checkpoint delivers the surprise. The intro card should say there are secrets to see, not list them. Keep at least one surprise vignette that no label mentions.
cards.use_when: discovery is a top feeling
do: Labels as invitations
One unlabelled surprise in the scenery
avoid: Labels that name the surprise ("See the giant octopus")
Hint labels in a race

cards.title: Fellowship words must not promise teamwork the engine lacks
cards.text: A shared floor lets players see each other's avatars and a race ranks them; there are no shared tasks, hand-offs or team scores. So write "together" as a shared journey ("Walk the ghost road together"), not as cooperation ("Lift the gate together", "One player holds the lamp"). Spectator cheering is real fellowship in MR: invite it on the card.
cards.use_when: fellowship is a feeling, or play_mode is together
do: "Together" as a shared journey
Invite spectators to cheer
avoid: Tasks that need two players
Team scores or roles per player

cards.title: Sensation: short punchy lines and sensory nouns
cards.text: Sensation games sell the wow, so text should be brief and physical: "Lava below. Steady steps.", "Into the storm!", "สะพานลอยฟ้า ค่อยๆ เดิน". Pair the words with the strongest visual at that checkpoint (void floor, giant models, neon). One exclamation mark per line at most.
cards.use_when: sensation is a top feeling, especially with void floor or big hero models
do: Sensory nouns: fire, ice, height, light
Put the punchiest label at the most dramatic spot
avoid: Long explanations
Wow words with no wow scenery beside them

cards.title: Use second person "you are" and keep the player silent
cards.text: Story text speaks to the player as "you" and gives them a role: "You are the night ranger." The player character never speaks, so never write lines for them ("I must hurry!") and never quote other characters as if they talk back. First- or third-person narration ("The hero walked...") distances players who are physically walking the route.
cards.use_when: writing any intro card, chapter line or board story
do: "You are..." early on the card
Imperatives in labels ("Free the fox")
avoid: First-person lines for the player
Narration about "the hero" in third person

cards.title: Pick a role that fits the genre's main verb
cards.text: Runner roles walk and visit: lantern carrier, ghost hunter on patrol, courier, explorer, pilgrim, rescuer. Battle roles fight with a sword and dodge: knight, temple guardian, ice ranger, monster hunter. Tactics roles are the piece: a jumping rider (knight), a sliding monk (bishop), a charging cart (rook), the queen. A ghost hunter in a runner "checks the haunted spots"; in battle she "cuts down the ghosts".
cards.use_when: choosing the player role for an option or the build
do: Match the role's main verb to the genre engine
Use the same role across labels, chapters and the card
avoid: A sniper or wizard role (no shooting or spells)
A runner role that fights

cards.title: Show a character's wish through the label, not through speech
cards.text: Characters cannot talk, but the label can carry what they want: "Bring Grandma her lost cat", "Wake the sleepy giant for the harvest", "พาลูกช้างไปหาแม่". Place the character model beside the checkpoint so players connect the want to a face. One clear want per character, and at most 2-3 named characters in a short game.
cards.use_when: the brief has characters the player should care about
do: Want + who in one label
The character model next to their checkpoint
avoid: Quoted speech ("Grandma: Find my cat!") that reads as dialogue
More than 3 named characters

cards.title: Vignettes tell what happened: show the aftermath beside the label
cards.text: Scenery tells story without words when it shows a result: a tipped cart and spilled fruit beside "Follow the thief's trail", broken lanterns beside "Relight the path", a sleeping dragon beside "Tiptoe past the dragon". In the layout brief, name the vignette for each labelled checkpoint so the words and the picture say the same thing.
cards.use_when: writing the layout brief for a story runner
do: One vignette per key label, described in the layout brief
Aftermath props (broken, spilled, frozen, sleeping)
avoid: Labels with no scenery support
Vignettes that contradict the label
cards.source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

cards.title: Make the goal visible from the spawn: a landmark that pulls players in
cards.text: Place the story's goal as the tallest or brightest model, seen from the start: the tower with the last bell, the volcano, the moon gate. The intro card names it ("Reach the moon gate"), and players see the promise the whole walk. In MR keep it inside the play area and away from real walls so it stays in view.
cards.use_when: a runner with a journey or climax, writing the layout brief
do: Name the landmark on the card and in the layout brief
Put it near the portal or the last checkpoint
avoid: A goal hidden until the last second in a narrative walk
A landmark outside the play area in MR

cards.title: The lighting preset and the story must say the same time and mood
cards.text: A Land has one lighting preset, so the story must fit it: night or spooky with midnight ghosts, morning with a journey starting, evening with lanterns and going home, neon with a future city, noon with bright festivals. Do not write "the sun sets as you walk"; the light will not change. In MR daylight, avoid stories that need darkness.
cards.use_when: choosing lighting and writing the story card
do: Name the time of day the preset shows
Pick spooky or night only indoors or after dark in MR
avoid: Stories where the light changes during play
A midnight story on a sunny outdoor MR floor

cards.title: Give red circles a red fiction: fire, lava, curse, alarm
cards.text: Runner hazards always look like red circles and battle warnings are red rings, so name them as something red or warning: lava pools, fire pits, curse rings, alarm zones, angry ant nests, dragon fire. Water or ice names fight the colour. Use one hazard name across the card, the rules and the layout brief ("lava pools" everywhere).
cards.use_when: naming hazards or warning rings in a story
do: A red fiction
The same name in rules and layout brief
avoid: Calling red circles "icy puddles"
A different hazard name on every line

cards.title: In MR, write the real room into the story
cards.text: Players see the real walls, windows and people, so the story should explain them: the walls are "the castle walls", the crowd is "the villagers watching", the window light is "the moon outside". One sentence on the intro card is enough: "The villagers watch from the hall. Show them the ghosts are gone." This turns the real room from a distraction into part of the world.
cards.use_when: an MR game in a visible real space with spectators
do: One intro sentence that names the real surroundings in story terms
Treat spectators as an audience in the fiction
avoid: A setting the room clearly contradicts ("deep under the sea") with no framing
Giving spectators a story task

cards.title: Void floor needs a story reason: a bridge, a sky island, a cliff path
cards.text: The void floor turns the real floor into a bottomless drop, which is dramatic and dizzy. Justify it in words so it feels intended: "The bridge over the abyss", "Islands in the clouds", "สะพานข้ามเหว". Keep labels calm and reassuring on void sections ("Steady steps"), and never write lines that dare players to jump or look down while walking fast.
cards.use_when: a design using void floor
do: Name the height in the story
Calm wording on void stretches
avoid: "Jump!" or "Look down!" labels
Void floor for kids or first-time VR without a gentle story
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Story props that a label names cannot be VR-only
cards.text: Decor marked "VR only" is hidden in MR. If a label points at a prop ("Wake the dragon"), that prop must be visible in MR, or the label points at empty floor. Use VR-only decor for background mood (sky, far walls, extra trees) and keep every story prop named by a label as normal scenery.
cards.use_when: an MR layout brief with story props and VR-only decor
do: Keep labelled story props visible in MR
Use VR-only for distant backdrop
avoid: A labelled hero prop set to VR only
Relying on hidden props to tell the story

cards.title: Humour: about one joke in every 3-4 lines, carried by the nouns
cards.text: Humour lands best in silly nouns and situations, not in wordplay that must be read twice: "Wake the snoring goat", "the Grumpy Cabbage King", "ปลุกแพะนอนกรน". Use about one funny line per 3-4 lines so the story still moves; a joke on every label tires players. Put the biggest laugh on the boss name or the last label.
cards.use_when: a light, family or kids game, or a comedy brief
do: Silly creatures and objects in labels
One running joke across the game
avoid: Puns that only work in one language
Humour that mocks people, accents or cultures

cards.title: Wonder: build up with small sights, end on one big one
cards.text: Wonder needs contrast. Let early labels be small and close ("Follow the fireflies"), then reveal a big sight with a big word near the end ("Under the sky whale"). Pair the wonder label with the largest model or the void floor. If every label says "amazing", nothing is.
cards.use_when: sensation or discovery games, all ages
do: Small to big across the route
Save one wonder word for the climax
avoid: "Amazing" or "magical" on every line
The biggest sight right at the spawn

cards.title: Mild scare: dread in words and light, never sudden shocks
cards.text: In MR, sudden scares make people run into real walls, so scare with mood, not jumps. Words do the work: "Something follows the lanterns", "Do not wake her". Use spooky or night lighting indoors, slow-reveal ghost models beside labels and a warm, safe ending ("Back to the light"). For kids, let the scary thing turn out friendly or silly by the last label.
cards.use_when: spooky, ghost or horror themes, especially in MR or for kids
do: Dread words + spooky lighting + a warm ending
For kids, reveal the ghost is friendly at the end
avoid: "Run!" labels or chase framing in MR
Gore, death or jump-scare promises
cards.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

cards.title: Heroism: raise the stakes one step each chapter or board
cards.text: Heroism grows when each step matters more: chapter 1 saves a farm, chapter 3 the town, the boss the kingdom. State the stake in a few words in each line ("The village is next.") and give the player the credit in the final line ("Only you stand at the gate."). Do not open at maximum stakes; there is nowhere left to go.
cards.use_when: battle or tactics with fantasy or challenge, or a heroic runner
do: Rising stakes across chapters or boards
The player as the one who decides it at the end
avoid: Saving the world in chapter 1
Ending with someone else saving the day

cards.title: Worked runner card (English, families): The Lantern River
cards.text: Story: "The river spirits lost their lights. You are the lantern child. Light 5 lanterns before the mist covers the river, then cross home." Goal: "Light 5 lanterns, then step through the moon gate." Rules: "Walk to the lanterns in order", "Walk, do not run", "Red circles are fire pits: they send you back", "Finish at the moon gate". Labels: "Lantern 1: the jetty", "Lantern 2: the reeds", "Past the sleeping frog", "Lantern 3: the old boat", "Lantern 4: the willow", "Last lantern: the bridge".
cards.use_when: a reference shape for a family runner card (do not copy)
do: Match counts across story, goal and labels
Mix numbered set labels with one moment label
avoid: Copying this text for a different brief

cards.title: Worked runner card (Thai, school kids): rescue the baby elephants
cards.text: Story: "ลูกช้าง 4 ตัวหลงป่าตอนพายุมา เราคือผู้พิทักษ์ป่าตัวน้อย ไปพาลูกช้างกลับหาแม่กันเลย!" Goal: "ช่วยลูกช้างครบ 4 ตัว แล้วเดินเข้าประตูป่า" Rules: "เดินไปตามจุดที่เรืองแสงทีละจุด", "เดินนะ ห้ามวิ่ง", "อย่าเหยียบวงแดง (รังมดแดง)". Labels: "ข้ามลำธาร", "ช่วยลูกช้างตัวแรก", "ลอดใต้ต้นไทร", "ช่วยตัวที่ 2", "ช่วยตัวที่ 3", "ช่วยตัวสุดท้าย".
cards.use_when: a reference shape for a Thai kids runner card (do not copy)
do: Spoken Thai with เรา and one particle
Digits for counts
avoid: Copying this text for a different brief

cards.title: Worked battle text (lava theme, teens): from chapters to boss
cards.text: Story: "The Ash King woke under the mountain and his hounds took the road. You are the last ember knight. Fight up the mountain and end him." Chapters: "The Ash Road" / "Imps pour out of the cracks." (grunts); "The Shield Gate" / "Stone guards lock shields. Hit them from the side." (shields + grunts); "Ember Storm" / "Fire falls from the sky. Keep moving." (rain); "The Hound Pit" / "His hounds smell you." (beast + grunts). Boss: "The Ash King" / "The Ash King rises from his throne. Break his crown."
cards.use_when: a reference shape for battle chapters and the boss (do not copy)
do: One foe meaning per chapter line
The boss named on the card first
avoid: Copying this text for a different brief

cards.title: Worked tactics text (heist, adults): The Moonstone Job
cards.text: Story: "Five moonstones sit in the duke's palace and his night watch never sleeps. You are the thief who becomes whatever the job needs. Take the stones in order and do not get caught." Boards: knight "Leap the garden hedges and take 2 stones."; rook "Charge down the long hall before the watch turns."; bishop "Slip along the chapel diagonals."; queen with king "The duke himself. Corner him for the last stone."
cards.use_when: a reference shape for tactics board stories (do not copy)
do: A piece role tied to each place
The king on the last board
avoid: Copying this text for a different brief

cards.title: Worked MR battle text (Thai, families, forest): the firefly forest
cards.text: Story: "ป่าหิ่งห้อยโดนเงามืดบุก เราคือองครักษ์ป่า ดาบอยู่ในมือขวาแล้ว ปกป้องหิ่งห้อยไว้ให้ได้!" Chapters (at most 6 foes each in MR): "ชายป่า" / "เงาตัวเล็กวิ่งเข้ามา"; "กำแพงโล่" / "ทหารเงาถือโล่ ฟันด้านข้างนะ"; "ฝนหนาม" / "หนามตกจากฟ้า ก้าวหลบให้ทัน". Boss: "ราชาเงามืด" / "ราชาเงามืดมาแล้ว ไล่มันออกไปจากป่า!" Rules include "ก้าวออกจากวงแดง ไม่ต้องวิ่ง".
cards.use_when: a reference shape for MR battle text in Thai (do not copy)
do: Step-not-run wording in MR
Short Thai lines under about 30 characters
avoid: Copying this text for a different brief

cards.title: Labels that promise mechanics: open, carry, shoot, choose
cards.text: Writers slip in verbs from other games: "Open the chest", "Carry the egg to the nest", "Shoot the target", "Choose your path". The engine only knows touching checkpoints in order, so players try the action and nothing happens. Rewrite as arrivals: "Reach the chest", "Visit the nest", "Pass the targets", and give a single route with no choices.
cards.use_when: reviewing labels, chapter lines or board stories
do: Rewrite every hand or choice verb as an arrival verb
Keep branching out of all text
avoid: "Choose" or "or" in labels
Verbs that need buttons in an MR runner

cards.title: Generic names ("Dark Lord", "Magic Forest") make the game forgettable
cards.text: Names are the cheapest way to make a world feel specific. Replace "Dark Lord" with "the Rust Abbot", "Magic Forest" with "Whisper Woods", "ป่ามหัศจรรย์" with "ป่าหิ่งห้อย". Make each name concrete (a material, an animal, a sound, a local place) and tie it to the theme and palette.
cards.use_when: naming places, bosses, the title or the role
do: Concrete noun + theme word
Local flavour for Thai themes (ตลาดน้ำ, ดอย, ลำธาร)
avoid: Fantasy clichés with no detail
Names copied from famous games or films

cards.title: Pick the aesthetic first, then the mechanics
cards.text: MDA says the designer builds mechanics, which create dynamics at play time, which the player feels as aesthetics; the player experiences it in the reverse order. So decide the target feeling from the brief first, then choose the genre and the knobs (enemy kinds, guard count, checkpoint labels) that produce it. If the brief has no feeling, infer one from the players and venue and write it down as an assumption.
cards.use_when: Any options or build step where the creator gave a theme but no feeling, or the mechanics are being chosen before the feeling.
do: State the primary MDA aesthetic before listing mechanics
Trace each mechanic to the dynamic it creates and the feeling it serves
Write inferred feelings into the brief as assumptions the creator can correct
avoid: Starting from "a game with a boss and rain" and hoping a feeling appears
Listing all 8 aesthetics as goals
cards.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

cards.title: Sensation: spectacle the body feels
cards.text: Sensation is pleasure of the senses: light, scale, motion and sound. In battle it comes from a big beast walking in, falling rain rings and a named boss reveal; in runner from the void floor, a dramatic lighting preset and hero scenery placed at the turn where the view opens; in tactics it is weakest, so carry it with theme and lighting. Put the biggest visual reveal at a moment when the player is standing still, not mid-dodge.
cards.use_when: The brief asks for "wow", "beautiful", "epic", or the venue is a showcase where first impressions matter.
do: Use night, neon or spooky lighting indoors for glow-heavy looks
Stage one hero piece visible from the spawn
Give the boss a name and an intro line so the reveal lands
avoid: Choosing tactics as the main sensation option
Putting a spectacle reveal where the player must also dodge
Glow themes outdoors at noon (they wash out)
cards.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

cards.title: Fantasy: give the player a role, not just a theme
cards.text: Fantasy is being someone else. The role must match what the body does: in MR battle the controller IS the sword, so "you are the last knight of the temple" fits the real swing; in tactics the player IS the chess piece, so "you are the knight sent to free the captives" fits walking L-shaped moves; in runner the player is a traveller, courier or explorer. Write the role into the intro story and echo it in labels so the fantasy holds from first to last second.
cards.use_when: The brief mentions being a character, a hero, an animal, or "feel like you are in the movie".
do: Name the role in one line of the story card
Choose the genre whose physical action matches the role
Use checkpoint labels and chapter lines in the role's voice ("Light the third lantern")
avoid: Promising a role whose action the engine lacks (a wizard casting spells, a gunslinger shooting)
Generic labels like "Checkpoint 3" that break the role
cards.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

cards.title: Narrative: tell the story through ordered beats
cards.text: Our engines have no dialogue, so story lives in the intro card (2-4 sentences), checkpoint labels touched in order, chapter titles and lines in battle, and each board's story line in tactics. Treat these as a beat sheet: setup, rising stakes, turn, climax, resolution. A 6-checkpoint runner can carry a complete three-act story if each label is a verb phrase that moves the plot.
cards.use_when: The brief asks for a story, a legend, a school lesson or a brand message told through play.
do: Write labels as story verbs ("Wake the guardian", "Cross the broken bridge")
Map acts to checkpoints: act 1 = first 2, act 2 = middle, act 3 = last 1-2 plus portal
Make the final chapter or board the story's confrontation
avoid: Long story text the player must read while walking
Promising NPC conversations or branching dialogue
Labels that do not change from beat to beat
cards.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

cards.title: Challenge: an obstacle the player can master
cards.text: Challenge is pleasure in overcoming a hard thing through skill. In battle it comes from mixing enemy kinds (shield forces flanking, beast forces stepping aside) and adding rain; in tactics from more guards, a faster beat and longer capture orders; in runner from tighter hazard spacing and a time limit. Challenge needs a visible score or time, a fair failure and a reason to try again.
cards.use_when: The brief asks for hard, skill, competitive, or players are gamers or teens.
do: Raise one variable per step (count, kind, speed, or spacing)
Show score or time so improvement is visible
Offer a race or leaderboard to give the challenge a social stake
avoid: Making it hard by hiding information
Raising every variable at once in the second chapter
Challenge for first-time VR seniors without a gentle first stage
cards.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

cards.title: Fellowship: design moments that are shared
cards.text: Fellowship is play as a social framework. The engine gives three tools: race mode (everyone walks their own copy, live leaderboard), shared floor (players see each other's avatars) and spectators who see bodies, not the game. There is no voice chat or co-op mechanic, so fellowship comes from shared timing, comparing scores, cheering and calling hints. Put dodges and the finish where watchers can see them.
cards.use_when: The brief is a family, a class, friends or a party, or "play together" appears.
do: Use race mode with the leaderboard on a wall screen for groups
Use shared floor when players are friends who want to see each other
Give spectators a role: cheer, call out the next target, watch the board
avoid: Promising teamwork mechanics like passing items or reviving each other
Putting the climax at the far side away from the audience
Putting spectators inside the play area
cards.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

cards.title: Discovery: reward looking around
cards.text: Discovery is the pleasure of exploring and finding. In runner, use a hub or spiral route where vignettes sit beside the path and each checkpoint reveals a new view; in tactics, discovery is finding the capture path a piece can take, which each new piece reopens; in battle it is weakest. Pace reveals so something new appears every 20-40 seconds, and keep the walking line clear so looking around is safe.
cards.use_when: The brief says explore, secrets, curious, or the scenery theme itself is the attraction.
do: Place vignettes beside the route, not on it
Introduce a new piece type each board in tactics
Let each checkpoint face a new view or vignette
avoid: A time limit so tight players cannot look around
Hiding checkpoints behind real obstacles
Asking players to look up while walking fast
cards.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

cards.title: Expression: let the player's style show
cards.text: Expression is self-discovery and showing off. The engine has no building or customisation in play, so expression comes from how a player solves things: their capture route in tactics, their line through hazards in runner, their swing style in battle seen by spectators. Make solutions plural (more than one valid path) and make the performance visible to watchers or a leaderboard.
cards.use_when: The brief says show off, creative, style, or "let them do it their way".
do: Design tactics boards with 2 or more valid capture paths
Leave room in runner for a bold line versus a safe line
Stage the battle so the spectators see the player's swings
avoid: Promising avatar customisation, crafting or level editing in play
Single-solution puzzles labelled as expressive
cards.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

cards.title: Submission: easy, calm, low-stakes fun
cards.text: Submission is play as pastime: relaxing, no pressure. Use a runner with no time limit, few hazards (0-2, far from the line), a soft lighting preset such as morning or evening, and a loop route that returns near the start. In battle use only grunts in small numbers and no rain; in tactics use 0 guards and 2-3 targets. Failure should cost little.
cards.use_when: The brief says relax, chill, for grandparents, for small kids, or a waiting-room or lobby setting.
do: Set timeLimit to null
Keep hazards away from the main line
Use gentle labels and a warm lighting preset
avoid: Adding a leaderboard that turns a calm walk into a race
Rain or beasts in a submission battle
Calling it relaxing but using a void floor
cards.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

cards.title: At most 3 feelings, and one leads
cards.text: A design can serve 2-3 aesthetics, but one must be primary and decide trade-offs. Rank them: primary sets the genre and loop, secondary sets theme and story, third is a seasoning (lighting or spectator moment). When two knobs disagree, the primary wins. The options axes field holds only the primary, so choose it deliberately.
cards.use_when: The brief lists 3 or more feelings, or the design feels muddled.
do: Rank the brief's feelings 1-2-3 and write the order
Use the primary in axes.aesthetic
Resolve every trade-off in favour of the primary
avoid: Treating all listed feelings as equal
Adding a fourth feeling during the build
cards.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

cards.title: Feeling pairs that reinforce each other
cards.text: Some aesthetics share mechanics and amplify each other: fantasy + sensation (a role plus spectacle, natural for battle), challenge + fellowship (a race with a leaderboard), discovery + narrative (a runner where each checkpoint reveals the next story beat), challenge + expression (tactics with several valid paths). Prefer these pairs when the brief allows a choice.
cards.use_when: Choosing a secondary feeling or combining parts of two options.
do: Pair battle with fantasy + sensation
Pair tactics with challenge + expression
Pair runner with discovery + narrative or submission
avoid: Forcing a pair onto a genre that only serves one half
cards.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

cards.title: Challenge and submission pull in opposite directions
cards.text: Challenge needs stakes, pressure and failure; submission needs calm and low cost of failure. One option cannot maximise both. If the brief lists both (common for "families"), split them: make the first half calm and the last chapter or board the challenge, or give the challenge only to those who opt into the race while the default is untimed.
cards.use_when: A brief asks for both "hard" and "relaxing", or a mixed-age group.
do: Split across options: one calm, one challenging
Or ramp from submission to challenge within one game
Ask the creator which matters more if unclear
avoid: A medium-difficulty compromise that is boring for gamers and stressful for grandparents
cards.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

cards.title: Racing makes players skip the story
cards.text: In race mode players optimise for time, so they ignore labels, scenery and the intro card. Narrative and discovery suffer. If the brief wants story and competition, keep the story in very short labels (3-5 words) read at a glance, or choose a solo or shared-floor mode for the story option and keep the race for a different option.
cards.use_when: An option combines race or time limit with narrative or discovery.
do: Keep labels short enough to read while walking
Put story weight on the intro card before the timer starts
Offer narrative and race in different options
avoid: Long labels in a race
Placing story vignettes that need stopping inside a timed route

cards.title: Tight time limits kill exploration
cards.text: Discovery needs dwell time. A time limit under about 30 seconds per checkpoint turns looking around into wasted time. For a discovery option, set timeLimit to null or generous (at least 45 s per checkpoint), and give the time bonus only as an optional extra.
cards.use_when: A discovery or sensation option also has a time limit.
do: Leave timeLimit null for discovery
If a limit is needed, allow 45+ seconds per checkpoint
avoid: A countdown on a tour-style route

cards.title: Keep challenge just ahead of skill
cards.text: Flow happens when challenge matches skill and both rise together; too hard causes anxiety, too easy causes boredom. Skill grows during a session, so difficulty must climb too. Our engines have no adaptive difficulty, so the ramp is authored: each chapter, board or checkpoint stretch should be a little harder than the last, with the first one easy enough for the least experienced player in the brief.
cards.use_when: Setting chapter, board or hazard counts for any game.
do: Design the first step for the weakest expected player
Raise difficulty a small step each stage
Tie the final step to the strongest expected player
avoid: A flat difficulty across all stages
A first stage tuned for gamers when the brief includes first-time VR players
cards.source: Csikszentmihalyi 1990, Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience

cards.title: Default battle chapter ramp
cards.text: A safe 4-chapter battle in MR: chapter 1 is 2-3 grunts (learn the swing and ring-dodge), chapter 2 adds 1-2 shields (learn to hit from the side), chapter 3 adds rain with mixed grunts and shields, chapter 4 introduces 1 beast, then the boss. Stay at or under 6 enemies per chapter in MR (9 on PC). The engine rejects a beast in chapter 1.
cards.use_when: Writing chapters for a battle build.
do: Introduce one new enemy kind or rain per chapter
Keep chapter 1 to grunts only
Save the beast for the second half
avoid: Beasts in chapter 1
More than 6 foes in an MR chapter
Rain and a new enemy kind introduced together

cards.title: Default tactics board ramp
cards.text: Start board 1 with 0-1 guards, 2-3 targets and a slow beat (3-3.5 s); the engine rejects more than 2 guards on board 1. Then add one guard or one crack per board, lengthen the capture order to 4-5 and, on PC, tighten the beat toward 2 s. In MR keep the beat at 3 s or slower on every board because the player walks. Change the piece type every 1-2 boards so the player relearns movement.
cards.use_when: Writing boards for a tactics build.
do: Board 1: 0-1 guard, 2-3 targets, beat 3.5
Add one guard or crack per board
Switch piece type to reset the puzzle space
avoid: A beat under 3 s in MR
Queen on board 1 (too many options to teach movement)
Changing piece and adding 2 guards on the same board

cards.title: Default runner hazard ramp
cards.text: Keep the stretch from spawn to checkpoint 1 and 2 free of hazards so players learn to walk in the headset and read the checkpoint order. Introduce a single hazard that is easy to see after checkpoint 2, then raise the count toward the last third, and keep the final stretch into the portal clear for a clean, visible finish. Hazards send players back to the last checkpoint, so later hazards cost more and should be fairer.
cards.use_when: Placing hazards along a runner route.
do: No hazards before checkpoint 2
Most hazards in the middle to last third
Clear run into the portal
avoid: Hazards right at the spawn
A hazard right after a checkpoint that resets players into a loop

cards.title: Sawtooth difficulty: rest after every peak
cards.text: Difficulty should climb in a sawtooth, not a straight line: each hard stage is followed by a slightly easier one that lets the player use their new skill with confidence, then the next peak is higher. In battle, follow a rain chapter with a smaller chapter before the boss; in tactics, follow a 3-guard board with a 2-guard board using a new piece.
cards.use_when: A game with 4 or more chapters, boards or stretches.
do: Place a breather stage after each spike
Make each new peak higher than the previous one
avoid: Monotonic increase with no relief
A breather right before the climax that kills the build-up
cards.source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

cards.title: There is no adaptive difficulty, so design the curve
cards.text: Creators often ask for "easy for kids, hard for adults" in one game. The engine has no difficulty setting or dynamic adjustment. Offer instead: an authored ramp where the first half suits beginners, an optional race for those who want stakes, or separate options tuned for different groups.
cards.use_when: The brief wants one game to fit very different skill levels.
do: Explain that the curve is fixed and authored
Use the early stages for beginners and the late stages for experts
Offer race mode as the opt-in challenge
avoid: Promising difficulty modes, handicaps or auto-scaling

cards.title: The first 30 seconds teach the one verb
cards.text: In the first 30 seconds the player should do the core action once and succeed. In MR battle: one or two slow grunts and a single red ring. In tactics: a first target reachable in one move. In runner: the first checkpoint visible from the spawn, 1.5-3 m away. Headset newcomers spend their first moments adjusting to passthrough, so nothing in that window should punish them.
cards.use_when: Designing the opening of any game, especially for first-time VR players.
do: Make the first checkpoint or target visible from the spawn
Guarantee a first success inside 30 s
Keep the first stage free of failure states
avoid: A hazard or beast in the opening
An intro card longer than 4 sentences

cards.title: The first stage is the tutorial
cards.text: There is no separate tutorial screen, and players will not read long rules in a headset. Teach by putting the player in a stage where the right action is obvious and the wrong one is cheap. Each later stage adds exactly one new element the player meets first in a safe form (a single shield, a single crack, a single hazard) before it appears under pressure.
cards.use_when: Any build; especially when rules are new for the players.
do: Introduce each element alone first
Keep the rules list to 3 short lines
Let the stage design explain the rule
avoid: Writing rules for things players will learn by doing
Introducing a new element at the climax
cards.source: Koster 2004, A Theory of Fun for Game Design

cards.title: Rule of threes: introduce, develop, twist
cards.text: Use each new element three times: once alone so it is learned, once combined with something known so it is practised, and once in a twist or under pressure so it is mastered. A 4-chapter battle fits one new element per chapter with its three uses spread across the next chapters. Also cap lists at three: 3 pillars, 3 rules, 3 feelings.
cards.use_when: Planning when elements appear across chapters, boards or checkpoints.
do: Plan three appearances for every new element
Cap the rules list at three main lines
avoid: Introducing an element and never using it again
Using a new element first in its hardest form

cards.title: Competence: let players feel themselves improve
cards.text: Self-determination research on games found that feeling competent strongly predicts enjoyment. Show progress (score, captured targets, chapter count), give clear success feedback, and make failure understandable so the next try is better. A short game that can be replayed and beaten faster serves competence better than a long one that is finished once.
cards.use_when: Any game, and especially for kids, newcomers and challenge briefs.
do: Make progress visible on the HUD
Make each failure explain itself
Let a replay be measurably better (time, score)
avoid: Random-feeling failures
Hiding the score
cards.source: Ryan, Rigby & Przybylski 2006, The Motivational Pull of Video Games (PENS/SDT)

cards.title: Autonomy: real choices inside a fixed structure
cards.text: Autonomy is the feeling of acting by choice. Our runner checkpoints are touched in order and tactics targets are captured in order, so autonomy must come from how, not what: the path between checkpoints, the moment to cross a guard's line, the route through a board, or the pace of a calm walk. Leave space between stops for two reasonable lines and say in the rules that any path is allowed.
cards.use_when: The brief wants freedom, or adults and gamers are the players.
do: Leave 2 viable lines between checkpoints
Give tactics boards several routes to each target
Let the player choose when to step, not only where
avoid: Corridors with only one way through
Promising open-world freedom or free locomotion in MR
cards.source: Ryan, Rigby & Przybylski 2006, The Motivational Pull of Video Games (PENS/SDT)

cards.title: Relatedness: connect players to each other and to watchers
cards.text: Relatedness is feeling connected to others. In our engines it comes from race mode (comparing on a live leaderboard), shared floor (seeing each other), spectators cheering at visible moments, and a story that casts the group as one side. Even a solo game gains relatedness if the finish faces the audience and the score can be compared afterwards.
cards.use_when: Groups, families, classes or events with an audience.
do: Face the finish toward the spectators
Use race mode for groups who know each other
Write the story so the group shares a goal
avoid: A solo game in a busy event with no visible finish
Mechanics that require talking (no voice chat)
cards.source: Ryan, Rigby & Przybylski 2006, The Motivational Pull of Video Games (PENS/SDT)

cards.title: Read which need the players lack most
cards.text: Different players arrive missing different needs. First-time VR players and small kids mostly need competence: a sure first win. Gamers and adults need autonomy: choices that matter. Families, classes and friends need relatedness: shared moments and comparison. Use the brief's players field to pick which need the recommended option should serve first.
cards.use_when: Choosing between options or deciding what the opening stage must deliver.
do: Newcomers: guarantee competence early
Gamers: add choice and stakes
Groups: add race or shared floor and visible moments
avoid: Designing for the creator's taste instead of the stated players
cards.source: Ryan, Rigby & Przybylski 2006, The Motivational Pull of Video Games (PENS/SDT)

cards.title: Agon: fair competition
cards.text: Agon is competition where skill decides. It needs equal starting conditions and a clear measure. Race mode gives every player their own identical copy of the course plus a live leaderboard; tactics races on time with a leaderboard. Agon options suit gamers, teens and events with a screen.
cards.use_when: The brief wants competition, a contest or a tournament.
do: Use race mode or time leaderboard
Keep the course identical for all
Show the leaderboard where spectators look
avoid: Competition where luck or hidden information decides
Agon for very young kids without a gentle mode

cards.title: Alea (chance) is weak in our engines
cards.text: Alea is play where chance decides: dice, loot, random draws. Our engines are authored and deterministic, with no random rewards or loot. If a creator wants luck or surprise, offer surprise through design instead: a reveal around a turn, a new piece each board, a boss with a dramatic intro, or rain chapters that add unpredictability of position. Say honestly that results depend on skill.
cards.use_when: The brief asks for luck, gacha, random prizes or a lottery feel.
do: Offer authored surprises as the closest match
Explain that outcomes depend on skill
avoid: Promising random loot, drops or prize draws in the game

cards.title: Mimicry: playing a part with the whole body
cards.text: Mimicry is make-believe, being someone else. MR is strong here because the body really moves: swinging the controller as a sword, walking as a chess piece, travelling a path as a pilgrim. Choose the role that matches the real motion and let spectators see the performance. This is Caillois' frame for the MDA fantasy aesthetic.
cards.use_when: Fantasy or role-play briefs, especially for kids and families.
do: Match the role to the physical action
Stage the performance toward spectators
avoid: Roles whose signature action is unavailable (flying, shooting, spellcasting)

cards.title: Ilinx: vertigo, used with care
cards.text: Ilinx is the pleasure of disturbed perception: dizziness, height, speed. The void floor turns the real floor into a bottomless drop, and a spiral route adds turning. It is the strongest wow in MR but can frighten or unsettle newcomers. Use it for teens and gamers, keep walking slow, avoid it for seniors and very young kids, and never combine it with a tight time limit.
cards.use_when: The brief wants thrill, height, scary-dramatic or "make them gasp".
do: Use void floor for one standout option
Keep hazards few on a void floor
Warn in the intro card
avoid: Void floor with a race
Void floor for first-time VR seniors
Spinning spirals plus fast pace

cards.title: Map 3 options to 3 different play types
cards.text: An easy way to make 3 options genuinely different is to let each lead with a different Caillois play type: one agon (a race or timed board), one mimicry (a role-heavy battle), one ilinx or calm paidia-style free play (a void-floor runner or a relaxed tour). This also fits the rule that the 3 options use 3 different genres.
cards.use_when: Generating the 3 options when the brief is open.
do: Assign a play type to each option before writing it
Check that the play types differ
avoid: Three agon options with different themes

cards.title: Fun is learning a pattern
cards.text: Koster argues that fun is the brain mastering a pattern, and boredom arrives when nothing is left to learn. Each chapter, board or stretch should contain something new to grasp: a new enemy kind, a new piece, a new hazard layout. When the pattern is fully mastered, end the game or change the pattern.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many stages to make and what each adds.
do: Give each stage one new pattern
End the game soon after the last pattern is mastered
avoid: Repeating the same stage with more enemies only
Adding stages that teach nothing new
cards.source: Koster 2004, A Theory of Fun for Game Design

cards.title: Stop before it becomes a grind
cards.text: Players remember a game that ends while they still want more. Prefer 3-4 strong stages over 6 thin ones. The engines allow up to 6 chapters or boards; use 5-6 only when the session is 8 minutes or more and each one teaches something new.
cards.use_when: Choosing chapter or board count.
do: Default to 4 chapters or boards
Cut any stage that teaches nothing new
avoid: Filling to the maximum because it is allowed
cards.source: Koster 2004, A Theory of Fun for Game Design

cards.title: Name the core loop in one line with one verb
cards.text: The core loop is what the player does again and again. If it cannot be said in one line with one main verb, it is not clear enough to build or to choose between. Good: "read the ring, step out, swing at the nearest enemy". Bad: "explore, fight, collect and solve puzzles". The options schema requires each option to have its own core loop.
cards.use_when: Writing core_loop for an option.
do: Write the loop as 2-3 steps of one cycle
Make each option's loop distinct
avoid: A list of activities instead of a cycle
The same loop with a different theme across options

cards.title: The native core loop of each genre
cards.text: Battle: watch enemies walk in, step out of red rings, swing to defeat them, survive the chapter. Tactics: read where guards attack, plan a legal move for your piece, walk onto the square, capture the next target. Runner: spot the next checkpoint, choose a line, avoid hazards, touch it. Theme and story change the meaning of the loop, not the loop itself. Start from the native loop and only reframe it.
cards.use_when: Turning a creator's idea into an option or build plan.
do: Start from the genre's native loop
Reframe it with theme and labels
avoid: Describing a loop the engine cannot run (collecting items into an inventory, shooting)

cards.title: Nest loops at three time scales
cards.text: A satisfying game has a moment loop (seconds: a step, a swing), a stage loop (a minute: clear a chapter, solve a board, reach a checkpoint) and a session loop (the whole play: beat the boss, finish the last board, reach the portal, then compare score). Make sure each has a clear end signal and that the session loop invites a replay.
cards.use_when: Checking whether a design has a satisfying rhythm.
do: Name the moment, stage and session loops in the prototype flow
Give each loop a clear success signal
avoid: A session with only a moment loop and no stage goals

cards.title: Risk and reward in the runner score
cards.text: The runner scores +100 per checkpoint, -25 per hazard and +300 plus a time bonus at the finish. A hazard also sends the player back to the last checkpoint, which costs time. So the real risk is time, and the reward is a shorter line. Place one or two hazards beside the shortest line between checkpoints so a bold player can save seconds and a careful player can walk around.
cards.use_when: Placing hazards in a race or time-limit runner.
do: Put hazards beside the short line, leaving a longer safe line
Make the safe detour 1-2 m longer
avoid: Hazards that fully block the route (no choice, just a wall)
Hazards with no shorter line next to them (pure punishment)

cards.title: Risk and reward on the tactics board
cards.text: In tactics, guards attack squares on a beat. A short route through squares that are safe only between beats rewards timing; a longer route around attacked squares is safe but slower in a time race. Cracked squares and tables block paths and create those trade-offs. Design at least one board where the fastest path needs timing and a slower safe path exists.
cards.use_when: Designing boards 2 and later.
do: Give one board a fast risky path and a slow safe path
Use cracks and tables to shape the two routes
avoid: Boards with only one path
Making the risky path the only path in MR with a fast beat

cards.title: A choice is meaningful only if its result is visible and matters later
cards.text: Salen and Zimmerman describe meaningful play as actions whose outcomes are discernible (the player sees what happened) and integrated (it affects what comes next). Check every choice in the design: does the player see the result, and does it change score, time or position later? If not, it is decoration, not a choice.
cards.use_when: Reviewing an option's mechanics or a build plan.
do: Show each choice's result immediately
Link choices to score, time or position
avoid: Choices that have no visible effect
Promising branching story the engine cannot run

cards.title: A dominant strategy erases the choice
cards.text: If one line or tactic is always best, every player does it and the choice disappears. In runner, a hazard nobody needs to go near; in tactics, a route that is both shortest and safest; in battle, standing in one corner where rings never fall. Look for the always-best answer in each stage and add a cost to it.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a layout, board or chapter for depth.
do: Ask "what is always best here?" for each stage
Give the best route a cost (a hazard, a guard beat, a crack)
avoid: Designs where the safest path is also the fastest

cards.title: Response: feedback must feel instant
cards.text: Swink describes game feel as real-time control, simulated space and polish. In MR the control is the player's own body, so the game must answer each action at once: a swing that hits, a checkpoint that lights the moment it is touched, a ring that clearly marks danger before it lands. A slow or missing response feels like the game ignored the player.
cards.use_when: Writing rules and HUD, or testing a prototype question about feel.
do: Add a test question about whether feedback reads in time
Keep checkpoints large enough to touch without searching
avoid: Tiny targets that need exact placement while walking
Relying on text to confirm an action

cards.title: Juice comes from the engine, the designer controls staging
cards.text: The engines already provide their own hit and pickup effects; the designer cannot add new particles, screen shake or custom sounds through the build plan. The designer's juice levers are staging: lighting preset, hero scenery at key moments, animated rides, the boss intro line, chapter titles, and where the finish sits relative to the audience. Promise polish through those, not through new effects.
cards.use_when: A creator asks for more effects, explosions or custom feedback.
do: Use lighting, hero pieces and animated rides for spectacle
Place key moments where they read best
avoid: Promising custom VFX, screen shake or new sound effects in the build plan

cards.title: Failure must be readable and fair
cards.text: Players accept failure when they see why it happened and that they could have avoided it. Red rings warn before they land; guards attack on a regular beat; hazards are red circles on the route. Never place a hazard where it cannot be seen in time, never put a guard's attack on the square the player must land on with no alternative, and keep MR beats slow enough to react while walking.
cards.use_when: Checking difficulty spikes and test questions.
do: Make every danger visible before it matters
Add a test question like "Can a 7-year-old read the rings in time?"
avoid: Hazards placed right behind a turn
Unavoidable damage

cards.title: Give short, mid and long goals at once
cards.text: Players stay engaged when a goal is always close: short (the next checkpoint, the next enemy, the next target, seconds away), mid (finish this chapter or board, about a minute) and long (beat the boss, reach the portal, top the leaderboard). The HUD and labels should always show the short goal; the intro card states the long one.
cards.use_when: Writing the goal line, HUD and labels.
do: State the long goal on the intro card
Show the short goal on the HUD
Name chapters or boards for the mid goal
avoid: Only a long goal with nothing close
Hiding which checkpoint or target is next

cards.title: Write the goal line as one action and one end state
cards.text: The game card goal is read once, often in a headset. Make it one sentence with the action and the end state: "Free the 4 captives, then reach the gate", "Survive 4 chapters and defeat the Ash King", "Capture the targets in order before the guards catch you". Numbers help players plan.
cards.use_when: Writing game.goal in the build step.
do: Use one sentence with a number if possible
Name the final thing (boss, portal, last target)
avoid: Vague goals like "Have fun exploring"
Goals with several clauses

cards.title: Alternate tension and release
cards.text: Interest curves rise and fall: a hook, a dip, rising peaks, the climax, then a short resolution. In battle, a chapter is tension and the gap before the next chapter title is release; in tactics, a hard board is tension and the next board's opening is release; in runner, hazard stretches are tension and open views at checkpoints are release. Plan release points as deliberately as peaks.
cards.use_when: Writing the prototype flow minute by minute.
do: Mark tension and release in the flow timeline
Put a release beat right after the first peak
avoid: Constant pressure from start to end
A long calm middle with no build
cards.source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

cards.title: Place the climax in the last 20 percent
cards.text: The climax should come near the end, after the player has learned everything it tests: the boss after the last chapter, the final board with the king or the most guards, the last checkpoint stretch before the portal. In MR, stage it where spectators can see it. Keep one short beat after it (the portal, the score) so it lands.
cards.use_when: Choosing the climax panel and the end of the flow.
do: Put the climax at about 80 percent of the session
Stage it facing the audience
Follow it with a short resolution
avoid: A climax in the middle and a long tail after
A climax that tests something never taught
cards.source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

cards.title: An ending feels earned when it uses what was learned
cards.text: Endings feel earned when the final challenge combines skills the player built and the story pays off the opening promise. Make the last chapter mix the enemy kinds already met, the last board use the hardest piece the player already knows, and the last checkpoint label answer the intro story ("Return the lantern to the temple"). Reaching the portal or defeating the boss then means something.
cards.use_when: Writing the last chapter, board or checkpoint and the story card.
do: Echo the intro story in the final label or boss name
Combine known elements in the finale
avoid: A new rule introduced at the end
An ending that ignores the opening story

cards.title: Fill the 8 formal elements before options
cards.text: Fullerton lists the formal elements every game has: players, objectives, procedures, rules, resources, conflict, boundaries and outcome. For a vague brief, check each one and fill the gaps with explicit defaults: players from group_size, objective from the genre, procedures from the native loop, boundaries from the venue size. If a missing element would change the options, ask; otherwise default and say so.
cards.use_when: The brief is short or vague and the interview is near its end.
do: Check all 8 elements against the brief
Ask only about elements that change the options
Write defaults into the brief
avoid: Producing options while the objective or boundary is unknown
Asking about elements that have an obvious default

cards.title: Defaults for players and objectives
cards.text: Players: in MR under 4 x 4 m, 1-2 at once; 4-10 m, 1-4; over 10 m, up to 6. Interaction pattern follows play_mode: solo, race (multilateral competition on separate copies) or together (shared floor). Objective by genre: battle is defeat the boss after the chapters, tactics is capture targets in order on each board, runner is reach the portal after all checkpoints. Reframe the objective with story but keep the underlying form.
cards.use_when: The brief does not state how many play or what winning is.
do: Derive player count from the floor size
Use the genre's native objective
avoid: More simultaneous MR players than the floor supports
Objectives the engine cannot check (collect 10 coins)

cards.title: Procedures are what players do, rules are what limits them
