cards.text: Procedures are the actions (walk, swing, step out of rings, move as a piece). Rules limit them and define consequences (a hazard sends you back, a guard's attacked square is forbidden, targets must be taken in order). In the rules list, write the 2-4 limits a player could not guess from the scene, in the player's language, and skip procedures they learn by doing.
cards.use_when: Writing game.rules for the build.
do: List only rules that cannot be seen
State consequences plainly ("Step on red, back to the last checkpoint")
avoid: Rules that describe obvious procedures
More than 6 rules

cards.title: Resources and boundaries in a walking game
cards.text: Resources are what players manage: time (time limit, time bonus), health in battle, position and safe squares in tactics, and score. Boundaries are the edges of play: in MR the real floor minus 0.6 m from its edge, which also sets how many checkpoints fit (small rooms 3-6, medium 4-8, large 4-10). Name the scarce resource in each option; if nothing is scarce, there is no tension.
cards.use_when: Making mechanics concrete for an option or build.
do: Name one scarce resource per option (time, health, safe squares)
Treat the real walls as the edge of the world
avoid: Inventory or currency resources (the engine has none)
Placing anything inside the 0.6 m edge margin

cards.title: Define conflict and outcome explicitly
cards.text: Conflict is what stops the player reaching the goal: enemies and rain in battle, guards and cracks in tactics, hazards and the clock in runner. Outcome is how it ends: win or lose, or a ranked score. Single-player walks with no conflict are tours, which is fine for submission but say so. Ranked outcomes (score, time) suit races; win or lose suits battle.
cards.use_when: Writing mechanics for an option or reviewing a build plan.
do: Name the source of conflict in one phrase
Say whether the outcome is win/lose or ranked
avoid: A challenge option with no real conflict
An outcome nobody can see (no score, no finish)

cards.title: Make options differ on at least 2 of 4 axes
cards.text: Each option sits on four axes: aesthetic (main MDA feeling), loop (explore, collect, race, story, escape, tour, dodge), social (solo, race, together) and route (loop, spiral, zigzag, lanes, hub, out-and-back). Any two options must differ on at least 2 axes and must use different genres. Choose the axis values first, then write the option, so difference is designed in rather than hoped for.
cards.use_when: Generating the 3 options.
do: Fill a 3 x 4 grid of axis values before writing
Vary social mode across options when the brief allows
Use 3 different genres
avoid: Writing options first and fixing axes afterward
Three options with the same social mode and feeling

cards.title: Avoid 3 skins of one idea
cards.text: Design fixation makes designers repeat the first idea with surface changes, such as the same course themed as jungle, space and candy. These are not real options because the creator's decision does not change the game. A real choice changes what the player does, how it feels, or who they play with. If the core loops read the same with theme words removed, rewrite.
cards.use_when: Reviewing the 3 options before sending them.
do: Remove theme words and compare the core loops
Change genre, loop and social mode between options
avoid: Options that differ only in theme, lighting or title

cards.title: Score options honestly and use the whole scale
cards.text: Scores (fun, mr_fit, players_fit, buildability, 1-5) are only useful if they differ and are tied to brief facts. A 5 means nothing to improve; most options should have at least one 3 or below. Each score_why must cite a fact (floor size, light, player age). Set confidence to low when the option depends on something untested, such as void floor with newcomers.
cards.use_when: Filling scores and scores_why for options.
do: Cite a brief or venue fact in each score_why
Give each option a weakest score
Use low confidence for untested combinations
avoid: All options scoring 4-5 on everything
Scores with no stated reason

cards.title: Recommend the option that serves the primary feeling and the players
cards.text: Recommend the option that best serves the brief's top feeling for the stated players in the real venue, not the most ambitious one. Tie-breaks: fits the venue and light better, safer for the least experienced player, simpler to build well. Say in one sentence which brief fact decided it. The creator chooses first, so the recommendation is a mirror, not a command.
cards.use_when: Setting recommend and recommend_why.
do: Name the deciding brief fact
Prefer venue fit and player safety in ties
avoid: Recommending the flashiest option by default
Recommending an option with a low players_fit

cards.title: Span the risk range: one safe, one bold
cards.text: A good set of 3 options spans risk: one safe option that clearly fits the brief, one bold option that stretches it (an unusual genre for the theme, a void floor, a race for a calm brief), and one in between. The bold option makes the creator think and often improves the final choice even when not picked. Mark the bold option's confidence honestly.
cards.use_when: Generating options when the brief is clear and a safe answer is obvious.
do: Label which option is the bold one in its why
Keep the bold option buildable
avoid: Three safe variations
A bold option that breaks safety rules or engine limits

cards.title: A 1-minute session
cards.text: One minute suits queues, booths and young kids. Use a runner with 4 checkpoints close together, or a battle with 3 short chapters of 2-3 grunts plus a boss; tactics needs more time per board, so use only 3 boards with 2 targets and 0-1 guard. The intro card must be 1-2 sentences. Consider timeLimit 60 s for a race.
cards.use_when: session_minutes is 1-2, or a high-throughput event.
do: Minimum stage counts
One-sentence story
First success within 15 s
avoid: 5+ chapters or boards
Long intro text

cards.title: A 3-minute session
cards.text: Three minutes is the default for events and first-time VR. Runner: 5-6 checkpoints with 2-4 hazards. Battle: 3-4 chapters with the boss. Tactics: 3-4 boards. There is room for one climax and one breather. For a race, timeLimit around 180 s gives a time bonus target.
cards.use_when: session_minutes is around 3, or not given for an event.
do: Use this as the default when session length is unknown
Plan one breather and one climax
avoid: Cramming 6 boards into 3 minutes

cards.title: A 5-minute session
cards.text: Five minutes fits a full arc with a sawtooth curve. Runner: 6-8 checkpoints in a medium or large space with a story told through every label. Battle: 4-5 chapters with rain introduced mid-way. Tactics: 4-5 boards with 2 piece changes. Headset comfort is fine at this length for most players.
cards.use_when: session_minutes is 4-6.
do: Use 2 tension peaks before the climax
Introduce one new element per stage
avoid: A flat middle stretch

cards.title: A 10-minute session
cards.text: Ten minutes is long for walking MR: fatigue, battery and headset comfort matter, and seniors or kids may tire. Use the maximum stages (6 chapters or boards, 8-10 checkpoints only in a large space), add clear release beats, and keep the climax near minute 8. On PC this length is comfortable. If the space is small, warn that a long walk will loop repeatedly.
cards.use_when: session_minutes is 8 or more.
do: Plan release beats every 2 minutes
Warn about headset fatigue for kids and seniors
avoid: 10 minutes of constant challenge in MR
A 10-minute runner in a small room

cards.title: Replay through time attack and the leaderboard
cards.text: The cheapest replay value is improvement: a fixed course and a clock. The runner time bonus and the tactics time race with a leaderboard both give players a reason to try again and beat their own time or a friend's. Keep the course short (1-3 minutes) so a retry costs little, and show the leaderboard where the queue can see it.
cards.use_when: The brief wants replayability, competition, or repeat visitors.
do: Keep a replayable course to 1-3 minutes
Show the leaderboard on a screen in view of the queue
avoid: Long courses for time attack
Time attack for a calm submission brief

cards.title: Replay through variety across stages
cards.text: When players should come back for more content rather than a better time, vary the stages: different pieces and guard layouts across tactics boards, different enemy mixes and rain across battle chapters, varied views and vignettes along a runner route. Variety within one session also keeps first-time play fresh. Persistent unlocks are not available, so variety must live inside the game.
cards.use_when: The brief wants depth or repeat visits but not competition.
do: Change piece type every 1-2 boards
Change the enemy mix every chapter
Give each runner stretch its own view
avoid: Promising unlocks, levels saved between visits or progression systems

cards.title: Design means turning open questions into decided facts
cards.text: Every brief field starts as unknown, and the interview exists to move as many fields as possible to decided before options are proposed. A field is decided when the engine could act on it without guessing: a number of metres, a play mode, a list of MDA feelings, a lighting preset. Treat each question as buying certainty on the field that would change the design most. Whatever is still open at the end must be written down as an assumption, not hidden.
cards.use_when: At every interview turn, when choosing what to ask next.
do: Keep a mental list of brief fields as decided, assumed or unknown
Ask about the unknown field with the biggest effect on the 3 options
Write leftover unknowns into the brief as explicit assumptions
avoid: Proposing options while platform or MR floor size is still unknown
Treating a vague answer like 'fun' as a decided field

cards.title: Ask the question whose answer splits the options most
cards.text: The best next question is the one where different answers would lead to clearly different game concepts. Platform and MR floor size split everything (genre list, route, player count), so they come first. Player age splits theme and difficulty. Colour preference or checkpoint names rarely change the concept, so do not spend a question on them. If every plausible answer leads to the same 3 options, skip the question and use a default.
cards.use_when: Deciding between two candidate questions with only a few questions left.
do: Imagine 2-3 likely answers and check if the options would change
Prefer questions that change genre, route, player count or theme
Leave cosmetic details to the prototype comments
avoid: Asking about colours, names or music during the interview
Asking a question just because it is next on the list

cards.title: Spend the 4-7 question budget on facts that cannot be defaulted
cards.text: Treat the interview as a budget: about 4-7 questions, never more than 9. Platform, players, feelings and (MR) floor size each need a question unless already answered; that is usually 4-5. The 1-3 remaining questions go to whichever optional field has no safe default for this creator, such as spectators at an event or brand rules for a sponsor. Session length, lighting and difficulty almost always fall back to defaults instead.
cards.use_when: Counting how many questions are left and what to spend them on.
do: Count required fields still open
Spend spare questions on fields with no safe default for this creator
avoid: Using spare questions on session length or lighting
Running out of budget before the MR floor size is known

cards.title: One question per turn, with one decision inside it
cards.text: Each turn asks exactly one question so the creator can answer by tapping a choice. Combining 'how many players and how old' makes choices impossible to list and answers hard to read. If two facts form one measurement, such as floor width and depth, ask them together with size choices like '3 x 3 m', '5 x 5 m', '10 x 10 m or more'.
cards.use_when: Writing the question text for the next interview turn.
do: Ask one thing and make the choices answer exactly that
Combine only facts that form one measurement or one picture
avoid: Two questions joined with 'and' in one turn
Choices that answer only half of the question

cards.title: Give 3-6 choices that are distinct and cover the likely answers
cards.text: Tappable choices are the main way novice creators answer, so they must be distinct and together cover most real answers. Each choice should lead to a different design, otherwise merge them. Include a middle choice and, when a default exists, a 'not sure, pick for me' choice. The creator can still type freely, so the list does not need to be exhaustive.
cards.use_when: Writing the choices array for any interview question.
do: Make each choice lead to a different design consequence
Include 'Not sure, pick for me' when a default exists
Use concrete numbers in choices (3 min, 5 x 5 m, 2 players)
avoid: Near-duplicate choices like 'fun' and 'enjoyable'
More than 6 choices
Only extreme choices with no middle

cards.title: Use multi-select only when several answers can be true at once
cards.text: Set multi to true for feelings (top 1-3 MDA aesthetics), surroundings and constraints, because several can apply together. Set multi to false for platform, floor size, play mode, session length and age band, because one answer drives the design. For feelings, say 'pick up to 3' in the question, since picking all 8 tells you nothing.
cards.use_when: Deciding the multi flag of an interview question.
do: multi false for platform, size, play mode, session length
multi true for feelings, constraints and surroundings, with a cap of 3 for feelings
avoid: Multi-select for platform
Letting the creator tick all 8 feelings without asking which matters most

cards.title: The why-line teaches one design idea in one sentence
cards.text: Each question carries a one-line why that tells the creator what the answer will change, so they learn how designers think. Good why-lines name a consequence: 'Floor size decides how many checkpoints fit and whether a race is safe.' Bad why-lines restate the question or flatter. Over 5 questions the creator should learn that space, players and feelings drive a design.
cards.use_when: Writing the why field for any interview question.
do: Name the concrete design consequence of the answer
Keep it under about 20 words
Match the creator's language and level
avoid: 'So I can make the best game for you'
Jargon like MDA or core loop without explanation for novices

cards.title: Never ask for names, schools, photos, phone numbers or addresses
cards.text: Many creators are children or teachers, and personal data is not needed to design a game. Ask for age bands and group types ('7-10 year olds', 'a school class of 30'), never a school or child's name. If the creator volunteers personal details, do not copy them into the brief; keep only the design fact. Describe a venue by kind and size ('a classroom 8 x 6 m'), not its address.
cards.use_when: Asking about players or venue, or when the creator types personal details.
do: Ask for age bands, group types and counts
Strip names and places from the brief, keep the design facts
avoid: 'What is your name?' or 'Which school?'
Asking for a photo of the room
Copying a child's name into the story

cards.title: Stop asking once platform, concept, players, feelings and the MR floor are decided
cards.text: The interview is done when platform, concept, players, feelings and, for MR, floor size and indoor or outdoor are known. Session length, play mode, lighting and constraints may be defaulted. Continuing past this point costs patience and rarely changes the 3 options. A good interview ends in 4-7 questions; at 9 you must stop and default the rest.
cards.use_when: After each answer, before writing the next question.
do: Check the required fields after each answer
Default the optional fields and mark them as assumed
Move to the summary as soon as the required fields are set
avoid: Asking about checkpoint names or colours before stopping
Going to options without the MR floor size

cards.title: Read the brief back in 2-3 sentences that expose assumptions
cards.text: The summary is the last cheap chance to catch a misunderstanding. Restate what the creator said in their words, then name what you assumed, for example 'I assumed about 3 minutes per play and a solo game; tell me if you want a race.' A creator corrects a wrong assumption far more easily when it is named than when it is buried. Keep it short so it is actually read.
cards.use_when: Writing the summary when the interview is done.
do: Lead with who plays, where and how it should feel
Name every defaulted field in one clause
Invite a one-tap correction
avoid: A summary that only repeats what the creator said
Hiding defaults so the options look certain

cards.title: 'Make it fun' or 'สนุกๆ' means the feelings are still unknown
cards.text: 'Fun' is not a design goal because every MDA aesthetic is fun to someone. Treat it as an empty feelings field and ask which kind of fun with plain choices: 'a hard challenge', 'a story', 'exploring and finding secrets', 'racing friends', 'relaxing and easy'. Ask for the top 1-3. Different picks lead to different genres, so this question has high value.
cards.use_when: The creator says fun, enjoyable, just a good game, or the Thai words for fun.
do: Translate MDA names into everyday words in the choices
Ask for the top 1-3 with multi true
Store the English MDA names in the brief
avoid: Writing 'fun' into the feelings field
Assuming fun means challenge
cards.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA; Koster, A Theory of Fun

cards.title: Missing group size: ask how many play at the same time
cards.text: Group size decides play mode (solo, race, together), route width and, in MR, whether the floor is big enough. Creators often say 'kids' or 'my friends' without a number, or confuse total visitors with players at once. Ask 'How many people play at the same time?' with choices 1, 2, 3-4, 5-6. For events, total visitors affect session length, not group size.
cards.use_when: Players are described but the number at once is unknown.
do: Ask 'at the same time' explicitly
Offer 1, 2, 3-4, 5-6 as choices
Cap MR players by floor size (under 4 x 4 m: 1-2)
avoid: Treating '30 students' as 30 players at once
Planning a 6-player race in a living room

cards.title: MR floor size is never guessed: ask in metres or paces
cards.text: In MR the empty floor is the whole game board; its size decides genre (under 3 x 3 m only runner fits), checkpoint count and player count. Ask for the width and depth of the empty floor, not the whole room. Offer choices like 'small room 3 x 3 m', 'classroom 6 x 8 m', 'hall 10 x 10 m or more', and accept paces (1 pace is about 0.75 m). If the creator does not know, ask them to pace it.
cards.use_when: Platform is MR and width_m or depth_m is unknown.
do: Ask for the empty floor only
Convert paces at 0.75 m each
Round down when the creator is unsure
avoid: Defaulting to a 10 x 10 m floor
Using a room size that includes sofas and tables

cards.title: Scary but for 5-year-olds: offer spooky-cute, not fear
cards.text: A wish for 'scary' with players under about 8 is a conflict between feeling and audience. Resolve it toward the audience: a spooky-cute theme (friendly ghosts, glowing lanterns, cartoon pumpkins), evening rather than spooky lighting, no sudden scares, and labels that make the child the brave hero. Name the trade-off openly and offer a slightly spookier option for older siblings.
cards.use_when: Feelings or theme say scary, horror or ghosts while players are young kids.
do: Name the conflict kindly in one line
Offer spooky-cute with friendly ghosts and warm light
Frame hazards as playful, not threatening
avoid: Jump scares or dark void floors for young children
Refusing the theme outright
cards.source: Meta VR comfort and MR design guidelines; design practice

cards.title: Relaxing but challenging: shape the session, do not average it
cards.text: When a creator picks both submission and challenge, medium difficulty everywhere often satisfies neither. Give a calm opening and a harder ending, or let one of the three options lean each way. In a runner, the first 3 checkpoints can be hazard-free and the last 2 dense with hazards and a time bonus. Ask which feeling should win if only one could.
cards.use_when: Feelings include both submission and challenge.
do: Ask which feeling wins if only one is possible
Easy start, hard finish
Let options lean different ways
avoid: Making every part medium difficulty
Dropping one of the two feelings silently

cards.title: A race wish in a small MR room: offer timed turns with a leaderboard
cards.text: Several players walking fast in under 4 x 4 m is unsafe, but the feeling behind a race is usually competition, not a shared floor. Offer the online race where each player walks their own copy, one at a time in the room, with a live leaderboard on a screen for friends watching. It keeps competition and fellowship while only one person walks.
cards.use_when: Creator wants a race but the MR floor is under 4 x 4 m.
do: Explain the safety reason in one line
Offer turn-based timed runs with a leaderboard
Make the waiting friends the cheering audience
avoid: Two or more players walking fast in a small room
Dropping competition completely
cards.source: Meta MR safety guidelines; FortalLand engine

cards.title: Shooting wish: offer the sword arena or a dodge course
cards.text: No genre can shoot. When a creator asks for guns, blasters or shooting, look for the feeling underneath: action and power. Offer battle, where in MR the right controller is the sword and enemies walk in from the edges, or a runner where hazards are 'laser beams' to dodge. Say clearly 'there is no shooting, but you can slash with a sword', so the creator is not surprised later.
cards.use_when: Creator mentions shooting, guns, blasters, or the Thai words for shoot or gun.
do: Say kindly that shooting is not available
Offer battle with the sword or a dodge runner
Keep the theme (sci-fi, space) they wanted
avoid: Promising a blaster with a sword engine underneath
Silently ignoring the wish

cards.title: NPC conversation wish: tell the story through the intro card and checkpoint labels
cards.text: There are no NPC conversations or dialogue choices. A creator who wants to 'talk to the villagers' usually wants narrative. Offer the story on the intro card, checkpoint labels written as story beats ('Wake the old monk', 'Return the lantern'), and a character model placed at each checkpoint as a silent storyteller. State the limit and the alternative in one line.
cards.use_when: Creator wants talking characters, dialogue or quests given by NPCs.
do: Map dialogue beats to 4-10 checkpoint labels
Place a character model at each story checkpoint
Write the setup in the intro story
avoid: Promising characters that answer back
Labels that imply choices the player cannot make

cards.title: Inventory or crafting wish: turn collecting into ordered checkpoints
cards.text: The engine has no inventory and no crafting. 'Collect ingredients and cook' becomes checkpoints touched in order with labels like 'Pick the mango', 'Grab the sticky rice', 'Cook at the stove', and the +100 per checkpoint shows progress. Be honest that items are not held or combined; the labels tell it.
cards.use_when: Creator mentions collecting items, a bag, crafting or recipes.
do: Use checkpoint order as the recipe order
Use labels to name each item
Show progress with the score
avoid: Promising a bag or item menu
Free-order collecting, since checkpoints are touched in order

cards.title: Flying, driving or joystick movement in MR: the player walks
cards.text: In MR players move only with their own legs. A wish to fly a dragon can become a void floor with scenery far below so walking feels like gliding above it; driving can become a racetrack walked on foot. Mention comfort: void floors are dramatic and dizzy, so avoid them for first-time VR players and young kids. If free movement is essential, suggest the PC platform.
cards.use_when: Creator wants flying, driving, riding, swimming or teleporting in MR.
do: Offer walking with a themed floor or a void floor
Warn about dizziness with void for beginners
Suggest PC if free movement is essential
avoid: Promising joystick or vehicle movement in MR
Void floor for first-time VR kids
cards.source: Meta VR comfort guidelines; FortalLand engine

cards.title: Voice chat or team messaging: use the shared floor and the real room
cards.text: There is no voice chat or in-game messaging. In MR players share the real room, so they can simply talk and point, and the shared floor mode shows each other's avatars. For players in different places, offer a race with a live leaderboard. Fellowship then comes from real people nearby, which MR does better than chat.
cards.use_when: Creator asks for voice chat, team chat or communication features.
do: Point out that co-located players can talk for real
Offer shared floor or race with a leaderboard
avoid: Promising team chat or pings
Puzzles that need remote players to talk

cards.title: Players building or decorating during play: put expression elsewhere
cards.text: Players cannot place objects or build during play. Expression can come from tactics boards where players plan their own path, from chasing a personal best on a leaderboard, or from the creator designing the land itself. If the creator is a kid who wants to build, point out that they are the builder: the game they design is their creation.
cards.use_when: Creator wants players to build, paint, decorate or customise during play.
do: Offer tactics planning or leaderboard bragging
Frame the creator's own design as the building part
avoid: Promising build modes or avatar customisation
Ignoring the expression wish

cards.title: Hidden assumption: spectators can see the game
cards.text: Creators often imagine parents watching the dragon, but in MR people outside the headset see only bodies walking and reacting. Surface this when spectators are mentioned and plan for it: a leaderboard on a wall screen, a key dodge near the audience side, and the finish portal where the crowd can cheer. Write the spectator plan into the brief.
cards.use_when: Creator mentions parents, an audience, a crowd or a stage.
do: Tell the creator spectators see bodies, not the virtual floor
Ask where spectators stand
Place key moments on their side
avoid: Visual spectacle aimed at spectators who cannot see it
Giving spectators tasks inside the play area

cards.title: Hidden assumption: a dark theme will look dark outdoors at noon
cards.text: Creators picture night or neon themes but plan to play in a sunny garden. Passthrough shows real daylight, which washes out glow and dark scenes. When the theme is dark and the venue is outdoors, ask the time of day. In daytime, offer a bright version of the theme (sunny temple fair instead of haunted temple) or suggest playing indoors or after dark.
cards.use_when: Theme is spooky, neon or night and the MR venue is outdoors.
do: Ask the time of day
Offer a daylight-readable version of the theme
Use noon or morning lighting outdoors in daytime
avoid: Night or neon lighting in midday sun
Assuming the headset darkens the real sky
cards.source: FortalLand engine; Meta MR design guidelines

cards.title: Hidden assumption: the whole room is empty floor
cards.text: People give the room size, not the empty floor. A 5 x 5 m living room with a sofa and table may have only 3 x 3 m clear. After size, ask about obstacles with choices like 'nothing inside', 'a table or sofa', 'a pillar', 'trees'. Write obstacles into the brief and keep the 1.2 m walking route and 0.6 m edge margin around them.
cards.use_when: Creator gives a room size for MR, especially homes and classrooms.
do: Ask what is inside the floor after the size
Subtract furniture from the usable size
Write obstacles or 'none' in the brief
avoid: Laying a route over a real sofa
Taking room size as play size
cards.source: Meta MR safety guidelines; FortalLand engine

cards.title: Hidden assumption: the creator is the player
cards.text: A creator describing what they like may be designing for someone else entirely: a parent for a 6-year-old, a teacher for a class, an organiser for strangers. Before feelings, make sure you know who plays; if the creator says 'I love hard games' but players are first-time families, design for the families and mention the gap. If the creator is the player, preferences and audience are the same and one question is saved.
cards.use_when: Creator states personal tastes before saying who plays.
do: Ask who plays before trusting taste as the feelings field
Name the gap when taste and audience differ
avoid: Designing a hard game for a family booth because the organiser likes hard games

cards.title: 'Adventure' or 'ผจญภัย': story, exploring, or danger
cards.text: 'Adventure' can mean a story journey (narrative: a quest told through checkpoint labels), exploring a world (discovery: hub and spokes, hidden scenery), or facing danger (challenge: hazards, or chapters and a boss in battle). Ask 'What is the best moment of the adventure?' with choices 'finding secret places', 'a story with an ending', 'beating a big monster'. That single answer picks the genre lean.
cards.use_when: Concept uses adventure, quest, journey, or the Thai words for adventure.
do: Ask for the best moment, not a definition
Map answers to discovery, narrative or challenge
avoid: Assuming adventure means combat
Writing 'adventure' as a feeling

cards.title: 'Challenge' or 'ท้าทาย': body skill, speed, or thinking
cards.text: A challenge can be body skill (battle: stepping out of red rings, slashing enemies), speed (a timed runner with a leaderboard), or thinking (a tactics board solved in order while avoiding guards). Ask 'What should be hard?' with choices 'moving and dodging', 'beating the clock or friends', 'figuring out the right path'. Each answer points to a different genre.
cards.use_when: Creator says challenge, hard, difficult, or the Thai words for these.
do: Ask what should be hard
Map to battle, runner race, or tactics
avoid: Making everything faster and calling it challenge
Hard puzzles for first-time VR players with no ramp

cards.title: 'Cute' or 'น่ารัก': the look, the mood, or easy play
cards.text: 'Cute' can describe the art (candy, toys, round animals, pastel palette), the mood (gentle, nothing scary), or a hidden request for easy play for small kids. Ask 'Cute like...?' with choices 'candy and toys', 'baby animals and farm', 'soft and easy to play'. The art reading changes theme only; the easy reading changes hazards and session length, so it matters which one.
cards.use_when: Creator says cute, adorable, kawaii, or the Thai words for cute.
do: Separate the look from the difficulty
Offer theme families from the model library (candy, toys, farm)
avoid: Assuming cute means babyish for teens
Only changing colours when they meant easy

cards.title: 'Epic' or 'อลังการ': scale, a boss climax, or spectacle
cards.text: 'Epic' usually means big scale (huge scenery models, a long route, the void floor drop), a climax (battle chapters ending in a boss), or wow visuals (dramatic lighting). Ask 'What makes it epic for you?' with choices 'giant monsters and places', 'a big final boss', 'wow light and views'. Check the venue: void floors and night lighting need indoor or dark conditions and experienced players.
cards.use_when: Creator says epic, huge, legendary, or the Thai words for grand.
do: Ask which part should feel big
Match to scenery scale, boss chapter or lighting
avoid: Adding everything at once and cluttering the route
Void floor for first-time VR kids

cards.title: 'Exciting' or 'ตื่นเต้น': speed, suspense, or surprise
cards.text: Excitement can come from speed (time limit, race, dense hazards), suspense (spooky lighting, a slow approach to a boss), or surprise (scenery revealed around corners). Ask 'Exciting like...?' with choices 'racing the clock', 'creepy and tense', 'surprises around every corner'. In MR there are no sudden scares that make people run, so suspense must stay walkable.
cards.use_when: Creator says exciting, thrilling, or the Thai words for exciting.
do: Ask which kind of excitement
Keep MR suspense walk-safe
avoid: Jump scares in MR
Making it exciting only by shortening the time limit
cards.source: Meta MR safety guidelines; design practice

cards.title: 'Scary' or 'น่ากลัว': spooky-fun, tense, or real horror
cards.text: Ask how scary with choices 'spooky but fun', 'creepy and tense', 'really scary (teens and adults only)'. The answer sets lighting (evening, spooky or night), which ghost models are used, and whether hazards are framed as threats. Combine with age: real horror is only for teens and adults, and even then no sudden scares in MR because players may run.
cards.use_when: Creator says scary, horror, haunted, ghosts, or the Thai words for scary.
do: Ask the intensity level
Check it against player age
Build dread with light and scenery, not startles
avoid: Real horror with kids or families
Startle effects in MR
cards.source: Meta MR safety guidelines; design practice

cards.title: 'Easy' or 'ง่ายๆ': easy to play, easy to understand, or quick to make
cards.text: 'Easy' can mean low difficulty (few hazards, no time limit), rules a first-timer understands in 10 seconds, or a quick project for the creator. Ask 'Easy for whom?' with choices 'players who never used VR', 'very young kids', 'I want to finish quickly'. Difficulty readings change hazards; the quick-project reading suggests fewer checkpoints and a simple loop.
cards.use_when: Creator says easy, simple, not complicated, or the Thai words for easy.
do: Ask who it should be easy for
Translate to hazard count, rule count or route simplicity
avoid: Removing all challenge when they meant simple rules
Assuming they mean themselves

cards.title: 'Like Minecraft' or 'like Roblox': find which part they mean
cards.text: Naming a famous game is a shortcut, not a spec, and those games use mechanics the engine lacks (building, shooting, open worlds). Ask 'What part of it do you love most?' with choices tied to buildable features: 'the blocky look', 'racing friends', 'exploring', 'fighting monsters'. Never copy names, characters or logos; borrow the feeling and a theme family.
cards.use_when: Creator references a known game, film or show.
do: Ask which part they love
Map it to a genre, theme or feeling
Use original names and library models
avoid: Promising the original game's mechanics
Using trademarked names or characters

cards.title: 'Educational' or 'ได้ความรู้' / 'สื่อการสอน': facts, a sequence, or planning skill
cards.text: Teachers ask for learning games. Readings: facts shown at checkpoint labels and the intro card, a process walked in order such as the water cycle (checkpoints as steps), or logical thinking (tactics boards). Ask 'What should students remember or be able to do?' with choices 'some facts', 'steps in the right order', 'think and plan'.
cards.use_when: Creator is a teacher or says learning or educational.
do: Ask for the learning outcome
Use checkpoint order for processes
Keep labels under about 5 words
avoid: Long text on checkpoints that walking players cannot read
Quiz mechanics the engine lacks

cards.title: 'Thai style' or 'แบบไทยๆ': temple, village, folklore, or festival
cards.text: Thai style can mean temple and palace architecture, village and farm life, folklore and ghosts, or festivals like Loy Krathong and Songkran. Ask 'Which Thai world?' with those four choices. Each picks a different model set and mood, and temples and ghosts bring cultural care rules.
cards.use_when: Concept says Thai or Thai style.
do: Ask which Thai world
Pick matching models from the library
Apply temple and ghost care rules when relevant
avoid: Mixing sacred temple items with hazards
A generic pan-Asian look

cards.title: 'Wow' or 'ว้าว' is sensation: views, light, or scale
cards.text: A creator wanting wow wants the sensation aesthetic. The engine delivers it through scale (huge scenery), light (neon, evening, night presets) and the void floor drop. Ask 'What should make players say wow?' with choices 'a huge creature or building', 'glowing lights', 'the floor dropping away'. Check light conditions: glow needs indoors or night.
cards.use_when: Creator says wow, amazing, or the Thai words for stunning.
do: Pick one wow moment and stage it as a reveal
Check lighting against the venue
avoid: Spreading wow evenly so nothing stands out
Void floor for first-time VR players
cards.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA; design practice

cards.title: 'Play together' or 'เล่นด้วยกัน': race, shared floor, or taking turns
cards.text: Together can mean competing (online race with a leaderboard), sharing one space and seeing each other (shared floor with avatars), or a family taking turns while the others watch. Ask 'How should they play together?' with choices 'race each other', 'walk the same world at once', 'take turns and cheer'. The answer sets play_mode and safety spacing.
cards.use_when: Creator says together, with friends, family play, or the Thai words for together.
do: Map to race, together, or solo turns with spectators
Check floor size for simultaneous walkers
avoid: Assuming together means everyone walking at once in a small room

cards.title: Default session length: 3 minutes at events, 5 at home or in class
cards.text: If session length is not given, use about 3 minutes for events and pop-ups where a queue waits, and 5 minutes for homes, classrooms and private play. First-time VR players and kids under 8 do best with short headset sessions. State it: 'I assumed about 3 minutes so the queue keeps moving; tell me if players can stay longer.'
cards.use_when: session_minutes is unknown when the interview stops.
do: Set 3 for events, 5 otherwise
State the assumption in the summary
avoid: Defaulting to 15-minute sessions
Spending a question when the venue already implies the answer
cards.source: Meta VR comfort guidelines; design practice

cards.title: Default play mode follows group size and floor size
cards.text: If play mode is unknown: one player means solo; 2-4 players on an MR floor over 4 x 4 m means together (shared floor), or race if challenge was picked with fellowship; any group on a floor under 4 x 4 m means solo turns with a leaderboard. On PC, solo unless friends were mentioned. State the choice so the creator can switch it.
cards.use_when: play_mode is unknown and group size is known.
do: Derive from group size, floor size and feelings
Prefer race when challenge and fellowship were both picked
avoid: Defaulting to race in a small room
Asking about play mode when the group is 1

cards.title: Default lighting: match the real light, not the theme wish
cards.text: If lighting was not discussed, choose from the venue: outdoors in daytime use noon or morning, indoors with steady light use default or studio, an indoor dark hall or evening event can use spooky, neon or night. Mention it only if it conflicts with the theme. On PC, pick the preset that best fits the theme mood.
cards.use_when: Choosing a lighting preset without an instruction from the creator.
do: Read indoor and time_of_day first
Flag any conflict between theme and real light
avoid: Neon lighting outdoors at noon
Spending an interview question on lighting

cards.title: Default difficulty: gentle start, one harder peak
cards.text: When difficulty is not specified, assume first-timers: the first 1-2 checkpoints or the first chapter have no hazards, hazards are spaced so a walking adult can step around them, and one climax is harder. For gamers or teens who picked challenge, raise hazard density and add a time limit. State 'I made it gentle at first; it is easy to make harder later.'
cards.use_when: Players' skill or the difficulty wish is unknown.
do: Start gentle and ramp to one peak
Raise difficulty only for challenge plus experienced players
avoid: Uniform high difficulty
No ramp for first-time VR players

cards.title: Default constraints: comfort and safety rules always apply
cards.text: If the creator lists no constraints, still write the standing ones into the brief: no sudden scares, a clear 1.2 m route, 0.6 m from the edge, nothing that needs looking up while walking fast, and no void floor for first-time players unless asked. Add age-based ones such as no real horror under 13. The creator should not have to ask for safety.
cards.use_when: constraints is empty when the interview ends.
do: Write standing safety constraints explicitly
Add age-based constraints from the players field
avoid: Leaving constraints empty
Asking 'any constraints?' with no choices
cards.source: Meta MR safety guidelines; FortalLand engine

cards.title: Default VR experience: first-time for public, schools and families
cards.text: If VR experience was not asked, assume first-time for events, schools, families and seniors, and some experience only for gamers or a creator who owns a Quest. First-time means short sessions, simple rules and no void floor. It is a safe default because experienced players still enjoy a clear game, while beginners suffer in a hard one.
cards.use_when: vr_experience is unknown.
do: Default to first-time for public audiences
State it in the summary
avoid: Assuming gamer comfort for a school class

cards.title: Missing concept: propose a theme from feelings and players, not a blank
cards.text: Some creators know who plays and how it should feel but have no theme ('anything is fine'). Do not spend more questions; pick 3 different themes from the model library that suit the players and feelings and let each option carry one. The option pick then resolves the theme. Say the themes were AI suggestions.
cards.use_when: concept is empty or 'anything' after players and feelings are known.
do: Let the 3 options carry 3 themes
Mark the concept as AI-suggested
avoid: Repeating 'what theme?' questions
One theme in three options

cards.title: Never default the platform
cards.text: MR and PC are different games: MR needs a real floor, walking and passthrough rules; PC has mouse and keyboard and no room. Guessing wrong wastes the whole design. If the creator has not said, ask in the first or second question with choices 'Quest headset walking a real floor', 'computer game', 'not sure'. If 'not sure', explain the difference in one line and ask again.
cards.use_when: platform is unknown.
do: Ask platform early
Explain MR vs PC in plain words if unsure
avoid: Assuming MR because the product is about headsets
Proposing options before platform is set

cards.title: Never default MR floor size, indoor or outdoor, or obstacles
cards.text: Real-space facts are safety facts: a guessed size can place a route through a wall or a table. Width, depth and indoor must come from the creator, and obstacles must be asked, with 'nothing inside' as a choice. If the creator cannot answer now, keep the brief open and say the game cannot be laid out until they measure or pace it.
cards.use_when: An MR brief is missing width_m, depth_m, indoor or obstacles.
do: Ask, or ask them to pace it
Accept 'none' for obstacles only from the creator
avoid: Inventing a typical room size
Guessing indoors or outdoors from the theme
cards.source: Meta MR safety guidelines; FortalLand engine

cards.title: State each assumption as value, reason and how to change it
cards.text: Assumptions are only useful if the creator can see and override them. Use one short form: 'I assumed 3 minutes because it is an event; tell me if players can stay longer.' Put it in the summary and repeat key ones in the prototype flow. Never present an assumption as something the creator said.
cards.use_when: Writing any defaulted value into the summary, options or prototype.
do: Value, reason and override hint in one clause
Group several assumptions into one sentence
avoid: Presenting defaults as facts
Listing assumptions as technical field names

cards.title: Track who decided each item: said, chose, inferred, or assumed
cards.text: Each brief value has a source: the creator said it in their own words, the creator chose it from offered choices, the AI inferred it from a card or a related answer, or the AI assumed a default. Said values are firmest; chosen values are firm but shaped by the choice list; inferred and assumed values must be shown back for confirmation. Never overwrite a said value with an inference.
cards.use_when: Building or updating the brief after each answer.
do: Remember the source for every field
Surface inferred and assumed items in the summary
avoid: Treating an inference as the creator's decision
Overwriting creator-said values with defaults

cards.title: Confidence: high when stated, medium when inferred, low when assumed
cards.text: Use three levels. High: the creator stated or chose it and it fits the rest. Medium: inferred from a strong clue (a school class implies 7-12 year olds and many players). Low: a default with no clue. Option confidence should drop when key fields are low, and low fields are the first things to check in the prototype test_questions.
cards.use_when: Setting the confidence of options or deciding what to verify.
do: Lower option confidence when players or feelings are assumed
Turn low-confidence fields into test_questions
avoid: High confidence on options built on defaults
Never reporting confidence

cards.title: Infer a field only from a strong clue, and say so
cards.text: Some answers imply others: 'my 6-year-old's birthday party' implies kids, families, first-time VR and watching parents. Fill these in as inferred and mention them in the next why-line or the summary instead of asking separately. Do not infer from weak clues, such as guessing age from a theme; adults love dinosaurs too.
cards.use_when: An answer strongly implies another brief field.
do: Fill obvious implications and mark them inferred
Confirm them in the summary instead of a new question
avoid: Inferring age from the theme
Silent inferences the creator never sees

cards.title: Each option names the assumption it depends on most
cards.text: If an option only works under an assumed fact, say so in its risks: 'Assumes 4 players at once; with 6 the route gets crowded.' The creator then picks with eyes open and sees which uncertainty matters. Options built on firm facts can carry higher confidence.
cards.use_when: Writing risks and confidence for each option.
do: Name the key assumption in risks
Tie confidence to how many assumed facts the option uses
avoid: Hiding a fragile assumption inside a confident pitch

cards.title: Show remaining assumptions inside the prototype so comments can fix them
cards.text: The prototype is where the creator sees the game, so remaining uncertainty should be visible there: the assumed session length in the flow ('0:00' to '3:00'), the assumed play mode in the HUD (leaderboard or not), and the riskiest assumption in test_questions. A creator who sees a 3:00 finish will say if they wanted 10 minutes.
cards.use_when: Writing the prototype while some brief fields are assumed.
do: Make assumed values visible in flow and HUD
Turn the riskiest assumption into a test question
avoid: Burying assumptions only in the brief JSON

cards.title: Leave low-stakes uncertainty for prototype comments
cards.text: Not everything must be settled in the interview. Cosmetic choices (palette, checkpoint names, music mood, exact theme details) are cheaper to settle by showing a prototype and letting the creator react, and reactions to a picture are more reliable than answers to abstract questions. Keep the interview for facts that change the genre or the safety of the layout.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to ask now or show it in the prototype.
do: Defer visual and naming choices to the prototype
Ask now only for structural and safety facts
avoid: Interview questions about colours
Deferring floor size to the prototype
cards.source: Fullerton, Game Design Workshop; design practice

cards.title: The creator decides; the AI mirrors and recommends
cards.text: The AI proposes and argues but never overrides a creator decision except for safety and engine limits. If the creator picks the option the AI scored lower, build it well. If a choice conflicts with safety (6 walkers in a small room), explain once, offer the safe version, then follow their decision within what is safe.
cards.use_when: Creator picks something the AI would not have picked.
do: Explain trade-offs once, then follow the choice
Hold firm only on safety and engine limits
avoid: Re-arguing a decided item every turn
Quietly changing the creator's pick

cards.title: When revising, say what changed and what stayed
cards.text: After a creator comment, the revised prototype should say in one line what changed and confirm what was kept: 'Made the boss bigger and the lighting neon; kept the route, story and 3-minute flow.' This keeps decisions traceable and reassures the creator that unmentioned parts were not lost.
cards.use_when: Producing a revised prototype or option after comments.
do: List changes and keeps briefly
Keep unmentioned fields identical
avoid: Regenerating everything from scratch
Silent changes to the story or route

cards.title: For an impossible wish, find the feeling and offer the closest buildable thing
cards.text: Every impossible request hides a feeling: shooting means power and action, flying means freedom and wow, NPC chat means story. Name the limit in one line, then offer 1-2 buildable ways to reach the same feeling. The creator keeps the heart of their idea, and trust grows because nothing is promised that cannot be built.
cards.use_when: Any request for a mechanic the engine does not have.
do: Say the limit plainly and kindly
Name the feeling behind the wish
Offer 1-2 buildable alternatives
avoid: A flat 'no'
Promising it and hoping the builder can fake it
cards.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA; design practice

cards.title: When wishes conflict, resolve in order: safety, audience, venue, feeling, theme
cards.text: Safety rules always win, then the audience's needs (age, VR experience), then what the real venue allows (size, light), then the chosen feelings, then theme details. Example: a neon theme in an outdoor noon garden for kids keeps the kids safe, uses a daylight version of the theme, and keeps the feeling. Explain which wish bent so the creator can change it.
cards.use_when: Two or more brief items cannot all be satisfied.
do: Apply the priority order
Explain which wish bent and why
avoid: Serving the theme at the cost of safety
Not telling the creator what was sacrificed

cards.title: Many players, small floor: rotate players, never shrink safety margins
cards.text: A class of 30 with a 4 x 4 m clear floor cannot have everyone walking. Offer 1-2 players at a time, 2-3 minute sessions, and the rest watching a leaderboard or cheering. Do not shrink the 1.2 m route or the 0.6 m edge margin to fit more people.
cards.use_when: Group size exceeds what the MR floor allows at once.
do: Compute players at once from floor size
Use short sessions and a leaderboard for the waiting group
avoid: Crowding players onto one floor
Cutting safety margins

cards.title: A long story in a 3-minute session: tell it in 5 beats
cards.text: Creators sometimes want an epic saga for an event booth. Compress it: a 2-4 sentence intro card, 5-7 checkpoint labels as story beats, and a finish that pays off the setup. Offer a longer home version with 8-10 checkpoints if the story matters more than queue speed.
cards.use_when: The narrative wish is big but the session is short.
do: Fit the story into intro, labels and finish
Offer a longer variant if time allows
avoid: Text walls on the intro card
More than 10 checkpoints

cards.title: Do not hide uncertainty behind 3 skins of one idea
cards.text: When the brief is thin, it is tempting to give three similar options. That hides the open question. Instead let each option take a different reading of the uncertain part (adventure as discovery, as narrative, as challenge), in 3 different genres. The creator's pick then resolves the uncertainty.
cards.use_when: Writing options from a brief with an ambiguous feeling or concept.
do: Map each reading of the ambiguity to one option
Use different genres and axes
avoid: Three runners with different colours
Options that differ only in theme

cards.title: Brand wants the product everywhere, players want a game: one hero moment
cards.text: Brand creators may ask for the product on every checkpoint. Too much placement turns a game into an ad and players disengage. Offer one hero moment (the product as the finish portal setting or the boss arena centrepiece) plus brand colours in the palette. Explain the trade-off and let the brand choose.
cards.use_when: A brand creator asks for heavy product placement.
do: Offer one hero placement and brand colours
Explain why less placement keeps players engaged
avoid: Product on every checkpoint
Inventing logos or slogans

cards.title: Novice creator: plain words, examples in choices, no jargon
cards.text: Most creators have never designed a game. Use everyday words ('race friends', not 'fellowship'), put concrete examples inside choices, and keep why-lines short. Offer a 'pick for me' choice on non-safety questions. Novices answer pictures and examples better than abstract categories.
cards.use_when: Creator writes short or vague answers, or says they are new to this.
do: Use everyday language and examples
Offer 'pick for me' where defaults exist
avoid: MDA terms or 'core loop' in questions
Long multi-part questions
cards.source: Fullerton, Game Design Workshop; design practice

cards.title: Experienced creator: accept precise specs, ask only the gaps
cards.text: A creator who speaks in mechanics and numbers ('6 checkpoints, 90 second limit, race mode') has already resolved much uncertainty. Accept their values, skip covered questions, and spend the rest on venue and audience facts they may have missed, often spectators and obstacles. Show trade-offs directly and use the terms they use.
cards.use_when: Creator uses design vocabulary or gives exact specs.
do: Fill fields from their spec at once
Ask only the gaps
avoid: Re-asking what they already specified
Over-explaining basics

cards.title: Kid creator designing for themselves: short, playful, decisive
cards.text: Children often design for themselves and friends. Keep questions very short, use playful choices, accept big imagination and map it to buildable pieces. For MR, phrase floor and safety questions so a grown-up can help ('Ask a grown-up to count steps across the room').
cards.use_when: The creator writes like a child or says they are a kid.
do: Very short questions with playful choices
Invite a grown-up for measuring
Turn wild ideas into checkpoints and scenery
avoid: Personal questions
Crushing an idea without an alternative

cards.title: Teacher creator: ask the learning outcome and how the class rotates
cards.text: Teachers need a game that teaches something and works for a whole class. The two most valuable questions are the learning outcome and how many play at once versus how many wait. Default short sessions (2-3 minutes) and a leaderboard or watching role for waiting students. Never ask about individual students.
cards.use_when: Creator is a teacher or mentions a class or lesson.
do: Ask the learning outcome
Plan rotation for a whole class
Keep checkpoint labels short and factual
avoid: Asking for the school name
Forgetting the students who are waiting

cards.title: Event organiser: queue speed, spectators and very few rules
cards.text: Event and booth organisers care about queue speed, a game that explains itself in seconds, and something the crowd can watch. Default 2-3 minute sessions, 1-2 rules, a leaderboard on a screen, and key moments on the audience side. Ask visitors per hour only if session length is unclear.
cards.use_when: Creator mentions an event, booth, festival, mall or pop-up.
do: Default short sessions and few rules
Plan for spectators and a leaderboard
avoid: Long narrative sessions at a busy booth
Rules that need staff to explain

cards.title: Brand creator: ask brand rules once, early, and store them as constraints
cards.text: A brand or sponsor brings rules: colours, product presence, words to avoid, audience age. Ask once for must-haves and must-nots with choices like 'brand colours', 'product appears in the game', 'no competitor themes', 'nothing scary'. Store them as constraints. Do not invent logos; scenery uses library models and the palette can follow brand colours.
cards.use_when: Creator represents a company, product or sponsor.
do: Ask brand must-haves and must-nots
Store them in constraints
Use brand colours in the palette
avoid: Inventing logos or slogans
Discovering brand rules only at the prototype

cards.title: Thai ghosts for kids: friendly versions only, and check first
cards.text: Thai folk ghosts such as Krasue or Pret can genuinely frighten Thai children who grew up with the stories. For kids, use friendly cartoon versions, warm lighting, and story roles where the ghost is helped or befriended. Ask the creator whether ghosts are fine for these children before using them.
cards.use_when: A Thai ghost theme with kids or families.
do: Ask if ghosts are fine for these kids
Use friendly ghost roles and warm light
avoid: Scary ghost models near young children
Ghosts as chasing threats

cards.title: Temples and Buddha images: never hazards, enemies or things to step on
cards.text: Temple themes are popular, but sacred items must be treated with respect. Never make a Buddha image, a monk or a sacred object a hazard, an enemy, or something on the walking floor that players step over. Use temples as backdrops and destinations, and keep Buddha images out of play unless the creator wants a respectful tour.
cards.use_when: Theme includes temples, wat, Buddha images or monks.
do: Use temples as backdrops and respectful checkpoints
Ask the creator about sensitivities
avoid: Hazards or enemies next to sacred items
Sacred images at foot level on the route

cards.title: 'Make it cooler' or 'เท่กว่านี้': look, action, or scale
cards.text: 'Cooler' usually means a stronger look (lighting, palette, hero scenery), more action (more hazards, a time limit, a tougher boss), or bigger scale (giant models, the void drop). Offer these three as quick choices, or change the one most likely from the chosen feelings and say which you changed.
cards.use_when: Creator comments 'cooler', 'more badass' or the Thai equivalent on a prototype.
do: Offer look, action or scale as choices
Change one dimension and name it
avoid: Changing everything at once
Changing the route when they meant visuals

cards.title: 'Not very wow' or 'ไม่ค่อยว้าว': add one stronger reveal moment
cards.text: This comment means sensation lacks a peak. Pick one moment, usually the climax panel or the finish portal, and make it bigger: a giant hero model revealed around a turn, a lighting change at the boss, or a void drop at the end for experienced players. Keep everything else and point to the changed panel.
cards.use_when: Creator says it is visually flat, not wow, or too ordinary.
do: Strengthen one reveal moment
Name which panel changed
avoid: Adding scenery everywhere until the route is cluttered
Rewriting the story

cards.title: 'Boring' or 'น่าเบื่อ': find whether pacing, choice or stakes is missing
cards.text: Boredom has three common causes: nothing changes over time (pacing), the player has nothing to decide (choice), or nothing is at risk (stakes). Fix with a ramp of hazards across the session, a planning element such as a tactics board, or a time limit and leaderboard. If the comment is general, ask which part felt boring.
cards.use_when: Creator calls the prototype boring or slow.
do: Ask which part felt boring
Add pacing, choice or stakes in that part
avoid: Only adding decoration
Making it hard for first-time players
cards.source: Koster, A Theory of Fun; design practice

cards.title: 'Too hard' or 'ยากไป': lower one difficulty lever, not all
cards.text: Difficulty has levers: hazard count and spacing, time limit, guard speed on a tactics board (keep 3 s or slower), enemy count per battle chapter. Lower the lever the comment points to, or the one that hurts first-timers most, usually the time limit. Keep the climax so the game still has a peak.
cards.use_when: Creator or a playtester says it is too hard.
do: Change one lever and say which
Keep one harder moment
avoid: Removing all hazards
Changing the theme

cards.title: 'Make it more Thai': change scenery, labels and palette, keep mechanics
cards.text: This is a theme comment. Add or swap Thai library models (temples, village, festival props), Thai-flavoured checkpoint labels, and a palette with gold, red and deep green, and leave route, genre and rules untouched. Apply the temple respect rules.
cards.use_when: Creator asks for more Thai flavour after seeing a prototype.
do: Change scenery, labels and palette
Keep the route and mechanics
avoid: Changing the genre
Sacred items as hazards

cards.title: Change what the comment names, keep everything it does not
cards.text: A creator who comments on the boss did not ask to change the route, story or palette. Keep all unmentioned parts exactly, because they are implicitly approved. If a requested change forces another (a bigger boss arena needs more space), say so in one line.
cards.use_when: Applying any comment to a prototype.
do: Change only the named parts
Explain any forced side effect
avoid: Regenerating the whole prototype
Renaming characters the creator liked

cards.title: Turn each comment into a concrete engine-level change
cards.text: Map every comment to something the builder can do: a lighting preset, checkpoint count or labels, hazard count and placement, time limit, scenery models, play mode. 'More spooky' becomes spooky lighting and ghost lantern models; 'longer' becomes 2 more checkpoints and a 5-minute flow. Write the mapping so the creator sees exactly what will change.
cards.use_when: Interpreting any prototype comment.
do: Name the engine field that changes
Use numbers (2 more checkpoints, a 60 s limit)
avoid: Vague promises like 'more atmosphere'
Changes outside the engine's abilities

cards.title: If a comment has two very different readings, ask one quick question
cards.text: Most comments can be applied with a stated interpretation, but some split badly: 'make it bigger' can mean bigger models or a longer route, which affects safety in MR. When readings lead to very different builds, ask one tappable question; when they are close, apply the likely one and say so.
cards.use_when: A comment is ambiguous and its readings diverge.
do: Ask once with 2-4 choices when readings diverge
Otherwise apply and state the interpretation
avoid: A question for every comment
Guessing on a safety-relevant comment

cards.title: Write test_questions from the biggest remaining uncertainty
cards.text: The prototype's test_questions should target what is still uncertain, not what is known. If difficulty for 6-year-olds was assumed, ask 'Can a 6-year-old step out of the rings in time?' If daylight readability is a risk, ask 'Are the red hazards visible in afternoon sun?' This carries design as uncertainty reduction into real play.
cards.use_when: Writing test_questions for the prototype.
do: Pick the 2-4 riskiest assumptions
Phrase each as an observable yes or no question
avoid: Generic 'Is it fun?'
Questions about things already decided
cards.source: Fullerton, Game Design Workshop; design practice

cards.title: Ask feelings with plain, picture-like choices
cards.text: Instead of MDA names, write choices like 'Wow, beautiful sights' (sensation), 'Be a hero or a monster' (fantasy), 'A story with an ending' (narrative), 'Hard, needs skill' (challenge), 'Play with friends' (fellowship), 'Find secrets' (discovery), 'Show off a high score' (expression), 'Relax, easy fun' (submission). Offer the 6 most relevant to the concept and ask for up to 3.
cards.use_when: Asking the feelings question.
do: Translate MDA into plain choices
Ask for up to 3 with multi true
avoid: Showing English MDA terms to Thai novices
All 8 when the concept rules some out

cards.title: Ask age as bands that change the design
cards.text: Use bands where design rules change: 'under 7', '7-12', 'teens', 'adults', 'mixed families', 'seniors'. Each band shifts scariness limits, hazard spacing, label length and session length. Do not ask exact ages or names.
cards.use_when: The players field is unknown or only says 'people'.
do: Use design-relevant age bands
Include mixed families when relevant
avoid: Exact ages
Bands that do not change the design

cards.title: Ask who watches and from where, with 'nobody' as a choice
cards.text: In MR, spectators shape where key moments go. Ask 'Who watches from the side?' with choices 'parents', 'friends waiting their turn', 'passers-by', 'nobody'. If someone watches, ask or assume the side they stand on so the finish and a key dodge face them. Skip this on PC.
cards.use_when: MR brief with unknown spectators, especially events and families.
do: Include 'nobody'
Note the side they stand on
avoid: Asking it on PC
Designing for spectators who do not exist

cards.title: When the creator says 'not sure', default or narrow, never repeat
cards.text: A 'not sure' or 'up to you' answer is information: the creator does not care strongly or lacks the knowledge. For defaultable fields, apply the default and state it. For required fields like MR floor size, narrow with familiar comparisons ('About a classroom? A living room? A badminton court?'). Never ask the identical question twice.
cards.use_when: Creator taps or types not sure, up to you, or the Thai equivalents.
do: Default optional fields
Reframe required fields with familiar comparisons
avoid: Repeating the same question
Treating 'up to you' as a firm decision on a safety fact

cards.title: Read free-typed answers for several fields at once
cards.text: Creators often type more than was asked: 'my class of 25 kids, in the gym after lunch'. Extract every field it covers (players, group size, venue, indoor, time of day) and skip those questions, then ask about the most valuable remaining gap. Confirm the extracted facts in the next why-line or the summary.
cards.use_when: Creator types a long free answer instead of tapping a choice.
do: Extract all fields mentioned
Skip questions already answered
avoid: Asking about what they just told you
Ignoring details outside the current question

cards.title: On PC, skip real-space questions and spend the budget on players and feelings
cards.text: When the platform is PC there is no real room: floor size, indoor, obstacles, venue and spectator side are not asked and not set. Use the saved questions to sharpen the genre: what kind of challenge, how long, solo or with friends watching the screen.
cards.use_when: platform is pc.
do: Skip venue, size, obstacles and indoor
Ask about the kind of challenge and session instead
avoid: Asking floor size for a PC game
Setting width_m on PC

cards.title: Order questions so early answers prune later ones
cards.text: Ask platform first because PC removes all space questions. Ask players before feelings because age limits what feelings fit (no real horror for 6-year-olds). Ask the MR floor before session and play mode because size caps players at once. A good order often lets the interview finish in 4-5 questions.
cards.use_when: Planning the sequence of the interview.
do: Platform, then players, then feelings, then space
Skip whatever earlier answers already settled
avoid: Asking session length before knowing the venue
Asking feelings before players

cards.title: Worked example: 'a fun ghost game for my kid's party' resolved in 5 questions
cards.text: Start (typed in Thai): 'a fun ghost game for my kid's birthday'. Inferred: kids, families, first-time VR, parents watching. Q1 platform: MR. Q2 age band: 5-7. Q3 how scary: 'spooky but fun' (resolves the conflict). Q4 floor: living room 4 x 5 m, with Q5 obstacles: a sofa on one side, so 4 x 3.5 m usable. Defaults stated: 3 minutes, solo turns with a leaderboard, evening lighting indoors, no sudden scares.
cards.use_when: A brief starts with several vague words and a child audience.
do: Infer from strong clues
Resolve the conflict with a scale question
State all defaults in the summary
avoid: Asking more than 7 questions
Using real horror

cards.title: 'Fun for everyone' or 'เล่นได้ทุกวัย': mixed ages playing together, or a wide public audience
cards.text: 'For everyone' can mean a family where a 6-year-old and a grandparent play the same session, or a public booth where any single visitor of any age walks in. For mixed groups, design the floor for the youngest and add an optional harder layer (time bonus, leaderboard) for older players. For a wide public, pick the safest settings: first-time VR, no void floor, 3 minutes, 1-2 rules. Ask 'Will different ages play at the same time, or one visitor at a time?'
cards.use_when: Creator says for everyone, all ages, family-friendly, or the Thai for all ages.
do: Design difficulty for the youngest likely player
Add an optional score layer for older players
avoid: Averaging difficulty so it suits nobody
Scary themes for an all-ages audience

cards.title: 'มันส์' or 'action-packed': fighting, high pace, or head-to-head
cards.text: The Thai word in the title means intense, energetic fun. It can mean constant action (battle with many grunts per chapter and falling warning rings), high pace with no pauses (a runner with a tight time limit and checkpoints close together), or the buzz of competing live (race mode with a leaderboard the crowd watches). Ask 'What makes it intense?' with choices 'slashing lots of enemies', 'non-stop rushing', 'beating friends'. In MR, intensity comes from density and timing, never from running.
cards.use_when: Creator says action-packed, hype, intense, or the Thai word for it.
do: Ask which source of intensity
Raise density and tempo, keep walking pace
avoid: Making MR players run
Long story pauses in an action brief
cards.source: Swink, Game Feel; Meta MR safety guidelines

cards.title: 'Relaxing' or 'ชิลๆ': no pressure, beautiful stroll, or light easy goals
cards.text: 'Chill' points to the submission aesthetic, but it can mean no failure pressure (no hazards, no time limit), a beautiful walk to look at (sensation: a scenic route with evening or morning light), or a small casual goal (touch 5 friendly checkpoints). Ask 'Chill like...?' with choices 'a pretty walk', 'easy goals, no losing', 'calm with a little surprise'. A tour or explore loop on the runner usually fits; battle rarely does.
cards.use_when: Creator says relaxing, chill, calm, or the Thai word for chill.
do: Remove time limits and most hazards
Invest in scenery and light along a loop
avoid: Adding a boss to a chill brief
A void floor, which is not relaxing for many

cards.title: 'Competitive' or 'แข่งกัน': live race, best time, or best score
cards.text: Competition can be a live race against people in the room or online (race mode), a personal best against the clock (time limit plus leaderboard), or a score fight where fewer hazard hits wins (score: checkpoint +100, hazard -25). Ask 'Who do they compete against?' with choices 'each other at the same time', 'the clock', 'the high score of the day'. Tactics boards also race on time with a leaderboard.
cards.use_when: Creator says competitive, versus, race, or the Thai word for compete.
do: Pick live race, timed run or score as the frame
Show the leaderboard on a screen for spectators
avoid: Live races in a floor under 4 x 4 m
Competition with no visible ranking
cards.source: Caillois 1961, Man, Play and Games (agon); FortalLand engine

cards.title: 'With a story' or 'มีเรื่องราว': a goal with a reason, a journey of beats, or a twist
cards.text: 'A story' can be light (a clear reason for the goal on the intro card: 'Return the lost lanterns'), a journey of beats (every checkpoint label is a story step leading to an ending), or a reveal (the finish or boss changes what the player thought). Ask 'How much story?' with choices 'just a reason to play', 'a story step at every stop', 'a surprise ending'. The engine tells stories only through the intro, labels, scenery and the finish.
cards.use_when: Creator says story, plot, narrative, or the Thai words for it.
do: Ask how much story
Use intro card, labels and scenery as the only story channels
avoid: Promising cutscenes or dialogue
Long intro text players will skip

cards.title: 'Realistic' or 'สมจริง': the art is always stylized, so find what should feel real
cards.text: Everything is stylized low-poly, flat shaded, so photoreal looks are not possible. 'Realistic' usually means believable scale (models at true 1:1 size, a house that is house-sized), real physical effort (walking the real floor in MR already gives this), or a real place or process (a local market, a real temple layout, the real order of steps). Say the style limit in one line, then ask which kind of real matters.
cards.use_when: Creator says realistic, real, lifelike, or the Thai word for realistic.
do: State that the art is stylized low-poly
Offer believable scale, real walking or a real-world sequence
avoid: Promising photoreal graphics
Copying a real brand's building or logo

cards.title: 'Like Pokemon', 'like Fortnite', 'like Roblox': borrow the feeling, never the IP
cards.text: Famous franchise names point to a feeling: Pokemon to cute creatures and discovery, Fortnite to competing and bright action, Roblox to playful blocky worlds. The engine cannot copy their mechanics (no creature catching, no shooting, no building), and their characters, names and logos are owned by others. Ask what part they love, then offer original creatures from the model library, a race or battle for competition, and a bright toy-like theme. Write original names in the brief and prototype.
cards.use_when: Creator names a franchise, its characters, or asks to use them.
do: Name the limit kindly: we make our own characters
Map the loved part to a genre and theme
avoid: Franchise names, characters or logos in labels or key art
Promising catching, shooting or building

cards.title: 'Something new' or 'แปลกใหม่': new place, new twist on the room, or new rule
cards.text: Novelty can come from an unusual theme (an underwater temple, a candy volcano), from using the real space in a surprising way (the real walls as the edge of a cliff, the void floor under a classroom), or from an unusual combination of engine rules (a tactics board as a heist). Ask 'New in what way?' with choices 'a world nobody has seen', 'surprise the room itself', 'a twist in how you play'. Never solve novelty with mechanics the engine lacks.
cards.use_when: Creator says unique, original, never seen before, or the Thai word for novel.
do: Ask where the novelty should live
Use the real surroundings as a source of surprise in MR
avoid: Inventing new mechanics to be novel
Novelty that confuses first-time players

cards.title: 'Looks plain' or 'ดูธรรมดา': add a hero piece and contrast, not clutter
cards.text: Plainness is usually a missing focal point or flat colour, not too few objects. Add one hero piece seen from the spawn (a giant statue, a dragon, a tower), raise palette contrast between the floor and the route, and group decor into 2-3 vignettes along the route. In MR, keep the 1.2 m route clear while adding. Say which of these you changed.
cards.use_when: Creator says the prototype looks plain, ordinary, or the Thai equivalent.
do: Add one hero piece visible from the spawn
Increase contrast between route and ground
Group decor into vignettes
avoid: Scattering more props everywhere
Blocking the walking route

cards.title: 'Make it scarier' or 'อยากให้น่ากลัวกว่านี้': darker mood and dread, within age and safety
cards.text: First check the players: for kids, scarier should mean spookier, not frightening. Levers: lighting preset from evening to spooky or night (only indoors or after dark in MR), scarier Thai ghost or haunted models along the route, a darker palette, and story labels that build dread toward the finish. No sudden scares and nothing that makes players run.
cards.use_when: Creator asks for more scary after seeing a prototype.
do: Check player age first
Change lighting, models, palette or labels and name which
avoid: Jump scares in MR
Night lighting outdoors in daylight
cards.source: Meta MR safety guidelines; FortalLand engine

cards.title: 'The colours are not nice' or 'สีไม่สวย': ask which way, then change the palette only
cards.text: Colour complaints can mean too dull, too loud, wrong mood, or not matching a brand. Offer 3-4 alternative palettes as tappable choices (warm, cool, pastel, high contrast), each with 4-6 named colours, or ask 'More bright, more soft, or more dark?'. Change only the palette and the lighting preset if needed; keep the route, story and scenery. In MR outdoors, keep enough contrast for sunlight.
cards.use_when: Creator dislikes the colours of the prototype.
do: Offer 3-4 palette alternatives
Change only palette and maybe lighting
avoid: Changing the theme or models for a colour comment
Low-contrast pastel for outdoor daylight

cards.title: 'Can kids play this?' or 'เด็กจะเล่นได้ไหม': answer with a checklist, then adjust
cards.text: Treat this as a concern, not a change request. Check and report: rules fit in 1-2 short lines, checkpoint labels under about 5 words, hazards spaced for small steps, no time limit or a generous one, session 3 minutes or less for under-8s, no scary or void moments, and the route clear by 1.2 m. Fix any item that fails and say which ones, and add a playtest question like 'Can a 6-year-old finish without help?'
cards.use_when: Creator asks whether children can play the prototype.
do: Run the kid checklist and report each item
Fix failing items and add a playtest question
avoid: Just answering yes
Making it babyish when the kids are 10-12
cards.source: Meta VR comfort guidelines; design practice

cards.title: 'Too long' or 'ยาวไป': cut checkpoints or chapters, keep the climax
cards.text: Length comes from checkpoint count, route length, the time limit, and battle chapters. Cut from the middle: remove 1-2 middle checkpoints or one chapter, shorten the route, and keep the opening and the climax. Update the flow so the new session length is visible ('ends at 2:30'). If 'too long' meant the intro text, shorten the story to 2 sentences instead.
cards.use_when: Creator says the game or intro is too long.
do: Ask or infer: the play or the text
Cut middle content, keep start and climax
Show the new length in the flow
avoid: Cutting the finish or boss
Fewer than 4 checkpoints in a runner

cards.title: 'Confusing' or 'งงๆ': find whether the goal, the order, or the danger is unclear
cards.text: Players get lost in three ways: they do not know the goal (fix the goal line and intro to one sentence), they do not know where to go next (fix checkpoint order with a clearer route shape and visible next stop), or they do not understand what hurts them (make hazards look like hazards and say so in the rules). Ask which part was confusing if unclear, and simplify rules to 1-3 lines.
cards.use_when: Creator or playtester says it is confusing or hard to understand.
do: Locate the confusion: goal, order or danger
Shorten rules to 1-3 lines
avoid: Adding more text to explain
Adding features to fix confusion
